chapters.title: Preface: From the Author to the Reader
paragraphs: If you are a person who plods so steadily through serious matters that you feel ashamed to spend even a few short moments in laughter and high spirits in the land of Fancy; if you believe life has nothing to do with innocent laughter that harms no one, then these pages are not for you. Close the book and go no further. I warn you plainly that if you read on, you will be shocked to see good, sober people out of real history frisking and capering in bright colors and jester’s clothes, so that you would hardly know them except for the names pinned to them. Here is a sturdy, vigorous fellow with a quick temper, though not a bad man for all that, who goes by the name of Henry II. Here is a fair and gentle lady to whom everyone else bows, and they call her Queen Eleanor. Here is a fat rascal dressed in the rich robes of a churchman, whom all the good people call my Lord Bishop of Hereford. Here is a man with a sour temper and a grim face, the worshipful Sheriff of Nottingham. And here, above all, is a great, tall, merry fellow who roams the greenwood, joins in plain country sports, and sits beside the Sheriff at a merry feast, and who bears the name of the proudest of the Plantagenets, Richard of the Lion’s Heart. Besides these there is a whole crowd of knights, priests, nobles, townsmen, yeomen, pages, ladies, young women, innkeepers, beggars, peddlers, and who knows what else, all living the merriest of merry lives. Nothing ties them together but a few odd strands of certain old ballads (snipped and clipped and knotted together again in a score of places), which pull these cheerful people this way and that, singing as they go.

Here you will find a hundred dull, sober, plodding places, all decked out with flowers and the like, until no one would recognize them in their fanciful dress. And here is a country with a well-known name, where no chilly mists weigh upon our spirits, and no rain falls except what rolls off our backs like April showers off the backs of sleek ducks. In it flowers bloom forever and birds are always singing, every fellow has a merry tune to sing as he travels the roads, and ale and beer and wine (the kind that never muddle anyone’s wits) flow like water in a brook.

This country is not Fairyland. What is it? It is the land of Fancy, and it is of such a pleasant kind that when you grow tired of it, whisk!—you simply slap the covers of this book together and it is gone, and you are ready for everyday life, with no harm done.
Now I will draw back the curtain that hangs between this place and No-man’s-land. Dear Reader, will you come along? Thank you. Take my hand.

chapters.title: How Robin Hood Came to Be an Outlaw
paragraphs: In Merry England, in the old days when good King Henry the Second ruled the land, there lived in the green glades of Sherwood Forest, near Nottingham Town, a famous outlaw named Robin Hood. No archer ever lived who could send a gray goose-feather arrow with such skill and cunning as his, and there were never such yeomen as the hundred and forty merry men who roamed with him through the greenwood shades. They lived very merrily in the depths of Sherwood Forest, with neither worry nor want. They passed the time in merry games of archery and bouts of cudgel play, and lived on the King’s venison, washed down with draughts of ale brewed in October.

Not only Robin himself but the whole band were outlaws and lived apart from other men. Yet the country people all around loved them, because no one ever came to jolly Robin for help in a time of need and went away again empty-handed.
And now I will tell how Robin Hood first ran afoul of the law.

When Robin was a youth of eighteen, strong of limb and bold of heart, the Sheriff of Nottingham announced a shooting match and offered a barrel of ale as the prize to whoever should shoot the best arrow in Nottinghamshire. “Well,” said Robin, “I will go too, for I would gladly draw a bowstring for the bright eyes of my lass and a barrel of good October ale.” So up he got, took his good strong yew bow and twenty or more broad clothyard arrows, and set off from Locksley Town through Sherwood Forest to Nottingham.

It was at the break of day in merry Maytime, when the hedgerows are green and flowers decorate the meadows: speckled daisies, yellow cuckoo buds, and fair primroses all along the briery hedges; when the apple trees are in bud and the sweet birds sing, the lark at dawn, the male thrush and the cuckoo; when lads and lasses look at one another with tender thoughts; and when busy housewives spread their linen on the bright green grass to bleach. The greenwood was sweet as he walked along its paths, and the green leaves rustled brightly, with little birds singing among them with all their might. Robin whistled cheerfully as he tramped along, thinking of Maid Marian and her bright eyes, for at such times a young man’s thoughts naturally turn to the girl he loves best.

As he walked along briskly, whistling merrily, he came suddenly upon some foresters sitting beneath a great oak tree. There were fifteen of them, having a merry time feasting and drinking around a huge pasty. Each man helped himself by plunging his hands into the pie, and they washed down their food with great horns of ale drawn foaming from a barrel that stood nearby. Each man was dressed in Lincoln green, and they made a fine sight sitting on the grass under that fair, spreading tree. Then one of them, with his mouth full, called out to Robin, “Hello, where are you going, little lad, with your one-penny bow and your farthing arrows?”
Then Robin grew angry, for no youngster likes to be mocked for his tender years.

“Well,” he said, “my bow and my arrows are as good as yours. Besides, I am going to the shooting match at Nottingham Town, which our good Sheriff of Nottinghamshire has announced. I will shoot there with other sturdy yeomen, for a fine barrel of ale has been offered as the prize.”

Then one who held a horn of ale in his hand said, “Ho! Listen to the lad! Why, boy, your mother’s milk is barely dry on your lips, and yet you talk of standing up with good strong men at the Nottingham butts, you who can scarcely pull the string of a two-stone bow.”
“I’ll bet any of you twenty marks,” said bold Robin, “that I can hit the target at sixty rods, with the good help of Our Lady.”
At this they all laughed aloud, and one said, “Well boasted, you fine infant, well boasted! And you know very well that there is no target near to prove your wager.”
And another cried, “Next he will be drinking ale with his milk!”

At this Robin grew truly furious. “Listen,” he said, “over there, at the end of the glade, I see a herd of deer, farther away even than sixty rods. I’ll bet you twenty marks that, by leave of Our Lady, I can bring down the best stag among them.”
“Done!” cried the man who had spoken first. “And here are twenty marks. I bet that you won’t kill any beast, with or without the help of Our Lady.”

Then Robin took his good yew bow in his hand, set the tip against his instep, and strung it very skillfully. Then he fitted a broad clothyard arrow to the string, raised the bow, and drew the gray goose feather back to his ear. The next moment the bowstring rang, and the arrow shot down the glade like a sparrowhawk skimming along in a northern wind. The noblest stag of the whole herd leaped high, only to fall dead, staining the green path red with his heart’s blood.
“Ha!” cried Robin. “How do you like that shot, my good fellow? I know the wager is mine, even if it were three hundred pounds.”
Then all the foresters were filled with rage, and the man who had spoken first and lost the wager was angrier than all the rest.

“No,” he cried, “the wager is not yours. Get out of here this minute, or, by all the saints in heaven, I’ll thrash your sides until you can never walk again.” “Don’t you know,” said another, “that you have killed the King’s deer, and that by the laws of our gracious lord and sovereign King Harry, your ears should be cropped close to your head?”
“Catch him!” cried a third.
“No,” said a fourth, “let him go, because he is so young.”

Robin Hood said never a word, but he looked at the foresters with a grim face. Then he turned on his heel and strode away from them down the forest glade. But his heart was bitterly angry, for his blood was hot and young and quick to boil.

Now, it would have been far better for the man who had spoken first if he had left Robin Hood alone. But his anger was hot, both because the youth had got the better of him and because of the deep drafts of ale he had been gulping. So suddenly, without any warning, he sprang to his feet, grabbed his bow, and fitted an arrow to it. “Yes,” he cried, “and I’ll hurry you along soon enough!” And he sent the arrow whistling after Robin.

Robin Hood was lucky that the forester’s head was swimming with ale; otherwise he would never have walked another step. As it was, the arrow hissed past just three inches from his head. He spun around, swiftly pulled back his own bowstring, and shot an arrow right back.
“You told me I was no archer,” he shouted. “Go on, say it again!”

The arrow flew straight. The archer fell forward with a cry and lay on his face on the ground, his arrows rattling out of his quiver around him, and the gray goose shaft wet with his heart’s blood. Then, before the others could collect their wits, Robin Hood was gone into the depths of the greenwood. Some started after him, but without much heart, for each feared meeting the same death as his fellow. So after a while they all came back, lifted the dead man up, and carried him away to Nottingham Town.

Meanwhile Robin Hood ran through the greenwood. All the joy and brightness had gone out of everything, for his heart was sick within him, and the truth sank deep into his soul that he had killed a man.

“Alas!” he cried, “you found in me an archer who will make your wife weep! I wish you had never said a word to me, or that I had never passed your way, or even that my right forefinger had been cut off before this happened! I struck in haste, and now I grieve long at leisure!” And then, even in his trouble, he remembered the old saying, “What is done is done; and a cracked egg cannot be mended.”

And so he came to live in the greenwood, which was to be his home for many years to come, and he never again saw the happy days with the lads and lasses of sweet Locksley Town. He was outlawed, not only because he had killed a man, but also because he had poached the King’s deer, and a reward of two hundred pounds was put on his head for whoever would bring him to the King’s court.

The Sheriff of Nottingham now swore an oath to hunt down that scoundrel Robin Hood himself and bring him to justice. He had two motives: he wanted the two hundred pounds, and the forester whom Robin had killed was his own kinsman.

But Robin Hood lay hidden in Sherwood Forest for a year, and in that time many others like himself gathered around him, people cast out from the rest of society for one reason or another. Some had shot deer in the hungry wintertime when they could get no other food, and had been seen doing it by the foresters, but had escaped and so saved their ears. Some had been thrown off their land so that their farms could be added to the King’s lands in Sherwood Forest. Some had been robbed by a great baron, a rich abbot, or a powerful squire. For one reason or another, all of them had come to Sherwood to escape wrong and oppression.

So in that one year, a hundred or more good, sturdy yeomen gathered around Robin Hood and chose him as their leader and chief. Then they vowed that just as they themselves had been robbed, they would rob their oppressors, whether baron, abbot, knight, or squire, and take from each of them whatever had been squeezed out of the poor through unjust taxes, land rents, or wrongful fines. But to the poor folk they would give a helping hand in times of need and trouble, and would give back to them what had been unjustly taken from them. They also swore never to harm a child or wrong a woman, whether maid, wife, or widow. So after a while, when the people began to find that no harm was meant to them, and that money or food came in times of want to many a poor family, they began to praise Robin and his merry men and to tell many tales about him and his doings in Sherwood Forest, for they felt he was one of their own.

Up rose Robin Hood one merry morning when all the birds were singing cheerfully among the leaves, and up rose all his merry men, each fellow washing his head and hands in the cold brown brook that leaped laughing from stone to stone. Then Robin said, “For fourteen days we have seen no sport, so now I will go out and look for adventures right away. But you, my merry men all, wait here in the greenwood, and only be sure you pay close attention to my call. I will blow three blasts on the bugle horn in my hour of need. Then come quickly, for I will want your help.”

So saying, he strode off through the leafy forest glades until he came to the edge of Sherwood. There he wandered for a long time, along highways and byways, through leafy dells and the outskirts of the forest. Now he met a fair, plump lass in a shady lane, and each gave the other a merry word and went on their way. Now he saw a fair lady upon an ambling horse, to whom he tipped his cap, and she bowed gravely in return to the handsome youth. Now he saw a fat monk on a donkey loaded with baskets. Now he saw a gallant knight, with spear and shield and armor that flashed brightly in the sunlight. Now he saw a page dressed in crimson, and now a stout townsman from good Nottingham Town, pacing along with solemn steps. All these sights he saw, but he found no adventure. At last he took a road along the edge of the forest, a side path that dipped toward a broad, pebbly stream crossed by a narrow bridge made from a single log. As he drew near this bridge, he saw a tall stranger coming from the other side. Robin quickened his pace, and so did the stranger, each of them thinking to cross first.
“Step aside,” said Robin, “and let the better man go over first.”
“No,” answered the stranger, “you stand back yourself, for I know that I am the better man.”

“We will see about that soon enough,” said Robin, “and meanwhile you stay right where you are, or else, by the bright brow of Saint AElfrida, I will show you some good Nottingham play with a clothyard arrow between your ribs.”
“Well,” said the stranger, “I will tan your hide until it is as many colors as a beggar’s cloak, if you dare so much as touch the string of that bow you are holding in your hands.”
“You talk like a donkey,” said Robin, “for I could send this arrow clean through your proud heart before a short-robed friar could say grace over a roast goose at Michaelmastide.”
“And you talk like a coward,” answered the stranger, “because you stand there with a good yew bow to shoot at my heart, while all I hold is a plain blackthorn staff to face you with.”

“Well,” said Robin, “on the faith of my heart, I have never been called a coward in all my life. I’ll set down my trusty bow and my arrows too, and if you dare wait for me, I’ll go cut a cudgel to test your manhood.”
“Yes indeed, I’ll wait for you, and gladly,” said the stranger, and he leaned sturdily on his staff to wait for Robin.

Then Robin Hood hurried to the edge of the thicket and cut a good staff of ground oak, straight and without a knot, six feet long. He came back trimming off the tender shoots, while the stranger waited for him, leaning on his staff and whistling as he looked around. As he trimmed his staff, Robin studied the man out of the corner of his eye, measuring him from head to foot, and thought he had never seen a stronger or sturdier fellow. Robin was tall, but the stranger was taller by a head and a neck, for he stood seven feet high. Robin was broad across the shoulders, but the stranger was broader by two full palms, and he measured at least an ell around the waist.

“All the same,” Robin said to himself, “I’ll give your hide a merry thrashing, my good fellow.” Then he said aloud, “Look, here is my staff, sturdy and tough. Wait for me, if you dare, and meet me, if you’re not afraid. We’ll fight until one of us tumbles into the stream from the blows.”
“Now that suits me down to the ground!” cried the stranger, twirling his staff over his head between finger and thumb until it whistled.

The Knights of Arthur’s Round Table never fought a harder fight than these two. In a moment Robin stepped onto the bridge where the stranger stood. First he made a feint, then swung a blow at the stranger’s head that would have knocked him straight into the water if it had landed. But the stranger turned the blow aside neatly and answered with one just as hard, which Robin turned aside in the same way. So they stood, each in his place, neither giving up a finger’s-breadth of ground, for a good hour. Many blows were given and taken in that time, until both had sore bones and bumps here and there, yet neither thought of crying “Enough,” and neither looked likely to fall off the bridge. Now and then they stopped to rest, and each thought he had never in his life met such a hand with a quarterstaff. At last Robin landed a blow on the stranger’s ribs that made his jacket smoke like damp thatch in the sun. The stroke was so sharp that the stranger came within a hair of falling off the bridge, but he caught himself quickly and, with a clever blow, cracked Robin on the crown of the head so that the blood ran. Then Robin grew mad with anger and struck out with all his might. But the stranger blocked the blow and thwacked Robin again, and this time so squarely that he fell head over heels into the water, the way the queen pin goes down in a game of bowls.
“So where are you now, my good lad?” the stranger shouted, roaring with laughter.

“Oh, in the flood and floating downstream with the tide,” cried Robin, and he could not help laughing himself at his sorry state. Then he got to his feet and waded to the bank, with the little fish darting this way and that, frightened by his splashing.

“Give me your hand,” he cried when he reached the bank. “I have to admit you are a brave and sturdy fellow, and a fine hand with the cudgels besides. By this and by that, my head is humming like a hive of bees on a hot June day.”

Then he put his horn to his lips and blew a blast that echoed sweetly down the forest paths. “Yes indeed,” he said again, “you are a tall lad and a brave one too, for I swear there is not a man between here and Canterbury Town who could do to me what you have done.”
“And you,” said the stranger, laughing, “take your drubbing like a brave heart and a sturdy yeoman.”
But now the distant twigs and branches rustled as men came near, and all at once twenty or more sturdy yeomen in Lincoln green burst out of the undergrowth, with merry Will Stutely leading them.
“Good master,” cried Will, “what is this? Why, you are wet from head to foot, right down to the skin.”
“Well,” answered jolly Robin, “that stout fellow over there has tumbled me neck and crop into the water, and given me a beating besides.”
“Then he won’t go without a ducking and a beating of his own!” cried Will Stutely. “At him, lads!”

Then Will and a score of yeomen leaped on the stranger. They sprang quickly, but they found him ready, and he struck out right and left with his stout staff. He went down in the end under their numbers, but not before some of them were rubbing cracked heads.

“No, stop!” cried Robin, laughing until his sore sides ached again. “He is a good man and true, and no harm will come to him. Now listen, good youth: will you stay with me and join my band? You’ll have three suits of Lincoln green each year, forty marks in pay besides, and a share of whatever good fortune comes our way. You’ll eat sweet venison and drink the strongest ale, and you’ll be my own right-hand man, for I never saw such a cudgel player in all my life. Speak! Will you be one of my good merry men?”

“That I don’t know,” said the stranger sullenly, for he was angry at being knocked about so. “If you handle a yew bow and an apple-wood arrow no better than you handle an oak cudgel, I’d say you’re not fit to be called yeomen in my country. But if there is anyone here who can shoot a better arrow than I can, then I will think about joining you.”

“By my faith,” said Robin, “you are a very saucy fellow, sir. Still, I will lower myself to you as I never have to any man before. Good Stutely, cut a fair white piece of bark four fingers wide and set it eighty yards away on that oak over there. Now, stranger, hit that squarely with a gray goose arrow and call yourself an archer.”
“Yes indeed, that I will,” he answered. “Give me a good stout bow and a fair broad arrow, and if I miss, strip me and beat me blue with bowstrings.”

Then he chose the stoutest bow among them all, after Robin’s own, and a straight gray goose arrow, smooth and well feathered. He stepped up to the mark while all the band, sitting or lying on the grass, watched him shoot. He drew the arrow to his cheek and loosed it neatly, sending it so straight down the path that it split the mark right in the center. “Aha!” cried he. “Beat that if you can!” And even the yeomen clapped their hands at so fine a shot.
“That is a keen shot indeed,” said Robin. “I can’t beat it, but perhaps I can spoil it.”

Then he took up his own good stout bow, fitted an arrow with care, and shot with every bit of his skill. The arrow flew straight and so true that it landed squarely on the stranger’s arrow and split it into splinters. Then all the yeomen leaped to their feet and shouted for joy that their master had shot so well.

“By the sturdy yew bow of good Saint Withold,” cried the stranger, “that is a shot indeed, and I never saw the like in all my life! Now I will truly be your man from this day on and forever. Good Adam Bell(1) was a fine shot, but he never shot like that!”

(1) Adam Bell, Clym o’ the Clough, and William of Cloudesly
were three famous bowmen from the north country whose names
were celebrated in many ballads of olden times.
“Then I have gained a very good man today,” said jolly Robin. “What name do you go by, good fellow?”
“Where I come from, men call me John Little,” answered the stranger.

Then Will Stutely, who loved a good joke, spoke up. “No, fair little stranger,” he said, “I don’t like your name and would gladly change it. You are little indeed, small of bone and sinew, so you shall be christened Little John, and I will be your godfather.”
At that, Robin Hood and his whole band burst out laughing, until the stranger started to get angry.
“If you make a joke of me,” he said to Will Stutely, “you’ll have sore bones and little pay, and soon at that.”

“No, my friend,” said Robin Hood, “keep your anger corked, for the name suits you well. Little John you shall be called from now on, and Little John it shall be. So come, my merry men, we’ll prepare a christening feast for this fine infant.”

So they turned their backs on the stream and plunged into the forest once more, tracing their steps until they reached the place where they lived in the depths of the woods. There they had built huts of bark and tree branches and made beds of sweet rushes covered with fallow-deer skins. Here stood a great oak tree with branches spreading wide, and under it was a seat of green moss where Robin Hood liked to sit at feasts and merrymaking with his sturdy men around him. Here they found the rest of the band, some of whom had come in with a pair of fat does. Then they all built great fires, and after a while they roasted the does and tapped a barrel of foaming ale. When the feast was ready they all sat down, but Robin put Little John at his right hand, for from then on he was to be second in the band.

Then, when the feast was done, Will Stutely spoke up. “I think it is time to christen our fine baby, isn’t it, merry boys?” And “Aye! Aye!” cried everyone, laughing until the woods echoed with their mirth.
“Then we shall have seven sponsors,” said Will Stutely, and he searched through the whole band and chose the seven strongest men of them all.
“By Saint Dunstan,” cried Little John, springing to his feet, “more than one of you will regret it if you lay a finger on me.”

But without a word they all rushed at him at once, seized him by the legs and arms, and held him tight in spite of his struggles. They carried him out while everyone gathered around to watch the fun. Then one came forward who had been chosen to play the priest because he had a bald crown, and in his hand he carried a brimming pot of ale. “Now, who brings this babe?” he asked, very solemnly.
“I do,” answered Will Stutely.
“And what name do you give him?”
“I call him Little John.”

“Now, Little John,” said the mock priest, “until now you have not lived, but only got yourself along through the world. From now on you will truly live. When you did not live you were called John Little, but now that you live indeed, Little John you shall be called, so I christen you.” And at these last words he emptied the pot of ale over Little John’s head.

Everyone shouted with laughter as the good brown ale ran down Little John’s beard and dripped from his nose and chin, and his eyes blinked at the sting. At first he felt like getting angry but found he could not, since the others were so merry, so he laughed along with the rest. Then Robin took this sweet, pretty babe, dressed him from top to toe in fresh Lincoln green, and gave him a good stout bow, and so made him a member of the merry band.

And that is how Robin Hood became an outlaw, how a band of merry companions gathered around him, and how he won his right-hand man, Little John; and so the prologue ends. Now I will tell how the Sheriff of Nottingham tried three times to catch Robin Hood, and how he failed each time.

chapters.title: Robin Hood and the Tinker
paragraphs: Now, it was told before how two hundred pounds were set on Robin Hood’s head, and how the Sheriff of Nottingham swore that he would seize Robin himself, both because he wanted the two hundred pounds and because the slain man was a kinsman of his own. The Sheriff did not yet know what a force Robin had around him in Sherwood. He thought he could serve a warrant for Robin’s arrest as he could on any other man who had broken the law, so he offered eighty golden angels to anyone who would serve it. But the men of Nottingham Town knew more about Robin Hood and his doings than the Sheriff did. Many laughed at the thought of serving a warrant on the bold outlaw, knowing well that all they would get for the trouble would be cracked heads, and so no one came forward to take the job. Thus two weeks passed, and in that time nobody came to do the Sheriff’s business. Then he said, “I have offered a very good reward to whoever will serve my warrant on Robin Hood, and I wonder that no one has come to take the task.”

Then one of his men who stood near him said, “Good master, you don’t know the force Robin Hood has around him, or how little he cares for the warrant of a king or a sheriff. Truly, no one likes to go on this errand, for fear of cracked heads and broken bones.”

“Then I say all Nottingham men are cowards,” said the Sheriff. “Show me the man in all Nottinghamshire who dares defy the warrant of our sovereign lord King Harry, for, by the shrine of Saint Edmund, I’ll hang him forty cubits high! But if no man in Nottingham has the courage to win eighty angels, I’ll look elsewhere, for there must be men of mettle somewhere in this land.”

Then he called in a messenger whom he trusted greatly and ordered him to saddle his horse and get ready to go to Lincoln Town, to see whether he could find anyone there who would do his bidding and win the reward. So that same morning the messenger set out on his errand.

The sun shone brightly on the dusty highway that ran from Nottingham to Lincoln, stretching away white over hill and valley. The road was dusty and the messenger’s throat was dusty too, so he was glad when he saw the sign of the Blue Boar Inn ahead, a little more than halfway through his journey. The inn looked fair to his eyes, and the shade of the oak trees around it seemed cool and pleasant, so he got down from his horse to rest for a while and called for a pot of ale to refresh his thirsty throat.

There he found a group of jolly fellows sitting under the big oak that shaded the grass in front of the door. They were a tinker, two barefoot friars, and six of the King’s foresters, all dressed in Lincoln green. Every one of them was gulping down foaming ale and singing cheerful ballads of the good old days. The foresters roared with laughter as jokes flew back and forth between songs, and the friars laughed even louder, for they were hearty men with beards as curly as the wool of black rams. But the Tinker laughed loudest of all, and he sang better than any of them. His bag and hammer hung from a twig of the oak, and close by leaned his sturdy cudgel, as thick as his wrist and knotted at the end.
“Come over here,” called one of the foresters to the weary messenger, “and join us for a round. Hey, landlord! Bring a fresh pot of ale for every man.”
The messenger was happy to sit down with the others, for his legs were tired and the ale was good.
“What news are you rushing along with?” asked one. “Where are you headed today?”

The messenger was a talkative fellow who dearly loved a bit of gossip, and the pot of ale had warmed his heart besides. So he settled into a comfortable corner of the inn bench, while the landlord leaned in the doorway and the landlady stood with her hands tucked under her apron, and he happily unpacked his bundle of news. He told everything from the very beginning: how Robin Hood had killed the forester, and how he had hidden in the greenwood to escape the law; how he lived there in defiance of the law, God knows, killing His Majesty’s deer and taking tolls from fat abbots, knights, and squires, so that nobody dared travel even the broad Watling Street or the Fosse Way for fear of him; and how the Sheriff meant to deliver the King’s warrant to this same rascal, though Robin would pay little heed to a warrant from either king or sheriff, for he was far from a law-abiding man. Then he told how no one in all of Nottingham Town could be found to deliver the warrant, for fear of cracked heads and broken bones, and how he himself was now on his way to Lincoln Town to find out what sort of stuff the Lincoln men were made of.

“Well, I come from good Banbury Town,” said the jolly Tinker, “and nobody near Nottingham, or Sherwood either, if that is where he hides, can match my grip on a cudgel. Why, lads, didn’t I meet that wild joker Simon of Ely at the famous fair in Hertford Town, and beat him in the ring right there, before Sir Robert of Leslie and his lady? This Robin Hood, whom I never heard of before, is a merry fellow, I’m sure, but if he is strong, am I not stronger? And if he is sly, am I not slyer? Now by the bright eyes of Nan o’ the Mill, and by my own name, which is Wat o’ the Crabstaff, and by my own mother’s son, which is myself, I swear that I, even I, Wat o’ the Crabstaff, will meet this sturdy rascal. And if he pays no mind to the seal of our glorious sovereign King Harry and the warrant of the good Sheriff of Nottinghamshire, I will bruise, beat, and batter his head so badly that he will never move a finger or a toe again! Do you hear that, my bully boys?”
“You’re just the man for my money,” cried the messenger. “And you’re coming back with me to Nottingham Town.”
“No,” said the Tinker, shaking his head slowly from side to side. “I go with no man unless it’s by my own free will.”
“No, no,” said the messenger, “there isn’t a man in Nottinghamshire who could make you go against your will, you brave fellow.”
“Aye, that’s right, I am brave,” said the Tinker.
“Indeed you are,” said the messenger, “a brave lad. And our good Sheriff has offered eighty angels of bright gold to whoever delivers the warrant to Robin Hood, though it won’t do much good.”

“Then I’ll go with you, lad. Just wait while I fetch my bag and hammer and my cudgel. Yes, just let me meet this Robin Hood, and we’ll see whether he pays attention to the King’s warrant.” So, after they had paid their bill, the messenger set off for Nottingham again, with the Tinker striding beside his nag.

One bright morning soon after this, Robin Hood set out for Nottingham Town to see what was going on there. He strolled cheerfully along the roadside, where the grass was sweet with daisies, letting his eyes wander and his thoughts too. His bugle horn hung at his hip and his bow and arrows at his back, and in his hand he carried a good stout oak staff, which he twirled in his fingers as he went.

As he walked down a shady lane, he saw a tinker coming toward him, humming a merry tune as he came near. On his back hung his bag and his hammer, and in his hand he carried a stout crabstaff a full six feet long. This is what he sang:

“_In pea-pod time, when hounds and horn
Listen till the buck is slain,
And little boys with reed-pipes sit
Tending cattle on the plain_—”
“Hello there, good friend!” cried Robin.
“I WENT TO GATHER STRAWBERRIES—”
“Hello!” cried Robin again.
“BY WOODS AND GROVES FULL FAIR—”
“Hello! Are you deaf, man? I said, good friend!”

“And who are you, to rudely interrupt a fine song?” said the Tinker, breaking off his singing. “Hello to you yourself, whether you’re a good friend or not. But let me tell you, my sturdy fellow, if you are a good friend, that’s well for both of us, but if you’re no good friend, it will be bad for you.”
“And where do you come from, my lusty lad?” asked Robin.
“I come from Banbury,” answered the Tinker.
“Alas!” said Robin. “I hear there is sad news this merry morning.”
“Ha! Is that so?” cried the Tinker eagerly. “Please tell it quickly, for I’m a tinker by trade, as you see, and in my trade I’m hungry for news, the way a priest is hungry for pennies.”
“Well then,” said Robin, “listen and I’ll tell you, but brace yourself, for the news is sad, I assure you. Here it is: I hear that two tinkers are in the stocks for drinking ale and beer!”
“A plague on you and your news, you scurvy dog,” said the Tinker, “for you speak ill of good men. But it is sad news indeed, if there are two stout fellows in the stocks.”
“No,” said Robin, “you’ve missed the point, and you’re weeping for the wrong pig. The sad part of the news is that there are only two in the stocks, while all the others roam the country free.”

“Now by the pewter plate of Saint Dunstan,” cried the Tinker, “I have half a mind to tan your hide for that wicked joke. But if men are put in the stocks for drinking ale and beer, I’d wager you wouldn’t miss your share.”

Robin laughed loudly and cried, “Well said, Tinker, well said! Why, your wits are like beer, and froth up most when they turn sour! But you’re right, man, for I do love ale and beer. So come with me right now to the Sign of the Blue Boar, close by. If you drink the way you look, and I’m sure you won’t make a liar of your looks, I’ll soak your throat with as good a home brew as was ever tapped in all of broad Nottinghamshire.”
“By my faith,” said the Tinker, “you’re a good fellow in spite of your nasty jokes. I like you, my sweet chick, and if I don’t go with you to that Blue Boar, you can call me a heathen.”
“Tell me your news, good friend, please,” said Robin as they tramped on together, “for I suspect tinkers are as stuffed with news as an egg is with meat.”

“I love you like a brother, my bully lad,” said the Tinker, “or I wouldn’t tell you my news. For I’m sly, man, and I have an important job in hand that needs all my wits. I’ve come looking for a bold outlaw whom folks around here call Robin Hood. In my pouch I have a warrant, neatly written out on parchment, mind you, with a great red seal to make it lawful. If I could only meet this Robin Hood, I’d serve it on his dainty body, and if he ignored it, I’d beat him until every one of his ribs cried Amen. But you live around here, so maybe you know Robin Hood yourself, good fellow.”

“Why yes, I do know him a little,” said Robin, “and I saw him this very morning. But, Tinker, people say he is a sly and wicked thief. You had better watch your warrant, man, or he might steal it right out of your pouch.”
“Just let him try!” cried the Tinker. “He may be sly, but so am I. I wish I had him here right now, man to man!” And he made his heavy cudgel spin again. “But what sort of man is he, lad?”
“Much like me,” said Robin, laughing, “and nearly the same in height and build and age. He has blue eyes, too.”
“No,” said the Tinker, “you’re just a green youth. I thought he was a big bearded man. The Nottingham folk were so afraid of him.”
“Truly, he is not as old or as stout as you are,” said Robin. “But people do say he is very handy with a quarterstaff.”

“That may be,” said the Tinker boldly, “but I’m handier, for didn’t I beat Simon of Ely in a fair bout in the ring at Hertford Town? But if you know him, my jolly lad, will you go with me and lead me to him? The Sheriff has promised me eighty bright angels if I serve the warrant on the rascal’s body, and I’ll give you ten of them if you show him to me.”
“Gladly,” said Robin, “but show me your warrant, man, so I can see whether it’s a good one or not.”
“That I will not do, not even for my own brother,” answered the Tinker. “No man will see my warrant until I serve it on that fellow’s own body.”
“Have it your way,” said Robin. “If you won’t show it to me, I don’t know whom you’ll show it to. But here we are at the Sign of the Blue Boar, so let’s go in and taste his brown October ale.”

No pleasanter inn could be found in all Nottinghamshire than the Blue Boar. None had such lovely trees around it, or was so covered with trailing clematis and sweet woodbine. None had such good beer and such foaming ale. And in winter, when the north wind howled and snow drifted around the hedges, no other inn had such a roaring fire on its hearth as the Blue Boar did. At such times you might find a fine company of yeomen or country folk sitting around the blazing fire, trading merry jokes, while roasted crabs(2) bobbed in bowls of ale on the hearthstone. Robin Hood and his band knew the inn well, for he and such merry companions as Little John, Will Stutely, or young David of Doncaster had often gathered there when the whole forest was filled with snow. As for the landlord, he knew how to keep a still tongue in his head and swallow his words before they passed his teeth, for he knew very well which side of his bread was buttered. Robin and his band were his best customers, and they paid their bills without having them chalked up behind the door. So now, when Robin Hood and the Tinker arrived and called loudly for two great pots of ale, no one could have guessed from his look or his speech that the landlord had ever laid eyes on the outlaw before.
(2) Small sour apples.

“Wait here,” Robin said to the Tinker, “while I go and make sure the landlord draws the ale from the right cask. He has good October ale, I know, brewed by Withold of Tamworth.” With that, he went inside and whispered to the landlord to add a measure of Flemish strong liquor to the good English ale, which the man did before bringing it out to them.

“By Our Lady,” said the Tinker, after a long swallow of the ale, “that Withold of Tamworth, a good Saxon name too, I’ll have you know, brews the headiest ale that ever passed the lips of Wat o’ the Crabstaff.”
“Drink up, man, drink,” cried Robin, barely wetting his own lips. “Landlord! Another pot of the same for my friend. And now, my jolly lad, let’s have a song.”

“Yes, I’ll give you a song, my lovely fellow,” said the Tinker, “for I never tasted such ale in all my days. By Our Lady, it makes my head hum already! Hey, Dame Hostess, come listen if you want to hear a song, and you too, you pretty lass, for I never sing so well as when bright eyes are looking at me.”

Then he sang an old ballad from the days of good King Arthur, “The Marriage of Sir Gawaine,” which you can read for yourself one day, in the solid English of early times. While he sang, everyone listened to that noble story of a noble knight and his sacrifice for his king. But well before the Tinker reached the last verse, his tongue began to stumble and his head to swim, thanks to the strong liquor mixed in the ale. First his tongue stumbled, then his words came out thick, then his head lolled from side to side, until at last he dropped off to sleep as if he would never wake.

Then Robin Hood laughed aloud and quickly pulled the warrant out of the Tinker’s pouch with his nimble fingers. “You are sly, Tinker,” he said, “but I vow you’re not yet as sly as that sly thief Robin Hood.”

Then he called the landlord over and said, “Here, good man, are ten broad shillings for the entertainment you’ve given us today. Take good care of your fine guest there, and when he wakes you may charge him another ten shillings, and if he doesn’t have it, you may take his bag and hammer, and even his coat, in payment. That is how I punish those who come into the greenwood to deal out blows to me. As for you, I never knew a landlord yet who wouldn’t charge twice if he could.”
At this the landlord gave a sly smile, as if telling himself the old country saying, “Teach a magpie to suck eggs.”

The Tinker slept on until the afternoon was nearly gone and long shadows lay beside the edge of the woods, and then he woke up. He looked up, then down, then east, then west, trying to gather his wits like barley straws blown apart by the wind. He thought first of his merry companion, but the man had vanished. Next he thought of his stout crabstaff, and he still had that in his hand. Then he thought of the warrant, and of the eighty angels he would earn by serving it on Robin Hood. He shoved his hand into his pouch, but there was not a scrap or a farthing inside. At that he leaped up in a fury.
“Hey, landlord!” he cried. “Where has that rascal gone who was with me just now?”

“What rascal does Your Worship mean?” said the landlord, calling the Tinker “Your Worship” to calm him, the way a man pours oil on rough water. “I saw no rascal with Your Worship. I swear no man would dare call that fellow a rascal this close to Sherwood Forest. I saw a sturdy yeoman with Your Worship, but I took it that you knew him, since there are few around here who pass him by without knowing him.”
“And how would I know him? I’ve never squealed in your sty, so how should I know all the pigs in it? Who was he, if you know him so well?”
“Why, that fellow is a sturdy chap the folk around here call Robin Hood, and he—”

“By our Lady!” cried the Tinker sharply, in a deep voice like an angry bull’s. “You saw me walk into your inn, a proud, honest craftsman, and you never told me who my company was, though you knew perfectly well who he was yourself. I have a good round piece of my mind to give you, and I mean to crack your rascally head for you!” Then he picked up his cudgel and glared at the landlord as though he would strike him on the spot.
“No!” cried the landlord, throwing up his elbow, for he feared the blow. “How was I to know you didn’t know him?”

“You may be truly thankful,” said the Tinker, “that I’m a patient man and spare your bald head, or you’d never cheat another customer. But as for this rascal Robin Hood, I’m going straight off to find him, and if I don’t crack his rascally head, you can chop my staff into kindling and call me a woman.” With that, he pulled himself together to leave.

“No,” said the landlord, planting himself in front of the Tinker and spreading his arms like a gooseherd, for the thought of his money made him bold. “You’re not leaving until you’ve paid me what you owe.”
“But didn’t he pay you?”
“Not so much as a farthing, and you’ve drunk ten good shillings’ worth of ale today. No, I tell you, you’re not leaving without paying me, or our good Sheriff will hear of it.”
“But I’ve nothing to pay you with, good fellow,” said the Tinker.

“‘Good fellow’ yourself, not me,” said the landlord. “I’m no good fellow when I’m about to lose ten shillings! Pay me what you owe in good coin, or else leave your coat and bag and hammer. Though I know they aren’t worth ten shillings, and I’ll lose by it. And if you so much as move, I have a big dog inside and I’ll set him on you. Maken, open the door and let Brian out if this fellow takes one step.”

“No,” said the Tinker, for from his roaming about the country he had learned what dogs were like. “Take whatever you like and let me leave in peace, and a plague go with you. But oh, landlord! If I catch that scurvy scoundrel, I swear he’ll pay back with interest everything he’s had!”
With that he strode off toward the forest, muttering to himself, while the landlord and his good wife and Maken stood watching him go, and they laughed once he was well out of sight.
“Robin and I stripped that donkey of his pack very neatly,” said the landlord.

Now it happened that about this time Robin Hood was walking through the forest toward Fosse Way to see what there was to see, for the moon was full and the night promised to be bright. In his hand he carried his stout oak staff, and at his side hung his bugle horn. As he walked up one forest path, whistling, the Tinker came down another, muttering to himself and shaking his head like an angry bull; and at a sudden bend they met face to face. Each stood still for a moment, and then Robin spoke.
“Hello there, my sweet bird,” he said, laughing merrily. “How did you like your ale? Won’t you sing me another song?”

At first the Tinker said nothing, but stood staring at Robin with a grim face. “Now,” he said at last, “I’m very glad I’ve met you, and if I don’t rattle your bones inside your hide today, you have my leave to put your foot on my neck.”

“With all my heart,” cried merry Robin. “Rattle my bones, if you can.” With that he gripped his staff and took his stance. The Tinker spat on his hands and, taking hold of his staff, came straight at him. He struck two or three blows, but soon found he had met his match, for Robin blocked and turned aside every one, and before the Tinker knew it, Robin gave him a rap on the ribs in return. Robin laughed out loud at this, and the Tinker grew angrier than ever and struck again with all his might and main. Again Robin blocked two of the strokes, but at the third his staff snapped under the Tinker’s mighty blows. “Curse you, traitor staff,” cried Robin as it fell from his hands. “You’re a rotten stick to fail me like this in my hour of need.”
“Now give up,” said the Tinker, “for you’re my prisoner; and if you don’t, I’ll beat your head to a pudding.”
Robin Hood gave no answer to this, but put his horn to his lips and blew three blasts, loud and clear.
“Go ahead and blow,” said the Tinker, “but you’re coming with me to Nottingham Town, for the Sheriff would dearly like to see you there. Now will you give up, or must I break your pretty head?”

“If I must drink sour ale, I must,” said Robin, “but I have never yielded to any man before, and that without a wound or mark on my body. And now that I think of it, I won’t yield now. Ho, my merry men! Come quickly!”
Then Little John and six stout yeomen dressed in Lincoln green leaped out of the forest.
“What is it, good master?” cried Little John. “What do you need, that you blow your horn so loudly?”
“There stands a tinker,” said Robin, “who would like to take me to Nottingham, to hang on the gallows tree.”
“Then he shall hang himself, and right now,” cried Little John, and he and the others rushed at the Tinker to seize him.

“No, don’t touch him,” said Robin, “for he’s a sturdy man. He’s a metal man by trade and a mettled man by nature; besides, he sings a lovely ballad. Tell me, good fellow, will you join all my merry men? You’ll have three suits of Lincoln green a year, and forty marks besides; you’ll share everything with us and lead a merry life in the greenwood. We have no cares, and misfortune never reaches us in the sweet shade of Sherwood, where we shoot the dun deer and feed on venison and sweet oatcakes, and curds and honey. Will you come with me?”

“Yes, indeed, I’ll join you all,” said the Tinker, “for I love a merry life, and I love you, good master, though you thumped my ribs and cheated me into the bargain. I’m glad to admit you’re both a sturdier and a slyer man than I am; so I’ll obey you and be your own true servant.”

So they all turned toward the depths of the forest, where the Tinker was to live from then on. For many a day he sang ballads to the band, until the famous Allan a Dale joined them, beside whose sweet voice all others sounded as harsh as a raven’s; but we shall hear of him later.

chapters.title: The Shooting Match at Nottingham Town
paragraphs: The Sheriff was furious at this failure to catch jolly Robin, for word reached him, as bad news always does, that the people were laughing at him and making a joke of his notion of serving a warrant on such a man as the bold outlaw. And a man hates nothing so much as being laughed at; so he said, “Our gracious lord and sovereign, the King himself, shall hear of this, and how his laws are twisted and scorned by this band of rebel outlaws. As for that traitor of a Tinker, I will hang him, if I catch him, from the very tallest gallows tree in all Nottinghamshire.”
He then told all his servants and followers to prepare for a trip to London Town, where he would see the King and talk with him.

At this there was a great bustle at the Sheriff’s castle, and men ran here and there on one errand and another, while the forge fires of Nottingham glowed red like twinkling stars far into the night, for all the smiths of the town were busy making or mending armor for the Sheriff’s escort. This work lasted two days, and on the third everything was ready for the journey. They set out in bright sunlight, from Nottingham Town to Fosse Way and from there to Watling Street; and they traveled for two days, until at last they saw the spires and towers of great London Town. Many people stopped along the way to gaze at the spectacle they made, riding down the highways with their flashing armor and bright plumes and trappings.
King Henry and his fair Queen Eleanor were holding court in London, which was full of ladies in silks and satins and velvets and cloth of gold, and of brave knights and gallant courtiers.
The Sheriff came there and was shown into the King’s presence.
“A favor, a favor,” he said, as he knelt on the ground.
“Well, what do you want?” said the King. “Let us hear what you desire.”
“My good Lord and Sovereign,” said the Sheriff, “a bold outlaw named Robin Hood lives in Sherwood Forest, in our own good shire of Nottingham.”
“In truth,” said the King, “his doings have reached even our own royal ears. He is a saucy, rebellious rogue, though I must admit he is a merry soul all the same.”

“But hear me, O my most gracious Sovereign,” said the Sheriff. “I sent a warrant to him with your own royal seal attached, by a strong and sturdy fellow, but he beat the messenger and stole the warrant. And he kills your deer and robs your own loyal subjects even on the great highways.”

“Why, what is this?” said the King angrily. “What would you have me do? You come to me with a great array of men-at-arms and retainers, and yet you can’t catch a single band of sturdy rogues with no armor on their chests, in your own county! What would you have me do? Are you not my Sheriff? Are my laws not in force in Nottinghamshire? Can you not take your own action against those who break the laws or do any harm to you or yours? Go, be gone, and think hard; devise some plan of your own, but trouble me no further. But take care, Master Sheriff, for I will have my laws obeyed by all men in my kingdom, and if you can’t enforce them, you are no sheriff for me. So look to yourself, I say, or ill may befall you as well as all the thieving rogues in Nottinghamshire. When the flood comes, it sweeps away the grain along with the chaff.”

The Sheriff turned away heavy-hearted and troubled, and he deeply regretted showing off such a fine crowd of followers, for he saw that the King was angry because he had so many men around him and still could not enforce the laws. As they all rode slowly back to Nottingham, the Sheriff brooded, full of worry. He spoke to no one, and not one of his men spoke to him, while the whole way he was busy working out some plan to catch Robin Hood.

“Aha!” he cried suddenly, slapping his thigh. “I have it now! Ride on, my merry men all, and let us get back to Nottingham Town as fast as we can. And mark my words: before two weeks have passed, that wicked rogue Robin Hood will be safely clapped into Nottingham jail.”
But what was the Sheriff’s plan?

A moneylender takes the silver angels out of a bag one by one, feeling each coin to find out whether it has been clipped. In the same way the Sheriff, as they all rode slowly and sadly back toward Nottingham, took up one thought after another, feeling around the edges of each one and finding a flaw in every one. At last he thought of the daring spirit of jolly Robin, and how, as the Sheriff knew, he often came even inside the walls of Nottingham.

“Now,” thought the Sheriff, “if I could only lure Robin close to Nottingham Town, so that I could find him, I’m sure I would lay hands on him so firmly that he would never get away again.” Then suddenly it came to him in a flash that if he announced a great shooting match and offered a splendid prize, Robin Hood’s spirit might be tempted to bring him to the butts; and it was this thought that made him cry “Aha!” and slap his thigh.

So as soon as he had returned safely to Nottingham, he sent messengers north and south and east and west to announce this grand shooting match through town, village, and countryside. Everyone who could draw a longbow was invited, and the prize was to be an arrow of pure beaten gold.
Robin Hood was in Lincoln Town when the news first reached him. He hurried back to Sherwood Forest, called all his merry men together, and told them this.

“Now listen, my merry men all, to the news I’ve brought from Lincoln Town today. Our friend the Sheriff of Nottingham has announced a shooting match and has sent messengers to spread word of it across the whole countryside, and the prize is to be a bright golden arrow. Now I would very much like one of us to win it, both because the prize is so fine and because our sweet friend the Sheriff is the one offering it. So we’ll take our bows and arrows and go there to shoot, for I know very well there will be merrymaking. What do you say, lads?”

Then young David of Doncaster spoke up and said, “Now, good master, please listen to what I have to say. I have come straight from our friend Eadom o’ the Blue Boar, and there I heard all the news of this match. But, master, I have it from him, and he got it from the Sheriff’s man Ralph o’ the Scar, that this rascal of a Sheriff has only set a trap for you with this shooting match and wants nothing so much as to see you there. So don’t go, good master, for I know well he is trying to trick you, but stay in the greenwood, or we will all meet with sorrow and woe.”

“Well,” said Robin, “you’re a wise lad, and you keep your ears open and your mouth shut, as a wise and crafty woodsman should. But shall it be said that the Sheriff of Nottingham frightened bold Robin Hood and a hundred and forty of the finest archers in all merry England? No, good David, what you tell me makes me want the prize even more than I would have otherwise. But what does our good gossip Swanthold say? Isn’t it, ‘A hasty man burns his mouth, and the fool who keeps his eyes shut falls into the pit’? So he says, and truly, therefore we must meet trickery with trickery. Now, some of you dress as friars in short habits, and some as country peasants, and some as tinkers or beggars, but see that each man carries a good bow or broadsword, in case of need. As for me, I will shoot for this golden arrow, and if I win it, we’ll hang it from the branches of our good greenwood tree for the joy of the whole band. How do you like the plan, my merry men all?”
Then “Good, good!” cried all the band heartily.

Nottingham Town was a fine sight on the day of the shooting match. Down on the green meadow beneath the town wall ran a long row of benches, rising tier above tier, set aside for knights and ladies, squires and their wives, and rich townsmen and their wives; only people of rank and quality were allowed to sit there. At the far end of the field, near the target, stood a raised seat hung with ribbons, scarfs and garlands of flowers, for the Sheriff of Nottingham and his lady. The field was forty paces wide. The target stood at one end, and at the other was a tent of striped canvas, with many-colored flags and streamers fluttering from its pole. Inside this booth were casks of ale, and any archer who was thirsty could tap one freely.

Facing the seats of the better folk, on the opposite side of the field, a railing kept the common people from crowding in front of the target. Early as it was, the benches were already filling with people of quality, who kept arriving in little carts or on palfreys that pranced gaily to the tinkle of silver bells on their bridles. The poorer folk came too, and sat or lay on the grass beside the railing that held them back from the field. In the great tent the archers were gathering in twos and threes. Some boasted loudly of the fine shots each had made in his day. Others were checking their bows, pulling a string between their fingers to be sure it was not frayed, or looking over their arrows, shutting one eye and peering down a shaft to see that it was not warped but straight and true, for neither bow nor arrow must fail at such a time, with such a prize at stake. And there had never been such a company of yeomen as the one gathered at Nottingham Town that day, for the very best archers in merry England had come to this match. Gill o’ the Red Cap was there, the Sheriff’s own chief archer, and Diccon Cruikshank of Lincoln Town, and Adam o’ the Dell, a man of Tamworth who was over sixty years old and still hale and hearty. In his time he had shot in the famous match at Woodstock and beaten the renowned archer Clym o’ the Clough there. Many more famous masters of the longbow were present too, men whose names have come down to us in fine old ballads.

At last, when every bench was full of guests, lords and ladies, townsmen and their wives, the Sheriff himself arrived with his lady. He rode proudly on his milk-white horse, and she rode a brown filly. On his head he wore a purple velvet cap, and his robe was purple velvet too, trimmed all around with rich ermine. His jerkin and hose were of sea-green silk, and his shoes were black velvet, with the pointed toes fastened to his garters by golden chains. A golden chain hung around his neck, and a great carbuncle set in red gold glittered at his collar. His lady wore blue velvet trimmed with swan’s down. They made a splendid sight riding side by side, and all the common people across the field shouted as they passed. So the Sheriff and his lady came to their seats, where men-at-arms in mail coats, carrying spears, stood around waiting for them.

When the Sheriff and his lady had taken their seats, he ordered his herald to blow his silver horn. The herald sounded three blasts, and they came echoing merrily back from the gray walls of Nottingham. Then the archers stepped forward to their places, while the crowd roared, each person calling out for a favorite yeoman. “Red Cap!” cried some. “Cruikshank!” cried others. “Hurrah for William o’ Leslie!” shouted still others, and ladies waved silk scarfs to urge each yeoman on to his best.
Then the herald stepped forward and called out the rules of the contest in a loud voice:

“Each man shall shoot from that mark over there, which is one hundred and fifty yards from the target. Every man shall shoot one arrow first, and of all the archers, the ten whose arrows land best shall be chosen to shoot again. Each of those ten shall shoot two arrows, and then the three whose arrows land best shall be chosen to shoot again. Each of those three shall shoot three arrows, and the prize shall go to the man whose arrows land best.”

The Sheriff leaned forward and searched the crowd of archers for Robin Hood, but no one was dressed in Lincoln green, the cloth that Robin and his band wore. “Even so,” the Sheriff said to himself, “he may be here, and I may simply be missing him among all the other men. But I’ll look again when only ten are left shooting, for I’m sure he will be among the ten, or I don’t know the man.”

Now the archers shot, one after another, and the good people had never seen such archery as they saw that day. Six arrows landed within the bull’s-eye, four within the black ring, and only two hit the outer ring. When the last arrow flew and struck the target, the whole crowd shouted aloud, for it was noble shooting.

Now only ten men were left of all who had shot before. Six of them were famous across the land, and most of the people gathered there knew them. These six were Gilbert o’ the Red Cap, Adam o’ the Dell, Diccon Cruikshank, William o’ Leslie, Hubert o’ Cloud and Swithin o’ Hertford. Two more were yeomen from merry Yorkshire. Another was a tall stranger in blue, who said he had come from London Town, and the last was a ragged stranger in scarlet, with a patch over one eye.
“Tell me,” the Sheriff said to a man-at-arms standing near him, “do you see Robin Hood among those ten?”

“No, I do not, Your Worship,” the man answered. “Six of them I know very well. Of those Yorkshire yeomen, one is too tall and the other too short for that bold rascal. Robin’s beard is yellow as gold, while that ragged beggar in scarlet has a brown beard, and he is blind in one eye besides. As for the stranger in blue, I’d say Robin’s shoulders are three inches broader than his.”
“Then,” said the Sheriff, slapping his thigh angrily, “that rascal is a coward as well as a rogue, and he doesn’t dare show his face among honest men.”

After a short rest, the ten sturdy men stepped forward to shoot again. Each shot two arrows. While they shot, not a word was spoken, and the crowd watched in near silence. But when the last man had loosed his arrow, another great shout went up, and many people tossed their caps into the air for joy at such marvelous shooting.

“By our gracious Lady,” said old Sir Amyas o’ the Dell, who sat near the Sheriff, bent with more than eighty years, “I never in all my life saw such archery, and I have watched the best hands with the longbow for sixty years and more.”

That left just three men standing out of everyone who had shot: Gill o’ the Red Cap, the ragged stranger in scarlet, and Adam o’ the Dell of Tamworth Town. The people all began calling out. Some cried, “Hurrah for Gilbert o’ the Red Cap!” and others, “Come on, stout Adam o’ Tamworth!” Yet not a single voice in the crowd cheered for the stranger in scarlet.
“Shoot well now, Gilbert,” cried the Sheriff, “and if yours is the best arrow, I’ll give you a hundred broad silver pennies on top of the prize.”

“I’ll do my best, truly,” said Gilbert stoutly. “A man can do no more than his best, but I’ll try to do that today.” With that, he drew out a fine smooth arrow with a broad feather and fitted it deftly to the string. Then he drew his bow with care and loosed the shaft. The arrow flew straight and landed in the bull’s-eye, a finger’s breadth from the center. “A Gilbert, a Gilbert!” shouted the whole crowd, and “Now, on my faith,” cried the Sheriff, clapping his hands together, “that is a clever shot.”

Next the ragged stranger stepped forward, and all the people laughed when they saw a yellow patch showing under his arm as he raised his elbow to shoot, and again when they saw him aim with only one eye. He drew his good yew bow quickly and loosed his arrow just as quickly, so fast that no one could have taken a breath between the drawing and the shooting. Yet his arrow lodged closer to the center than Gilbert’s, by twice the length of a barleycorn.
“By all the saints in Paradise!” cried the Sheriff. “That is a beautiful shot, truly!”

Then Adam o’ the Dell shot, slowly and carefully, and his arrow landed close beside the stranger’s. After a short pause, all three shot again. Once more every arrow landed in the bull’s-eye, but this time Adam o’ the Dell’s was farthest from the center, and again the ragged stranger’s was the best. After another rest, they shot for the third time. This time Gilbert took great care with his aim, measuring the distance closely and shooting with the utmost skill. His arrow flew straight, and the crowd shouted so loudly that the very flags waving in the breeze seemed to shake, and the rooks and jackdaws flew squawking around the roofs of the old gray tower, for the shaft had landed right beside the spot that marked the exact center.
“Well done, Gilbert!” cried the Sheriff joyfully. “I’m ready to believe the prize is yours, and fairly won. Now, you ragged rascal, let me see you shoot a better shot than that.”

The stranger said nothing but took his place. All was hushed. No one spoke, no one even seemed to breathe, so deep was the silence as everyone wondered what he would do. He stood perfectly still for a moment, holding his bow in his hand, as long as it takes to count five. Then he drew his trusty yew, held it drawn for just an instant, and let the string go. The arrow flew straight and so true that it sliced a gray goose feather from Gilbert’s shaft, and the feather went fluttering down through the sunlit air as the stranger’s arrow lodged in the very center, right beside the Red Cap’s. For a while no one said a word and no one cheered. Each man simply stared at his neighbor in amazement.

“No,” said old Adam o’ the Dell after a moment, drawing a long breath and shaking his head. “I’ve been shooting arrows for more than forty years, and maybe not always badly, but I’ll shoot no more today, for no man can match that stranger, whoever he is.” Then he shoved his arrow into his quiver with a rattle and unstrung his bow without another word.

Then the Sheriff came down from his platform, in all his silks and velvets, and walked over to where the ragged stranger stood leaning on his stout bow, while the good people crowded around to see the man who shot so wonderfully well. “Here, good fellow,” said the Sheriff, “take the prize. You have won it well and fairly, I admit. What is your name, and where do you come from?”
“Men call me Jock o’ Teviotdale, and that is where I come from,” said the stranger.

“Then, by Our Lady, Jock, you are the finest archer my eyes have ever seen. If you will join my service, I will dress you in a better coat than the one on your back. You shall eat and drink of the best, and every Christmastide you shall be paid eighty marks. I’d wager you draw a better bow than that coward Robin Hood, who didn’t dare show his face here today. Tell me, good fellow, will you join my service?”
“No, that I will not,” said the stranger roughly. “I’ll be my own man, and no one in all merry England shall be my master.”

“Then be gone, and a plague on you!” cried the Sheriff, his voice shaking with anger. “On my faith and honor, I have half a mind to have you beaten for your insolence!” Then he turned on his heel and strode away.

A very mixed company gathered around the noble greenwood tree deep in Sherwood that same day. There were twenty or more barefoot friars, and some who looked like tinkers, and some who seemed to be sturdy beggars and country laborers. On a mossy seat sat a man dressed all in tattered scarlet, with a patch over one eye, and in his hand he held the golden arrow that was the prize of the great shooting match. Amid the noise of talk and laughter, he pulled the patch from his eye and stripped off the scarlet rags, and there he stood, dressed all in fine Lincoln green. “These things come off easily,” he said, “but walnut stain doesn’t wash out of yellow hair so quickly.” Then everyone laughed louder than before, for it was Robin Hood himself who had won the prize right out of the Sheriff’s hands.

Then they all sat down to the woodland feast and talked among themselves about the merry joke they had played on the Sheriff, and about the adventures each member of the band had met with in his disguise. But when the feast was over, Robin Hood took Little John aside and said, “I tell you, my blood is boiling. I heard the Sheriff say today, ‘You shoot better than that coward Robin Hood, who didn’t dare show his face here this day.’ I’d dearly like to let him know who it was that won the golden arrow from his hand, and also that I am no coward, whatever he takes me for.”
Then Little John said, “Good master, take me and Will Stutely with you, and we will send that fat Sheriff word of all this by a messenger he doesn’t expect.”

That day the Sheriff sat at dinner in the great hall of his house in Nottingham Town. Long tables ran down the hall, and at them sat men-at-arms, household servants and good sturdy villains,(1) more than eighty in all. They talked about the day’s shooting as they ate their meat and drank their ale. The Sheriff sat at the head of the table on a raised seat under a canopy, with his lady beside him.
(1) Bond-servants.

“On my word,” he said, “I was quite sure that rascal Robin Hood would be at the contest today. I never thought he was such a coward. But who could that saucy fellow have been, who answered me to my face so boldly? I wonder I didn’t have him beaten. Yet there was something about him that suggested something other than rags and tatters.”

Just as he finished speaking, something came clattering down among the dishes on the table, and those sitting nearby jumped up wondering what it was. After a while, one of the men-at-arms found the courage to pick it up and bring it to the Sheriff. Then everyone saw that it was a blunted gray goose arrow, with a fine scroll, about as thick as a goose quill, tied close to its head. The Sheriff opened the scroll and glanced at it, and the veins on his forehead swelled and his cheeks turned red with rage as he read, for this is what he saw:

“_May Heaven bless Your Grace today,
So say we all in sweet Sherwood,
For you have given the prize away
To merry Robin Hood_.”
“Where did this come from?” cried the Sheriff in a mighty voice.
“Straight through the window, Your Worship,” said the man who had handed him the arrow.

chapters.title: Will Stutely Rescued by his Companions
paragraphs: When the Sheriff saw that neither law nor trickery could beat Robin Hood, he was badly troubled. “What a fool I am!” he said to himself. “If I hadn’t told the King about Robin Hood, I wouldn’t be in this mess. Now I must either catch him or face the anger of His Majesty. I’ve tried the law, and I’ve tried trickery, and I’ve failed with both. So now I’ll see what force can do.”

Turning the matter over in his mind, he called his constables together and told them his plan. “Each of you take four men, all in good armor,” he said, “and go off to the forest by different routes and lie in wait for this Robin Hood. If any constable finds himself facing too many men, let him blow a horn, and every band within hearing must hurry to join the one that calls. That way, I think, we’ll catch this green-clad rascal. What’s more, whoever is first to meet Robin Hood will get a hundred pounds in silver, if he brings him to me dead or alive. And whoever meets any of his band will get forty pounds, if he brings the man to me dead or alive. So be bold, and be clever.”

So they marched off to Sherwood Forest in sixty companies of five, to capture Robin Hood. Every constable hoped to be the one to find the bold outlaw, or at least one of his men. For seven days and nights they searched the forest glades, but they never saw so much as one man in Lincoln green, because Eadom o’ the Blue Boar, a faithful friend, had carried word of all this to Robin Hood.

When Robin first heard the news, he said, “If the Sheriff dares to send force against force, he will be sorry, and so will many better men than he, for blood will be spilled and there will be great trouble for everyone. But I would gladly avoid blood and battle, and I would gladly spare the women and wives from sorrow because good, sturdy yeomen have lost their lives. Once I killed a man, and I never want to kill another, for it weighs bitterly on the soul to think of it. So for now we will stay quietly in Sherwood Forest, so that all may go well. But if we are forced to defend ourselves, or any of our band, then let every man draw bow and sword with all his might.”

Hearing this, many of the band shook their heads and said to themselves, “Now the Sheriff will think we are cowards, and people all over the countryside will laugh and say we are afraid to face his men.” But they said nothing aloud. They swallowed their words and did as Robin told them.

So they stayed hidden in the depths of Sherwood Forest for seven days and seven nights, and never showed their faces outside it in all that time. But early in the morning of the eighth day, Robin Hood called the band together and said, “Now, who will go and find out what the Sheriff’s men are up to? For I know very well they won’t stay forever in the shade of Sherwood.”

At this a great shout went up, and every man waved his bow in the air and cried out that he should be the one to go. Robin Hood’s heart swelled with pride as he looked around at his strong, brave fellows. “You are all brave and true, my merry men,” he said, “and a fine band of good fellows you are, but you can’t all go. So I will choose one of you, and it will be good Will Stutely, for he is as sly as any old dog fox in Sherwood Forest.”

Then Will Stutely leaped high in the air and laughed out loud, clapping his hands for sheer joy that he had been picked from among them all. “Thank you, good master,” he said, “and if I don’t bring you news of those rascals, never call me your sly Will Stutely again.”

Then he dressed himself in a friar’s gown, and under the robe he hung a good broadsword, in a spot where he could grab it easily. Dressed like this, he set out on his errand until he reached the edge of the forest and then the highway. He passed two bands of the Sheriff’s men, but he turned neither right nor left. He only pulled his hood closer over his face and folded his hands as if deep in thought. At last he came to the Sign of the Blue Boar. “For,” he said to himself, “our good friend Eadom will tell me all the news.”

At the Sign of the Blue Boar he found a group of the Sheriff’s men drinking heartily. Without speaking to anyone, he sat down on a bench far off, with his staff in his hand and his head bowed as though he were deep in thought. There he sat, waiting for a chance to see the landlord alone. Eadom did not recognize him and took him for some poor, tired friar, so he let him sit without a word or any trouble, though he did not like the friar’s habit. “For,” he said to himself, “it takes a hard heart to kick a lame dog off the doorstep.” As Stutely sat there, a big house cat came and rubbed against his knee, lifting his robe a hand’s breadth. Stutely quickly pushed the robe back down, but the constable in charge of the Sheriff’s men had seen it, and he had seen handsome Lincoln green under the friar’s robe too. He said nothing at the time, but thought to himself, “That is no friar of the gray order. And I know that no honest yeoman goes about dressed as a priest, nor does a thief dress that way for nothing. I truly think this is one of Robin Hood’s own men.” So after a while he said aloud, “Holy father, won’t you have a good pot of March beer to wet your thirsty soul?”
But Stutely shook his head without a word, for he said to himself, “There may be someone here who knows my voice.”
Then the constable spoke again. “Where are you headed, holy friar, on this hot summer’s day?”
“I’m going as a pilgrim to Canterbury,” answered Will Stutely, speaking gruffly so that no one would know his voice.

Then, for the third time, the constable said, “Now tell me, holy father, do pilgrims to Canterbury wear good Lincoln green under their robes? Ha! By my faith, I take you for some sturdy thief, and perhaps one of Robin Hood’s own band! Now, by Our Lady’s grace, if you move a hand or a foot, I’ll run you through with my sword!”

With that he drew his bright sword and leaped at Will Stutely, thinking to catch him off guard. But Stutely had his own sword gripped tightly in his hand beneath his robe, and he drew it out before the constable reached him. The stout constable struck a mighty blow, but he never struck another in that fight, for Stutely turned the blow aside neatly and struck the constable back with all his strength. Stutely would then have gotten away, but he could not, because the constable, dizzy from the wound and the flowing blood, wrapped his arms around Stutely’s knees as he reeled and fell. Then the others rushed at Stutely, and he struck at another of the Sheriff’s men, but the steel cap turned the blow, and although the blade cut deep, it did not kill. Meanwhile the constable, faint as he was, dragged Stutely down, and the others, seeing the yeoman held back like that, rushed at him again. One of them struck him on the head so that blood ran down his face and blinded him. Then he staggered and fell, and they all sprang on him, though he fought so bravely that they could hardly hold him down. At last they tied him with strong hempen cords so that he could not move hand or foot, and so they overpowered him.

Robin Hood was standing under the greenwood tree, thinking about Will Stutely and how he might be doing, when he suddenly saw two of his strong yeomen come running down the forest path, and between them ran plump Maken of the Blue Boar. Robin’s heart sank, for he knew they were bringing bad news.
“Will Stutely has been captured,” they cried as soon as they reached him.
“And are you the one who has brought such sad news?” Robin asked the girl.

“Yes, indeed, for I saw it all,” she cried, panting like a hare that has just escaped the hounds. “And I fear he is badly hurt, for one of them struck him a cruel blow on the head. They have tied him up and taken him to Nottingham Town, and before I left the Blue Boar I heard that he is to be hanged tomorrow.”
“He shall not be hanged tomorrow,” cried Robin, “or if he is, many a man will bite the dust, and many will have cause to cry, ‘Alas the day!’”
Then he put his horn to his lips and blew three loud blasts, and soon his good yeomen came running through the greenwood until a hundred and forty bold blades were gathered around him.

“Now listen, all of you!” cried Robin. “Our dear companion Will Stutely has been taken by that wicked Sheriff’s men, so it is our duty to take up bow and sword and bring him back. I know we ought to risk life and limb for him, as he has risked life and limb for us. Isn’t that so, my merry men all?” Then they all cried, “Aye!” in one great voice.

The next day they all made their way out of Sherwood Forest, but by different paths, because they had to be very careful. The band split up into parties of two and three, and all were to meet again in a tangled dell near Nottingham Town. When they had all gathered at the meeting place, Robin spoke to them like this:
“Now we will lie here in ambush until we can get news, for we must be cunning and careful if we want to rescue our friend Will Stutely from the Sheriff’s clutches.”
