So they lay hidden for a long time, until the sun stood high in the sky. The day was warm, and the dusty road was empty of travelers except for an old palmer, who walked slowly along the highroad that ran close beside the gray castle wall of Nottingham Town. When Robin saw that no other traveler was in sight, he called young David of Doncaster, who was shrewd for his age, and said to him, “Now go out, young David, and speak to that palmer walking beside the town wall. He has only just come from Nottingham Town, and he may be able to tell you news of good Stutely.”

So David strode out, and when he reached the pilgrim, he greeted him and said, “Good morning, holy father. Can you tell me when Will Stutely will be hanged on the gallows tree? I would hate to miss the sight, for I have come from far away to see such a sturdy rogue hanged.”

“Shame on you, young man,” cried the Palmer, “to talk like that when a good, strong man is about to be hanged for nothing but protecting his own life!” And he struck his staff on the ground in anger. “Alas, I say, that this should happen! For this very day, toward evening, when the sun sinks low, he will be hanged, eighty rods from the great town gate of Nottingham, where three roads meet. The Sheriff swears he will die there as a warning to all outlaws in Nottinghamshire. But still I say again, alas! For though Robin Hood and his band may be outlaws, he takes only from the rich, the powerful and the dishonest, while there is not a poor widow or a peasant with a houseful of children near Sherwood who doesn’t have enough barley flour all year long because of him. It grieves my heart to see a man as gallant as this Stutely die, for I was a good Saxon yeoman in my day, before I became a palmer, and I know well what a strong hand it is that strikes hard at a cruel Norman or a proud abbot with fat moneybags. If only good Stutely’s master knew what dangers his man was surrounded by, perhaps he might send help to get him out of his enemies’ hands.”

“Yes indeed, that is true,” cried the young man. “If Robin and his men are anywhere near this place, I know well they will try to rescue him from his danger. But farewell, good old man, and believe me, if Will Stutely dies, he will be well avenged.”

Then he turned and walked quickly away, but the Palmer looked after him, muttering, “I’m sure that young man is no country farmhand come to see a good man die. Well, well, perhaps Robin Hood is not so far away, and there will be stirring deeds this day.” And he went on his way, still muttering to himself.
David of Doncaster went back and repeated the Palmer’s words to Robin Hood. Robin gathered the band close around him and said:

“Now let’s go straight into Nottingham Town and mix with the people there. But keep each other in sight, and press as close to the prisoner and his guards as you can when they come outside the walls. Strike no man unless you must, for I would rather avoid bloodshed, but if you do strike, strike hard, so that there’s no need to strike again. Then stay together until we are back in Sherwood, and let no man leave his fellows.”

The sun was low in the western sky when a bugle sounded from the castle wall. Then all was bustle in Nottingham Town, and crowds filled the streets, for everyone knew that the famous Will Stutely was to be hanged that day. Soon the castle gates swung wide, and a great company of men-at-arms came out with noise and clatter, with the Sheriff riding at their head, dressed in shining mail of linked chain. In the middle of the guard, in a cart with a rope around his neck, rode Will Stutely. His face was pale from his wound and the loss of blood, like the moon in broad daylight, and his fair hair was clotted into spikes on his forehead where the blood had dried. When he came out of the castle he looked up and he looked down, and although he saw some faces that showed pity and some that showed kindness, he saw none that he knew. Then his heart sank within him like a lead weight, but he still spoke up boldly.
“Put a sword in my hand, Sir Sheriff,” he said, “and wounded as I am, I will fight you and all your men until my life and strength are gone.”
“No, you wicked scoundrel,” said the Sheriff, turning his head and looking grimly at Will Stutely. “You will have no sword, but will die a shameful death, as a vile thief like you deserves.”
“Then just untie my hands, and I will fight you and your men with nothing but my bare fists. I ask for no weapon, only don’t let me be hanged like a dog this day.”

Then the Sheriff laughed out loud. “Why, what’s this?” he said. “Is your proud spirit failing? Confess your sins, you vile rogue, for I intend you to hang this day, and at the place where three roads meet, so that all men will see you hang, for the carrion crows and jackdaws to peck at.”

“You cowardly wretch!” cried Will Stutely, gnashing his teeth at the Sheriff. “You craven hound! If my good master ever meets you, you will pay dearly for this day’s work! He despises you, and so does every brave heart. Don’t you know that you and your name are a joke on the lips of every brave yeoman? A man like you, you miserable coward, will never be able to defeat bold Robin Hood.”

“Ha!” cried the Sheriff in a rage. “Is that so? Am I a joke to your master, as you call him? Then I will make a joke of you, and a sorry one, for after you are hanged I will cut you into quarters.” With that he spurred his horse ahead and said nothing more to Stutely.

At last they came to the great town gate, and through it Stutely saw the lovely countryside beyond, with its hills and valleys all dressed in green, and far away the dim edge of Sherwood. He saw the slanting sunlight lying on field and fallow, shining red here and there on cottage and farmhouse. He heard the sweet birds singing their evening songs and the sheep bleating on the hillside, and he watched the swallows flying in the bright air. His heart swelled so full that everything blurred before his eyes through salt tears, and he bowed his head so that people would not think him unmanly when they saw the tears in his eyes. He kept his head bowed until they had passed through the gate and were outside the town walls. But when he looked up again, his heart leaped and then stood still for pure joy, for he saw the face of one of his own dear companions from merry Sherwood. Glancing quickly around, he saw familiar faces on every side, crowding close against the men-at-arms who guarded him. Then the blood rushed to his cheeks, for in the crowd he caught sight of his own good master, and seeing him, he knew that Robin Hood and all his band were there. Still, between him and them stood a line of men-at-arms.
“Stand back!” cried the Sheriff in a mighty voice, for the crowd was pressing in on every side. “What do you mean, you rascals, pushing against us like this? Stand back, I say!”
Then came a bustle and a noise, as someone struggled to squeeze between the men-at-arms to reach the cart, and Stutely saw that it was Little John who was causing all the commotion.
“You stand back!” cried one of the men-at-arms, whom Little John was shoving with his elbows.
“Stand back yourself,” said Little John, and he promptly struck the man a blow beside the head that felled him the way a butcher fells an ox. Then he leaped onto the cart where Stutely sat.

“Say farewell to your friends before you die, Will,” he said, “or perhaps I will die with you if you must, for I could never ask for better company.” Then with one stroke he cut the ropes that bound Stutely’s arms and legs, and Stutely leaped straight out of the cart.
“As I live,” cried the Sheriff, “I know that fellow well, and he is a sturdy rebel! Seize him, all of you, I order you, and do not let him escape!”

Saying this, he spurred his horse at Little John and, rising in his stirrups, struck with all his might. But Little John ducked quickly under the horse’s belly, and the blow whistled harmlessly over his head.

“No, good Sir Sheriff,” he cried, springing up again once the blow had passed, “I must borrow your most worshipful sword.” And he deftly twitched the weapon out of the Sheriff’s hand. “Here, Stutely,” he cried, “the Sheriff has lent you his sword! Stand back to back with me, man, and defend yourself, for help is near!”

“Cut them down!” bellowed the Sheriff in a voice like an angry bull. He spurred his horse at the two men, who now stood back to back, forgetting in his rage that he had no weapon to defend himself with.

“Stand back, Sheriff!” cried Little John. Even as he spoke, a bugle horn sounded shrilly and a clothyard arrow whistled within an inch of the Sheriff’s head. Then came a swaying this way and that, with curses, shouts and groans, the clash of steel, swords flashing in the setting sun, and a score of arrows whistling through the air. Some cried, “Help, help!” and others, “A rescue, a rescue!”
“Treason!” cried the Sheriff in a loud voice. “Fall back! Fall back! Or we will all be dead men!” And he backed his horse out through the thickest part of the crowd.

Robin Hood and his band could have slain half the Sheriff’s men if they had wanted to. Instead they let them push their way out of the crowd and get away, sending only a flight of arrows after them to hurry them along.

“Oh, wait!” shouted Will Stutely after the Sheriff. “You will never catch bold Robin Hood if you won’t stand and meet him face to face.” But the Sheriff, bent low along his horse’s back, gave no answer and only spurred on faster.

Then Will Stutely turned to Little John and looked him in the face until the tears ran from his eyes and he wept aloud. Kissing his friend’s cheeks, he said, “O Little John! My own true friend, whom I love better than any man or woman in all the world! I little thought to see your face today, or to meet you this side of Paradise.” Little John could make no answer, but wept too.

Then Robin Hood gathered his band into a tight formation with Will Stutely in the middle, and so they moved slowly off toward Sherwood and were gone, the way a storm cloud drifts away from the place where a tempest has swept across the land. But they left ten of the Sheriff’s men lying on the ground, wounded, some badly and some lightly, and no one knew who had struck them down.

So the Sheriff of Nottingham tried three times to catch Robin Hood and failed every time. The last time he was frightened, for he realized how close he had come to losing his life. So he said, “These men fear neither God nor man, neither king nor king’s officers. I would rather lose my office than my life, so I will trouble them no more.” He stayed shut up in his castle for many a day and did not dare show his face outside his own household. All that time he was gloomy and would speak to no one, for he was ashamed of what had happened that day.

chapters.title: Robin Hood Turns Butcher
paragraphs: After all this had happened, and Robin Hood learned how the Sheriff had tried three times to take him prisoner, he said to himself, “If I get the chance, I will make our worshipful Sheriff pay dearly for what he has done to me. Perhaps I can bring him into Sherwood Forest someday and give him a merry feast with us.” For whenever Robin Hood caught a baron or a squire, or a fat abbot or bishop, he brought him to the greenwood tree and feasted him before he lightened his purse.

In the meantime, Robin Hood and his band lived quietly in Sherwood Forest and stayed out of sight, for Robin knew it would be unwise to be seen near Nottingham, since those in authority were very angry with him. But though they did not go abroad, they lived a merry life in the woods. They spent their days shooting at garlands hung on a willow wand at the end of the glade, while the leafy aisles rang with jokes and laughter, for anyone who missed the garland was given a sound slap, and when Little John delivered it, the unlucky yeoman always went tumbling. Then they had wrestling bouts and cudgel play, so that every day they grew in skill and strength.

They lived like this for nearly a year, and in that time Robin Hood often turned over in his mind ways of settling accounts with the Sheriff. At last he grew restless at being shut in. One day he took up his stout cudgel and set out to look for adventure, strolling cheerfully along until he came to the edge of Sherwood. There, as he rambled down the sunny road, he met a sturdy young butcher driving a fine mare and riding in a stout new cart hung all about with meat. The Butcher whistled merrily as he jogged along, for he was going to market, and the day was fresh and sweet and made his heart light.
“Good morning to you, jolly fellow,” said Robin. “You seem happy this fine morning.”

“Yes, I am,” said the jolly Butcher, “and why shouldn’t I be? Am I not healthy in wind and limb? Don’t I have the prettiest girl in all Nottinghamshire? And last of all, am I not going to marry her next Thursday in sweet Locksley Town?”

“Ha,” said Robin, “you come from Locksley Town? I know that fair place well for miles around, and I know every hedgerow and gentle pebbly stream, and even all the bright little fishes in them, for I was born and raised there. Now, where are you taking your meat, my good friend?”
“I’m going to the market at Nottingham Town to sell my beef and mutton,” answered the Butcher. “But who are you, who come from Locksley Town?”
“I am a yeoman, and men call me Robin Hood.”

“By Our Lady’s grace,” cried the Butcher, “I know your name well, and many a time I have heard your deeds sung and spoken of. But Heaven forbid that you should take anything from me! I am an honest man and have wronged neither man nor maid, so don’t trouble me, good master, since I have never troubled you.”

“Heaven forbid indeed,” said Robin, “that I should take from a man like you, jolly fellow! I wouldn’t take so much as one farthing from you, for I like a fair Saxon face like yours very well, especially when it comes from Locksley Town, and most of all when its owner is about to marry a pretty girl next Thursday. But come, tell me what price you want for all your meat and your horse and cart together.”
“I value meat, cart, and mare at four marks,” said the Butcher, “but if I don’t sell all my meat, I won’t get four marks’ worth.”

Robin Hood took the purse from his belt. “There are six marks in here,” he said. “I would like to play the butcher for a day and sell meat in Nottingham Town. Will you make a deal with me and take six marks for everything you have here?”
“God bless you, and may all the saints bless your honest head!” cried the Butcher happily. He jumped down from the cart and took the purse Robin was holding out.

“No,” said Robin, laughing loudly, “many people like me and wish me well, but few call me honest. Now go back to your lass, and give her a sweet kiss from me.” With that he put on the Butcher’s apron, climbed into the cart, took the reins in his hand, and drove off through the forest to Nottingham Town.

When he reached Nottingham, he went to the part of the market where the butchers stood and took his inn(2) in the best spot he could find. Then he opened his stall and spread his meat on the bench, and, clattering his cleaver and steel together, he sang out in a merry voice:
(2) A place to sell from.

“Come, you lasses, and you ladies too,
And buy your meat from me;
For three pennyworths of meat I sell
For the price of just one penny.

“I have lamb that has fed on nothing
But the pretty daisies there,
And the sweet violet and the daffodil
That grow by streams so fair.

“And I have beef from the heathery moors,
And mutton from valleys green,
And veal as white as a maiden’s brow,
With its mother’s milk, I’d say.

“So come, you lasses, and you ladies too,
Come, buy your meat from me,
For three pennyworths of meat I sell
For the price of just one penny.”

So he sang cheerfully while everyone nearby listened in amazement. When he had finished, he clattered the steel and cleaver even louder and shouted heartily, “Now, who’ll buy? Who’ll buy? I have four fixed prices. Three pennyworths of meat I sell to a fat friar or priest for sixpence, because I don’t want their business. Stout aldermen I charge threepence, for it makes no difference to me whether they buy or not. To plump housewives I sell three pennyworths of meat for one penny, because I like their business well. But to the pretty lass who has a liking for a good, trim butcher I charge nothing but one fair kiss, for I like her business best of all.”

Everyone began to stare and wonder and crowd around, laughing, for no one in Nottingham Town had ever seen such selling. When they came to buy, they found he had told the truth: a goodwife or dame got as much meat for one penny as she would pay three for anywhere else, and a widow or poor woman got hers for nothing. When a merry lass gave him a kiss, he charged not one penny for his meat, and many came to his stall, for his eyes were as blue as June skies and he laughed merrily as he gave everyone full measure. He sold his meat so fast that none of the butchers near him could sell a thing.

Then they began to talk among themselves, and some said, “This must be some thief who has stolen the cart, horse, and meat.” But others said, “No, when did you ever see a thief who gave away his goods so freely and cheerfully? This must be some spendthrift who has sold his father’s land and wants to live merrily while the money lasts.” Since these were the larger number, the others came around one by one to their way of thinking.

Then some of the butchers came to make his acquaintance. “Come, brother,” said the one who was the head of them all, “we are all of one trade, so will you come and dine with us? Today the Sheriff has invited the whole Butchers’ Guild to feast with him at the Guild Hall. There will be hearty fare and plenty to drink, and you will like that, or I am much mistaken.”

“A curse on the heart of anyone who would turn down a fellow butcher,” said jolly Robin. “And what is more, I will dine with you all, my good lads, and as fast as I can go.” Then, having sold all his meat, he closed his stall and went with them to the great Guild Hall.

The Sheriff had already arrived in state, and with him many butchers. When Robin and his companions came in, all of them laughing at some merry joke he had been telling, those near the Sheriff whispered to him, “That fellow over there is a wild one, for today he sold more meat for one penny than the rest of us could sell for three, and to any merry lass who gave him a kiss he gave meat for nothing.” Others said, “He is some spendthrift who has sold his land for silver and gold, and means to spend it all merrily.”

Then the Sheriff called Robin over, not recognizing him in his butcher’s clothes, and sat him close beside him on his right hand. He loved a rich young spendthrift, especially when he thought he could move that spendthrift’s money into his own most worshipful purse. So he made much of Robin, and laughed and talked with him more than with any of the others.

At last dinner was ready to be served, and the Sheriff told Robin to say the blessing. So Robin stood up and said, “Heaven bless us all, and bless the good meat and the good wine in this house, and may every butcher be and stay as honest as I am.”

At this everyone laughed, the Sheriff loudest of all. He said to himself, “This must be some spendthrift, and perhaps I can empty his purse of some of the money the fool tosses around so freely.” Then he said aloud to Robin, “You are a jolly young fellow, and I like you enormously,” and he slapped Robin on the shoulder.
Then Robin laughed loudly too. “Yes,” he said, “I know you love a jolly fellow. Didn’t you have jolly Robin Hood at your shooting match, and didn’t you gladly hand him a bright golden arrow to keep?”
At this the Sheriff looked grim, and so did the whole guild of butchers, so that no one laughed but Robin, though a few of them winked slyly at one another.

“Come, pour us some wine!” cried Robin. “Let’s always be merry while we can, for man is only dust, and he has just a short span to live here before the worm gets him, as our good neighbor Swanthold says. So let life be merry while it lasts, I say. Come now, don’t be down in the mouth, Sir Sheriff. Who knows, you may catch Robin Hood yet, if you drink less good wine and Malmsey, and work the fat off your belly and the dust out of your brain. Be merry, man.”

Then the Sheriff laughed again, though not as if he liked the joke, while the butchers said to one another, “By Heaven, we never saw such a mad, rollicking fellow. Still, he may well make the Sheriff angry.”

“What is this, brothers?” cried Robin. “Be merry! Don’t go counting your farthings, for by this and by that I will pay the bill myself, even if it costs two hundred pounds. So let no man pull a long face or shove his hand into his purse, for I swear that neither butcher nor Sheriff shall pay one penny for this feast.”
“Now you are a truly merry soul,” said the Sheriff, “and I’m sure you must own many a head of horned cattle and many an acre of land, to spend your money so freely.”

“Yes, I do,” said Robin, laughing loudly again. “My brothers and I have five hundred head of horned cattle and more, and we haven’t been able to sell a single one, or I would not have become a butcher. As for my land, I have never asked my steward how many acres I have.”

At this the Sheriff’s eyes twinkled, and he chuckled to himself. “Well, good youth,” he said, “if you can’t sell your cattle, perhaps I can find a man to take them off your hands. Perhaps that man might even be me, for I like a merry young fellow and would gladly help one along in life. Now, how much do you want for your horned cattle?”
“Well,” Robin replied, “at the very least they’re worth five hundred pounds.”

“No,” answered the Sheriff slowly, as if thinking it over, “I like you well, and I would gladly help you along, but five hundred pounds in cash is a good round sum, and besides, I don’t have it with me. Still, I will give you three hundred pounds for the lot, and in good hard silver and gold.”

“You old miser!” said Robin. “You know very well that so many horned cattle are worth seven hundred pounds and more, and even that is a small price for them. Yet here you are, with your gray hairs and one foot in the grave, ready to profit from the folly of a wild young man.”

At this the Sheriff gave Robin a grim look. “Come,” said Robin, “don’t look at me as if you had sour beer in your mouth, man. I will take your offer, for my brothers and I do need the money. We lead a merry life, and nobody leads a merry life on a farthing, so I will close the bargain with you. But make sure you bring a full three hundred pounds, for I don’t trust a man who drives such a hard bargain.”
“I’ll bring the cash,” the Sheriff said. “But tell me, good youth, what do they call you?”
“Men call me Robert of Locksley,” said bold Robin.

“Then, good Robert of Locksley,” said the Sheriff, “I will come today to see your horned beasts. But first my clerk will draw up a paper binding you to the sale, for you won’t get my money unless I get your cattle in return.”
Then Robin Hood laughed again. “So be it,” he said, slapping his palm into the Sheriff’s hand. “My brothers will certainly be grateful to you for your money.”
So the bargain was made. But many of the butchers murmured among themselves about the Sheriff, saying it was a shabby trick to cheat a poor spendthrift youth like that.

By the time the Sheriff mounted his horse and joined Robin Hood, the afternoon had come. Robin was standing outside the gateway of the paved court, waiting for him, for he had sold his horse and cart to a trader for two marks. Then they set out, the Sheriff riding his horse and Robin running beside him. So they left Nottingham Town and went on along the dusty highway, laughing and joking together as if they had been old friends. But all the while the Sheriff was saying to himself, “Your joke about Robin Hood will cost you dearly, my good fellow, a full four hundred pounds, you fool.” For he reckoned he would make at least that much on his bargain.

So they traveled on until they reached the edge of Sherwood Forest. There the Sheriff looked up and down and to the right and left, then grew quiet and stopped laughing. “Now,” he said, “may Heaven and its saints keep us safe today from a rogue men call Robin Hood.”
Then Robin laughed aloud. “Don’t worry,” he said, “you can set your mind at rest, for I know Robin Hood well, and I know you are in no more danger from him today than you are from me.”
At this the Sheriff eyed Robin sideways and said to himself, “I don’t like that you seem so well acquainted with this bold outlaw, and I wish I were safely out of Sherwood Forest.”

But still they went deeper into the forest shade, and the deeper they went, the quieter the Sheriff became. At last they came to a sudden bend in the road, and ahead of them a herd of dun deer went trotting across the path. Then Robin Hood moved close to the Sheriff, and pointing with his finger, he said, “These are my horned beasts, good Master Sheriff. How do you like them? Aren’t they fat and fine to look at?”
At this the Sheriff quickly reined in his horse. “Now, fellow,” he said, “I wish I were out of this forest, for I don’t like your company. Go your own way, good friend, and let me go mine.”

But Robin only laughed and caught hold of the Sheriff’s bridle. “No,” he cried, “stay a while, for I want you to meet my brothers, who own these fine horned beasts along with me.” With that he put his bugle to his mouth and blew three merry notes, and soon up the path came bounding a hundred good, sturdy yeomen with Little John at their head.
“What do you want, good master?” said Little John.

“Why, can’t you see?” Robin answered. “I’ve brought splendid company to feast with us today! Shame on you! Don’t you recognize our good and worshipful master, the Sheriff of Nottingham? Hold his bridle, Little John, for he does us the honor of dining with us today.”

Then all of them took off their hats humbly, without smiling or seeming to joke, while Little John took the bridle and led the horse still deeper into the forest. All marched in order, with Robin Hood walking beside the Sheriff, hat in hand.

All this time the Sheriff said not a word, but only looked around him like a man suddenly woken from sleep. When he found himself going into the very depths of Sherwood, his heart sank, for he thought, “Surely they will take my three hundred pounds, even if they don’t take my life itself, for I have plotted against their lives more than once.” But everyone seemed humble and meek, and not a word was said of danger to his life or his money.

So at last they came to the part of Sherwood Forest where a noble oak spread its branches wide. Beneath it was a seat made all of moss, and there Robin sat down, placing the Sheriff at his right hand. “Now get busy, all my merry men,” he said, “and bring out the best we have, both food and wine, for his worship the Sheriff feasted me in Nottingham Guild Hall today, and I don’t want him to go back hungry.”
Nobody had mentioned the Sheriff’s money all this while, so he started to feel hopeful. “Perhaps,” he told himself, “Robin Hood has forgotten the whole thing.”

Meanwhile, off in the forest, bright fires crackled, and savory smells of sweetly roasting venison and fat capons filled the glade, while brown pasties warmed beside the blaze. And Robin Hood entertained the Sheriff in truly royal style. First, several pairs of men came forward to fight with quarterstaffs. They were so skilled at the game, and struck and parried so quickly, that the Sheriff, who loved to watch any lively sport of the kind, clapped his hands, forgetting where he was, and shouted, “Well struck! Well struck, you fellow with the black beard!” He had no idea that the man he was cheering was the Tinker who had tried to serve his warrant on Robin Hood.

Then several yeomen came forward and spread cloths on the green grass and laid out a royal feast, while others tapped barrels of wine and Malmsey and good strong ale, and set them out in jars on the cloth with drinking horns all around. Then everyone sat down and feasted and drank merrily together until the sun was low and the half-moon shone with a pale light between the leaves of the trees overhead.

Then the Sheriff got up and said, “I thank you all, good yeomen, for the merry entertainment you have given me today. You have treated me most courteously, which shows that you have great respect for our glorious King and for his deputy in brave Nottinghamshire. But the shadows are growing long, and I must be off before dark, or I may lose my way in the forest.”
Then Robin Hood and all his merry men stood up too, and Robin said to the Sheriff, “If you must go, worshipful sir, then go you must. But you have forgotten one thing.”
“No, I forgot nothing,” said the Sheriff, though all the same his heart sank.
“But I say you have forgotten something,” said Robin. “We keep a merry inn here in the greenwood, but whoever becomes our guest must pay his bill.”

Then the Sheriff gave a laugh, but it rang hollow. “Well, jolly lads,” he said, “we’ve had a merry time together today. Even if you hadn’t asked, I’d have gladly given you twenty pounds for such pleasant entertainment.”

“No,” said Robin seriously, “it would be unworthy of us to treat Your Worship so meanly. On my faith, Sir Sheriff, I would be ashamed to show my face if I did not charge the King’s deputy three hundred pounds. Isn’t that so, all my merry men?”
Then “Aye!” cried all of them in a loud voice.
“Three hundred devils!” the Sheriff roared. “You think that miserable feast of yours was worth three pounds, never mind three hundred?”

“Now,” said Robin gravely, “don’t speak so bluntly, Your Worship. I do love you for the fine feast you gave me today in merry Nottingham Town, but some men here don’t love you quite so much. If you look down the cloth you will see Will Stutely, who thinks little of you. Then there are two other sturdy fellows here whom you don’t know, who were wounded in a brawl near Nottingham Town some time ago, and you know when. One of them was badly hurt in the arm, though he has got the use of it back. Good Sheriff, take my advice: pay your bill without more fuss, or it may go badly for you.”

While Robin spoke, the Sheriff’s ruddy cheeks went pale. He said nothing more, but stared at the ground and bit his lower lip. Then slowly he pulled out his fat purse and flung it on the cloth before him.
“Now take the purse, Little John,” said Robin Hood, “and see that the bill is paid in full. We would never doubt our Sheriff, but he might not like it if he found out he hadn’t paid his whole share.”

Little John counted out the money, and the bag held three hundred pounds in silver and gold, exactly. To the Sheriff, though, each ring of the shining coins felt like a drop of blood drawn from his veins. When he saw it all piled up in a heap, filling a wooden platter, he turned away without a word and climbed back onto his horse.
“We have never had so worshipful a guest before!” said Robin. “And since the day is growing late, I will send one of my young men to guide you out of the depths of the forest.”
“Heaven forbid!” the Sheriff cried in haste. “I can find my own way, good man. I need no help.”

“Then I will set you on the right track myself,” said Robin, and taking the Sheriff’s horse by the bridle, he led him onto the main forest path. Before letting him go, he said, “Now, farewell, good Sheriff, and the next time you think of robbing some poor spendthrift, remember your feast in Sherwood Forest. ‘Never buy a horse, good friend, without first looking in its mouth,’ as our good old Swanthold says. And so, once more, farewell.” Then he slapped the horse on the back, and off went nag and Sheriff through the forest glades.

Then the Sheriff bitterly regretted the day he first meddled with Robin Hood, for everyone laughed at him, and folk all over the country sang many ballads about how the Sheriff went out to shear and came home shorn to the very quick. For that is how men sometimes outsmart themselves through greed and trickery.

chapters.title: Little John Goes to Nottingham Fair
paragraphs: Spring had gone by since the Sheriff’s feast in Sherwood, and summer with it, and now the mellow month of October was here. The air was cool and crisp. The harvests were brought in, the young birds had all their feathers, the hops were picked, and the apples were ripe. Time had smoothed things over, and men no longer spoke of the horned beasts the Sheriff had wanted to buy. Still, he was sore about it, and he could not stand to hear Robin Hood’s name spoken in his presence.

October brought the time for the great Fair, held every five years in Nottingham Town, and people came to it from all over the country, near and far. Archery was always the main sport of the day, since the yeomen of Nottinghamshire were the finest hands with a longbow in all of merry England. But this year the Sheriff put off announcing the Fair for a long while, afraid that Robin Hood and his band might turn up. For a time he was more than half inclined not to hold it at all, but on second thought he knew that people would laugh at him and tell one another he was scared of Robin Hood, so he dropped the idea. In the end he made up his mind to offer a prize that Robin’s men would not bother to shoot for. On these occasions the prize had always been ten marks or a barrel of ale, so this year he announced that the best bowman would win two fat steers.

When Robin Hood heard what the Sheriff had announced, he was annoyed. “A curse on this Sheriff,” he said, “for offering a prize that nobody but shepherd boys will want to shoot for! Nothing would have pleased me more than another go at merry Nottingham Town, but if I won this prize it would bring me neither pleasure nor profit.”

Then Little John spoke up. “No, but listen, good master,” he said. “Just today Will Stutely, young David of Doncaster, and I were at the Sign of the Blue Boar, and there we heard all the news of this merry Fair. We also heard that the Sheriff has offered this prize so that we men of Sherwood won’t care to come. So, good master, if you’re willing, I would gladly go and try to win even this poor prize among the sturdy yeomen who will shoot at Nottingham Town.”

“No, Little John,” said Robin. “You are a sound, sturdy fellow, but you lack the cunning that good Stutely has, and I would not have harm come to you for all of Nottinghamshire. Still, if you want to go, wear a disguise, in case anyone there might recognize you.”

“Very well, good master,” said Little John. “The only disguise I want is a good suit of scarlet in place of this Lincoln green. I will pull the hood of my jacket over my head to hide my brown hair and beard, and then, I trust, no one will know me.”

“I am very much against it,” said Robin Hood, “but if you truly wish it, then go. Only conduct yourself properly, Little John, for you are my own right-hand man and I could hardly bear to see you harmed.”
Little John put on his scarlet outfit from head to foot and headed for the Nottingham Fair.

Those Fair days at Nottingham were merry indeed. On the green before the great town gate, rows of booths stood side by side with tents of many-colored canvas, hung with streamers and garlands of flowers, and people came from all over the countryside, gentlefolk and common folk alike. In some booths there was dancing to lively music, in others ale and beer were flowing, and in others sweet cakes and barley sugar were sold. There was entertainment outside the booths too: here a minstrel sang ballads of olden times and played an accompaniment on the harp, and there wrestlers struggled with one another inside a ring of sawdust. But the biggest crowd of all gathered around a raised platform where sturdy fellows were playing at quarterstaff.

So Little John came to the Fair. His hose and jerkin were all scarlet, and so was his hooded cap, which had a scarlet feather stuck in the side. A stout bow of yew was slung over his shoulders, and a quiver of good round arrows hung across his back. Many people turned to look after such a big, tall fellow, for his shoulders were a hand’s breadth broader than anyone else’s there, and he stood a full head taller than all the other men. The girls glanced at him sideways, too, thinking they had never seen a more vigorous young man.

First he went to the booth where strong ale was sold, and standing high on a bench, he called to everyone nearby to come and drink with him. “Hey, good lads!” he cried. “Who will drink ale with a hearty yeoman? Come, all of you! Come, all! Let’s be merry, for the day is fine and the ale is sharp. Come here, good yeoman, and you, and you, for not one of you will pay a farthing. No, turn this way, you sturdy beggar, and you jolly tinker, for everyone shall be merry with me.”

So he shouted, and everyone crowded around, laughing, while the brown ale flowed. They called Little John a fine fellow, and each swore he loved him like his own brother; for when a man is entertained and has nothing to pay, he loves whoever provides it.

Then he strolled over to the platform where they were playing at cudgels, for he loved a bout at quarterstaff as much as he loved food and drink. And here an adventure happened that was sung in ballads all across the Midlands for many a day.

There was one fellow there who had been cracking the head of everyone who tossed a cap into the ring. This was Eric o’ Lincoln, a man of great fame, whose name had been sung in ballads all over the countryside. When Little John reached the stand, he found nobody fighting, only bold Eric walking up and down the platform, swinging his staff and shouting at the top of his voice, “Now, who will come and strike a blow for the girl he loves best, against a good Lincolnshire yeoman? Well, lads? Step up! Step up! Either the girls around here aren’t pretty, or the blood of Nottingham’s young men runs sluggish and cold. Lincoln against Nottingham, I say! For no one has set foot on these boards today whom we in Lincoln would call a cudgel player.”
At this, one man would nudge another with his elbow, saying, “Go on, Ned!” or “Go on, Thomas!” but no lad wanted to get his head cracked for nothing.

Soon Eric spotted Little John standing among the others, a head and shoulders above them all, and he called out to him loudly, “Hello there, you long-legged fellow in scarlet! Your shoulders are broad and your head is thick. Isn’t your girl pretty enough for you to pick up a cudgel for her sake? Truly, I think Nottingham men turn to nothing but bone and sinew, for they have neither heart nor courage! Now, you great lout, won’t you twirl a staff for Nottingham?”

“Yes,” said Little John, “if only I had my own good staff here, it would please me enormously to crack your rascal’s head, you cheeky braggart! I think it would be better for you if your cockscomb were clipped!” He spoke slowly at first, for he was slow to move, but his anger gathered speed like a great stone rolling down a hill, so that by the end he was full of fury.

Then Eric o’ Lincoln laughed out loud. “Well spoken for a man who is afraid to meet me fairly, man to man,” he said. “You’re cheeky yourself, and if you set foot on these boards, I’ll make that cheeky tongue of yours rattle in your teeth!”

“Now,” said Little John, “is there no man here who will lend me a good sturdy staff, so I can test the mettle of that fellow over there?” At this, ten men held out their staves to him, and he took the stoutest and heaviest of them all. Then, looking the cudgel up and down, he said, “Now, all I have in my hand is a splinter of wood, a barley straw, you might say, but I suppose it will have to do, so here goes.” With that he tossed the cudgel onto the stand and, leaping lightly up after it, snatched it up again.

Then each man stood in his place and sized up the other with fierce looks, until the man in charge of the sport cried, “Play!” At this they stepped forward, each gripping his staff tightly in the middle. And those standing around saw the stoutest game of quarterstaff that Nottingham Town had ever witnessed. At first Eric o’ Lincoln thought he would gain an easy advantage, and he came forward as if to say, “Watch, good people, how I carve up this young rooster in no time!” But he soon found it was not going to be quick at all. He struck cleverly and with great skill at fencing, but he had met his match in Little John. Once, twice, three times he struck, and three times Little John turned the blows aside, to the left and to the right. Then, quickly and with a neat backhanded blow, he rapped Eric under his guard so smartly that it made his head ring. Eric stepped back to gather his wits, while a great shout went up and everyone was glad that Nottingham had cracked Lincoln’s crown; and so the first bout of the game ended.

Soon the man in charge cried “Play!” again, and they came together once more. But now Eric played carefully, for he saw that his opponent was a man of good mettle, and he had no pleasant memory of the blow he had taken. So in this bout neither Little John nor the Lincoln man landed a stroke inside the other’s guard. After a while they parted again, and that was the second bout.

Then for the third time they came together, and at first Eric tried to be careful, as he had been before. But growing furious at being so thwarted, he lost his head and began to rain down blows so fiercely and so fast that they rattled like hail on a lean-to roof; yet in spite of it all, he did not get inside Little John’s guard. At last Little John saw his chance and took it cleverly. Once more, with a quick blow, he rapped Eric on the side of the head, and before Eric could recover, Little John slid his right hand down to meet his left and, with a swinging blow, struck the other man so hard on the crown that he fell flat as though he would never move again.

The crowd roared so loudly that people came running from every side to find out what the fuss was about. Little John hopped down from the stand and returned the staff to its owner. That was how the famous match between Little John and the renowned Eric o’ Lincoln came to an end.

But now the time had come for those who were to shoot with the longbow to take their places, and the people began to flock to the butts where the shooting would be. Near the target, in a good spot, the Sheriff sat on a raised platform with many gentlefolk around him. When the archers had taken their places, the herald stepped forward and announced the rules of the contest: each man would shoot three shots, and the prize of two fat steers would go to whoever shot best. A score of fine marksmen were gathered there, among them some of the keenest hands with a longbow in Lincolnshire and Nottinghamshire, and among them all Little John stood taller than the rest. “Who is that stranger dressed all in scarlet?” some asked, and others answered, “He’s the one who just now so soundly cracked the head of Eric o’ Lincoln.” So the people talked among themselves, until at last it reached even the Sheriff’s ears.

And now each man stepped forward and shot in turn. Though every one of them shot well, Little John was the best of all, for three times he hit the bull’s-eye, and the one other time he missed the center by only the length of a barleycorn. “Hurrah for the tall archer!” shouted the crowd, and some of them shouted, “Hurrah for Reynold Greenleaf!” for that was the name Little John had given himself that day.

Then the Sheriff came down from his raised seat and walked over to where the archers stood, and everyone who saw him coming took off his cap. He looked keenly at Little John but did not recognize him, though after a while he said, “Well, good fellow, I think there is something about your face that I have seen before.”
“Maybe so,” said Little John, “for I have often seen Your Worship.” And as he spoke, he looked steadily into the Sheriff’s eyes, so that the Sheriff did not suspect who he was.
“You are a fine fellow, my friend,” said the Sheriff, “and I hear you have upheld the skill of Nottinghamshire against that of Lincoln today. What is your name, good fellow?”

“People call me Reynold Greenleaf, Your Worship,” answered Little John. The old ballad that tells this story adds, “And a green leaf he truly was, though the Sheriff had no idea what sort of tree he came from.”

“Now, Reynold Greenleaf,” said the Sheriff, “you are the finest hand with a longbow that my eyes have ever seen, next to that wicked rogue Robin Hood, from whose tricks Heaven protect me! Will you join my service, good fellow? You will be paid very well: you shall have three suits of clothes a year, good food, and as much ale as you can drink; and besides this, I will pay you forty marks each Michaelmas.”
“Then here I stand, a free man, and I will gladly enter your household,” said Little John, for he thought he might find some merry joke to play if he joined the Sheriff’s service.

“You have fairly won the fat steers,” said the Sheriff, “and I will add to them a barrel of good March beer, for the joy of having got such a man. For I’m sure you shoot as fine an arrow as Robin Hood himself.”

“Then,” said Little John, “for the joy of having got myself into your service, I will give the fat steers and the brown ale to all these good folk, to make them merry.” At this a great shout went up, and many threw their caps in the air, delighted with the gift.

Some people built big fires and roasted the steers, while others broke open the barrel of ale, and everyone had a merry time of it. When they had eaten and drunk their fill, and the day was fading and the great moon rose, red and round, above the spires and towers of Nottingham Town, they joined hands and danced around the fires to bagpipes and harps. But long before the merrymaking started, the Sheriff and his new servant Reynold Greenleaf had gone up to Nottingham Castle.

chapters.title: How Little John Lived at the Sheriff’s
paragraphs: So Little John entered the Sheriff’s service and found the life he led there easy enough, for the Sheriff made him his right-hand man and thought highly of him. He sat near the Sheriff at meals and ran beside his horse when the Sheriff went hunting. Between a little hunting and hawking, eating rich dishes, drinking good sack, and sleeping late in the mornings, he grew as fat as a stall-fed ox. Things floated along easily like this with the tide, until one day, when the Sheriff went hunting, something happened that broke the smooth surface of things.

That morning the Sheriff rode out with many of his men to meet some noble lords and go hunting. He looked everywhere for his good man, Reynold Greenleaf, and was annoyed not to find him, because he wanted to show off Little John’s skill to his fine friends. As for Little John, he lay in bed snoring loudly until the sun stood high in the sky. At last he opened his eyes and looked around, but he made no move to get up. The sun shone brightly in at the window, and the air was sweet with the scent of the honeysuckle that hung in sprays along the outer wall, for the cold winter was over and spring had come again. Little John lay still, thinking how lovely everything was on this fair morning. Just then he heard a bugle, faint and far away, sounding thin and clear. The sound was small, but it was like a pebble dropped into a still, glassy pool: it broke the smooth surface of his thoughts, and his whole soul was stirred up. His spirit seemed to wake from its laziness, and his memory brought back all the merry life of the greenwood—how the birds were singing happily there this bright morning, and how his dear friends were feasting and making merry, or perhaps talking about him in serious tones. For he had first entered the Sheriff’s service as a joke; but the hearth was warm in winter, and the food was plentiful, so he had stayed, putting off his return to Sherwood from one day to the next, until six long months had passed. Now, though, he thought of his good master and of Will Stutely, whom he loved better than anyone in the world, and of young David of Doncaster, whom he had trained so well in all manly sports. A great and bitter longing for them all came over his heart, until his eyes filled with tears. Then he said aloud, “Here I am growing fat like an ox in a stall, and all my manliness is draining away while I turn into a lazy fool. But I will rouse myself and go back to my own dear friends, and I will never leave them again as long as I live.” With that he leaped out of bed, for he hated his own laziness now.

When he came downstairs, he saw the Steward standing near the pantry door—a big, fat man with a huge bunch of keys hanging from his belt. Little John said, “Hey, Master Steward, I’m a hungry man. I’ve had nothing all this blessed morning. So give me something to eat.”

The Steward gave him a grim look and rattled the keys at his belt, for he hated Little John because the Sheriff had taken a liking to him. “So, Master Reynold Greenleaf, you’re hungry, are you?” he said. “But my fine young fellow, if you live long enough, you’ll find that the man who sleeps too much for the sake of a lazy head goes about with an empty stomach. What does the old saying tell us, Master Greenleaf? Isn’t it ‘The late bird gets poor pickings’?”

“Now, you great bag of lard!” cried Little John. “I’m not asking you for a fool’s wisdom, but for bread and meat. Who are you, to refuse me food? By Saint Dunstan, you had better tell me where my breakfast is, if you want to keep your bones unbroken!”
“Master Fireblaze, your breakfast is in the pantry,” the Steward replied.
“Then fetch it here!” cried Little John, who was getting angry by now.
“Go and fetch it yourself,” said the Steward. “Am I your slave, to run and carry things for you?”
“I say, you go and bring it to me!”
“And I say, you go and fetch it for yourself!”

“Yes, indeed, that I will, and quickly!” said Little John in a rage. With that he strode to the pantry and tried the door, but found it locked, at which the Steward laughed and rattled his keys. Then Little John’s anger boiled over. He raised his clenched fist and struck the pantry door, knocking out three panels and making a hole so large that he could easily stoop and walk through it.

When the Steward saw what had been done, he went mad with rage. As Little John stooped to look into the pantry, the Steward grabbed him from behind by the back of the neck, pinching him hard and beating him about the head with his keys until the yeoman’s ears rang. At this, Little John turned on the Steward and gave him such a blow that the fat man fell to the floor and lay there as if he would never move again. “There,” said Little John, “think well of that blow, and never keep a good breakfast from a hungry man again.”

With that he crept into the pantry and looked around for something to ease his hunger. He saw a great venison pie and two roast capons, and beside them a platter of plovers’ eggs; there was also a flask of sack and another of canary wine—a sweet sight to a hungry man. He took these down from the shelves, set them on a sideboard, and got ready to enjoy himself.

Now the Cook, in the kitchen across the courtyard, had heard the loud argument between Little John and the Steward, and the blow Little John had struck. So he came running across the courtyard and up the stairs to the Steward’s pantry, carrying the spit with the roast still on it. Meanwhile the Steward had pulled himself together and got to his feet. When the Cook arrived, he found the Steward glaring through the broken door at Little John, who was getting ready for a fine meal, the way one dog glares at another that has a bone. When the Steward saw the Cook, he went over to him and put one arm over his shoulder, for the Cook was a tall, stout man. “Alas, dear friend!” he said. “Do you see what that wretched rascal Reynold Greenleaf has done? He has broken into our master’s stores and hit me on the ear so hard that I thought I was dead. Good Cook, I am very fond of you, and you shall have a good pottle of our master’s best wine every day, for you are an old and faithful servant. And, good Cook, I have ten shillings that I mean to give you as a present. But don’t you hate to see a low upstart like this Reynold Greenleaf carrying on so boldly?”

“Yes, indeed I do,” said the Cook boldly, for he liked the Steward because of his talk about the wine and the ten shillings. “Go straight to your room, and I will bring this rascal out by his ears.” With that he put down his spit and drew the sword that hung at his side, and the Steward left as fast as he could, for he hated the sight of bare steel.
Then the Cook walked straight to the broken pantry door, and through it he saw Little John tucking a napkin under his chin and getting ready to enjoy himself.
“Why, what is this, Reynold Greenleaf?” said the Cook. “You are no better than a thief, I’d say. Come straight out here, man, or I will carve you the way I would carve a suckling pig.”

“No, good Cook, mind your manners, or else I will come out and give you what you deserve. Most of the time I’m as gentle as a yearling lamb, but when someone comes between me and my meal, I’m a raging lion, you might say.”
“Lion or no lion,” said the brave Cook, “come straight out, or else you’re a coward as well as a thieving rascal.”
“Ha!” cried Little John. “Nobody has ever called me a coward, so look to yourself, good Cook, for I’m coming out right now, the roaring lion I just told you about.”

Then he, too, drew his sword and came out of the pantry. They took their positions and came slowly together with grim and angry looks, but suddenly Little John lowered his point. “Hold on, good Cook!” he said. “It strikes me that it would be wrong of us to fight with good food sitting so close by, and such a feast as would suit two sturdy fellows like us. Truly, good friend, I think we should enjoy this fine feast before we fight. What do you say, jolly Cook?”

At this speech the Cook looked Little John up and down, scratching his head in doubt, for he loved good feasting. At last he drew a long breath and said to Little John, “Well, good friend, I like your plan very much. So, my fine lad, I say let’s feast, and gladly, for one of us may be having supper in Paradise before nightfall.”

So each pushed his sword back into its sheath and went into the pantry. When they had sat down, Little John drew his dagger and stuck it into the pie. “A hungry man must be fed,” he said, “so, my sweet friend, I’ll help myself without asking.” But the Cook was not far behind, for right away his hands, too, were deep in the fine pie. After this neither of them said another word, but put their teeth to better use. Yet though neither spoke, they looked at each other, and each thought to himself that he had never seen a sturdier fellow than the one across the table.

At last, after a long while, the Cook drew a deep, full breath, as if in great regret, and wiped his hands on the napkin, for he could eat no more. Little John, too, had had enough, for he pushed the pie aside as if to say, “I don’t want you near me anymore, good friend.” Then he picked up the pottle of sack and said, “Now, good fellow, I swear by all that is bright that you are the stoutest eating companion I ever had. Look! I drink your health.” With that he put the flask to his lips and rolled his eyes upward while the good wine poured down his throat. Then he passed the pottle to the Cook, who also said, “Look, I drink your health, sweet fellow!” And he was no slower at drinking than he had been at eating.
“Now,” said Little John, “you have a round, sweet voice, jolly lad. I don’t doubt you can sing a ballad very merrily. Can you not?”
“Well, I’ve belted out a tune or two in my time,” said the Cook, “but I won’t sing by myself.”
“No, indeed,” said Little John, “that would be poor manners. Start up your tune, and afterward I will sing one to match it, if I can.”
“So be it, my fine lad,” said the Cook. “And have you ever heard the song of the Deserted Shepherdess?”
“No, I don’t know it,” answered Little John, “but sing it, and let me hear.”
Then the Cook took another swallow from the pottle, cleared his throat, and sang very sweetly:
The song of the deserted shepherdess

“_In Lenten time, when leaves grow green,
And pretty birds begin to mate,
When lark and thrush sing, I believe,
And stockdove coos both soon and late,
Fair Phillis sat beside a stone,
And this I heard her make her moan:
‘O willow, willow, willow, willow!
I’ll take from you a branch so fair
And twine a wreath to deck my hair.

“‘The thrush has gone and found a mate,
The robin, too, and so the dove;
My Robin has deserted me,
And left me for another love.
So here, beside the brook, alone,
I sit me down and make my moan.
O willow, willow, willow, willow!
I’ll take from you a branch so fair
And twine a wreath to deck my hair.’

“But never came a herring from the sea
But there was one as good within the tide;
Young Corydon came over the meadow lea,
And sat himself by Phillis’s side.
So soon she changed her tone,
And began to cease her moan,
‘O willow, willow, willow, willow!
You may keep your garlands fair,
I do not want them for my hair_.’”
“Now, on my word,” cried Little John, “that is a very good song, and there is truth in it, too.”
“I’m glad you like it, sweet lad,” said the Cook. “Now sing one yourself, for a man should never make merry alone, or sing with no one listening.”

“Then I will sing you a song of a good knight of Arthur’s court, and how he cured his heart’s wound without running onto the dart again, as your Phillis did; for I’d say she only cured one sting by giving herself another. So listen while I sing:”
The good knight and his love

“_When Arthur was king and ruled this land,
A good king he was, they say,
And he had of stout knights a band
Of merry company.

“Among them all, both great and small,
A good strong knight was there,
A lusty youth, and tall as well,
Who loved a lady fair.

“But she would have nothing to do with him,
But turned her face away;
So off he went to a far country,
And left that lady gay.

“Alone there in that land he grieved,
He sobbed and sighed all day,
And wept enough to move a rock,
And nearly pined away.

“But still his heart did feel the smart,
And bitter grief and woe,
And his pain grew sharper day by day
As his body grew thin and low.

“Then he went back where good sack was found
And merry company,
And soon he ceased to cry ‘Alack!’
When glad and gay was he.

“From which I hold, and feel quite bold
To say, and I believe,
That if the belly does not go cold
The heart will cease to grieve_.”
“By my word,” cried the Cook, banging the pottle on the sideboard, “I like that song enormously, and its meaning, too, which sits inside it like a sweet kernel in a hazelnut.”
“Now you are a man of sharp opinions,” said Little John, “and I love you truly, as if you were my brother.”
“And I love you, too. But the day is wearing on, and I have my cooking to do before our master comes home; so let’s go and settle this grand fight we have on our hands.”

“Yes indeed,” said Little John, “and right away. I have never been slower at fighting than at eating and drinking. So come out into the passageway, where there is good room to swing a sword, and I will do my best to serve you.”

Then they both stepped out into the broad passage that led to the Steward’s pantry. Each man drew his sword again and, without more ado, fell on the other as though he meant to cut his fellow limb from limb. Their swords clashed together with a great din, and sparks flew from every blow in showers. So they fought up and down the hall for an hour and more, and neither landed a blow on the other, though both tried their best, for both were skillful at fencing, and so all their labor came to nothing. Every now and then they stopped to rest, panting; then, once they had caught their breath, they went at it again more fiercely than before. At last Little John cried out, “Hold, good Cook!” and each of them leaned on his sword, panting.
“Now I’ll swear this,” said Little John, “you are the very best swordsman my eyes ever saw. Truly, I thought I would have carved you long ago.”
“And I thought to do the same to you,” said the Cook, “but somehow I have missed the mark.”
“Now I have been wondering,” said Little John, “what we are fighting for; and the truth is, I don’t rightly know.”
“Why, neither do I,” said the Cook. “I have no love for that pot-bellied Steward, but I thought we had agreed to fight each other and that it had to be done.”

“Listen,” said Little John, “it seems to me that instead of trying to cut each other’s throats, we would do better to be good friends. What do you say, jolly Cook? Will you come with me to Sherwood Forest and join Robin Hood’s band? You will lead a merry life in the woods, with a hundred and forty good companions, and I am one of them. Every year you will get three suits of Lincoln green, and forty marks in wages.”

“Why, you are a man after my own heart!” the Cook cried warmly. “Now that you mention it, that is exactly the job for me. I will go with you, and gladly. Shake my hand, friend, and from this moment I am your companion. What is your name, lad?”
“Men call me Little John, my good fellow.”

“What? You are really Little John, Robin Hood’s own right-hand man? I have heard of you many a time, but I never hoped to see you with my own eyes. So you truly are the famous Little John!” And the Cook stood amazed, staring at his companion with wide eyes.

“I am Little John indeed, and today I will bring Robin Hood a sturdy fellow to join his merry band. But before we go, my friend, it seems a great pity to me that, after eating so much of the Sheriff’s food, we shouldn’t also carry some of his silver plate off to Robin Hood, as a gift from his worship.”

“Yes, by Our Lady, it is a pity,” said the Cook. So they began searching the house and took as much silver as they could lay their hands on, stuffing it into a bag. When the sack was full, they set out for Sherwood Forest.

They plunged into the woods and came at last to the greenwood tree, where they found Robin Hood and sixty of his merry men lying on the fresh green grass. When Robin and his men saw who was coming, they jumped to their feet. “Welcome!” cried Robin Hood. “Welcome, Little John! It has been a long time since we heard from you, though we all knew you had joined the Sheriff’s service. How have you fared all these long days?”

“I have lived merrily at the Lord Sheriff’s,” answered Little John, “and I have come straight from there. Look, good master! I have brought you his cook, and even his silver plate.” Then he told Robin Hood and the merry men gathered there everything that had happened to him since he left them to go to the Fair at Nottingham Town. They all roared with laughter, except Robin Hood, who looked serious.

“No, Little John,” he said, “you are a brave lad and a loyal fellow. I am glad you have come back to us, and with such a good companion as the Cook, whom we all welcome to Sherwood. But I do not like it so well that you stole the Sheriff’s plate like some petty thief. We have punished the Sheriff already, and he lost three hundred pounds, because he tried to rob another man. But he has done nothing to deserve having his household plate stolen from him.”

Little John was annoyed at this, but he tried to laugh it off with a joke. “Well, good master,” he said, “if you think the Sheriff didn’t give us the plate, I will fetch him, and he can tell us with his own lips that he gives it all to us.” With that he jumped up and was gone before Robin could call him back.

Little John ran a full five miles until he found the Sheriff of Nottingham and a cheerful company hunting near the forest. When he reached the Sheriff, he took off his cap and bent his knee. “God save you, good master,” he said.
“Why, Reynold Greenleaf!” cried the Sheriff. “Where have you come from, and where have you been?”

“I have been in the forest,” answered Little John, speaking in wonder, “and there I saw a sight like nothing anyone has ever seen! I saw a young stag dressed in green from head to toe, and around him was a herd of sixty deer, all green from head to foot as well. But I didn’t dare shoot, good master, for fear they would kill me.”
“Why, what is this, Reynold Greenleaf?” cried the Sheriff. “Are you dreaming, or are you mad, to bring me a tale like that?”

“No, I am not dreaming and I am not mad,” said Little John, “and if you will come with me, I will show you this fine sight, for I saw it with my own eyes. But you must come alone, good master, or the others will frighten the deer and they will get away.”
The whole party then rode on, with Little John guiding them down into the forest.
“Now, good master,” he said at last, “we are close to where I saw the herd.”

Then the Sheriff got down from his horse and told the others to wait until he came back. Little John led him on through a thick patch of brush until they suddenly came out into a wide open glade. At the far end of it Robin Hood sat in the shade of the great oak tree, with his merry men all around him. “Look, good Master Sheriff,” said Little John, “there is the stag I told you about.”
At this the Sheriff turned to Little John and said bitterly, “A while ago I thought I remembered your face, but now I know you. Curse you, Little John, for you have betrayed me today.”
Meanwhile Robin Hood had come over to them. “Welcome, Master Sheriff,” he said. “Have you come today to share another feast with me?”
“No, Heaven forbid!” said the Sheriff, in deadly earnest. “I want no feast, and I am not hungry today.”

“Even so,” said Robin, “if you are not hungry, perhaps you are thirsty, and I know you will take a cup of sack with me. But I am sorry you won’t feast with me, because you could have food just to your liking. There stands your cook.”
Then, willing or not, the Sheriff was led by Robin to the familiar seat under the greenwood tree.
“Hey, lads!” cried Robin. “Fill our good friend the Sheriff a cup of sack, right to the brim, and bring it here, for he is faint and tired.”

One of the band then stepped up and handed the Sheriff a cup of sack with a deep bow. But the Sheriff couldn’t bring himself to drink, because the cup was one of his own silver flagons, and it sat on one of his own silver plates.
“Well now,” said Robin, “don’t you like our new silver service? We got a whole bag of it today.” And he held up the sack of silver that Little John and the Cook had brought with them.

The Sheriff’s heart was bitter inside him, but he did not dare say a word and only stared at the ground. Robin looked hard at him for a while before he spoke again. Then he said, “Now, Master Sheriff, the last time you came to Sherwood Forest, you came to rob a poor spendthrift, and you were robbed yourself. This time you have come meaning no harm, and I do not know that you have robbed anyone. I take my share from fat priests and lordly squires, to help the people they rob and to lift up the people they push down. But I do not know that you have any tenants of your own whom you have wronged. So take back what is yours, and I will not take from you today so much as one farthing. Come with me, and I will lead you out of the forest, back to your own party.”

Then he slung the bag over his shoulder and turned away, and the Sheriff followed, too bewildered to speak. They walked on until they were within a furlong of the place where the Sheriff’s companions were waiting for him. Then Robin Hood gave the sack of silver back to the Sheriff. “Take back what is yours,” he said, “and listen to me, good Sheriff, for I give you a piece of advice along with it. Test your servants well before you hire them so quickly again.” Then he turned and left the Sheriff standing there, stunned, with the sack in his hands.

The company waiting for the Sheriff were amazed to see him come out of the forest with a heavy sack on his shoulders. They questioned him, but he never said a word and acted like a man walking in a dream. Silently he laid the bag across his horse’s back, mounted, and rode away, with all of them following. All the while his head was in a great turmoil, with thoughts tumbling one over another. And so ends the merry tale of Little John and how he entered the Sheriff’s service.

chapters.title: Little John and the Tanner of Blyth
paragraphs: One fine day, not long after Little John had left the Sheriff’s house and come back to the merry greenwood with his worship’s cook, as has just been told, Robin Hood and a few chosen fellows of his band lay on the soft turf beneath the greenwood tree where they lived. The day was warm and sultry. Most of the band were scattered through the forest on one errand or another, but these few sturdy fellows lay lazily in the shade of the tree in the soft afternoon, trading jokes and telling merry stories, with plenty of laughter and fun.

The air was heavy with the sharp fragrance of hawthorn blossom, and the leafy shadows of the woods beyond rang with the sweet singing of birds, the thrush, the cuckoo, and the wood pigeon. Mingled with the birdsong was the cool sound of a brook that came bubbling out of the shady forest and ran, tumbling among its rough gray stones, across the sunlit open glade in front of the meeting tree. It was a fine sight, those ten tall, strong yeomen, all dressed in Lincoln green, lying under the wide-spreading branches of the great oak, where the sunlight trembled through the quivering leaves and fell in dancing patches on the grass.
Suddenly Robin Hood slapped his knee.

“By Saint Dunstan,” he said, “I had almost forgotten that quarter day is coming fast, and we have no cloth of Lincoln green in all our store. We must see to it, and quickly. Come, get ready, Little John! Stir those lazy bones of yours, for you must go straight to our good friend the draper, Hugh Longshanks of Ancaster. Tell him to send us four hundred yards of fine Lincoln green cloth right away. Maybe the journey will work off some of the fat you put on from lazy living at our dear Sheriff’s.”

“No,” muttered Little John (for he had heard so much about this that he was touchy on the subject), “no, it may be true that I have more flesh on my bones than I once had. But flesh or no flesh, I am sure I could still hold my place and footing on a narrow bridge against any yeoman in Sherwood, or in Nottinghamshire for that matter, even if he had no more fat on his bones than you have, good master.”

This answer set everyone roaring with laughter, and all eyes turned to Robin Hood, because they all knew Little John meant the fight he once had with their master, the fight that first brought the two of them together.

“No,” said Robin Hood, laughing louder than anyone. “Heaven forbid that I should doubt you, for I want no taste of your staff myself, Little John. I must admit that there are men in my band who can handle a seven-foot staff better than I can. Yet no man in all Nottinghamshire can draw a gray goose shaft as I do. Still, a trip to Ancaster may do you good, so go as I tell you. You had better go this very evening, because since you stayed at the Sheriff’s, many people know your face, and if you go in broad daylight you may get yourself into trouble with some of his worship’s men-at-arms. Wait here until I bring you money to pay our good Hugh. I am sure he has no better customers in all Nottinghamshire than we are.” With that, Robin left them and went into the forest.

Not far from the meeting tree was a great rock with a chamber cut into it. The entrance was closed by a massive oak door two hand-widths thick, studded with spikes and fastened with a big padlock. This was the band’s treasure house, and Robin Hood went there, unlocked the door, and entered the chamber. He came out with a bag of gold, which he gave to Little John to pay Hugh Longshanks for the cloth of Lincoln green.
Then Little John got up, thrust the bag of gold into his shirt, tied a belt around his waist, took a stout pikestaff a full seven feet long in his hand, and set out on his journey.

So he strode along the leafy forest path that led to Fosse Way, whistling as he went and turning neither right nor left, until at last he came to a place where the path forked. One way led on to Fosse Way, and the other, as Little John knew very well, led to the merry Blue Boar Inn. Here Little John suddenly stopped whistling and stood still in the middle of the path. First he looked up and then he looked down, and then, tilting his cap over one eye, he slowly scratched the back of his head. For this was how it was: at the sight of these two roads, two voices began to clamor inside him. One cried, “There lies the road to the Blue Boar Inn, a mug of brown October ale, and a merry night with the sweet companions you will find there.” The other cried, “There lies the way to Ancaster and the duty you were sent to do.” Now the first of these voices was by far the louder, for Little John had grown very fond of good living during his stay at the Sheriff’s house. So after a moment he looked up into the blue sky, where bright clouds were sailing like silver boats and swallows skimmed in circling flight, and said, “I am afraid it will rain this evening, so I may as well stop at the Blue Boar until it passes by, for I know my good master would not want me soaked to the skin.” And without more ado, off he strode down the path that led the way of his own liking. There was no sign of bad weather at all, but when a man wants to do something, as Little John did, he never lacks reasons for doing it.

Four merry rascals were at the Blue Boar Inn: a butcher, a beggar, and two barefoot friars. Little John heard them singing from far off as he walked through the hush of the mellow twilight that was now settling over hill and dale. They were delighted to welcome such a merry fellow as Little John. Fresh mugs of ale were brought, and with jokes and songs and merry tales the hours flew by. None of them gave a thought to time or tide until the night was so far gone that Little John gave up the idea of setting out again that night, and stayed at the Blue Boar Inn until morning.
It was a piece of bad luck for Little John that he put his pleasure ahead of his duty, and he paid a heavy price for it, as we are all likely to do in the same case, as you shall see.
He got up at dawn the next day, took his stout pikestaff in his hand, and set out on his journey once more, as if he meant to make up for lost time.

In the good town of Blyth lived a sturdy tanner who was known far and wide for his strength and for the many hard bouts he had fought at wrestling and quarterstaff. For five years he had held the mid-country wrestling belt, until the great Adam o’ Lincoln threw him in the ring and cracked one of his ribs. At quarterstaff, though, he had never met his match anywhere in the country around. He also loved the longbow dearly, and a sly trip into the forest when the moon was full and the dun deer were in season. The King’s rangers therefore kept a sharp eye on him, for Arthur a Bland’s house always seemed to hold plenty of meat that looked a good deal more like venison than the law allowed.

Arthur had gone to Nottingham Town the day before Little John set out on his errand, to sell half a score of tanned cowhides. On the very morning that Little John left the inn, he started home from Nottingham to Blyth. His road ran, in the dewy morning, along the edge of Sherwood Forest, where the birds were welcoming the lovely day with a great merry chorus. His stout quarterstaff was slung across his shoulders, always near enough to grab in a moment, and on his head he wore a cap of doubled cowhide, so tough that even a broadsword could hardly split it.

“Now,” Arthur a Bland said to himself, when he reached the place where the road cut through a corner of the forest, “at this time of year the dun deer must be coming out of the deep woods toward the open meadows. Perhaps I might catch a glimpse of the dainty brown darlings, early as it is.” For he loved nothing better than to watch a herd of deer go tripping by, even when he could not tickle their ribs with a clothyard arrow. So he left the path and went peeping this way and that through the underbrush, searching first here and then there, with all the cunning of a master of woodcraft, which he was, and of a man who had more than once put on a coat of Lincoln green.

Meanwhile Little John was strolling cheerfully along, thinking of nothing but the sweetness of the hawthorn buds that decked the hedges, or gazing up at the lark that had sprung from the dewy grass and hung high on quivering wings in the yellow sunlight, pouring out a song that dropped like a falling star from the sky. His luck led him off the highway, not far from where Arthur a Bland was peeping through the leaves of the thickets. Hearing branches rustle, Little John stopped, and soon he spotted the Tanner’s brown cowhide cap moving among the bushes.

“I wonder,” Little John said to himself, “what that fellow is up to, peeping and peering around like that. I truly believe that scurvy rascal is nothing but a thief, and he has come here after our deer and the good King’s.” For after so much roaming in the forest, Little John had come to think that all the deer in Sherwood belonged to Robin Hood and his band just as much as to good King Harry. “No,” he said again after a while, “I must look into this.” So he left the highroad and went into the thickets too, and began to spy around after sturdy Arthur a Bland.

For a long while the two of them went hunting about, Little John after the Tanner and the Tanner after the deer. At last Little John stepped on a stick, which snapped under his foot. Hearing the noise, the Tanner spun around and caught sight of the yeoman. Seeing that the Tanner had found him out, Little John put on a bold front.

“Hello there,” he said, “what are you doing here, you rascal? Who are you, to come prowling along Sherwood’s paths? Truly, you have a wicked look about you, and I really think you are nothing but a thief, come after our good King’s deer.”

“No,” said the Tanner boldly—for though he was taken by surprise, he was not a man to be frightened by big words—“you lie in your teeth. I am no thief, but an honest craftsman. As for my looks, they are what they are, and for that matter, yours are none too pretty either, you saucy fellow.”

“Ha!” said Little John in a great loud voice, “do you talk back to me? I have a good mind to crack your skull for you. I will have you know, fellow, that I am, in a manner of speaking, one of the King’s foresters. At least,” he muttered to himself, “my friends and I take good care of our sovereign’s deer.”
“I don’t care who you are,” answered the bold Tanner, “and unless you have a good many more like you with you, you will never make Arthur a Bland cry ‘Mercy.’”

“Is that so?” cried Little John in a rage. “By my faith, you saucy rogue, your tongue has led you into a pit that you will have a hard time climbing out of, for I will give you such a thrashing as you have never had in all your life. Take your staff in your hand, fellow, for I will not strike an unarmed man.

“Oh, go on with you, and a plague on you!” cried the Tanner, for he had talked himself into a fume as well. “Big words never killed so much as a mouse. Who are you, to talk so freely of cracking the head of Arthur a Bland? If I do not tan your hide today as I never tanned a calf’s hide in all my life, split my staff into skewers for roasting lamb and never call me a brave man again! Now look to yourself, fellow!”
