“Wait!” said Little John. “First let us measure our cudgels. I reckon my staff is longer than yours, and I would not take an advantage of you by even an inch.”
“No, I don’t care about length,” answered the Tanner. “My staff is long enough to knock down a calf, so look to yourself, fellow, I say again.”
So without more talk, each gripped his staff in the middle, and with fierce, angry looks they slowly moved toward each other.

Now word had reached Robin Hood that Little John, instead of doing as he was told, had put pleasure before duty and stayed overnight in merry company at the Blue Boar Inn, rather than going straight to Ancaster. Robin was vexed to the heart by this, so at dawn he set out to find Little John at the Blue Boar, or at least to meet him on the road, and tell him exactly what he thought of the matter. As he strode along in anger, putting together the words he would use to scold Little John, he suddenly heard loud, angry voices, like men in a rage trading fierce words back and forth. Robin Hood stopped and listened. “Surely,” he said to himself, “that is Little John’s voice, and he is talking angrily too. The other voice is strange to me. Heaven forbid that my good, trusty Little John has fallen into the hands of the King’s rangers. I must see to this, and quickly.”

So Robin Hood spoke to himself, and all his anger vanished like breath from a windowpane at the thought that his trusty right-hand man might be in danger of his life. He crept carefully through the thickets toward the voices, pushed aside the leaves, and peeped into the small open space where the two men, staffs in hand, were slowly closing in on each other.

“Ha!” Robin said to himself, “here is some merry sport! I would give three golden angels out of my own pocket if that sturdy fellow would give Little John a good, sound drubbing! It would please me to see him well thumped for failing to do as I told him. I fear, though, that there is little chance of my seeing such a pleasant sight.” With that, he stretched himself out on the ground, so that he could see the sport better and enjoy the merry sight at his ease.

You may have seen two dogs that mean to fight, walking slowly round and round each other, neither one wanting to begin. In just that way the two stout yeomen circled, each watching for a chance to catch the other off guard and land the first blow. At last Little John struck like lightning, and—“rap!”—the Tanner met the blow and turned it aside, then struck back at Little John, who turned that blow too, and so the great battle began. Up and down and back and forth they trod, the blows falling so thick and fast that from a distance you would have thought half a score of men were fighting. They fought for nearly half an hour, until the ground was plowed up by their heels and their breathing grew as heavy as an ox’s in the furrow. But Little John suffered most, for he had grown unused to such hard work, and his joints were not as limber as they had been before he went to live with the Sheriff.

All this time Robin Hood lay beneath the bush, delighted with such a fine bout of quarterstaff. “By my faith!” he said to himself, “I never thought I would see Little John so evenly matched in all my life. Still, he would probably have beaten that fellow long ago if he were in his old shape.”

At last Little John saw his chance. Throwing into one blow all the strength he could feel draining from him, a blow that might have felled an ox, he struck at the Tanner with all his might. Now the Tanner’s cowhide cap stood him in good stead, and without it he might never have held a staff again. Even so, the blow he took beside the head was so sharp that it sent him staggering across the little glade, and if Little John had had the strength to press his advantage, it would have gone badly for sturdy Arthur. But the Tanner recovered quickly and, at arm’s length, struck back at Little John. This time the stroke found its mark, and down went Little John at full length, his cudgel flying from his hand as he fell. Then, raising his staff, sturdy Arthur gave him another blow across the ribs.
“Stop!” roared Little John. “Would you strike a man when he is down?”
“Yes, I would,” said the Tanner, giving him another whack with his staff.
“Stop!” roared Little John. “Help! Hold, I say! I give up! I give up, I say, good fellow!”
“Have you had enough?” asked the Tanner grimly, holding his staff high.
“Yes, indeed, and more than enough.”
“And do you admit that I am the better man of the two?”
“Yes, truly, and a plague take you!” said Little John, saying the first part aloud and the last part into his beard.
“Then you may go your way, and thank your patron saint that I am a merciful man,” said the Tanner.

“A plague on mercy like yours!” said Little John, sitting up and rubbing his ribs where the Tanner had cudgeled him. “I swear, it feels as if every one of my ribs were broken in two. I tell you, good fellow, I never thought there was a man in all Nottinghamshire who could do to me what you have done this day.”

“And I thought so too,” cried Robin Hood, bursting out of the thicket and roaring with laughter till tears ran down his cheeks. “Oh, man, man!” he said, as well as he could for laughing, “you went over like a bottle knocked off a wall. I saw the whole merry bout, and I never thought to see you give in, hand and foot, to any man in all merry England. I was looking for you to scold you for leaving my errand undone, but this good fellow has paid you everything I owed you, full measure, pressed down and running over. Why, he reached out his arm full length while you stood gaping at him, and with one pretty rap he tumbled you over as I have never seen anyone tumbled before.” So bold Robin spoke, and all the while Little John sat on the ground looking as though he had sour curds in his mouth. “What is your name, good fellow?” Robin said next, turning to the Tanner.
“Men call me Arthur a Bland,” the Tanner spoke up boldly, “and now what is your name?”

“Ha, so you are Arthur a Bland!” said Robin. “Your name is familiar to me, good fellow. At the Ely fair last October you broke the head of a friend of mine. People there call him Jock o’ Nottingham, but to us he is Will Scathelock. The poor man you have just thrashed is reckoned the finest quarterstaff player in all merry England. He is Little John, and I am Robin Hood.”

“What!” cried the Tanner. “Are you truly the great Robin Hood, and is this the famous Little John? Why, if I had known who you were, I would never have been bold enough to raise my hand against you. Let me help you up, good Master Little John, and brush the dust off your coat.”

“No,” said Little John crossly, getting up carefully, as though his bones were made of glass, “I can help myself, good fellow, without your aid. And let me tell you, if it had not been for that wretched cowskin cap of yours, things would have gone badly for you this day.”
At this Robin laughed again, and turning to the Tanner he said, “Will you join my band, good Arthur? For I swear you are one of the sturdiest men my eyes have ever seen.”

“Will I join your band?” cried the Tanner joyfully. “Yes, indeed I will! Hurrah for a merry life!” he cried, leaping into the air and snapping his fingers, “and hurrah for the life I love! Away with tanbark and filthy vats and foul cowhides! I will follow you to the ends of the earth, good master, and there won’t be a herd of dun deer in the whole forest that doesn’t know the twang of my bowstring.”

“As for you, Little John,” said Robin, turning to him with a laugh, “you will start once more for Ancaster, and we will go part of the way with you, for I will not have you turn right or left until you are well clear of Sherwood. There are other inns around here that you know of yet.” With that, they left the thickets, took to the highway again, and went off about their business.

chapters.title: Robin Hood and Will Scarlet
paragraphs: So they traveled along the sunny road, three stout fellows such as you could hardly find anywhere else in all merry England. Many people stopped to gaze after them as they strode by, their shoulders were so broad and their walk so sturdy.
Robin Hood said to Little John, “Why didn’t you go straight to Ancaster yesterday, as I told you? You would not have gotten yourself into such a mess if you had done as I ordered.”
“I was afraid of the rain that threatened,” said Little John in a sullen tone, for he was annoyed that Robin teased him so about what had happened.

“Rain!” cried Robin, halting abruptly in the middle of the road and gazing at Little John in amazement. “Why, you big oaf! Not one drop has fallen in three days, and no rain has threatened either. There has been no hint of bad weather anywhere, in the sky, on the land or on the water.”

“All the same,” growled Little John, “holy Saint Swithin keeps the waters of heaven in his pewter pot, and he could have tipped them out on us even from a clear sky. Would you have had me soaked to the skin?”
At this Robin Hood burst out laughing. “Oh, Little John!” he said, “what soft wits you have in that head of yours! Who could stay angry with a man like you?”
With that, they all set out on the road again, starting off on the right foot, as the saying goes.

They had gone some distance when Robin Hood began to feel thirsty, for the day was warm and the road dusty. Just behind the hedgerow there was a spring of water as cold as ice, so they climbed over the stile and came to the place where it bubbled up from under a mossy stone. There they knelt, scooped up water in their cupped hands, and drank their fill. The spot was cool and shady, so they stretched out their legs and rested for a while.

Beyond the hedge in front of them the dusty road ran off across the plain. Behind them, meadows and bright green fields of young corn lay wide open in the sun, and above them spread the cool, rustling leaves of the beech tree. The soft scent of purple violets and wild thyme, growing in the dewy damp around the edge of the little spring, drifted pleasantly to them, and so did the gentle gurgle of the water. Everything was so pleasant and so full of the quiet joy of bright Maytime that for a long while none of the three felt like talking. Each of them lay on his back, gazing up through the trembling leaves at the sky. At last Robin, whose mind was not quite so far off wandering as the others’, and who had been glancing around now and then, broke the silence.
“Well, well!” he said. “There is a gaily feathered bird, I swear.”

The others looked and saw a young man walking slowly along the highway. He was gay indeed, just as Robin had said, and he cut a fine figure. His jacket and stockings were of scarlet silk, and a handsome sword hung at his side in an embossed leather scabbard picked out with fine threads of gold. His cap was scarlet velvet, with a broad feather hanging down behind one ear. His long yellow hair curled on his shoulders, and in his hand he carried an early rose, which he sniffed delicately now and then.
“Upon my life!” said Robin Hood, laughing, “did you ever see such a pretty, mincing fellow?”

“His clothes are far too pretty for my taste, I admit,” said Arthur a Bland, “but even so, his shoulders are broad and his waist is narrow. And do you see, good master, how his arms hang from his body? They don’t dangle like spindles. They hang stiff and bend at the elbow. I swear there are no bread-and-milk limbs inside those fine clothes, only firm joints and tough muscles.”
“I think you are right, friend Arthur,” said Little John. “I truly believe that fellow is no rose-petal, whipped-cream gallant, whatever he would like us to think.”

“Pah!” said Robin Hood. “The sight of a fellow like that leaves a nasty taste in my mouth! Look how he holds that pretty flower between his thumb and finger, as if he were saying, ‘Good rose, I don’t dislike you so much that I can’t put up with your smell for a little while.’ I think you are both wrong. I truly believe that if an angry mouse ran across his path, he would cry, ‘La!’ or ‘Alack-a-day!’ and faint away on the spot. I wonder who he can be.”
“Some great baron’s son, no doubt,” answered Little John, “with honest men’s money lining his purse.”

“Yes, indeed, that must be so,” said Robin. “What a shame that men like him, who think of nothing but strutting about in fine clothes, should have good fellows dancing to their orders, when they are not fit to tie those fellows’ shoes. By Saint Dunstan, Saint Alfred, Saint Withold, and all the good men in the Saxon calendar, it makes me furious to see these fine lordlings from over the sea walking on the necks of good Saxons, who owned this land before their great-grandfathers ever chewed a rind of boar’s meat! By the bright bow of Heaven, I will have their ill-gotten gains from them, even if I hang for it as high as any tree in Sherwood!”

“Why, master,” said Little John, “what a temper is this? You set your pot boiling when you may have no bacon to cook in it! That fellow’s hair seems too light for Norman locks to me. For all you know, he may be an honest, good man.”

“No,” said Robin, “I’ll bet my head against a lead farthing that he is just what I say he is. So both of you lie right here, and I’ll show you how I thrash this fellow.” With that, Robin Hood stepped out of the shade of the beech tree, crossed the stile, and stood in the middle of the road with his hands on his hips, right in the stranger’s path.

All this talk had gone on while the stranger was still some way off, because he was walking so slowly. He neither hurried his steps nor seemed to notice that a man like Robin Hood existed in the world. So Robin stood in the middle of the road and waited while the other strolled forward, smelling his rose and looking this way and that, at everything except Robin.
“Halt!” cried Robin, when the other had finally come close to him. “Halt! Stay where you are!”

“Why should I halt, good fellow?” said the stranger in a soft, gentle voice. “And why should I stay where I am? Still, since you want me to stop, I will wait a short while, so that I may hear what you have to say to me.”

“Well then,” said Robin, “since you do as I tell you so nicely, and speak to me so softly, I will treat you with all due courtesy as well. I would have you know, fair friend, that I am something of a devotee at the shrine of Saint Wilfred, who, as you may know, took all the gold from the heathen whether they liked it or not, and melted it down into candlesticks. So I charge a certain toll on those who come this way, and I hope I use it for a better purpose than making candlesticks. Therefore, sweet chuck, I would like you to hand over your purse, so that I may look into it and judge, as well as my poor powers allow, whether you carry more wealth than our law permits. For, as our good Gaffer Swanthold says, ‘The man who is fat from overliving must lose some blood.’”

All this time the young man had been sniffing the rose he held between his thumb and finger. “No,” he said with a gentle smile when Robin Hood had finished, “I love to hear you talk, you pretty fellow, and if by chance you are not done yet, please go on. I still have a little time to spare.”

“I have said all,” said Robin, “and now, if you will give me your purse, I will let you go on your way without any trouble as soon as I have seen what is in it. If you have only a little, I will take nothing from you.”
“Alas! It grieves me deeply,” said the other, “that I cannot do as you wish. I have nothing to give you. Please let me go on my way. I have done you no harm.”
“No, you are not going,” said Robin, “until you have shown me your purse.”
“Good friend,” said the other gently, “I have business elsewhere. I have given you plenty of time and listened to you patiently. Please let me leave in peace.”

“I have spoken to you, friend,” said Robin sternly, “and now I tell you again that you will not move one step forward until you have done as I say.” With that, he raised his quarterstaff above his head, as a threat.
“Alas!” said the stranger sadly, “it grieves me that this must happen. I am very much afraid that I will have to kill you, you poor fellow!” With that, he drew his sword.

“Put your weapon away,” said Robin. “I would take no unfair advantage of you. Your sword can’t stand up to an oak staff like mine. I could snap it like a barley straw. There is a good thicket of oak by the roadside over there. Take a cudgel from it and defend yourself fairly, if you have a taste for a good thrashing.”

The stranger first looked Robin up and down, and then looked at the oak staff. “You are right, good fellow,” he said at last. “My sword is truly no match for that cudgel of yours. Wait a little while I fetch myself a staff.” With that, he tossed aside the rose he had been holding all this time and pushed his sword back into its scabbard. Then he walked, faster than he had moved so far, to the roadside, where the little clump of young oaks that Robin had mentioned was growing. After looking over the trees, he soon found a sapling he liked. He did not cut it down. Instead he rolled up his sleeves a little, took hold of it, planted his heel against the ground, and with one mighty pull tore the young tree out of the earth, roots and all. Then he came back, trimming off the roots and tender shoots with his sword, as calmly as if he had done nothing worth mentioning.

Little John and the Tanner had been watching everything that happened. But when they saw the stranger drag the sapling out of the ground, and heard the roots tearing and snapping, the Tanner pursed his lips and drew his breath in through them in a long, low whistle.

“By the breath of my body!” said Little John, as soon as he could pull his wits together after the shock. “Did you see that, Arthur? I think our poor master is going to have a bad time of it with that fellow. By Our Lady, he pulled up that green tree as if it were a barley straw.”
Whatever Robin Hood was thinking, he stood his ground, and now he and the stranger in scarlet faced each other.

Robin Hood held his own well that day, for a plain country yeoman. They fought this way and that, back and forth, Robin’s skill against the stranger’s strength. The dust of the highway rose around them like a cloud, so that at times Little John and the Tanner could see nothing and could only hear the staves clattering against each other. Three times Robin Hood hit the stranger, once on the arm and twice on the ribs, and he had fended off all the other man’s blows. Yet just one of those blows, had it landed, would have laid stout Robin lower in the dust than he had ever been. At last the stranger struck Robin’s cudgel so squarely in the middle that Robin could hardly keep hold of his staff. He struck again, and Robin bent under the blow. The third time he struck, he not only beat down Robin’s guard but gave him such a rap that Robin tumbled down into the dusty road.
“Stop!” cried Robin Hood, when he saw the stranger raise his staff once more. “I give up!”
“Stop!” cried Little John, bursting out of hiding with the Tanner right behind him. “Stop! Give over, I say!”
Calmly the stranger answered, “If two more have joined in, and each is as strong as this good fellow, I may well have my hands full. Still, come ahead, and I will try my best to deal with you all.”

“Stop!” cried Robin Hood. “We will fight no more. I swear this is an unlucky day for you and me, Little John. I truly believe my wrist, and my arm too, are numbed by the shock of the blow this stranger gave me.”
Then Little John turned to Robin Hood. “Why, good master,” he said, “alas! You are in a sorry state. Your jacket is all spoiled with the dust of the road. Let me help you up.”
“Plague take your help!” Robin shouted angrily. “I can get to my feet without any help from you, good fellow.”
“No, but at least let me dust your coat for you. I am afraid your poor bones are terribly sore,” said Little John solemnly, but with a sly twinkle in his eyes.
“Give over, I say!” said Robin in a huff. “My coat has been dusted enough already, without any help from you.” Then he turned to the stranger and said, “What is your name, good fellow?”
“My name is Gamwell,” answered the other.
“Ha!” cried Robin, “is that so? I have close kin of that name. Where do you come from, fair friend?”

“I come from Maxfield Town,” answered the stranger. “I was born and raised there, and from there I have come to look for my mother’s younger brother, whom men call Robin Hood. So, if perhaps you can direct me—”

“Ha! Will Gamwell!” cried Robin, putting both hands on the other’s shoulders and holding him off at arm’s length. “It can be no one else! I might have known you by that pretty, maidenly air of yours, and that dainty, finicky way you walk. Don’t you know me, lad? Take a good look at me.”

“Now, by the breath of my body!” cried the other, “I truly believe in my heart that you are my own Uncle Robin. Yes, it is certainly so!” And each threw his arms around the other and kissed him on the cheek.

Then once more Robin held his kinsman off at arm’s length and looked him keenly over from head to foot. “Why,” he said, “what a change is here! Some eight or ten years ago I left you a gangly lad, with big joints and badly hung limbs, and here you are now, as fine a fellow as I ever set eyes on. Don’t you remember, lad, how I showed you the proper way to pinch the goose feather between your fingers and hold your bow arm steady? You showed great promise of becoming a keen archer. And don’t you remember how I taught you to guard and parry with the cudgel?”

“Yes,” said young Gamwell, “and I looked up to you so much, and thought you so far above all other men, that I swear, if I had known who you were, I would never have dared to raise a hand against you today. I hope I did you no great harm.”

“No, no,” said Robin hastily, glancing sideways at Little John, “you did me no harm. But say no more about that, please. I will say this much, lad: I hope I never feel another blow like the one you gave me. By’r Lady, my arm is tingling still from fingernail to elbow. Truly, I thought I was crippled for life. I tell you, cousin, you are the strongest man I ever laid eyes on. I swear my stomach quaked when I saw you pluck up that green tree the way you did. But tell me, how did you come to leave Sir Edward and your mother?”

“Alas!” answered young Gamwell. “It’s a sorry story I have to tell you, uncle. After old Giles Crookleg died, my father hired a new steward, and he was always an insolent rascal. I don’t know why my father kept him, except that he managed the estate very well. It used to make my blood boil to hear him talk back so boldly to my father, who, as you know, was always a patient man with the people around him, slow to anger and slow to say a harsh word. Well, one day—and an unlucky day it was for that insolent fellow—he started scolding my father while I stood there. I couldn’t stand it any longer, good uncle, so I stepped forward and gave him a box on the ear, and—would you believe it?—the man dropped dead on the spot. I think they said I broke his neck, or something like that. So they packed me off to find you and get away from the law. I was on my way when you saw me, and here I am.”

“Well, by my heart’s faith,” said Robin Hood, “of all the men I’ve ever seen running from the law, you were taking it the easiest! Who in the whole world ever saw a man who had killed someone, and was fleeing for it, strolling down the highway like a dainty court lady, sniffing at a rose all the while?”

“Now, uncle,” answered Will Gamwell, “as the old saying goes, haste never churned good butter. Besides, I truly believe my great strength has taken the quickness out of my heels. Why, you just rapped me three times a moment ago, and I never hit you once, except by overpowering you with my strength.”

“No,” said Robin, “let’s say no more about that. I’m very glad to see you, Will, and you’ll bring great honor and credit to my band of merry fellows. But you must change your name, because warrants will soon be out against you. So, because of your bright clothes, from now on and forever you shall be called Will Scarlet.”

“Will Scarlet,” said Little John, stepping forward and holding out his great palm, which the other man took. “Will Scarlet, the name suits you well. I’m very glad to welcome you among us. I’m called Little John, and this is a new member who has just joined us, a sturdy tanner named Arthur a Bland. You’re likely to become famous, Will, let me tell you, because many a merry ballad will be sung across the country, and many a merry story told in Sherwood, about how Robin Hood taught Little John and Arthur a Bland the right way to use the quarterstaff. And about how our good master bit off such a big piece of cake that he choked on it, too, so to speak.”

“No, good Little John,” said Robin gently, for he did not like the thought of such a joke being told about him. “Why should we talk about this little matter? Please, let’s keep this day’s doings among ourselves.”

“With all my heart,” said Little John. “But, good master, I thought you loved a merry story, since you’ve so often made a joke about a certain thickening of my joints, flesh I gathered while staying with the Sheriff of—”
“No, good Little John,” said Robin hastily, “now that I think of it, I’ve said quite enough on that subject.”
“That’s well,” said Little John, “because truthfully I’m a little tired of it myself. But now I remember, you also seemed ready to make a joke about the rain that threatened last night, so—”
“Oh, enough,” said Robin Hood crossly. “I was mistaken. I remember now that it did look like rain.”
“Truly, I thought so myself,” said Little John, “so no doubt you think it was wise of me to stay all night at the Blue Boar Inn instead of venturing out in such stormy weather, don’t you?”
“A plague on you and your doings!” cried Robin Hood. “If you insist, you were right to stay wherever you pleased.”

“Once more, that’s well,” said Little John. “As for me, I’ve been blind today. I didn’t see you get thrashed. I didn’t see you tumble head over heels in the dust. And if any man says you did, I can with a clear conscience rattle his lying tongue between his teeth.”
“Come on,” cried Robin, biting his lower lip while the others couldn’t help laughing. “We’ll go no farther today. We’ll go back to Sherwood, and you can go to Ancaster another time, Little John.”
Robin said this because his bones were sore now, and a long journey seemed a bad idea to him. So they turned around and walked back the way they had come.

chapters.title: The Adventure with Midge, the Miller’s Son
paragraphs: The four yeomen had been traveling toward Sherwood for a long time, and noon had passed, when they began to grow hungry. Robin Hood said, “I wish I had something to eat. I think a good loaf of white bread, a piece of snow-white cheese, and a drink of foaming ale would be a feast fit for a king.”
“Now that you mention it,” said Will Scarlet, “I wouldn’t mind that myself. Something inside me is crying out, ‘Food, good friend, food!’”
“I know a house close by,” said Arthur a Bland, “and if I only had the money, I’d bring you just what you’re describing: a sweet loaf of bread, a fine cheese, and a skin of brown ale.”
“As for that, you know I have money with me, good master,” said Little John.
“Yes, you do, Little John,” said Robin. “Good Arthur, how much will it cost to buy us food and drink?”
“Six broad pennies should buy enough to feed a dozen men, I’d say,” answered the Tanner.

“Then give him six pennies, Little John,” said Robin, “since I think food for three men will just about meet my needs. Now be off with you, Arthur, with the money, and bring the food back here. There’s pleasant shade in that thicket over there beside the road, and that’s where we’ll eat our meal.”
So Little John handed Arthur the money, and the others went over to the thicket to wait for the Tanner to come back.

After a while he returned, carrying a big brown loaf of bread and a fine round cheese, with a goatskin full of strong March beer slung over his shoulders. Then Will Scarlet took his sword and cut the loaf and the cheese into four fair shares, and each man helped himself. Robin Hood took a long swallow of the beer. “Aha!” he said, catching his breath. “I’ve never tasted a sweeter drink than this.”
After that nobody spoke, but each man munched away heartily at his bread and cheese, taking a pull at the beer every now and then.
At last Will Scarlet looked at a small piece of bread still in his hand and said, “I think I’ll give this to the sparrows.” He tossed it away and brushed the crumbs from his jerkin.
“I’ve had enough too, I think,” said Robin. As for Little John and the Tanner, they had by now eaten every crumb of their bread and cheese.

“Now,” said Robin, “I feel like a new man, and I’d gladly enjoy something pleasant before we go any farther on our journey. I remember, Will, that you used to have a pretty voice, one that was sweet on a song. Please, give us one before we travel on.”
“Truly, I don’t mind singing a tune,” answered Will Scarlet, “but I wouldn’t want to sing alone.”
“Don’t worry, others will follow. Start up, lad,” said Robin.

“In that case, all right,” said Will Scarlet. “I remember a song a certain minstrel used to sing in my father’s hall now and then. I don’t know its name, so I can’t tell you one, but it goes like this.” Then he cleared his throat and sang:

“_In the happy time of blossoms,
When longing for love fills the heart,
When the linden is in flower,
When the small birds build their nests,
Sweetly sings the nightingale
And the bold thrush on the bough;
The cuckoo in the dewy dale
And the dove in the wood.
But the robin is the one I love,
For he sings the whole year through.
Robin! Robin!
Merry Robin!
That’s how I’d have my true love be:
Never to flee
At the near
Sight of cold hard times_.

“_When spring brings its sweet delights,
When the lark climbs up on high,
Lovers court on mellow nights,
And young men gaze in maidens’ eyes,
That’s when the wild rose blooms,
Spotted daisies on the hill,
Fair cowslips and columbine,
Dark violets by the stream.
But the ivy stays green
When the north wind brings the snow.
Ivy! Ivy!
Steady and true!
That’s how I’d have her love be:
Never to die
At the near
Breath of cold hard times_.”

“That was well sung,” said Robin, “but, cousin, I’ll tell you plainly, I’d rather hear a sturdy fellow like you sing a lusty ballad than a fussy song about flowers and birds and whatnot. Still, you sang it nicely, and for that matter it’s not a bad little snatch of song. Now, Tanner, it’s your turn.”

“I don’t know,” said Arthur, smiling, with his head on one side like a bashful girl who’s been asked to dance. “I don’t know that I can match our sweet friend’s song. Besides, I really think I’ve caught a cold, and I have a tickle and a huskiness in my windpipe.”
“Come, sing up, friend,” said Little John, who sat next to him, patting him on the shoulder. “You have a fine, round, mellow voice. Let’s hear a bit of it.”
“Well, if you’re set on having a poor thing,” said Arthur, “I’ll do my best. Have you ever heard of the wooing of Sir Keith, the sturdy young Cornish knight, in good King Arthur’s time?”
“I think I’ve heard something of it,” said Robin, “but start up your ditty anyway and let’s hear it. As I remember, it’s a gallant song, so out with it, good fellow.”
Then the Tanner cleared his throat and, without any more fuss, began to sing:
The Wooing of Sir Keith

“_King Arthur sat in his royal hall,
And all around him there
Sat many a tall and noble lord,
The greatest in the land.

“Sir Lancelot sat with raven hair,
Gawaine with hair of gold,
Sir Tristram, Kay the keeper of keys,
And many another knight.

“And through the stained-glass panes
Over the red-tiled eaves,
The sun poured down in colored light
On golden helms and shin guards.

“But suddenly a hush fell
Around the Round Table,
For up the hall there walked a woman
Bent nearly to the ground.

“And so she crept up slowly
And knelt at Arthur’s feet;
Said Kay, ‘She is the foulest woman
That ever met my eyes.’

“‘O mighty King, I beg of you
A favor on bended knee’;
That was how she spoke. ‘What do you want?’
Said Arthur the King, ‘of me_?’

“_Said she, ‘A dreadful sickness
Gnaws at my very heart,
And only one thing can bring me ease
Or cure my bitter pain.

“‘There is no rest, no ease for me
North, east, or west, or south,
Until a Christian knight will gladly
Kiss me three times on the mouth.

“‘He must not be a married man
Who gives this ease to me;
Nor may he be forced, I think,
But kiss me willingly.

“‘So is there here one Christian knight
Of such a noble line
That he will give a suffering soul
Sweet ease from deadly pain?’

“‘A married man,’ said Arthur the King,
‘A married man am I,
Or else I would think it a noble deed
To kiss you willingly.

“‘Lancelot, all men look to you
As the head and chief of all
Chivalry. Come, noble knight,
And bring her swift relief.’

“But Lancelot turned away
And stared down at the floor,
For it stung his haughty pride
To hear them laughing all around.

“‘You come, Sir Tristram,’ said the King.
Said he, ‘It cannot be,
For I can never make my stomach
Do it willingly.’

“‘Will you, Sir Kay, you scornful man?’
Said Kay, ‘No, on my word!
What lady would kiss a knight
Who had kissed so foul a mouth_?’

“_‘Will you, Gawaine?’ ‘I cannot, King.’
‘Sir Geraint?’ ‘No, not I;
My kisses could bring no relief,
For I would sooner die.’

“Then up spoke the youngest man
Of all around the table,
‘Whatever help a Christian can give
I’ll give her, my lord.’

“This was Sir Keith, a youthful knight,
Strong of limb and bold,
His chin was dusted with a beard
Like finest threads of gold.

“Said Kay, ‘He has no sweetheart yet
That he can call his own,
But here is one who’s quickly won,
As she herself has shown.’

“He kissed her once, and then again,
A third time, too, he pressed;
A wondrous change came in a flash,
And she was foul no more.

“Her cheeks bloomed red as any rose,
Her forehead pale as lawn,
Her bosom white as winter snow,
Her eyes were like a fawn’s.

“Her breath was sweet as summer air
Across a meadow’s flowers;
Her voice was soft as whispering leaves,
No longer cracked and harsh.

“Her hair now shone like spun gold,
Her hands were white as cream;
The ragged, dirty clothes she wore
Were changed to robes of silk.

“In great amazement the knights stared.
Said Kay, ‘I give my vow,
If it would please you, lovely lady,
I’ll gladly kiss you now_.’

“_But young Sir Keith knelt on one knee
And kissed her gown so fair.
‘Oh, let me be your slave,’ said he,
‘For none compare with you.’

“She bent and kissed his forehead,
His lips, his eyes as well.
Said she, ‘You are my master now,
My lord, my love, arise!

“‘And all the wealth that I own,
My lands, I give to you,
For never has a knight shown a lady
Such noble courtesy.

“‘A spell was on me, and great pain,
But you have set me free;
Now that I am myself once more,
I give myself to you_.’”
“Yes, truly,” said Robin Hood when the Tanner had finished singing, “it’s just as I remembered it, a fine ditty, and a ballad with a pleasing tune.”

“It has often seemed to me,” said Will Scarlet, “that there’s a certain point to it, something like this: a duty that sometimes seems ugly and harsh to us, when we kiss it squarely on the mouth, so to speak, turns out to be no such foul thing after all.”

“I think you’re right,” said Robin, “and the other way around, too: when we kiss a pleasure that looks gay, it turns foul on us. Isn’t that so, Little John? Such a thing has certainly brought you some sore thumps today. No, man, don’t look so down in the mouth. Clear your pipes and sing us a ditty.”

“No,” said Little John, “I have none as fine as the one merry Arthur has just trolled. The ones I know are all poor things. Besides, my voice is out of tune today, and I wouldn’t want to spoil even a halfway decent song by singing it badly.”

At this they all pressed Little John to sing, and when he had refused for a proper length of time, as is only polite for a man who’s been asked to sing, he finally gave in. He said, “Well, if you will have it so, I’ll give you what I can. Like fair Will, I have no title for my ditty, but here it goes.”

“_O my lady, spring is here,
With a hey nonny nonny;
The sweet love season of the year,
With a ninny ninny nonny;
Now lad and lass
Lie in the grass
That grows so green
With flowers between.
The buck lies down to rest,
The leaves start to unfold,
The rooster crows,
The breeze blows,
And all things laugh in_—”
“Who’s that fellow coming along the road?” said Robin, breaking into the song.
“I don’t know,” said Little John in a sour voice. “But I do know it’s a bad business to cut off a good song in the middle.”

“Now, Little John,” said Robin, “don’t be cross, I beg you. But ever since you started your song, I’ve been watching that fellow trudging toward us, bent double under the big sack on his back. Look, Little John, and tell me if you know him.”

Little John looked where Robin Hood was pointing. “Well, now,” he said after a while, “I think that fellow is a young miller I’ve seen now and then along the edge of Sherwood. A poor creature, if you ask me, to spoil a good song over.”
“Now that you mention him,” said Robin Hood, “I think I’ve seen him now and then myself. Doesn’t he have a mill over past Nottingham Town, close to the Salisbury road?”
“You’re right, that’s the man,” said Little John.
“A fine, sturdy fellow,” said Robin. “About two weeks ago I saw him crack Ned o’ Bradford’s head, and I never saw a scalp lifted so neatly in all my life.”

By now the young miller had come close enough for them to see him clearly. His clothes were dusted with flour, and on his back he carried a great sack of meal. He was bent over so that the whole weight rested on his shoulders, and a thick quarterstaff lay across the top of the sack. His limbs were big and strong, and he strode along the dusty road very sturdily under the heavy load. His cheeks were as red as a winter rose hip, his hair was the color of flax, and on his chin grew a soft fuzz of flaxen beard.

“A good, honest fellow,” said Robin Hood, “and just the kind who does credit to the yeomen of England. Now let’s have some merry sport with him. We’ll jump out as if we were ordinary thieves and pretend to rob him of his honest earnings. Then we’ll take him into the forest and give him a feast bigger than his stomach ever held in all his life. We’ll wash his throat with good canary wine and send him home with a crown in his purse for every penny he has. What do you say, lads?”
“It’s a merry idea, truly,” said Will Scarlet.
“It’s a fine plan,” said Little John, “but may all the saints keep us from any more beatings today! Goodness, my poor bones ache so much that I—”
“Please be quiet, Little John,” said Robin. “That foolish tongue of yours will get us both laughed at yet.”
“My foolish tongue, indeed,” growled Little John to Arthur a Bland. “I only wish it could keep our master from dragging us into another scrape today.”
Just then the Miller, plodding down the road, drew level with the spot where the yeomen lay hidden, and all four of them sprang out and ringed him in.

“Stop, friend!” Robin cried to the Miller. He turned slowly, with the weight of the bag still on his shoulder, and looked at each of them in turn, completely bewildered, for though he was a strong man, his wits did not jump about like roasting chestnuts.
“Who tells me to stop?” said the Miller in a deep, gruff voice, like the growl of a big dog.
“I do, and no mistake,” said Robin, “and let me tell you, friend, you had better do as I say.”
“And who might you be, good friend?” asked the Miller, swinging the big sack off his shoulder and dropping it on the ground. “And who are the men with you?”
“We are four good Christian men,” said Robin, “and we would gladly help you by carrying part of your heavy load.”
“Thank you all,” said the Miller, “but my bag isn’t so heavy that I can’t carry it by myself.”

“No, you misunderstand,” said Robin. “I meant that you might have some heavy farthings or pennies about you, not to mention silver and gold. Our good Gaffer Swanthold says that gold is too heavy a burden for a two-legged donkey to carry, so we would like to lift some of that load from you.”

“Oh no!” cried the Miller. “What do you want to do to me? I don’t have so much as a clipped groat on me. Don’t hurt me, I beg you, but let me go in peace. And let me tell you that you are on Robin Hood’s ground, and if he finds you trying to rob an honest craftsman, he will crop your ears close to your heads and whip you all the way to the walls of Nottingham.”
“Truly, I fear Robin Hood no more than I fear myself,” said jolly Robin. “Today you must hand over every penny you have on you. And if you move an inch, I’ll rattle this staff about your ears.”
“No, don’t hit me!” cried the Miller, throwing up his elbow as if he feared the blow. “Search me if you like, but you’ll find nothing on me, in pouch, pocket, or skin.”

“Is that so?” said Robin Hood, looking hard at him. “Well, I don’t believe a word of it. Unless I’m badly mistaken, you have something at the bottom of that fat sack of meal. Good Arthur, empty the bag onto the ground. I’ll bet you find a shilling or two in the flour.”
“Oh no!” cried the Miller, dropping to his knees. “Don’t spoil all my good meal! It will do you no good and it will ruin me. Spare it, and I will hand over the money that’s in the bag.”

“Ha!” said Robin, nudging Will Scarlet. “Is that so? So I’ve found where your money lies? Goodness, I have a wonderful nose for the blessed face of good King Harry. I thought I smelled gold and silver under that barley meal. Bring it right out, Miller.”

Then the Miller slowly got to his feet, and slowly, unwillingly, he untied the mouth of the bag. Slowly he pushed his hands into the meal and began to fumble about, with his arms buried to the elbows in the barley flour. The others crowded around him with their heads together, looking and wondering what he would bring out.

So they stood, all of them with their heads close together, staring down into the sack. But while he pretended to be searching for the money, the Miller scooped up two big handfuls of meal. “Ha,” he said, “here they are, the beauties.” Then, as the others leaned even farther forward to see what he had, he suddenly flung the meal into their faces, filling their eyes and noses and mouths with flour, blinding them and half choking them. Arthur a Bland was worse off than anyone, for his mouth was hanging open in wonder at what was coming, so that a great cloud of flour went down his throat and set him coughing until he could hardly stand.

Then, while all four of them stumbled about, roaring from the sting of the meal in their eyeballs, and rubbing their eyes until the tears cut wide channels through the meal on their faces, the Miller seized another handful of flour, and another, and another, and threw them in their faces. Even if they had still had a glimmer of light before, they were now as blind as any beggar in Nottinghamshire, while their hair and beards and clothes were as white as snow.

Then the Miller snatched up his great crabtree staff and began laying about him as if he had gone completely mad. The four of them hopped this way and that like peas on a drumhead, but they could see neither to defend themselves nor to run away. Thwack! Thwack! went the Miller’s cudgel across their backs, and with every blow great white clouds of flour rose from their jackets and drifted away on the breeze.
“Stop!” Robin roared at last. “Enough, good friend, I am Robin Hood!”

“You lie, you rascal,” cried the Miller, giving him a rap on the ribs that sent up a great cloud of flour like a puff of smoke. “Stout Robin never robbed an honest tradesman. Ha! You wanted my money, did you?” And he gave him another blow. “No, you’re not getting your share, you long-legged rascal. Share and share alike.” And he struck Little John across the shoulders so hard that he sent him hopping halfway across the road. “Don’t worry, it’s your turn now, black beard.” And he gave the Tanner a whack that made him roar in spite of his coughing. “Well now, red coat, let me brush the dust off you!” he cried, hitting Will Scarlet. And so he gave them merry words and blows until they could hardly stand, and whenever he saw one of them about to clear his eyes, he threw more flour in his face. At last Robin Hood found his horn, put it to his lips, and blew three loud blasts on it.

Now it happened that Will Stutely and a party of Robin’s men were in the glade not far from where this merry sport was going on. They heard the hubbub of voices and blows that sounded like a flail in the barn in wintertime, and they stopped to listen, wondering what was going on. Will Stutely said, “Unless I’m mistaken, there’s a hearty battle with cudgels going on not far from here. I’d like to see this fine sight.” With that, he and the whole party turned toward the noise. When they had come close to where all the uproar was, they heard the three blasts of Robin’s bugle horn.
“Quick!” cried young David of Doncaster. “Our master is in great need!” So without stopping for a moment, they dashed forward with all their might and burst out of the thicket onto the highroad.
What a sight met their eyes! The road lay white with meal, and five men stood in it, white from head to toe, for a good deal of the barley flour had rained back down on the Miller.
“What do you need, master?” cried Will Stutely. “And what does all this mean?”

“Why,” said Robin, in a towering rage, “that traitor, that low-bred fellow over there, has come as close to killing me as any man in the world. If you hadn’t come so quickly, good Stutely, your master would be dead.”

Then, while he and the other three rubbed the meal from their eyes, and Will Stutely and his men brushed their clothes clean, Robin told them everything: how he had meant to play a joke on the Miller, and how it had turned so badly against them.

“Quick, men, seize the wicked Miller!” cried Stutely, who was almost choking with laughter, as were the rest. Several of them ran at the sturdy fellow, grabbed him, and tied his arms behind his back with bowstrings.

“Ha!” cried Robin, when they brought the trembling Miller to him. “You wanted to murder me, did you? By my faith—” Here he stopped and stood glaring grimly at the Miller. But Robin’s anger could not last. First his eyes twinkled, and then, in spite of everything, he burst out laughing.

When the yeomen standing around saw their master laugh, they could hold back no longer, and a mighty shout of laughter went up from all of them. Many could not stand, but rolled on the ground from pure merriment.
“What is your name, good fellow?” Robin said at last to the Miller, who stood gaping as if he were in a daze.
“Please, sir, my name is Midge, the Miller’s son,” he answered in a shaky voice.

“I swear,” said merry Robin, slapping him on the shoulder, “you are the mightiest Midge my eyes have ever seen. Now will you leave your dusty mill and join my band? By my faith, you’re too strong a man to spend your days between the hopper and the till.”
“Then truly, if you forgive me for the blows I struck without knowing who you were, I will join you gladly,” said the Miller.

“Then today I have gained,” said Robin, “the three strongest yeomen in all Nottinghamshire. Let’s go to the greenwood tree and hold a merry feast there in honor of our new friends. Perhaps a cup or two of good sack and canary will ease the soreness of my poor joints and bones, though I’m sure it will be many a day before I’m the man I was.” With that, he turned and led the way, the rest following, and so they entered the forest once more and disappeared from sight.

So that night the woods were ablaze with crackling fires. Robin and the others we have mentioned, all except Midge, the Miller’s son, had plenty of sore bumps and bruises here and there on their bodies, but their joints were not so sore that they couldn’t enjoy a jolly feast held to welcome the new members of the band. So with songs and jokes and laughter that echoed through the deeper, quieter corners of the forest, the night passed quickly, as such merry times do, until at last every man went to his bed, silence fell over everything, and everything seemed to sleep.

But Little John could never keep a rein on his tongue, so bit by bit the whole story came out, both his own fight with the Tanner and Robin’s fight with Will Scarlet. And I have told it here so that you can laugh at the merry tale along with me.

chapters.title: Robin Hood and Allan a Dale
paragraphs: You have just heard how three unlucky adventures befell Robin Hood and Little John in a single day and left them with sore ribs and aching bones. Next we will tell how they made up for those mishaps by a good deed, which cost Robin some small pain along the way.

Two days passed, and some of the soreness had left Robin Hood’s joints. Even so, whenever he moved suddenly without thinking, a pain here or there would jab him, as if to say, “You’ve had a thrashing, my good fellow.”

The day was bright and cheerful, and the morning dew still lay on the grass. Robin Hood sat under the greenwood tree. On one side Will Scarlet lay stretched out on his back, gazing into the clear sky with his hands clasped behind his head. On the other side Little John sat shaping a cudgel from a stout crabtree limb. Elsewhere on the grass many others of the band sat or lay.

“By the faith of my heart,” said merry Robin, “it occurs to me that we haven’t had anyone to dine with us for a long time. Our money is running low in the purse, for no one has come to pay a bill for many a day. Now hurry, good Stutely, pick six men, and go to Fosse Way or thereabouts, and make sure you bring someone back to eat with us this evening. Meanwhile we will prepare a grand feast, to do whoever comes the greater honor. And wait, good Stutely. I want you to take Will Scarlet with you, for it’s only right that he should become familiar with the ways of the forest.”

“I thank you, good master,” said Stutely, springing to his feet, “for choosing me for this adventure. Truly, my limbs are growing slack from sitting around here idle. As for two of my six, I will choose Midge the Miller and Arthur a Bland, for, as you well know, good master, they are strong fists with the quarterstaff. Isn’t that so, Little John?”

Everyone laughed at this except Little John and Robin, who screwed up his face. “I’ll answer for Midge,” he said, “and for my cousin Scarlet too. This very morning I looked over my ribs and found them as many colors as a beggar’s cloak.”
So Will Stutely picked four more sturdy fellows and led his band off to Fosse Way, to see if they could find some rich guest to feast in Sherwood that day with Robin and his men.

They stayed close to the highway for the whole long day. Each man had brought a good supply of cold meat and a bottle of strong March beer to keep his stomach quiet until they got home. So when noon came, they sat down on the soft grass beneath a wide green hawthorn bush and had a hearty, cheerful feast. After that, one man kept watch while the others dozed, for the day was still and sultry.

So the time passed pleasantly enough, but not one of the guests they wanted showed his face all the while they lay hidden there. Plenty of people went along the dusty road in the glare of the sun. First came a bunch of chattering girls, tripping merrily along; then a plodding tinker; then a cheerful shepherd boy; then a sturdy farmer. All of them stared straight ahead down the road, never guessing that seven strong fellows lay hidden so close by. Those were the travelers who came that way, but of fat abbots, rich squires or moneylenders loaded with gold, not one came.

At last the sun began to sink low in the sky, the light turned red and the shadows grew long. A great stillness settled over the air, the birds twittered drowsily, and from far away came the clear, faint, musical call of a milkmaid bringing the cows home to be milked.

Then Stutely got up from where he had been lying. “A plague on this bad luck!” he said. “We have waited here all day, and not one bird worth shooting has come within range of our arrows, so to speak. If I had gone out on some harmless errand, I would have met a dozen stout priests or a score of pot-bellied moneylenders. But it is always the way: the brown deer are never so scarce as when you have a gray goose feather pinched between your fingers. Come on, lads, I say let us pack up and go home.”

So the others got up, came out of the thicket, and turned their toes back toward Sherwood. When they had gone some distance, Will Stutely, who was leading the party, suddenly stopped. “Hush!” he said, for his ears were as sharp as those of a five-year-old fox. “Listen, lads! I think I hear something.” At this they all stopped and listened, holding their breath, though for a while they could hear nothing, since their ears were duller than Stutely’s. At last they heard a faint, sad sound, like someone crying out in grief.
“Ha!” said Will Scarlet. “We must look into this. Someone near here is in trouble.”

“I don’t know about that,” said Will Stutely, shaking his head doubtfully. “Our master is always too quick to stick his finger in a boiling pot. For my part, I see no point in getting ourselves into a mess. That is a man’s voice over there, unless I am mistaken, and a man ought to be able to get himself out of his own troubles.”
Then Will Scarlet spoke up boldly. “Shame on you for talking like that, Stutely! Stay here if you like. I am going to find out what is wrong with this poor creature.”

“No,” said Stutely, “you jump so fast you’ll tumble into a ditch. Who said I wouldn’t go? Come along, I say.” With that, he led the way and the others followed. After a short distance they came to a little clearing in the woods, where a brook came gurgling out from under a tangle of overhanging bushes and spread into a broad pool with a bed of shining pebbles. By the edge of this pool, under the branches of a willow, a young man lay face down, weeping aloud. It was his crying that Stutely’s sharp ears had caught first. His golden hair was tangled, his clothes were all in disorder, and everything about him spoke of sorrow and misery. Above his head, from a branch of the willow, hung a beautiful harp of polished wood, inlaid with gold and silver in curious patterns. Beside him lay a strong ash bow and half a score of fine, smooth arrows.
“Hello there!” shouted Will Stutely, when they had come out of the forest into the little clearing. “Who are you, fellow, lying there and killing all the green grass with salt water?”
At the sound of the voice, the stranger sprang to his feet, snatched up his bow, fitted an arrow to it, and stood ready for whatever harm might come.

“Truly,” said one of the yeomen, when they had seen the young stranger’s face, “I know that lad very well. He is a minstrel I have seen around here more than once. Only a week ago I saw him skipping across the hill like a yearling doe. He was a fine sight then, with a flower at his ear and a rooster’s plume stuck in his cap. But now, it seems to me, our young rooster has lost all his bright feathers.”

“Pah!” cried Will Stutely, coming up to the stranger. “Wipe your eyes, man! I hate to see a tall, strong fellow snivel like a fourteen-year-old girl over a dead tomtit. Put down your bow, man! We mean you no harm.”

But Will Scarlet saw that the stranger, who looked young and boyish, was stung by Stutely’s words. He went over and laid a hand on the youth’s shoulder. “You are in trouble, poor boy!” he said kindly. “Don’t mind what these fellows said. They are rough, but they mean well by you. Perhaps they simply don’t understand a lad like you. Come with us, and maybe we can find someone who can help you with your troubles, whatever they are.”
“Yes, come along,” said Will Stutely gruffly. “I meant you no harm, and I may do you some good. Take your singing tool down from that fine tree, and come with us.”

The youth did as he was told and went along with the others, head bowed and step heavy, walking beside Will Scarlet. So they made their way through the forest. The bright light faded from the sky, and a gray shimmer settled over everything. From the deeper parts of the forest came the strange whispering sounds of night. All else was silent except for the rustle of their footsteps in the crisp, dry leaves left over from last winter. At last a ruddy glow showed here and there through the trees ahead. A little farther on, they came to the open glade, now bathed in pale moonlight. In the middle of the clearing a great fire crackled, casting a red glow on everything around it. Juicy venison steaks, pheasants, capons, and fresh fish from the river were roasting over it. The whole air was filled with the sweet smell of good things cooking.

The little band crossed the glade. Many yeomen turned and stared curiously after them, but none spoke or asked them anything. So, with Will Scarlet on one side and Will Stutely on the other, the stranger came to the place where Robin Hood sat on a seat of moss under the greenwood tree, with Little John standing beside him.
“Good evening, fair friend,” said Robin Hood, rising as the other came near. “Have you come to feast with me today?”

“Alas, I can’t say,” said the lad, staring around him with dazed eyes, for everything he saw bewildered him. “Truly, I can’t tell whether I am awake or lost in a dream,” he murmured to himself in a low voice.
“Why, no,” said Robin, laughing. “You are awake, as you will soon find out, for a fine feast is cooking for you. You are our honored guest today.”

The young stranger kept looking around him as if in a dream. After a while he turned to Robin. “I think,” he said, “I know now where I am and what has happened to me. Are you not the great Robin Hood?”

“You have hit the bull’s-eye,” said Robin, clapping him on the shoulder. “Men around here do call me by that name. Since you know me, you also know that whoever feasts with me must pay his bill. I trust you have a full purse with you, fair stranger.”
“Alas!” said the stranger, “I have no purse and no money either, except half of a sixpence. The other half is carried by my own dear love, hung around her neck on a strand of silken thread.”

At this speech a great shout of laughter went up from everyone around, and the poor boy looked as if he would die of shame. But Robin Hood turned sharply to Will Stutely. “Well, well,” he said, “is this the guest you brought us to fill our purse? It seems to me you have brought a skinny rooster to market.”
“No, good master,” answered Will Stutely, grinning. “He is no guest of mine. It was Will Scarlet who brought him here.”

Then Will Scarlet spoke up and told how they had found the lad in tears, and how he had brought him to Robin, thinking Robin might be able to help him in his trouble. Then Robin Hood turned to the youth, put a hand on his shoulder, and held him at arm’s length, studying his face closely.

“A young face,” he said in a low voice, half to himself, “a kind face, a good face. It is as pure as a maiden’s, and the fairest my eyes have ever seen. But if I may judge by your looks, grief comes to the young as well as the old.” At these words, spoken so kindly, the poor lad’s eyes filled with tears. “No, no,” said Robin quickly, “cheer up, lad. I am sure your case is not so bad that it cannot be mended. What is your name?”
“Allen a Dale is my name, good master.”

“Allen a Dale,” Robin repeated, thinking. “Allen a Dale. That name does not sound altogether strange to me. Yes, surely you are the minstrel we have been hearing about lately, whose voice charms all men. Don’t you come from the Dale of Rotherstream, over beyond Stavely?”
“Yes, indeed,” answered Allan. “I do come from there.”
“How old are you, Allan?” said Robin.
“I am only twenty years old.”

“I think you are far too young to be worried by trouble,” said Robin kindly. Then, turning to the others, he cried, “Come, lads, bustle about and get our feast ready. Only you, Will Scarlet, and you, Little John, stay here with me.”

Then, when the others had gone, each man to his own business, Robin turned once more to the youth. “Now, lad,” he said, “tell us your troubles, and speak freely. A flow of words always eases the heart of its sorrows. It is like opening the spillway when the mill pond is too full. Come, sit down beside me and speak at your ease.”

Then the youth poured out everything in his heart to the three yeomen. At first the words came in broken pieces, but they flowed more freely once he saw that everyone was listening closely. He told them how he had come from York to the pleasant valley of the Rother, wandering the countryside as a minstrel and stopping by turns at castles, halls and farmhouses. One sweet evening, he said, he had stopped at a certain broad, low farmhouse and sung for a stout franklin and a maiden as pure and lovely as the first snowdrop of spring. He had played and sung for her, and sweet Ellen o’ the Dale had listened and had come to love him. Then, in a low, soft voice that was barely a whisper, he told how he had watched for her and met her now and then when she went out, but had been too timid in her sweet company to say a word, until at last, on the banks of the Rother, he spoke of his love, and she whispered an answer that set his heartstrings trembling with joy. They broke a sixpence in two between them and swore to be true to each other forever.

Next he told how her father had found out what was going on and had taken her away from him, so that he never saw her again and his heart was sometimes ready to break. He told how this very morning, only a month and a half after he had last seen her, he had heard, and knew it to be true, that she was to marry old Sir Stephen of Trent in two days. Ellen’s father thought it would be a grand thing to have his daughter marry so high, though she did not want it. And no wonder a knight should want to marry his own sweet love, who was the most beautiful maiden in all the world.

The yeomen listened to all this in silence. The clatter of many voices, joking and laughing, sounded around them, and the red light of the fire shone on their faces and in their eyes. The poor boy’s words were so simple and his sorrow so deep that even Little John felt a knotty lump rise in his throat.

“I am not surprised,” said Robin, after a moment’s silence, “that your true love loved you, for you must have a silver cross under your tongue, like good Saint Francis, who could charm the birds of the air with his speech.”

“By the breath of my body,” burst out Little John, trying to hide his feelings with angry words, “I have a great mind to go right now and beat the miserable life out of that vile Sir Stephen. Hold on there, I say, what in the world! Does a withered old man think tender young girls are to be bought like chickens on market day? Shame on him! I—but no matter, only let him look out for himself.”

Then Will Scarlet spoke up. “I think it was badly done of the girl to change so quickly at others’ bidding, especially when it comes to marrying a man as old as this same Sir Stephen. I don’t like it in her, Allan.”

“No,” said Allan hotly, “you are unfair to her. She is as soft and gentle as a dove, and I know her better than anyone alive. She may obey her father, but if she weds Sir Stephen her heart will break and she will die. My own sweet dear, I—” He stopped and shook his head, unable to say more.

While the others were speaking, Robin Hood had been lost in thought. “I think I have a plan that might fit your case, Allan,” he said. “But first tell me, lad, do you think your true love has spirit enough to marry you if you were together in church, the banns published and the priest found, even if her father said no?”
“Yes, indeed she would,” cried Allan eagerly.

“Then, if her father is the man I take him to be, I promise that he will give you both his blessing as husband and wife, in place of old Sir Stephen, on her very wedding morning. But wait, now that I think of it, there is one thing we have not counted on: the priest. Truly, men of the cloth do not love me very much, and when it comes to doing what I want in such a matter, they are likely to prove stubborn. As for the lesser clergy, they are afraid to do me a favor because of their abbot or bishop.”

“Well,” said Will Scarlet, laughing, “as far as that goes, I know a certain friar who, if you could only get on his good side, would do your business even if Pope Joan herself stood up to forbid him. He is known as the Curtal Friar of Fountain Abbey, and he lives in Fountain Dale.”

“But,” said Robin, “Fountain Abbey is a good hundred miles from here. If we are to help this lad, we have no time to go there and back before his true love is married. Nothing can be gained there, cousin.”

“Yes,” said Will Scarlet, laughing again, “but this Fountain Abbey isn’t nearly as far off as the one you’re talking about, uncle. The one I mean is no rich and stately place like that other. It’s a plain little cell, though as snug a spot as any sturdy hermit ever lived in. I know the way well and can guide you there. It’s a good distance, but I think a pair of strong legs could get a man there and back in a single day.”

“Then give me your hand, Allan,” cried Robin, “and listen to me. I swear by the bright hair of Saint AElfrida that two days from now Ellen a Dale will be your wife. Tomorrow I’ll go looking for this Friar of Fountain Abbey, and I promise I’ll get on his good side, even if I have to thump him soft first.”

Will Scarlet laughed again at this. “Don’t be too sure of that, good uncle,” he said. “Still, from what I know of him, I think this Curtal Friar will gladly marry two such fine lovers, especially if there’s good food and drink to follow.”

Just then one of the band came to say that the feast was laid out on the grass. Robin led the way, and the others followed him to the spread. It was a merry meal. Jokes and stories flew around freely, and everyone laughed until the forest rang. Allan laughed along with the rest, for his cheeks glowed with the hope Robin Hood had given him.

At last the feast was over, and Robin Hood turned to Allan, who was sitting beside him. “Now, Allan,” he said, “we’ve heard so much about your singing that we’d like a taste of your skill ourselves. Can’t you give us something?”

“Gladly,” answered Allan at once. He was no third-rate singer who must be begged again and again, but said “yes” or “no” the first time he was asked. So he took up his harp and ran his fingers lightly over the sweet-sounding strings, and a hush fell around the cloth. Then, backing his voice with the music of his harp, he sang:
May Ellen’s wedding
(Telling how a fairy prince loved her and carried her off to his own home.)

“_May Ellen sat beneath a thorn
And in a shower around
The blossoms fell with every breeze
Like snow upon the ground,
And in a linden tree close by
A strange wild bird sang sweet and high.

“O sweet, sweet, sweet, so piercing sweet,
So sweetly long the notes did ring!
May Ellen’s heart grew still and hushed
With joy that was half sting;
Her face turned up, she listened there
As if she’d died in that bright air.

“’Come down from out the blossoms, bird!
Come down from out the tree,
And on my heart I’ll let you lie,
And love you tenderly!’
Thus cried May Ellen, soft and low,
From where the hawthorn shed its snow.

“Down dropped the bird on trembling wing,
From out the blooming tree,
And nestled in her snowy breast.
‘My love! my love!’ cried she;
Then straight home, ’mid sun and flower,
She bore him to her own sweet bower.

“The day has melted into night,
The moon rides o’er the lea,
And in its cold and ghostly light
A youth stands silently:
A youth with beauty strange and rare
Stands in May Ellen’s chamber there.

“He stood upon the cold stone floor
Where moonbeams shimmered pale.
May Ellen stared with wide, scared eyes,
Unable to look away,
For, like a spirit in a dream,
He stood there still, with silent gleam.

“In a low and breathless voice,
‘Where do you come from?’ said she;
‘Are you a creature of a dream,
Or a vision that I see?’
Then soft he spoke, like night winds shiver
Through straining reeds beside the river.

“’A bird I was, on feathered wing,
From far-off Faeryland,
Where gentle waters hum and sing
Beside the golden sand,
Where trees stay green the whole year through;
And there my mother is the queen.’

“May Ellen leaves her room no more
To see the blossoms fair;
But in the hushed and midnight hour
They hear her talking there,
Or, when the moon is shining white,
They hear her singing through the night.

“’Oh, put on your silks and jewels fine,’
May Ellen’s mother said,
‘For here comes the Lord of Lyne
And this lord you must wed.’
May Ellen said, ‘It cannot be.
He’ll never find his wife in me.’

“Up spoke her brother, dark and grim:
‘Now by the bright blue sky,
Before another day goes by
Your wicked bird shall die!
For he has done you bitter harm,
By some strange art or cunning charm.’

“Then, with a sad and mournful song,
Away the bird did fly,
Over the castle eaves, and through
The gray and windy sky.
‘Come forth!’ then cried the brother grim,
‘Why do you gaze so after him?’

“It is May Ellen’s wedding day,
The sky is clear and blue,
And lords and ladies, bright and gay,
Fill up the church pews, too.
The bridegroom was Sir Hugh the Bold,
Dressed all in silk and cloth of gold.

“The bride walked in, in samite white,
A wreath upon her hair;
Her eyes were fixed in a glassy stare,
Her face was deathly fair,
And standing in the crowded hall,
She sang a wild and wondrous call.

“Then came a strange and rushing sound
Such as a coming wind will bring,
And in the open windows shot
Nine swans on whistling wing,
And high above the heads they flew,
In gleaming flight the darkness through.

“Round May Ellen’s head they sped
In wide and windy flight,
And three times circled, wheeling round;
The guests all shrank in fright,
And the priest beside the altar there
Crossed himself with muttered prayer.

“But when they wheeled the third time round,
Fair Ellen was not there,
And where she stood, upon the ground,
A snow-white swan stood fair.
With a wild and lovely cry,
It joined the winged throng in the sky.

“There are old men who’ve been at weddings
For sixty years and more,
But such a wondrous wedding day
They never saw before.
But none could check and none could stay
The swans that bore the bride away_.”

Not a sound broke the stillness when Allan a Dale had finished. Everyone sat gazing at the handsome singer, for his voice and music were so sweet that each man held his breath, afraid that one more drop might fall and he would miss it.

“By my faith and my word,” said Robin at last, drawing a deep breath, “lad, you are—you must not leave our company, Allan! Won’t you stay with us here in the sweet green forest? Truly, I feel my heart going out to you with great love.”
Then Allan took Robin’s hand and kissed it. “I will stay with you always, dear master,” he said, “for I have never known such kindness as you have shown me today.”
Then Will Scarlet held out his hand and shook Allan’s as a sign of friendship, and Little John did the same. And so the famous Allan a Dale became one of Robin Hood’s band.

chapters.title: Robin Hood Seeks the Curtal Friar
paragraphs: The sturdy yeomen of Sherwood Forest were always early risers in the morning, especially once summer had come, for then, in the freshness of dawn, the dew shone at its brightest and the small birds sang their sweetest.

Said Robin, “Now I’m going to look for that Friar of Fountain Abbey we talked about last night. I’ll take four of my good men with me: Little John, Will Scarlet, David of Doncaster, and Arthur a Bland. The rest of you stay here, and Will Stutely will be your chief while I’m gone.” Then Robin Hood promptly put on a fine steel coat of chain mail, and over it a light jacket of Lincoln green. On his head he clapped a steel cap, and over that he pulled one of soft white leather, with a nodding cock’s plume stuck in it. At his side he hung a good broadsword of tempered steel, its bluish blade engraved all over with strange figures of dragons, winged women, and who knows what else. Robin made a gallant sight dressed like that, I can tell you, with the glint of steel showing here and there whenever the sunlight caught the links of polished mail beneath his green coat.

Once he was dressed, he and the four yeomen set off on their way, with Will Scarlet in front, since he knew better than the others where to go. Mile after mile they strode along, crossing a rushing stream, then following a sunny road, then going down some lovely forest path where the trees met overhead in a green, rustling canopy, and at the end of which a herd of startled deer bolted away with a rattle of leaves and a crackle of branches. On they walked with song and joking and laughter until noon was past, and at last they reached the banks of a wide, glassy stream covered with lily pads. Here a broad, well-trodden path ran along beside the water. On this path the horses had labored, pulling slow barges loaded with barley meal and other goods from the countryside to the many-towered town. But now, in the hot silence of midday, there was no horse to be seen, and no man except themselves. The river stretched out behind them and ahead of them, its calm surface ruffled here and there by the purple shadow of a small breeze.

“Now, good uncle,” said Will Scarlet at last, when they had walked a long while beside this sweet, bright river, “just past that bend ahead of us is a shallow ford that’s nowhere deeper than your mid-thigh. On the other side of the stream there’s a little hermitage hidden in the tangled thickets, and that is where the Friar of Fountain Dale lives. I’ll lead you there, for I know the way, though it isn’t very hard to find.”

“No,” said jolly Robin, stopping suddenly, “if I’d known I’d have to wade through water, even a stream as clear as this one, I would have put on different clothes. But never mind now, for after all, a wetting won’t wash the skin off, and what must be, must be. But you lads stay here, for I’d like to enjoy this merry adventure alone. Still, listen well, and if you hear me blow my bugle horn, come quickly.” With that, he turned and left them, striding on alone.

Robin had gone no farther than the place where the bend of the road hid his good men from view when he stopped suddenly, for he thought he heard voices. He stood still and listened, and soon he heard words passing back and forth between what seemed to be two men, though the two voices were strangely alike. The sound came from behind the bank, which was steep and high here, dropping some ten feet from the edge of the road to the reedy shore of the river.

“That’s strange,” Robin muttered to himself after a while, when the voices had stopped talking. “Surely two people were speaking to each other, and yet their voices sound very much alike. I swear I’ve never heard anything like it in all my life. Truly, if these two are to be judged by their voices, no two peas were ever more alike. I’ll look into this.” With that, he crept softly to the river bank, lay down on the grass, and peered over the edge at what was below.

It was cool and shady beneath the bank. A sturdy willow grew there, not straight up but leaning out across the water, shading the spot with its soft leaves. All around grew a mass of feathery ferns, the kind that hide and nestle in cool places, and up to Robin’s nose came the sweet smell of wild thyme, which loves the damp edges of running streams. There, with his broad back against the rough trunk of the willow tree, half hidden by the soft ferns around him, sat a stout, brawny fellow, but there was no other man in sight. His head was as round as a ball, covered with a mat of close-cropped, curly black hair that grew low on his forehead. But the top of his head was shaved as smooth as the palm of your hand, and that, together with his loose robe, hood, and string of beads, showed what his looks never would have: that he was a friar. His cheeks were as red and shiny as a winter crab apple, though they were nearly covered by a thick curly black beard, which also covered his chin and upper lip. His neck was thick like a north country bull’s, and his round head sat snugly on shoulders that were a match even for Little John’s. Beneath his bushy black brows danced a pair of small gray eyes that could not keep still for sheer fun. No one could look into his face without feeling his heartstrings tickled by the merriment in those eyes. Beside him lay a steel cap, which he had taken off to cool his head. His legs were stretched wide apart, and between his knees he held a great pie made of juicy meats of many kinds, seasoned with tender young onions, with both meat and onions mixed in a good rich gravy. In his right fist he held a big piece of brown crust, which he munched on sturdily, and every now and then he thrust his left hand into the pie and pulled it out full of meat. From time to time he took a mighty swig from a big bottle of Malmsey that lay beside him.

“Upon my word,” said Robin to himself, “this must be the merriest feast, the merriest fellow, the merriest spot, and the merriest sight in all merry England. I thought there was someone else down there, but it must have been this holy man talking to himself.”

So Robin lay watching the Friar, and the Friar, not knowing that anyone was looking down at him, calmly ate his meal. At last he was finished, and after wiping his greasy hands on the ferns and wild thyme (no king in all the world ever had a sweeter napkin), he picked up his flask and began talking to himself as though he were another man, and answering himself as though he were somebody else.

“Dear lad, you are the sweetest fellow in all the world. I love you as a lover loves his lass. Goodness, you make me ashamed to speak so to me in this lonely place, with nobody around, and yet if you want me to say so, I do love you as you love me. Well then, won’t you take a drink of good Malmsey? After you, lad, after you. No, I beg you, sweeten the drink with your lips (here he passed the flask from his right hand to his left). If you’re going to press it on me like that, I have to do as you ask, though I’m all the happier to do it as I drink your very good health (here he took a long, deep swallow). And now, sweet lad, it’s your turn next (here he passed the bottle from his left hand back to his right). I’ll take it, sweet chuck, and here’s wishing you as much good as you wish me.” Saying this, he took another swallow, and truly he drank enough for two.

All this time merry Robin lay on the bank and listened, and his belly shook so hard with laughter that he had to press his palm over his mouth to keep it from bursting out. For truly, he would not have spoiled such a fine joke for half of Nottinghamshire.

After catching his breath from his last swallow, the Friar started talking again. “Now, sweet lad, can’t you sing me a song? Oh, I don’t know, my voice is poor today, so please don’t ask me. Can’t you hear me croaking like a frog? No, no, your voice is as sweet as any bullfinch’s. Come, sing, I beg you. I would rather hear you sing than eat a fine feast. Alas, I would rather not sing in front of someone who can whistle so well and has heard so many fine songs and ballads. Still, if you insist, I will do my best.
