But now I think you and I could sing a pretty song together. Don’t you know a certain dainty little round called ‘The Loving Youth and the Scornful Maid’? Why, I think I have heard it before. Then don’t you think you could take the girl’s part if I take the boy’s? I don’t know, but I will try. You begin with the boy’s part and I will follow with the girl’s.”
Then he sang first in a deep, gruff voice and then in a high, squeaky one, and cheerfully rattled off the merry round of
The loving youth and the scornful maid

“_Ah, will you come with me, my love?
And will you, love, be mine?
For I will give you, my love,
Gay knots and ribbons so fine.
I’ll woo you, love, on bended knee,
And I’ll play sweet songs for you alone.
So it’s hark! hark! hark!
To the soaring lark,
And it’s hark to the cooing dove!
The bright daffodil
Grows down by the rill,
So come and be my love.

SHE
“Now get away from me, young man so fine;
Now get away, I say;
My true love will never be thine,
So you had better not stay.
You’re not a fine enough lad for me,
So I’ll wait till a better young man I see.
For it’s hark! hark! hark!
To the soaring lark,
And it’s hark to the cooing dove!
The bright daffodil
Grows down by the rill,
Yet I’ll never be your love.

HE
“Then I’ll go and look for another fair she,
For many a maid can be found,
And since you will have nothing of me,
To you I’ll never be bound.
No blossom in the field is ever so rare
That others can’t be found just as fair.
So it’s hark! hark! hark!
To the joyous lark,
And it’s hark to the cooing dove!
The bright daffodil
Grows down by the rill,
And I’ll find me another dear love.

SHE
“Young man, don’t turn away so quick
Another fair lass to find.
I think I spoke in haste today,
And I haven’t made up my mind,

And if you’ll only stay with me,
I’ll love no other, sweet lad, but you_.”

At this Robin could hold himself in no longer and burst into a mighty roar of laughter. Then, as the holy Friar went on with the song, he joined in the chorus, and together they sang, or rather, you might say, bellowed:

“_So it’s hark! hark! hark!
To the joyous lark,
And it’s hark to the cooing dove!
For the bright daffodil
Grows down by the rill,
And I’ll be your own true love_.”

So they sang together. The stout Friar seemed not to have heard Robin laugh, and he seemed not to know that the yeoman had joined the song. With his eyes half closed, staring straight ahead and wagging his round head from side to side in time to the music, he carried on bravely to the end, and he and Robin finished with a roar that could have been heard a mile away. But no sooner was the last word sung than the holy man snatched up his steel cap, clapped it on his head, jumped to his feet, and shouted in a great voice, “What spy is this? Come out, you limb of evil, and I will carve you into as fine a pudding meat as any wife in Yorkshire ever cooked on a Sunday.” With that he pulled a great broadsword from under his robes, every bit as stout as Robin’s.

“No, put away your pinking iron, friend,” said Robin, standing up with tears of laughter still on his cheeks. “Folk who have sung so sweetly together should not fight afterward.” Then he leaped down the bank to where the other stood. “I tell you, friend,” he said, “my throat is as dry from that song as any barley stubble in October. Do you happen to have any Malmsey left in that stout flask?”

“Truly,” said the Friar in a sour voice, “you help yourself freely where you are not invited. Still, I trust I am too good a Christian to refuse a drink to any man who is thirsty. Such as there is of it, you are welcome to a drink.” And he held the flask out to Robin.

Robin took it without another word, put it to his lips, and tilted his head back, while what was inside said “glug!” “lug! glug!” for more than three winks, I can tell you. The stout Friar watched Robin anxiously all the while, and when he was done he snatched the flask back. He shook it, held it between his eyes and the light, gave the yeoman a reproachful look, and promptly put it to his own lips. When it came away again, there was nothing left in it.
“Do you know the country around here, you good and holy man?” asked Robin, laughing.
“Yes, somewhat,” answered the other dryly.
“And do you know of a certain place called Fountain Abbey?”
“Yes, somewhat.”
“Then perhaps you also know of a certain man who goes by the name of the Curtal Friar of Fountain Abbey.”
“Yes, somewhat.”
“Well, then, my good fellow, holy father, whatever you may be,” said Robin, “tell me this: is that same Friar to be found on this bank of the river, or on the far one?”
“That,” said the Friar, “is a practical question that the subtle rules of logic do not touch. I advise you to find it out with your own five senses: sight, feeling, and what not.”
“I very much wish,” said Robin, looking thoughtfully at the stout priest, “to cross that ford and try to find this same good Friar.”
“Truly,” said the other piously, “that is a fine wish in one so young. Far be it from me to hold you back from so holy a quest. Friend, the river is free to all.”

“Yes, good father,” said Robin, “but you see that my clothes are of the finest, and I would rather not get them wet. I think your shoulders are stout and broad. Couldn’t you find it in your heart to carry me across?”

“Now, by the white hand of the holy Lady of the Fountain!” burst out the Friar in a mighty rage, “do you, you poor puny stripling, you kiss-my-lady-la popinjay, you—you—what shall I call you? Do you ask me, the holy Tuck, to carry you? Now I swear—” Here he suddenly stopped, and then slowly the anger left his face, and his little eyes twinkled once more. “But why should I not?” he said piously.

“Didn’t the holy Saint Christopher once carry the stranger across the river? And should I, a poor sinner, be ashamed to do the same? Come with me, stranger, and I will do as you ask in a humble frame of mind.” With these words he clambered up the bank, with Robin close behind, and led the way to the shallow, pebbly ford, chuckling to himself all the while as though he were enjoying some fine joke inside.

When they reached the ford, he hitched his robes up around his waist, tucked his good broadsword under his arm, and bent his back so that Robin could climb on. Suddenly he straightened up. “I think,” he said, “you will get your weapon wet. Let me tuck it under my arm along with my own.”
“Oh, there’s no need, good father,” said Robin. “I would load you with nothing of mine except myself.”
“Do you think,” said the Friar mildly, “that the good Saint Christopher would have sought his own ease like that? No, give me your tool as I tell you, for I would carry it as a penance for my pride.”

At this, without another word, Robin Hood unbuckled his sword from his side and handed it to the other, who thrust it under his arm with his own. Then the Friar bent his back once more, and when Robin had climbed on, he stepped sturdily into the water and strode onward, splashing through the shallows and breaking the smooth surface into ever-widening rings. At last he reached the other side, and Robin leaped lightly from his back.
“Many thanks, good father,” he said. “You are indeed a good and holy man. Please give me my sword and let me go, for I am in a hurry.”

At this the stout Friar looked at Robin for a long time, with his head on one side and a most waggish twist to his face. Then he slowly winked his right eye. “No, good youth,” he said gently, “I don’t doubt that you are in a hurry with your affairs, but you think nothing of mine. Yours are of a worldly nature; mine are spiritual, a holy work, so to speak. Moreover, my affairs lie on the other side of this stream. I can see from your search for this same holy recluse that you are a good young man and very respectful to the cloth. I got wet coming here, and I am sadly afraid that if I wade the water again I might get certain cricks and pains in the joints that would spoil my devotions for many a day to come. I know that since I have so humbly done your bidding, you will carry me back again. You see how Saint Godrick, the holy hermit whose birthday this is, has put two swords in my hands and not one in yours. So be persuaded, good youth, and carry me back again.”

Robin Hood looked up and he looked down, biting his lower lip. “You cunning Friar,” he said, “you have me fair and square. Let me tell you that no man of your cloth has ever tricked me like this in all my life. I might have known from your looks that you were no such holy man as you pretended to be.”
“No,” the Friar broke in, “and I tell you not to talk so abusively either, or you may feel the prick of an inch or so of blue steel.”

“Tut, tut,” said Robin, “don’t talk like that, Friar. The loser always has the right to use his tongue as he pleases. Give me my sword. I promise to carry you back at once. No, I will not raise the weapon against you.”
“Well, well,” said the Friar, “I don’t fear you, fellow. Here is your skewer, and get yourself ready right away, for I want to hurry back.”
Robin took back his sword and strapped it on. Then he stooped his sturdy back and hoisted the Friar up onto it.

Now, I can tell you, Robin Hood had a heavier load to carry in the Friar than the Friar had in him. What is more, he did not know the ford, so he went stumbling among the stones, now stepping into a deep hole and now nearly tripping over a boulder, while sweat ran down his face in beads from the hard going and the weight of his load. Meanwhile the Friar kept digging his heels into Robin’s sides, telling him to hurry and calling him many bad names. To all this Robin answered never a word. Instead he softly felt around until he found the buckle of the belt that held the Friar’s sword, and slyly worked at the fastenings to loosen them. So by the time he reached the other bank with his load, the Friar’s sword belt was loose, though the Friar did not know it. When Robin stood on dry land and the Friar leaped from his back, the yeoman grabbed the sword, and blade, sheath, and strap all came away from the holy man, leaving him without a weapon.

“Now then,” said merry Robin, panting as he spoke and wiping the sweat from his brow, “I have you, fellow. This time that same saint you spoke of just now has put two swords in my hands and stripped yours away from you. Now if you don’t carry me back, and quickly, I swear I will prick your skin until it is as full of holes as a slashed doublet.”

The good Friar said nothing for a while, but gave Robin a grim look. “Now,” he said at last, “I thought your wits were of the heavy sort, and I did not know you were so cunning. Truly, you have me beaten. Give me my sword, and I promise not to draw it against you except in self-defense. I also promise to do as you say and take you on my back and carry you.”

So jolly Robin gave him his sword again, and the Friar buckled it to his side, this time making sure the fastenings were more secure. Then he tucked up his robes once more, took Robin Hood on his back, and without a word stepped into the water and waded on in silence while Robin sat laughing on his back. At last he reached the middle of the ford, where the water was deepest. There he stopped for a moment, and then, with a sudden lift of his hand and heave of his shoulders, he flung Robin clean over his head as if he were a sack of grain.
Down went Robin into the water with a mighty splash. “There,” said the holy man, turning calmly back toward the shore, “maybe that will cool your hot temper.”

Meanwhile, after much splashing, Robin had gotten to his feet and stood gazing around, all bewildered, with the water running off him in pretty little streams. At last he shook the water out of his ears and spat some out of his mouth, and when he had gathered his scattered wits, he saw the stout Friar standing on the bank, laughing. Then, I can tell you, Robin Hood was a madman. “Stay there, you villain!” he roared. “I’m coming after you right now, and if I don’t carve your brawn for you this day, may I never lift a finger again!” With that he dashed, splashing, to the bank.

“You needn’t hurry yourself too much,” said the stout Friar. “Don’t worry, I will wait right here, and if you don’t cry ‘Alack-a-day’ before long, may I never again peep through the brush at a fallow deer.”

And now Robin, having reached the bank, began without another word to roll his sleeves up above his wrists. The Friar also tucked his robes up around him, showing a great, stout arm on which the muscles stood out like the knobs of an ancient tree. Then Robin saw what he had not known before: the Friar also had a coat of chain mail under his gown.
“Look to yourself,” cried Robin, drawing his good sword.

“Aye, indeed,” said the Friar, who already held his in his hand. And with that they came together, and a fierce and mighty battle began. Right and left, up and down, and back and forth they fought. The swords flashed in the sun and then met with a clash that sounded far and near. I can tell you this was no playful bout at quarterstaff, but a grim and serious fight in real earnest. They struggled for an hour or more, stopping every now and then to rest, and each time each looked at the other with wonder and thought he had never seen so stout a fellow. Then once again they would go at it more fiercely than ever. Yet in all this time neither had hurt the other or drawn his blood. At last merry Robin cried, “Hold your hand, good friend!” and both lowered their swords.

“Now I’d like to ask a favor before we start again,” said Robin, wiping the sweat from his forehead. They had fought so long that he had begun to feel it would be a poor thing either to be struck down himself or to strike down so sturdy and brave a man.
“What do you want from me?” asked the Friar.
“Only this,” said Robin. “Let me blow my bugle horn three times.”

The Friar knit his brows and looked sharply at Robin Hood. “I truly think you have some sly trick in mind,” he said. “Even so, I’m not afraid of you, and I’ll grant your wish, provided you let me blow three times on this little whistle.”
“Gladly,” said Robin, “so here goes the first.” With that, he lifted his silver horn to his lips and blew three clear, high notes.

Meanwhile the Friar stood watching closely for whatever might happen. In his fingers he held a pretty silver whistle, the kind knights use to call their hawks back to their wrists. It always hung from his belt alongside his rosary.

The echo of Robin’s last note had barely come winding back from across the river when four tall men in Lincoln green came running around the bend in the road. Each had a bow in his hand and an arrow already fitted to the string.

“Aha! So that’s how it is, you treacherous rascal!” cried the Friar. “Then, by my faith, look out for yourself!” With that, he put the hawk’s whistle straight to his lips and blew a loud, shrill blast. At once the bushes along the far side of the road began to crackle, and out of the thicket burst four great shaggy hounds. “After him, Sweet Lips! After him, Bell Throat! After him, Beauty! After him, Fangs!” cried the Friar, pointing at Robin.

It was lucky for that yeoman that a tree stood close by the road, or he would have fared badly. Quicker than you could say “Gaffer Downthedale,” the hounds were on him. He had just time to drop his sword and spring up into the tree, and the hounds gathered around its foot, staring up at him as if he were a cat on a roof. But the Friar soon called off his dogs. “After them!” he cried, pointing down the road to where the yeomen stood frozen, amazed at what they saw. As a hawk dives on its prey, the four dogs raced at the yeomen. But when the four men saw the hounds coming, all of them except Will Scarlet drew their goose-feather arrows back to their ears and let fly.

Now the old ballad tells of a marvelous thing that happened here. It says that each dog that was shot at sprang lightly aside, and as the arrow whistled past, caught it in his mouth and bit it in two. It would have gone badly for those four good fellows if Will Scarlet had not stepped in front of the others and met the hounds as they came charging. “Why, what is this, Fangs!” he cried sternly. “Down, Beauty! Down, you rascal! What does this mean?”

At the sound of his voice every dog shrank back, then came straight to him, licking his hands and fawning on him, as dogs do when they meet someone they know. Then the four yeomen came forward, with the hounds leaping happily around Will Scarlet. “Well, now!” cried the sturdy Friar. “What does this mean? Are you a wizard, to turn these wolves into lambs? Ha!” he cried, as they came still nearer. “Can I believe my eyes? What is young Master William Gamwell doing in such company?”

“No, Tuck,” said the young man, as the four came up to where Robin was now climbing down from the tree he had been perched in, having seen that the danger was over for the moment. “No, Tuck, my name is no longer Will Gamwell but Will Scarlet. And this is my good uncle, Robin Hood, with whom I am staying just now.”

“Truly, good master,” said the Friar, looking rather ashamed and holding out his big hand to Robin, “I’ve often heard your name, both sung and spoken, but I never thought to meet you in a fight. I beg your pardon, and I’m not surprised I found you such a tough man to face.”

“Truly, most holy father,” said Little John, “I have never been more thankful in all my life that our good friend Scarlet knew you and your dogs. I tell you in earnest, I felt my heart melt away when I saw my arrow miss its mark and those great beasts of yours coming straight at me.”
“You may well be thankful, friend,” said the Friar gravely. “But Master Will, how is it that you are living in Sherwood now?”
“Why, Tuck, don’t you know about my bad luck with my father’s steward?” answered Scarlet.
“Yes, indeed, but I didn’t know you were in hiding because of it. By my faith, the times are all upside down when a gentleman must hide for so small a thing.”
“But we’re wasting time,” said Robin, “and I still have to find that Curtal Friar.”
“Why, uncle, you don’t have far to go,” said Will Scarlet, pointing at the Friar, “for there he stands beside you.”
“What?” said Robin. “Are you the man I’ve gone to such trouble to find all day, and been ducked in the water for?”
“Why, truly,” said the Friar with a straight face, “some call me the Curtal Friar of Fountain Dale. Others call me, as a joke, the Abbot of Fountain Abbey. And others again call me plain Friar Tuck.”

“I like the last name best,” said Robin, “for it slips off the tongue more easily. But why didn’t you tell me you were the man I was looking for, instead of sending me off to hunt for black moonbeams?”
“Why, truly, you never asked me, good master,” said sturdy Tuck. “But what did you want of me?”
“Well,” said Robin, “the day is getting late, and we can’t stand here talking any longer. Come back with us to Sherwood, and I’ll explain everything as we go.”
So without any more delay they all set off, with the big dogs at their heels, and made their way back to Sherwood. But it was long after dark before they reached the greenwood tree.
Listen on, for next I will tell you how Robin Hood won happiness for two young lovers, with the help of the jolly Friar Tuck of Fountain Dale.

chapters.title: Robin Hood Compasses a Marriage
paragraphs: And now the morning had come when fair Ellen was to be married, the morning on which merry Robin had sworn that Allan a Dale should, as it were, eat from the dish that had been prepared for Sir Stephen of Trent. Robin Hood got up cheerful and gay, and all his merry men got up too, and last of all got up sturdy Friar Tuck, blinking the sleep out of his eyes. Then, while the air seemed to overflow with the songs of many birds all mingled together and rejoicing in the misty morning, each man washed his face and hands in the leaping brook, and so the day began.

“Now,” said Robin, when they had eaten breakfast and every man had had his fill, “it is time for us to set out on the business we have in hand for today. I will pick twenty of my good men to go with me, for I may need help. And you, Will Scarlet, will stay here and be the leader while I’m gone.” Then Robin went through the whole band, every man crowding forward, eager to be chosen, and called out the ones he wanted by name until he had twenty sturdy fellows, the very pick of his yeomen. Besides Little John and Will Stutely, nearly all those famous lads I have already told you about were among them. Then, while those chosen ran off in high spirits to arm themselves with bow and arrows and broadsword, Robin Hood stepped aside into the thicket and put on a gaudy, beribboned coat like one a wandering minstrel might wear. He slung a harp across his shoulder to play the part better.
The whole band stared, and many laughed, for they had never seen their master dressed in such a fanciful way.

“Truly,” said Robin, holding out his arms and looking down at himself, “I do think it’s a bit of a bright, gaudy, grasshopper outfit. But it’s a pretty thing all the same, and it suits my looks well enough, even though I’m only wearing it for the occasion. But wait, Little John. Here are two bags I want you to carry in your pouch for safekeeping. I can’t very well look after them myself under this motley.”
“Why, master,” said Little John, taking the bags and weighing them in his hand, “I hear the clink of gold in here.”

“Well, what if there is?” said Robin. “It’s my own money, and the band is none the worse for what’s in there. Come, get moving, lads,” and he turned quickly away. “Get ready at once.” Then he gathered the twenty into a tight group, with Allan a Dale and Friar Tuck in the middle, and led them out of the forest shade and on their way.

So they walked on for a long time until they had left Sherwood and come to the vale of Rotherstream. Here the sights were different from those in the forest: hedgerows, broad fields of barley, pastures rolling upward until they met the sky and dotted all over with flocks of white sheep, and hayfields that sent up the smell of new-mown hay lying in smooth rows, over which the swifts skimmed in rapid flight. All this they saw, and it was different, I know, from the tangled depths of the sweet woodlands, but just as lovely. So Robin led his band, walking cheerfully with his chest out and his head thrown back, breathing in the scents of the gentle breeze drifting in from the hayfields.

“Truly,” he said, “the dear world is as fair here as in the woodland shade. Who calls it a vale of tears? I think it is only the darkness in our own minds that brings gloom to the world. For what does that merry song you sing, Little John, say? Doesn’t it go like this?

“_When my love’s eyes shine on mine, on mine,
And when her lips smile so sweet,
The day is merry and fine, so fine,
Whether it’s wet or it’s fair.
And when the good ale is flowing so fast,
Our sorrows and troubles are things of the past_.”

“No,” said Friar Tuck piously, “you think of worldly things and nothing else. Yet truly, there are better protections against care and woe than ale drinking and bright eyes, namely fasting and meditation. Look at me. Do I look like a sorrowful man?”
At this, a roar of laughter went up on every side, because the night before, the hearty Friar had drained twice as many mugs of ale as any other man in the band.
“Truly,” said Robin, when he could speak for laughing, “I’d say your sorrows are about equal to your holiness.”

So they strode along, talking, singing, joking, and laughing, until they came to a certain little church that belonged to the great estates of the rich Priory of Emmet. This was where fair Ellen was to be married that morning, and this was the place the yeomen had been heading for. Across the road from the church, which stood among waving fields of barley, ran a stone wall. On the far side of the wall from the highway was a fringe of young trees and bushes, and here and there the wall itself was covered with a mass of blossoming woodbine, which filled the warm air far and wide with its sweet summer scent. Then the yeomen promptly leaped over the wall and landed on the tall, soft grass on the other side, scaring a flock of sheep lying in the shade so that they scattered in every direction. Here was sweet, cool shade from the wall and from the fair young trees and bushes, and here the yeomen sat down, glad enough to rest after their long tramp that morning.

“Now,” said Robin, “I want one of you to keep watch and tell me when he sees anyone coming to the church, and the one I choose is young David of Doncaster. So climb up on the wall, David, and hide under the woodbine to keep watch.”

So young David did as he was told, while the others stretched out at full length on the grass, some talking together and others sleeping. Then everything was quiet, except for the low voices of those who were talking, and Allan’s restless footsteps as he paced up and down, for his heart was so troubled that he could not stand still, and also except for the mellow snoring of Friar Tuck, who enjoyed his sleep with a noise like someone very slowly sawing soft wood. Robin lay on his back and gazed up into the leaves of the trees, his thoughts miles away, and so a long time passed.
Then Robin spoke up. “Now tell us, young David of Doncaster, what do you see?”
David replied, “I see the white clouds drifting by, I feel the wind blowing, and three black crows are flying across the open land. But nothing else do I see, good master.”
So silence fell again, and more time passed, broken only as I have said, until Robin grew impatient and spoke again. “Now tell me, young David, what do you see this time?”
David answered, “I see the windmills turning, three tall poplars swaying against the sky, and a flock of fieldfares winging over the hill. But I see nothing else, good master.”

More time slipped by, until Robin finally asked young David again what he could see. This time David said, “I hear the cuckoo singing, and the wind is rolling waves through the barley. And now an old friar is coming over the hill toward the church, with a great bunch of keys in his hands. Look! He’s reached the church door.”

Then Robin Hood stood up and shook Friar Tuck by the shoulder. “Come, wake up, holy man!” he cried. With much grunting, sturdy Tuck got to his feet. “Get moving, by my faith,” said Robin, “for there, in the church door, is one of your own kind. Go and talk to him, and get yourself into the church so that you’ll be there when you’re needed. Meanwhile, Little John, Will Stutely, and I will follow you shortly.”

So Friar Tuck scrambled over the wall and crossed the road to the church. There the old friar was still wrestling with the big key, since the lock was somewhat rusty and he was somewhat old and feeble.
“Hello, brother,” said Tuck, “let me help you.” With that, he took the key from the other’s hand and quickly opened the door with a single turn.
“Who are you, good brother?” asked the old friar in a high, wheezing voice. “Where do you come from, and where are you going?” And he winked and blinked at sturdy Friar Tuck like an owl at the sun.

“Here is my answer to your questions, brother,” said the other. “My name is Tuck, and I will go no farther than this spot, if you will only let me stay while the wedding goes on. I come from Fountain Dale, and I am, you might say, a poor hermit, for I live in a cell beside the fountain blessed by the holy Saint Ethelrada. But if I have heard right, there is to be a gay wedding here today. So if you don’t mind, I would like to rest in the cool shade inside, because I would love to see the sight.”

“You are welcome indeed, brother,” said the old man, and he led the way inside. Meanwhile Robin Hood, disguised as a harper, had reached the church with Little John and Will Stutely. Robin sat down on a bench beside the door, but Little John, carrying the two bags of gold, went inside, and so did Will Stutely.

So Robin sat by the door, watching the road in both directions to see who might come. After a while he saw six horsemen riding up slowly and solemnly, as suited them, for they were churchmen of high rank. When they drew nearer, Robin saw who they were and recognized them. The first was the Bishop of Hereford, and I can tell you he made a fine show. His robes were of the richest silk, and around his neck hung a handsome chain of beaten gold. The cap covering his shaved crown was black velvet, and its edges were lined with rows of jewels, each set in gold, that sparkled in the sunlight. His stockings were flame-colored silk, and his shoes were black velvet, with long pointed toes that curled up and were fastened to his knees, and a cross of gold thread was embroidered on the top of each foot. Beside the Bishop, on a prancing little horse, rode the Prior of Emmet. His clothes were rich too, but not as showy as the stout Bishop’s. Behind them came two of the senior brothers of Emmet, and behind those, two of the Bishop’s servants. The Lord Bishop of Hereford tried to look as much like a great baron as a man in holy orders possibly could.

When Robin saw this company approaching, with the flash of jewels and silk and the jingle of silver bells on the horses’ harness, he scowled at them. He said to himself, “That Bishop is far too showy for a holy man. I wonder whether his patron saint, who I think was Saint Thomas, wore golden chains around his neck, silk clothes on his body, and pointed shoes on his feet. God knows the money for all of it was squeezed out of poor tenants by their sweat. Bishop, Bishop, your pride may take a fall before you know it.”

So the holy men arrived at the church, with the Bishop and the Prior joking and laughing together about some pretty ladies, in words that suited laymen better, I think, than holy clerks. Then they dismounted, and the Bishop looked around and soon noticed Robin standing in the doorway. “Hello there, my good fellow,” he said in a cheerful voice. “Who are you, strutting about in such fine feathers?”

“I am a harper from the north country,” said Robin, “and I can play the strings, I tell you, as no other man in all merry England can. Truly, good Lord Bishop, many a knight and townsman, clerk and layman, has danced to my music whether he liked it or not, and most of the time very much against his will. Such is the magic of my harping. Now today, my Lord Bishop, if I may play at this wedding, I promise I will make the fair bride love the man she marries, with a love that will last as long as the two of them live together.”

“Ha! Is that so?” cried the Bishop. “Do you really mean it?” And he looked hard at Robin, who looked boldly back into his eyes. “Now, if you can make this girl love the man she is to marry, as you say you can (she has truly bewitched my poor cousin Stephen), I will give you anything you ask, within reason. Let me have a taste of your skill, fellow.”
“No,” said Robin, “my music does not come unless I choose, not even at a lord bishop’s command. Truly, I will not play until the bride and bridegroom arrive.”
“You are a saucy rascal to speak that way to a man of my rank,” said the Bishop, frowning at Robin. “Still, I must put up with you. Look, Prior, here comes our cousin Sir Stephen with his lady love.”

Now, around the bend of the highroad came more riders on horseback. First of all was a tall, thin man with the bearing of a knight, dressed entirely in black silk, wearing a black velvet cap trimmed with scarlet. Robin looked, and had no doubt this was Sir Stephen, both because he carried himself like a knight and because of his gray hair. Beside him rode a stout Saxon landowner, Ellen’s father, Edward of Deirwold. Behind the two came a litter carried by two horses, and in it was a maiden who Robin knew must be Ellen. Behind the litter rode six men-at-arms, the sun flashing on their steel caps as they jingled up the dusty road.

So these riders also came to the church, and there Sir Stephen jumped from his horse, went to the litter, and helped fair Ellen out. Then Robin Hood looked at her, and he could no longer wonder how a knight as proud as Sir Stephen of Trent came to want to marry a common farmer’s daughter. Nor did he wonder that no fuss had been made over it, for she was the loveliest maiden he had ever seen. But now she was pale and drooping, like a white lily snapped at the stem. With her head bowed and a sorrowful look, she went into the church, with Sir Stephen leading her by the hand.
“Why don’t you play, fellow?” said the Bishop, glaring at Robin.
“Well,” said Robin calmly, “I will play far better than Your Lordship expects, but not until the right time has come.”
The Bishop said to himself, glowering at Robin, “When this wedding is over, I will have this fellow soundly whipped for his saucy tongue and bold talk.”

Now fair Ellen and Sir Stephen stood before the altar, and the Bishop himself came in his robes and opened his book. At this, fair Ellen looked up and around her in bitter despair, like a fawn that finds the hounds at its heels. Then Robin Hood, in all his fluttering tags and ribbons of red and yellow, strode forward. He took three steps away from the pillar he had been leaning on, and stood between the bride and the bridegroom.

“Let me look at this girl,” he said in a loud voice. “Well, now! What have we here? There are lilies in her cheeks, not the roses that suit a bonny bride. This is no proper wedding. You, Sir Knight, so old, and she so young, and you think to make her your wife? I tell you it cannot be, for you are not her own true love.”

At this everyone stood amazed. They did not know where to look or what to think or say, for they were all bewildered by what was happening. While they all stared at Robin as if turned to stone, he put his bugle horn to his lips and blew three blasts, so loud and clear that they echoed from floor to rafters as if sounded by the trumpet of doom. Then Little John and Will Stutely came leaping out at once, stood on either side of Robin Hood, and quickly drew their broadswords. Meanwhile a mighty voice rolled over everyone’s heads, “Here I am, good master, whenever you want me!” For it was Friar Tuck calling from the organ loft.

Now everything was uproar and noise. Stout Edward strode forward in a rage and would have grabbed his daughter to drag her away, but Little John stepped between them and shoved him back. “Stand back, old man,” he said. “You are a hobbled horse today.”
“Down with the villains!” cried Sir Stephen, and he felt for his sword, but it was not at his side, since it was his wedding day.

Then the men-at-arms drew their swords, and it looked as if blood would soon wet the stones. But suddenly there was a commotion at the door and loud voices, steel flashed in the light, and the crash of blows rang out. The men-at-arms fell back, and up the aisle came leaping eighteen stout yeomen, all dressed in Lincoln green, with Allan a Dale at their head. In his hand he carried Robin Hood’s good, stout, trusty bow of yew, and he gave it to Robin, kneeling on one knee as he did so.
Then Edward of Deirwold spoke up in a deep voice of anger. “Is it you, Allan a Dale, who has stirred up all this trouble in a church?”
“No,” said merry Robin, “I did that, and I don’t care who knows it, for my name is Robin Hood.”

At this name a sudden silence fell. The Prior of Emmet and his people huddled together like a flock of frightened sheep when the wolf is near, while the Bishop of Hereford put down his book and crossed himself devoutly. “Heaven protect us today,” he said, “from that wicked man!”
“No,” said Robin, “I mean you no harm. But here is fair Ellen’s promised husband, and she shall marry him, or some of you will be hurt.”
Then stout Edward spoke up in a loud and angry voice. “Well, I say no! I am her father, and she shall marry Sir Stephen and no one else.”

All this time, while everything was in turmoil around him, Sir Stephen had been standing in proud, scornful silence. “No, fellow,” he said coldly, “you may take your daughter back. I would not marry her after today’s doings if I could gain all of merry England by it. I tell you plainly, I loved your daughter, old as I am, and would have lifted her like a jewel out of the pigsty. But truly, I did not know that she loved this fellow, and that he loved her. Maiden, if you would rather choose a beggarly minstrel than a high-born knight, take your choice. I feel it a shame to stand here talking in the midst of this herd, and so I will leave you.” With these words he turned, gathered his men around him, and walked proudly down the aisle. All the yeomen fell silent, struck by the scorn of his words. Only Friar Tuck leaned over the edge of the choir loft and called to him before he was gone, “Good evening, Sir Knight. You know old bones must always make room for young blood.” Sir Stephen neither answered nor looked up, but walked out of the church as though he had heard nothing, with his men following him.

Then the Bishop of Hereford spoke hastily. “I have no business here either, so I will leave.” And he made as if to go. But Robin Hood caught hold of his clothes and held him. “Stay, my Lord Bishop,” he said. “I still have something to say to you.” The Bishop’s face fell, but he stayed as Robin told him, for he saw he could not get away.

Then Robin Hood turned to stout Edward of Deirwold and said, “Give your blessing to your daughter’s marriage to this yeoman, and all will be well. Little John, give me the bags of gold. Look, farmer. Here are two hundred bright golden angels. Give your blessing, as I say, and I will count them out to you as your daughter’s dowry. If you don’t give your blessing, she will be married all the same, but not even a cracked farthing will cross your palm. Choose.”

Then Edward stared at the ground with a furrowed brow, turning the matter over and over in his mind. But he was a shrewd man, one who would make the best use even of a cracked pot. So at last he looked up and said, though not cheerfully, “If the girl will go her own way, let her go. I had hoped to make a lady of her, but if she chooses to be what she is likely to be, I will have nothing to do with her from now on. Still, I will give her my blessing once she is properly wed.”
“That cannot be,” spoke up one of the men from Emmet. “The banns have not been properly announced, and there is no priest here to marry them.”

“What do you say?” roared Tuck from the choir loft. “No priest? Why, here stands a man as holy as you are, any day of the week, a clerk in orders, I’ll have you know. As for the banns, don’t stumble over that bit of straw, brother, for I will announce them myself.” With that, he called out the banns, and, as the old ballad says, in case three times was not enough, he announced them nine times over. Then he came straight down from the loft and at once performed the marriage service, and so Allan and Ellen were properly wed.

Now Robin counted out two hundred golden angels to Edward of Deirwold, and Edward, for his part, gave his blessing, though not, I can tell you, as if he meant it with much good will. Then the stout yeomen crowded around and shook Allan’s hand, and he, holding Ellen’s hand in his own, looked around him, dizzy with happiness.

Then at last jolly Robin turned to the Bishop of Hereford, who had watched everything that happened with a grim look. “My Lord Bishop,” he said, “you may remember that you promised me, if I played in such a way as to make this fair lass love her husband, you would give me whatever I asked within reason. I have played my play, and she loves her husband, which she would not have done without me. So now keep your promise. You are wearing something that I think you would be better off without, so I beg you, give me the golden chain that hangs around your neck, as a wedding present for this fair bride.”

Then the Bishop’s cheeks turned red with rage and his eyes flashed. He gave Robin a fierce look, but he saw something in the yeoman’s face that made him stop. Then slowly he took the chain from around his neck and handed it to Robin, who flung it over Ellen’s head so that it hung glittering on her shoulders. Then merry Robin said, “I thank you, on the bride’s behalf, for your handsome gift, and truly you look better without it. Now, if you ever come near Sherwood, I hope very much to give you there such a feast as you have never had in all your life.”
“Heaven forbid!” cried the Bishop earnestly, for he knew very well what kind of feast Robin Hood gave his guests in Sherwood Forest.

But now Robin Hood gathered his men together, and with Allan and his young bride in their midst, they all turned their steps toward the woods. On the way, Friar Tuck came up close to Robin and tugged at his sleeve. “You lead a merry life, good master,” he said, “but don’t you think it would be good for all your souls to have a sturdy chaplain like me to look after holy matters? Truly, I love this life mightily.” At this, merry Robin Hood laughed heartily and told him he could stay and join their band if he wished.

That night such a feast was held in the greenwood as Nottinghamshire had never seen. You and I were not invited to that feast, and what a pity that is. So, to keep us both from feeling the loss more sharply, I will say no more about it.

chapters.title: Robin Hood Aids a Sorrowful Knight
paragraphs: And so the gentle spring slipped away in budding beauty, with its silver showers and sunshine, its green meadows and its flowers. The summer went the same way, with its yellow sunlight, its shimmering heat and its deep, leafy shade, its long twilights and mellow nights, when the frogs croaked and the fairy folk were said to be abroad on the hillsides. All of that was over now, and autumn had arrived with pleasures and joys of its own. The harvest was gathered in, and cheerful bands of gleaners roamed the countryside, singing along the roads by day and sleeping under hedges and haystacks by night. Now the rose hips glowed red in the tangled thickets and the hawthorn berries turned black in the hedgerows. The stubble lay crisp and bare beneath the sky, and the green leaves were turning quickly to russet and brown. This was also the cheerful season when the good things of the year are stored away in plenty. Brown ale ripens in the cellar, hams and bacon hang in the smokehouse, and crab apples are packed in straw to be roasted in wintertime, when the north wind heaps the snow in drifts against the gables and the fire crackles warm on the hearth.
The seasons went by like that then, as they go by now and will go by in the years ahead, while we ourselves come and go like leaves on a tree, falling and soon forgotten.

Robin Hood sniffed the air and said, “This is a fine day, Little John, and we can’t afford to waste it sitting idle. Pick whatever men you need and go east, while I head west, and let each of us bring back a worthy guest to dine with us today beneath the greenwood tree.”
“Indeed!” cried Little John, clapping his hands together for joy. “Your order fits my liking like a hilt fits a blade. I’ll bring you back a guest today, or I won’t come back myself.”
Then each of them picked the men from the band that he wanted, and they left the forest by different paths.

Now, you and I can’t go two ways at once while we share in this merry business, so we’ll let Little John follow his own road while we hitch up our skirts and tramp along after Robin Hood. And it’s good company, too: Robin Hood, Will Scarlet, Allan a Dale, Will Scathelock, Midge the Miller’s son, and others. Twenty or more sturdy fellows had stayed behind in the forest with Friar Tuck to get everything ready for the homecoming, but all the rest had gone with either Robin Hood or Little John.

They traveled on, Robin following his fancy and the others following Robin. First they made their way through an open valley with cottages and farms scattered through it, and then they entered woodland again. They passed fair Mansfield Town, with its towers and battlements and spires all smiling in the sun, and at last came out of the forest country. On they went, along highways and byways, through villages where goodwives and merry lasses peeped out of their windows at the fine show of young men, until finally they had gone beyond Alverton in Derbyshire. By now it was high noon, and they had met no guest worth taking back to Sherwood. So they came to a spot where a shrine stood at the crossing of two roads, and Robin called a halt. On either side there was shelter behind high hedgerows, and they could hide there and watch the roads at their ease while they ate their midday meal. Merry Robin said, “This looks to me like a good lodging, where peaceful folk like us can eat in quiet. We’ll rest here and see what may drop into our luck-pot.” So they climbed over a stile and went behind a hedgerow, where the mellow sunlight was bright and warm and the grass was soft, and there they sat down. Then each man took out of the pouch at his side whatever he had brought to eat, for a cheerful walk like this one sharpens the appetite until it is as keen as a March wind. So nobody said a word, but each man saved his teeth for better work and munched heartily on brown crust and cold meat.

In front of them, one of the highroads crawled up a steep hill and then dipped suddenly over the crest, sharply outlined against the sky by its hedgerow and shaggy grass. Over the top of the windy hill peeped the roofs of a few houses from the village that lay back in the valley behind it. The top of a windmill showed there too, its sails rising and dipping slowly against the clear blue sky behind the hill, as the light wind turned them with a creaking, heavy swing.

So the yeomen lay behind the hedge and finished their meal, but time went on and still no one came. At last a man came riding slowly over the hill and down the stony road toward the place where Robin and his band lay hidden. He was a stout, fine-looking knight, but his face was sorrowful and his bearing dejected. His clothes were plain but rich, yet no gold chain hung around his neck, such as people of his rank usually wore, and he had no jewel on him; still, nobody could have taken him for anything but a man of proud and noble blood. His head was bowed upon his chest and his hands hung limp at his sides. So he came riding slowly along, as if lost in sad thoughts, and even his good horse walked with its head hanging and the reins loose on its neck, as though it shared its master’s grief.

Robin Hood said, “That one is certainly a sorry-looking gentleman, and he seems to have put on ill humor with his jerkin this morning. All the same, I’ll go out and talk with him, for there may be some pickings here for a hungry jackdaw. His clothes look rich to me, though he himself is so downcast. Stay here while I look into this.” With that he got up and left them, crossed the road to the shrine, and stood there waiting for the sorrowful knight to come near. When the knight came riding slowly up, jolly Robin stepped forward and laid his hand on the bridle. “Hold, Sir Knight,” he said. “Please stop for a little while, for I have a few words to say to you.”
“Who are you, friend, to stop a traveler like this on His Majesty’s own highway?” said the Knight.

“Well now,” said Robin, “that’s a hard question to answer. One man calls me kind, another calls me cruel; this one calls me a good honest fellow, and that one a vile thief. The world has as many ways of looking at a man as a toad has spots, so which pair of eyes you see me with is entirely up to you. My name is Robin Hood.”

“Truly, good Robin,” said the Knight, a smile twitching at the corners of his mouth, “you have a quaint way of putting things. As for the eyes I see you with, I would say they are as favorable as can be, for I hear a great deal of good about you and very little ill. What do you want of me?”

“Now I swear, Sir Knight,” said Robin, “you must have learned your wisdom from good Gaffer Swanthold, for he says, ‘Fair words are as easily spoken as foul ones, and they bring goodwill instead of blows.’ Now I’ll show you that this saying is true. If you will come with me today to Sherwood Forest, I’ll give you as merry a feast as you ever had in your life.”
“You are kind indeed,” said the Knight, “but I think you will find me a poor and sorrowful guest. You had better let me go on my way in peace.”

“No,” said Robin, “you might go your own way, except for one thing, which I’ll tell you. We keep an inn, so to speak, deep in Sherwood, but so far from the highroads and beaten paths that guests seldom come near us. So when we grow dull by ourselves, my friends and I set out cheerfully to look for them. That’s how matters stand, Sir Knight. And I’ll tell you something more: we expect our guests to pay their bill.”
“I understand you, friend,” said the Knight gravely, “but I am not your man, for I have no money on me.”

“Is that the truth?” said Robin, looking at the Knight keenly. “I can hardly help believing you. Still, Sir Knight, there are some of your order whose word can’t be trusted as far as they would like others to think. You won’t mind if I look into the matter myself.” Then, still holding the horse by the bridle, he put his fingers to his lips and blew a shrill whistle. At that, eighty yeomen came leaping over the stile and ran to where the Knight and Robin stood. “These,” said Robin, looking at them proudly, “are some of my merry men. They share and share alike with me in all joys and troubles, gains and losses. Sir Knight, please tell me how much money you have on you.”

For a while the Knight said not a word, but a slow flush rose in his cheeks. At last he looked Robin in the face and said, “I don’t know why I should be ashamed, for there is no shame in it. But, friend, I tell you the truth when I say that there are ten shillings in my purse, and that this is every penny that Sir Richard of the Lea has in all the wide world.”
When Sir Richard had finished, a silence fell, until at last Robin said, “And do you give me your knightly word that this is all you have with you?”

“Yes,” answered Sir Richard, “I give you my most solemn word, as a true knight, that it is all the money I have in the world. And here is my purse, so that you can see for yourselves that I speak the truth.” And he held his purse out to Robin.

“Put away your purse, Sir Richard,” said Robin. “I would never doubt the word of so gentle a knight. I try to bring the proud down, but I would help those who walk in sorrow if I could. Come, Sir Richard, cheer up and come with us into the greenwood. Even I may be able to help you, for surely you know how good Athelstane was saved by the little blind mole that dug a trench, over which the man who was hunting the king’s life stumbled.”

“Truly, friend,” said Sir Richard, “I think you mean well in your own way. All the same, my troubles are such that you are unlikely to cure them. But I will go with you into Sherwood today.” With that he turned his horse’s head, and they all made their way to the woodlands, with Robin walking on one side of the Knight and Will Scarlet on the other, while the rest of the band trudged along behind.
After they had traveled like this for a while, Robin Hood spoke. “Sir Knight,” he said, “I wouldn’t trouble you with idle questions, but can you find it in your heart to tell me your sorrows?”

“Truly, Robin,” said the Knight, “I see no reason why I shouldn’t. This is how it stands: my castle and my lands are pawned for a debt I owe. Three days from now the money must be paid, or else my whole estate is lost forever, for then it falls into the hands of the Priory of Emmet, and what they swallow they never give back.”
Robin said, “I don’t understand why men of your kind live in a way that lets all their wealth melt away like snow under the spring sun.”

“You wrong me, Robin,” said the Knight, “for listen. I have a son only twenty years old, and yet he has already won his spurs as a knight. Last year, on an evil day, the jousts were held at Chester, and my son went there, as did I and my lady wife. I tell you it was a proud time for us, for he unhorsed every knight he rode against. At last he ran a course against a great knight, Sir Walter of Lancaster, and though my son was so young, he kept his seat, even though both spears were shattered down to the hilt. But it happened that a splinter of my boy’s lance went through the visor of Sir Walter’s helmet and pierced his eye and his brain, so that he died before his squire could unlace his helm. Now, Robin, Sir Walter had powerful friends at court, so his kinsmen stirred up trouble against my son, and to save him from prison I had to pay a ransom of six hundred pounds in gold. Even then all might have gone well, but through the twists and crookedness of the law I was fleeced like a sheep that is clipped to the quick. So I had to pawn my lands to the Priory of Emmet for more money, and they drove a hard bargain with me in my hour of need. Yet I want you to understand that I grieve for my lands only because of my dear lady wife.”
“And your son, where is he now?” asked Robin, who had been listening closely to every word.

“He is in Palestine,” said Sir Richard, “fighting as a brave Christian soldier for the cross and the holy sepulcher. England was no place for him after Sir Walter died, with all the Lancastrian’s kinsmen hating him.”
“Truly,” said Robin, much moved, “yours is a hard lot. But tell me, how much do you owe the Priory of Emmet for your estates?”
“Only four hundred pounds,” said Sir Richard.
At this Robin slapped his thigh in anger. “Oh, the bloodsuckers!” he cried. “A noble estate lost for four hundred pounds! But what will become of you if you lose your lands, Sir Richard?”

“In that case it is not my own lot that troubles me,” said the Knight, “but my dear lady’s. If I lose my land, she will have to go to some kinsman and live there on charity, which I think would break her proud heart. As for me, I will cross the salt sea to Palestine and join my son in the fight for the holy sepulcher.”
Then Will Scarlet spoke up. “But have you no friend who will help you in your dire need?”

“Not a man,” said Sir Richard. “While I was rich at home and had friends, they made great boasts of how they loved me. But when the oak falls in the forest, the swine run out from under it so they won’t be struck down too. So my friends have left me, for I am not only poor but I have powerful enemies.”

Then Robin said, “You tell me you have no friends, Sir Richard. I won’t boast, but plenty of people in trouble have found a friend in Robin Hood. Take heart, Sir Knight, for I may be able to help you yet.”

The Knight shook his head with a faint smile, but for all that, Robin’s words made his heart lighter. For hope, however faint, brings a gleam into the darkness, like a little rushlight that costs only a groat.

The day was nearly over when they drew close to the greenwood tree. Even from far off they could tell, from the crowd of men gathered there, that Little John had come back with a guest. But when they got near enough, who should it be but the Lord Bishop of Hereford! The good Bishop was in a fine fury, I can tell you. He paced back and forth under the tree like a fox caught in a henhouse. Behind him three Black Friars huddled together in a frightened bunch, like three black sheep in a storm. Tied to the branches of the nearby trees stood six horses. One was a Barbary horse with showy trappings, which the Bishop usually rode. The others were loaded with packs of all shapes and sizes, and one of them made Robin’s eyes shine, for it was a box, not very large, but strongly bound with bands and ribs of iron.

When the Bishop saw Robin and his companions come out into the open, he made as if to run toward the yeoman. But the fellow who was guarding the Bishop and the three friars shoved his quarterstaff in the way, so that his lordship had to stay where he was, though he scowled and spoke angrily.

“Stay there, my Lord Bishop,” cried jolly Robin in a loud voice, as soon as he saw what had happened. “I’ll come to you as fast as I can, for there’s no man in merry England I’d rather see.” With that he hurried his steps and soon reached the spot where the Bishop stood fuming.

“Well, now,” said the Bishop in a loud, angry voice, as soon as Robin had come up to him, “is this how you and your band treat a man as high in the Church as I am? These brethren and I were traveling peacefully along the highroad with our pack horses and ten men to guard them, when a great strapping fellow, a full seven feet tall, came up with eighty men or more behind him and ordered me to halt. Me, the Lord Bishop of Hereford, mark you! And my armed guards, curse them for cowards, ran off at once. But listen to this: not only did the fellow stop me, he threatened me. He said Robin Hood would strip me as bare as a winter hedge. And besides all that, he called me names like ‘fat priest,’ ‘man-eating bishop,’ and ‘money-gorging usurer,’ and who knows what else, as though I were nothing but a wandering beggar or tinker.”

At this the Bishop glared like an angry cat, and even Sir Richard laughed. Only Robin kept a straight face. “Oh, my lord,” he said, “what a shame that my band has treated you so badly! I tell you truly, we have great respect for your robe. Little John, step forward at once.”

Little John stepped up at this, pulling a comical face as if to say, “Have mercy on me, good master.” Robin then turned to the Bishop of Hereford. “Is this the man who talked so boldly to Your Lordship?” he asked.
“Yes, it was the very same,” said the Bishop. “A wicked fellow, I tell you.”
“Is it true, Little John,” said Robin sadly, “that you called his lordship a fat priest?”
“Yes,” said Little John sorrowfully.
“And a man-eating bishop?”
“Yes,” said Little John, even more sorrowfully than before.
“And a money-gorging usurer?”
“Yes,” said Little John, in a voice so sorrowful that it could have drawn tears from the Dragon of Wentley.
“What a shame that such things should happen!” said jolly Robin, turning to the Bishop, “for I have always found Little John to be a truthful man.”

At this a roar of laughter went up, and the blood rushed into the Bishop’s face until it was cherry red from forehead to chin. But he said nothing. He only swallowed his words, though they nearly choked him.

“Come now, my Lord Bishop,” said Robin, “we are rough fellows, but after all, I hope we are not such bad men as you think. Not one man here would harm a hair on your reverence’s head. I know our joking has stung you, but here in the greenwood we are all equal. There are no bishops or barons or earls among us, only men, so you must share our life while you stay here. Come on, my merry men, hurry and get the feast ready. In the meantime, we’ll show our guests our woodland sports.”

So while some went off to light the fires for roasting meat, others ran, leaping, to fetch their cudgels and longbows. Then Robin brought Sir Richard of the Lea forward. “My Lord Bishop,” he said, “here is another guest we have with us today. I’d like you to get to know him better, for I and all my men will do our best to honor you both at this merrymaking.”

“Sir Richard,” said the Bishop in a reproachful tone, “I think you and I are companions and fellow sufferers in this den of—” He was about to say “thieves,” but he stopped short and glanced sideways at Robin Hood.
“Say it, Bishop,” said Robin, laughing. “Here in Sherwood we don’t check a free flow of words. ‘Den of thieves’ is what you were about to say.”

The Bishop said, “Perhaps that is what I meant, Sir Richard. But I will say this: I saw you just now laughing at the coarse jokes of these fellows. It would have been more proper, I think, to frown at them instead of egging them on with your laughter.”
“I meant you no harm,” said Sir Richard, “but a merry joke is a merry joke, and I can honestly say I would have laughed at it even if it had been aimed at me.”

Now Robin Hood called on some of his band, who spread soft moss on the ground and laid deerskins over it. Then Robin invited his guests to sit, and the three of them took their places. Some of the chief men, such as Little John, Will Scarlet, Allan a Dale, and others, stretched out on the ground nearby. A garland was then set up at the far end of the glade, and the bowmen shot at it, and the shooting that day was so fine that it made one’s heart leap to watch. And all the while Robin talked so amusingly to the Bishop and the Knight that the one forgot his annoyance and the other his troubles, and both of them laughed out loud again and again.

Then Allan a Dale stepped forward and tuned his harp. Everything around fell quiet, and he sang in his wonderful voice songs of love, of war, of glory, and of sadness, and everyone listened without moving or making a sound. Allan sang on until the great round silver moon shone with its clear white light among the tangled upper branches of the trees. At last two fellows came to say that the feast was laid out. So Robin, leading his guests by either hand, brought them to where great steaming dishes, sending savory smells far and wide, stood along the white linen cloth spread on the grass. Torches blazed all around and lit everything with a red glow. Then everyone sat down at once and fell to eating, with a great racket and hubbub, the clatter of platters mixing with loud talk and laughter. The feast lasted a long time, but at last it was over, and the bright wine and foaming ale went briskly around. Then Robin Hood called loudly for silence, and all was still until he spoke.

“I have a story to tell you all, so listen to what I have to say,” he said. Then, without further ado, he told them all about Sir Richard and how his lands were in pawn. As he went on, the Bishop’s face, which had been smiling and red with good cheer, grew serious. He set down the horn of wine he was holding, for he knew Sir Richard’s story, and his heart sank with dark misgivings. When Robin Hood had finished, he turned to the Bishop of Hereford. “Now, my Lord Bishop,” he said, “don’t you think this is a wrong thing for anyone to do, much more so for a churchman, who ought to live humbly and with charity?”
The Bishop did not answer a word but stared at the ground with a gloomy look.
Robin said, “You are the richest bishop in all England. Can’t you help this needy brother?” But still the Bishop did not say a word.

Then Robin turned to Little John and said, “You and Will Stutely go and bring out those five pack horses over there.” So the two yeomen did as they were told. The men around the cloth made room on the green, where the light was brightest, for the five horses that Little John and Will Stutely soon led forward.
“Which of you holds the list of the goods?” Robin Hood asked, turning to the Black Friars.
Then the smallest of them spoke up in a trembling voice. He was an old man with a gentle, wrinkled face. “I have it, but please, don’t hurt me.”

“No,” said Robin, “I have never yet harmed a harmless man. But hand it over, good father.” So the old man did as he was told and gave Robin the tablet on which the account of the various packages on the horses was written down. Robin passed it to Will Scarlet and told him to read it out. So Will Scarlet raised his voice so that everyone could hear, and began:
“Three bales of silk to Quentin, the mercer at Ancaster.”
“We won’t touch that,” said Robin, “for this Quentin is an honest fellow who has risen by his own hard work.” So the bales of silk were set aside unopened.
“One bale of silk velvet for the Abbey of Beaumont.”

“What do these priests want with silk velvet?” said Robin. “Still, though they have no need of it, I won’t take it all from them. Measure it off into three lots: one to be sold for charity, one for us, and one for the abbey.” This, too, was done as Robin Hood ordered.
“Forty large wax candles, for the Chapel of Saint Thomas.”

“Those rightly belong to the chapel,” said Robin, “so put them to one side. We would never take from the blessed Saint Thomas what belongs to him.” This too was done as Robin ordered, and the candles were laid aside along with honest Quentin’s unopened bales of silk. So they went through the whole list, and the goods were judged according to what Robin thought fitting. Some things were set aside untouched, and many were opened and divided into three equal parts: for charity, for themselves, and for the owners. Soon the whole ground in the torchlight was covered with silks and velvets and cloths of gold and cases of rich wines, and they came to the last line on the tablet: “A box belonging to the Lord Bishop of Hereford.”
Hearing this, the Bishop trembled as though chilled, and the box was placed on the ground.
“My Lord Bishop, do you have the key to this box?” asked Robin.
The Bishop shook his head.

“Go, Will Scarlet,” said Robin, “you are the strongest man here. Fetch a sword right away and cut this box open, if you can.” Then Will Scarlet got up and left them, and in a short time he came back carrying a great two-handed sword. Three times he struck that strong, iron-bound box, and at the third blow it burst open and a great heap of gold came rolling out, gleaming red in the torchlight. At the sight a murmur ran through the band, like the sound of wind in distant trees, but no man stepped forward or touched the money.
Robin said, “You, Will Scarlet, and you, Allan a Dale, and you, Little John, count it over.”

It took a long time to count all the money. When it had been properly tallied, Will Scarlet announced that there were fifteen hundred golden pounds in all. But among the gold they found a paper, which Will Scarlet read out loudly, and everyone heard that this money was the rents, fines, and forfeits from certain estates belonging to the Bishopric of Hereford.

“My Lord Bishop,” said Robin Hood, “I won’t strip you bare like a winter hedge, as Little John said, for you shall take back one third of your money. One third you can well spare us as payment for your entertainment and that of your party, for you are very rich. Another third you can better spare for charity, because I hear, Bishop, that you are a hard master to those beneath you, and that you hoard gains greedily, which it would be better, and more to your credit, to give to charity than to spend on your own pleasures.”
The Bishop glanced up at this, though he still had no words. But he was grateful to be keeping part of his riches.

Then Robin turned to Sir Richard of the Lea and said, “Now, Sir Richard, the Church seemed likely to rob you, so some of the surplus church money may well be used to help you. You shall take the five hundred pounds set aside for people who need it more than the Bishop does, and pay your debts to Emmet with it.”

Sir Richard looked at Robin until his eyes filled with something that made all the lights and faces blur together. At last he said, “I thank you from my heart, friend, for what you are doing for me. But don’t think badly of me if I can’t take your gift freely. This I will do: I will take the money and pay my debts, and a year and a day from now I will return it safely, either to you or to the Lord Bishop of Hereford. I pledge my most solemn word as a knight. I feel free to borrow, for I know of no man who ought to be more bound to help me than one so high in that Church which drove such a hard bargain.” “Truly, Sir Knight,” said Robin, “I don’t understand those fine scruples that weigh on men of your kind. But nevertheless it shall be just as you wish. Still, you had better bring the money to me at the end of the year, for perhaps I can make better use of it than the Bishop.” Then he turned to the men near him and gave his orders, and five hundred pounds were counted out and tied up in a leather bag for Sir Richard. The rest of the treasure was divided: part was taken to the band’s treasure house, and part was put aside with the other goods for the Bishop.
Then Sir Richard stood up. “I can’t stay any longer, good friends,” he said, “for my lady will worry if I don’t come home. So I ask your leave to go.”
Then Robin Hood and all his merry men rose, and Robin said, “We can’t let you go from here without an escort, Sir Richard.”

Then Little John spoke up. “Good master, let me pick twenty sturdy fellows from the band, and let us arm ourselves handsomely and serve as Sir Richard’s retainers until he can find others to take our place.”
“Well said, Little John, and it shall be done,” said Robin.
Then Will Scarlet spoke up. “Let us give him a golden chain to wear around his neck, as befits a man of his blood, and golden spurs for his heels.”
Then Robin Hood said, “Well said, Will Scarlet, and it shall be done.”
Then Will Stutely spoke up. “Let us give him that bale of rich velvet and that roll of cloth of gold to take home to his noble lady wife, as a present from Robin Hood and all his merry men.”
At this everyone clapped their hands for joy, and Robin said, “Well said, Will Stutely, and it shall be done.”

Sir Richard of the Lea looked around at them all and tried to speak, but his feelings choked him so badly that he could hardly manage it. At last he said in a husky, shaking voice, “You will all see, good friends, that Sir Richard of the Lea will always remember your kindness today. If you are ever in great need or trouble, come to me and my lady, and the walls of Castle Lea will be torn down before any harm comes to you. I—” He could say no more, and turned quickly away.

Now Little John came forward with the nineteen sturdy fellows he had picked for his company, all ready for the journey. Every man wore a coat of linked mail over his chest, a steel cap on his head, and a good strong sword at his side. They made a splendid sight, standing there in a row. Then Robin came and hung a gold chain around Sir Richard’s neck, and Will Scarlet knelt and buckled the golden spurs onto his heels. Little John led up Sir Richard’s horse, and the Knight mounted. For a little while he looked down at Robin, then suddenly leaned over and kissed his cheek. A great shout went up that echoed through all the forest glades as the Knight and the yeomen marched away through the woods, with flaring torches and gleaming steel, and then they were gone.
Then the Bishop of Hereford spoke up in a mournful voice. “I must be on my way too, good fellow, for the night is getting late.”

But Robin put a hand on the Bishop’s arm and held him back. “Don’t be in such a hurry, Lord Bishop,” he said. “Sir Richard must pay his debts to Emmet three days from now. Until then you will have to stay here with me, so that you can’t cause the Knight any trouble. I promise you good sport, for I know you are fond of hunting the dun deer. Put aside your cloak of gloom and try to live a cheerful yeoman’s life for three whole days. I promise you will be sorry to leave when the time comes.”

So the Bishop and his company stayed with Robin for three days, and his lordship had a great deal of sport in that time. Just as Robin had said, when the day came for him to go, he was sorry to leave the greenwood. At the end of the three days Robin let him go and sent him out of the forest with a guard of yeomen, to keep outlaws from taking what was left of his packs and bundles.
But as the Bishop rode away, he swore to himself that someday he would make Robin regret the day he stopped him in Sherwood.
But now we will follow Sir Richard. Listen, and you will hear what happened to him, and how he paid his debts at Emmet Priory, and in good time to Robin Hood as well.

chapters.title: How Sir Richard of the Lea Paid his Debts
paragraphs: The long highway ran straight ahead, gray and dusty in the sun. On both sides lay ditches full of water, lined with willows, and far off in the distance stood the towers of Emmet Priory, ringed with tall poplar trees.

A knight was riding along the causeway with twenty sturdy men-at-arms behind him. He wore a plain, long robe of gray serge, belted at the waist with a broad leather belt that held a long dagger and a strong sword. But for all his plain clothes, the horse he rode was a splendid Barbary steed, and its harness was rich with silk and silver bells.

So the company traveled along the causeway between the ditches until they finally reached the great gate of Emmet Priory. There the Knight called one of his men and told him to knock at the porter’s lodge with the hilt of his sword.

The porter had been dozing on his bench inside the lodge, but at the knock he woke up, opened the little gate, and came limping out to greet the Knight. Meanwhile a tame starling in a wicker cage hanging inside chirped out, “_In coelo quies! In coelo quies!_”, which were the words the poor old lame porter had taught it to say.
“Where is your prior?” the Knight asked the old porter.
“He is at dinner, good knight, and he is expecting you,” said the porter, “for unless I am mistaken, you are Sir Richard of the Lea.”
“I am Sir Richard of the Lea, so I will go and find him at once,” said the Knight.

“But shall I not take your horse to the stable?” said the porter. “By Our Lady, it is the finest animal, and the best harnessed, that I have ever seen in all my life.” And he patted the horse’s flank with his palm.

“No,” said Sir Richard. “The stables of this place are not for me, so please step aside.” With that he pushed forward, and when the gates were opened he rode into the stone courtyard of the Priory, with his men behind him. They came in with a rattle of armor, a clash of swords, and the ring of hooves on cobblestones, and a flock of pigeons that had been strutting in the sun flew up flapping to the high eaves of the round towers.

While the Knight was riding along the causeway toward Emmet, a merry feast was under way in the dining hall there. The afternoon sun streamed through the great arched windows and lay in broad squares of light on the stone floor and across the table, which was covered with a snowy linen cloth and loaded with a princely feast. At the head of the table sat Prior Vincent of Emmet, dressed in soft robes of fine cloth and silk. On his head was a black velvet cap trimmed with gold, and around his neck hung a heavy gold chain with a large locket. On the arm of his great chair beside him perched his favorite falcon, for the Prior loved the gentle sport of hawking. On his right sat the Sheriff of Nottingham in rich purple robes trimmed with fur, and on his left a famous doctor of law in dark, sober clothes. Below them sat the high cellarer of Emmet and the other leading brothers.

Jokes and laughter went around the table, and everyone was as merry as could be. The withered face of the man of law was twisted into a wrinkled smile, for in his pouch were eighty golden angels that the Prior had paid him as his fee for the case between the Prior and Sir Richard of the Lea. The learned doctor had been paid in advance, because he did not trust the holy Vincent of Emmet very far.
The Sheriff of Nottingham said, “But are you sure, Sir Prior, that you have the lands so safely in your grip?”
“Yes, indeed,” said Prior Vincent, smacking his lips after a deep drink of wine. “I have kept a close watch on him, though he never knew it, and I know very well that he has no money to pay me with.”

“True,” said the man of law in a dry, husky voice. “His land is surely forfeit if he doesn’t come to pay. But, Sir Prior, you must get a release signed by his own hand, or you can’t hope to keep the land without trouble from him.”
“Yes,” said the Prior, “you have told me so before. But I know this knight is so poor that he will gladly sign away his lands for two hundred pounds in hard cash.”

Then the high cellarer spoke up. “I think it is a shame to drive an unlucky knight into the ditch like this. It saddens me that the finest estate in Derbyshire should pass out of his hands for a miserable five hundred pounds. Truly, I—”

“How dare you!” the Prior broke in, his voice shaking, his eyes glittering and his cheeks red with anger. “Do you lecture me to my very face, fellow? By Saint Hubert, you had better save your breath to cool your soup, or it may scald your mouth.”

“No,” said the man of law smoothly. “I would swear that this knight will never come to a settlement today, but will prove a coward. Even so, we will find some way to get his lands from him, so never fear.”

But just as the doctor finished speaking, there came a sudden clatter of horses’ hooves and a jingle of iron mail in the courtyard below. The Prior spoke up and called to one of the brothers sitting below the salt, telling him to look out of the window and see who was down there, though he knew perfectly well it could be no one but Sir Richard.

So the brother got up, went to look, and said, “I see below twenty strong men-at-arms and a knight just getting down from his horse. He is wearing long gray robes that look rather poor to me, but the horse he rides has the richest harness I ever saw. The Knight is dismounting, and they are coming this way. They are in the great hall right now.”

“Well, look at that,” said Prior Vincent. “Here you have a knight with so thin a purse that he can hardly buy himself a crust of bread to chew, yet he keeps a band of followers and puts rich trappings on his horse’s hide while his own back goes bare. Is it not right that such men should be brought low?”

“But are you sure,” said the little doctor nervously, “that this knight will do us no harm? Men like him are fierce when crossed, and he has a band of rough men at his heels. Perhaps you had better give him more time on his debt.” He said this because he was afraid Sir Richard might hurt him.
“You need not be afraid,” said the Prior, looking down at the little man beside him. “This knight is gentle, and would as soon think of hurting an old woman as of hurting you.”

As the Prior finished, a door at the lower end of the dining hall swung open, and in came Sir Richard with his hands folded and his head bowed on his chest. He walked slowly up the hall in this humble way while his men-at-arms stood around the door. When he reached the place where the Prior sat, he knelt on one knee. “God save and keep you, Sir Prior,” he said. “I have come to keep my day.”
The first thing the Prior said to him was, “Have you brought my money?”
“Alas! I do not have so much as one penny on me,” said the Knight, and at this the Prior’s eyes sparkled.
“Well, you are a clever debtor, I must say,” said the Prior. Then he added, “Sir Sheriff, I drink to you.”
But the Knight still knelt on the hard stones, so the Prior turned to him again. “What do you want?” he asked sharply.

At these words a slow red flush rose in the Knight’s cheeks, but still he knelt. “I beg your mercy,” he said. “As you hope for Heaven’s mercy, show mercy to me. Do not strip me of my lands and so reduce a true knight to poverty.”
“Your day is past and your lands are forfeit,” said the man of law, gaining courage at the Knight’s humble words.
Sir Richard said, “You, man of law, will you not befriend me in my hour of need?”
“No,” said the other, “I side with this holy Prior. He has paid my fees in hard gold, and that binds me to him.”
“Then will you take my part, Sir Sheriff?” asked Sir Richard.

“No, by Heaven,” said the Sheriff of Nottingham, “this is none of my business, though I will do what I can.” And he nudged the Prior under the tablecloth with his knee. “Will you not relieve him of some of his debt, Sir Prior?”
At this the Prior smiled grimly. “Pay me three hundred pounds, Sir Richard,” he said, “and I will give you a full release from your debt.”
