“You know very well, Sir Prior, that paying four hundred pounds would be no harder for me than paying three hundred,” said Sir Richard. “But can you not grant me one more year to settle my debt?”
“Not another day,” said the Prior sternly.
“And is this all you will do for me?” asked the Knight.
“Away with you, false knight!” cried the Prior, bursting out in anger. “Either pay your debt as I have said, or give up your land and get out of my hall.”

Then Sir Richard rose to his feet. “You false, lying priest!” he said, in so stern a voice that the man of law shrank back in fright. “I am no false knight, as you know perfectly well, but have held my place in the thick of battle and in the tournament. Have you so little courtesy that you would let a true knight kneel all this time, or see him come into your hall and never offer him food or drink?”
Then the man of law said in a trembling voice, “This is surely a poor way to talk about matters of business. Let us speak mildly. What will you pay this knight, Sir Prior, for a release of his land?”
“I would have given him two hundred pounds,” said the Prior, “but since he has spoken so vilely to my face, he will not get one groat over one hundred pounds.”

“If you had offered me a thousand pounds, false prior,” said the Knight, “you would not have got an inch of my land.” Then he turned to where his men-at-arms stood near the door, called “Come here,” and beckoned with his finger. The tallest of them all stepped forward and handed him a long leather bag. Sir Richard took the bag and poured out onto the table a glittering stream of golden coins. “Remember, Sir Prior,” he said, “that you promised me a release for three hundred pounds. You will not get one farthing more than that.” With that he counted out three hundred pounds and pushed it toward the Prior.

But now the Prior’s hands dropped to his sides and his head sank onto his shoulder, for not only had he lost all hope of the land, but he had forgiven the Knight one hundred pounds of his debt and had paid the man of law eighty angels for nothing. He turned to him and said, “Give me back the money you have.”
“No,” cried the other shrilly, “it was only my fee that you paid me, and you will not get it back.” And he hugged his gown tight around him.

“Now, Sir Prior,” said Sir Richard, “I have kept my day and paid all the dues demanded of me. Since there is nothing more between us, I am leaving this wretched place at once.” With that he turned on his heel and strode away.

The whole while, the Sheriff had been gaping at the tall man-at-arms with wide eyes and his mouth hanging open, while the man stood stiff as a stone statue. Finally the Sheriff gasped, “Reynold Greenleaf!”

At this the tall man-at-arms, who was none other than Little John, turned to the Sheriff with a grin. “A good day to you, fair neighbor,” he said. “What I mean to say, sweet Sheriff, is that I have heard all your pretty talk today, and Robin Hood shall be told every word of it. So farewell for now, until we meet again in Sherwood Forest.” Then he too turned and followed Sir Richard down the hall, leaving the Sheriff pale and stunned, shrunk together in his chair.

It was a merry feast that Sir Richard had walked in on, but he left behind a sorry company, who had little appetite for the princely food spread before them. Only the learned doctor was happy, for he had his fee.

A year and a day had passed since Prior Vincent of Emmet sat at his feast, and once again the mellow days of autumn had arrived. But the year had brought great changes to the lands of Sir Richard of the Lea, I can tell you. Where shaggy wild grass had once covered the meadows, golden stubble now stretched away in every direction, showing that a rich and plentiful crop had been brought in. The castle had changed as well. Where there had been empty moats and crumbling neglect, everything was now orderly and well kept.

The sun shone brightly on battlement and tower, and in the blue air above, a flock of clattering jackdaws wheeled around the gilded weather vane and spire. Then, in the brightness of the morning, the drawbridge came down across the moat with a rattle and clank of chains, and the castle gate swung slowly open. Out of the courtyard came a fine company of steel-clad men-at-arms, flashing in the light, with a knight in the middle of them dressed in chain mail as white as frost on briar and thorn on a winter morning. In his hand the Knight carried a great spear, and from its point fluttered a blood-red pennant no wider than the palm of a hand. So the troop came out of the castle, and in the middle of them walked three pack horses loaded with parcels of all shapes and sizes.

So good Sir Richard of the Lea rode out to pay his debt to Robin Hood on that bright and merry morning. They made their way along the highway with the steady tramp of feet and the rattle and jingle of swords and harness. They marched on until they came close to Denby, where, from the top of a hill, they saw many gay flags and streamers waving in the bright air on the far side of the town. Then Sir Richard turned to the man-at-arms nearest him. “What is going on at Denby today?” he asked.

“If it please Your Worship,” answered the man-at-arms, “there is a merry fair there today, with a great wrestling match, and many people have come for it. The prize is a cask of red wine, a fine golden ring, and a pair of gloves, and all of it goes to the best wrestler.”

“By my faith,” said Sir Richard, who loved a good manly sport, “that will be well worth seeing. I think we can spare a little time on our journey to watch the fun.” So he turned his horse aside toward Denby and the fair, and he and his men rode that way.

There they found the whole place buzzing with merriment. Flags and streamers waved, tumblers turned somersaults on the green, bagpipes played, and lads and lasses danced to the music. But most of the crowd had gathered around a ring where the wrestling was under way, and Sir Richard and his men walked over to it.

When the judges of the wrestling saw Sir Richard coming and recognized who he was, the chief judge left the bench where he and the others sat. He went over to the Knight, took him by the hand, and begged him to come and sit with them and help judge the contest. So Sir Richard dismounted and went with the judges to the raised bench beside the ring.

The morning had already been full of excitement. A certain yeoman named Egbert, who came from Stoke over in Staffordshire, had thrown every man who faced him, and with ease. But a man of Denby, known throughout the countryside as William of the Scar, had been waiting for his chance at the Stoke man. When Egbert had thrown everyone else, sturdy William jumped into the ring. A hard bout followed, and in the end William threw Egbert heavily. There was a great deal of shouting and handshaking at that, for all the Denby men were proud of their wrestler.

By the time Sir Richard arrived, he found sturdy William, swollen with pride at his friends’ cheering, strutting up and down the ring and daring anyone to try a fall with him. “Come one, come all!” he cried. “Here I stand, William of the Scar, ready for any man. If there is nobody in Derbyshire to face me, then let them come from Nottingham, Stafford, or York, whoever dares. If I don’t make every last one of them grub in the dirt with their noses like pigs in the forest, never call me brave William the wrestler again.”

Everyone laughed at this, but above the laughter a loud voice was heard to shout, “Since you talk so big, fellow, here comes one from Nottinghamshire to try a fall with you!” At once a tall young man with a stout quarterstaff in his hand came pushing through the crowd and at last sprang lightly over the rope into the ring. He was not as heavy as sturdy William, but he was taller and broader in the shoulders, and every joint of him was well knit. Sir Richard looked at him keenly. Then he turned to one of the judges and said, “Do you know who this youth is? I think I have seen him before.”
“No,” said the judge, “he is a stranger to me.”

Meanwhile the young man said not a word. He put down his quarterstaff and began taking off his jerkin and the rest of his upper clothing, until he stood there bare to the waist. He made a handsome sight stripped like that, for his muscles stood out round and smooth and sharp, like the ripples of swift-running water.

Now each man spat on his hands, clapped them to his knees, and crouched down, watching the other closely to get the better of him in the grip. Then they leaped together like a flash, and a great shout went up, because William had got the better hold of the two. For a short while they strained and struggled and twisted, and then sturdy William tried his craftiest trip and throw. But the stranger met it with even greater skill, and the trip came to nothing. Then, all of a sudden, with a twist and a wrench, the stranger freed himself, and the man of the scar found himself locked in a pair of arms that made his ribs crack. So they stood there for a while, breathing hard and hot, straining against each other, their bodies glistening with sweat and great drops running down their faces. But the stranger’s hug was so tight that at last sturdy William’s muscles went soft under it, and he gave a sob. Then the young man put forth all his strength, hooked William’s leg with his heel, and flung him over his right hip. Down went sturdy William with a sickening thud, and he lay there as though he would never move hand or foot again.

But now no cheer went up for the stranger. Instead an angry murmur ran through the crowd, because he had won so easily. Then one of the judges, a kinsman of William of the Scar, rose to his feet with a trembling lip and a threatening look. “If you have killed that man,” he said, “it will go badly for you, I can tell you, fellow.” But the stranger answered boldly, “He took his chance with me as I took mine with him. No law can touch me, even if I had killed him, as long as it was done fairly in the wrestling ring.”
“We shall see about that,” said the judge, scowling at the young man, while another angry murmur went around the crowd. As I have said, the men of Denby were proud of sturdy William of the Scar.
Then Sir Richard spoke up gently. “No,” he said, “the young man is right. If the other man dies, he dies in the wrestling ring, where he took his chance, and he was thrown fairly enough.”

But in the meantime three men had come forward and lifted sturdy William from the ground, and they found that he was not dead, though badly shaken by his heavy fall. Then the chief judge stood up and said, “Young man, the prize is rightly yours. Here is the red-gold ring, here are the gloves, and over there stands the cask of wine, to do with as you please.”

At this the young man, who had put his clothes back on and picked up his staff, bowed without a word. He took the gloves and the ring, tucked the gloves into his belt and slipped the ring onto his thumb, and then he turned and leaped lightly over the ropes again. He made his way through the crowd and was gone.

“Now I wonder who that young fellow can be,” said the judge, turning to Sir Richard. “From his red cheeks and fair hair, he looks like a sturdy Saxon. Our William is a sturdy man too, and I have never seen him thrown in the ring before, though he has not yet gone up against great wrestlers like Thomas of Cornwall, Diccon of York, and young David of Doncaster. Doesn’t he have a firm footing in the ring, Sir Richard, don’t you think?”
“Yes, truly, and yet this young man threw him fairly and with marvelous ease. I do wonder who he can be.” Sir Richard said this in a thoughtful voice.

For a while the Knight stood talking with the people around him, but at last he got up and prepared to leave. He called his men together, tightened the girths of his saddle, and mounted his horse once more.

Meanwhile the young stranger had pushed his way through the crowd, but as he passed he heard mutterings all around him: “Look at the cockerel!” “See how he preens himself!” “I’ll swear he threw good William unfairly!” “Yes, indeed, didn’t you see birdlime on his hands?” “Someone ought to clip his comb!” The stranger paid no attention to any of this, but walked proudly along as though he heard nothing. He strolled slowly across the green to the booth where the dancing was going on, and stood at the door looking in at the fun. As he stood there, a stone suddenly struck his arm with a sharp jolt. He turned and saw that an angry crowd of men had followed him from the wrestling ring. When they saw him turn, they all broke out in hooting and yelling, so that the people came running out of the dancing booth to see what was happening. At last a tall, broad-shouldered, burly blacksmith strode out from the crowd, swinging a mighty blackthorn club in his hand.

“Did you have to come to our fair town of Denby, you Jack in the Box, and beat a good honest lad with your wicked, juggling tricks?” he growled in a deep voice like the bellow of an angry bull. “Take that, then!” And suddenly he swung a blow at the young man that could have felled an ox. But the other turned the blow neatly aside and gave back one so terrible that the man of Denby dropped with a groan, as though struck by lightning. When the crowd saw their leader fall, they gave another angry shout. But the stranger put his back against the tent beside him and swung his terrible staff, and the blow he had dealt the stout smith had been so fierce that nobody dared come within reach of his cudgel. So the crowd shrank back, like a pack of dogs from a bear at bay. But then some coward behind him hurled a sharp, jagged stone that struck the stranger on the crown of his head. He staggered back, and red blood gushed from the cut and ran down his face and over his jerkin. Seeing him dazed by this vile blow, the crowd rushed upon him, overwhelmed him, and he fell beneath their feet.

Things might have gone badly for the young man, even to the loss of his young life, if Sir Richard had not come to this fair. For all at once shouts were heard, steel flashed in the air, and blows were dealt with the flat of swords, while through the middle of the crowd Sir Richard of the Lea came spurring on his white horse. Then the crowd, seeing the steel-clad knight and his armed men, melted away like snow on a warm hearth, and left the young man lying bloody and dusty on the ground.
Finding himself free, the young man got up, wiped the blood from his face, and looked up. “Sir Richard of the Lea,” he said, “you may have saved my life today.”
“Who are you, that you know Sir Richard of the Lea so well?” said the Knight. “I think I have seen your face before, young man.”
“You have,” said the young man, “for men call me David of Doncaster.”

“Ha!” said Sir Richard. “I am surprised I did not know you, David, but your beard has grown longer, and you are more settled in manhood than you were this day last year. Come into the tent, David, and wash the blood from your face. And you, Ralph, bring him a clean jerkin at once. I am sorry for what has happened to you, but I am very glad to have had the chance to pay back a part of my debt of kindness to your good master Robin Hood, for it might have gone badly for you if I had not come, young man.”
The Knight took David into the tent, where the young man cleaned his face of blood and changed into the fresh jerkin.

Meanwhile a whisper had gone around among the people standing nearest that this was none other than the great David of Doncaster, the best wrestler in all the Midlands. Only last spring he had thrown sturdy Adam o’ Lincoln in the ring at Selby, in Yorkshire, and he now held the Midlands champion’s belt. So when young David came out of the tent with Sir Richard, with the blood washed from his face and his soiled jerkin changed for a clean one, no angry sounds were heard. Instead everyone pressed forward to see him, proud that one of the great wrestlers of England had stepped into the ring at Denby fair. That is how fickle a crowd can be.

Then Sir Richard called out, “Friends, this is David of Doncaster, so do not think it a shame that your Denby man was thrown by such a wrestler. He bears you no ill will for what has happened, but let it be a warning to you about how you treat strangers from now on. If you had killed him, it would have been a black day for you, for Robin Hood would have swooped down on your town as a kestrel swoops on a dovecote. I bought the cask of wine from him, and now I give it to you freely, to drink as you please. But never again attack a man just because he is a sturdy yeoman.”

The crowd cheered at this, though the truth is they were thinking more about the wine than about what the Knight had said. Then Sir Richard, with David at his side and his men-at-arms around them, rode away from the fair.

But in later days, when the men who had seen that wrestling bout were bent with age, they would shake their heads whenever they heard of any strong man’s game and say, “Aye, aye, but you should have seen the great David of Doncaster throw sturdy William of the Scar at Denby fair.”

Robin Hood stood in the merry greenwood with Little John and most of his sturdy yeomen around him, waiting for Sir Richard to arrive. At last a glint of steel showed through the brown forest leaves, and Sir Richard rode out of the thicket into the open at the head of his men. He came straight to Robin Hood, jumped down from his horse, and threw his arms around the yeoman.
“Well, well,” said Robin after a while, holding Sir Richard at arm’s length and looking him up and down, “I think you are a gayer bird than when I saw you last.”

“Yes, and I have you to thank, Robin,” said the Knight, resting his hand on the yeoman’s shoulder. “If it weren’t for you, I would be wandering in misery in some foreign land by now. But I have kept my word, Robin. I have brought back the money you lent me, and I have doubled it four times over, so that I am rich again. Along with it I have brought a small gift for you and your brave men, from my dear lady and myself.” Then he turned to his men and called out, “Bring up the pack horses.”

But Robin stopped him. “No, Sir Richard,” he said, “don’t think me rude for crossing your order, but here in Sherwood we do no business until we have eaten and drunk.” With that, he took Sir Richard by the hand and led him to the seat under the greenwood tree, while the other leading men of the band came and sat down around them. Then Robin said, “How is it that I saw young David of Doncaster with you and your men, Sir Knight?”

At once the Knight told him everything: about his stay at Denby, what had happened at the fair, and how things had been likely to go badly for young David. When he had told the whole tale, he said, “That is what kept me on the road so late, good Robin. Otherwise I would have been here an hour ago.”

When he had finished, Robin reached out and gripped the Knight’s hand. “I owe you a debt I can never hope to repay, Sir Richard,” he said, his voice trembling. “I tell you, I would rather lose my right hand than see young David of Doncaster suffer what seemed about to happen to him at Denby.”

They went on talking until, after a while, someone came to say that the feast was ready, and everyone got up and went to it. When it was over, the Knight told his men to bring the pack horses forward, and they did as he ordered. Then one of them brought him a strongbox. He opened it, took out a bag, and counted out five hundred pounds, the sum he had borrowed from Robin.
“Sir Richard,” said Robin, “you would please us all if you would keep that money as a gift from us in Sherwood. Isn’t that so, my lads?”
Then they all shouted “Aye!” in one mighty voice.
“I thank you all deeply,” said the Knight earnestly, “but please don’t think badly of me if I can’t accept it. I was glad to borrow it from you, but I cannot take it as a gift.”

Robin Hood said no more, but handed the money to Little John to put away in the treasury. He was shrewd enough to know that nothing breeds ill will and bitterness like a gift forced on someone who has no choice but to take it.

Then Sir Richard had the packs set on the ground and opened. A great shout went up that made the forest ring, for there lay two hundred bows of the finest Spanish yew, polished until they gleamed, each inlaid with fanciful figures in silver, though not so deeply as to weaken them. Beside these were two hundred leather quivers embroidered with golden thread, and in each quiver were twenty arrows with polished heads that shone like silver. Every arrow was feathered with peacock plumes and had its notch trimmed with silver.
Sir Richard gave each yeoman a bow and a quiver of arrows. To Robin he gave a sturdy bow inlaid with gold in the most skillful workmanship, and every arrow in his quiver had a golden notch.
Then they all cheered again, delighted with the splendid gift, and vowed among themselves to die for Sir Richard and his lady if it ever came to that.

At last the time came when Sir Richard had to leave. Robin Hood called his band around him, and each yeoman took a torch to light the way through the woods. They went together to the edge of Sherwood, and there the Knight kissed Robin on both cheeks, left him, and was gone.
So Robin Hood rescued a noble knight from terrible misfortunes that would otherwise have choked all the happiness out of his life.

chapters.title: Little John Turns Barefoot Friar
paragraphs: The cold winter was over and spring had come. The woods had not yet put on their thick leaves, but the budding foliage hung around the trees like a soft mist. In the open country the meadows lay a shimmering green, and the cornfields a deep velvety color, thick and soft with growing blades. The plowboy shouted in the sunshine, and flocks of birds hunted fat worms in the purple, freshly turned furrows. The whole broad, damp earth smiled in the warm light, and every little green hill seemed to clap its hands for joy.

Robin Hood sat on a deer’s hide spread on the ground in the open, in front of the greenwood tree, basking in the sun like an old dog fox. He leaned back with his hands clasped around his knees and lazily watched Little John twist a strong bowstring out of long strands of hemp thread, wetting his palms every now and then and rolling the cord along his thigh. Nearby, Allan a Dale sat fitting a new string to his harp.

At last Robin said, “I think I would rather roam this forest in the gentle spring than be King of all merry England. What palace in the wide world is as fair as this sweet woodland right now? And what king has as much appetite for plovers’ eggs and lampreys as I have for juicy venison and sparkling ale? Gaffer Swanthold is right when he says, ‘Better a crust with contentment than honey with a sour heart.’”

“Aye,” said Little John, rubbing his new bowstring with yellow beeswax, “the life we lead is the life for me. You talk of the springtime, but I think even winter has its own joys. You and I, good master, spent more than one merry day at the Blue Boar this past winter. Don’t you remember the night you and Will Stutely and Friar Tuck and I spent at that same inn with the two beggars and the wandering friar?”
“Aye,” said merry Robin, laughing, “that was the night Will Stutely just had to steal a kiss from the stout hostess, and got a mug of ale emptied over his head for his trouble.”
“That’s the very night,” said Little John, laughing too. “And I thought it was a fine song the wandering friar sang. Friar Tuck, you have a quick ear for a tune. Don’t you remember it?”

“I did catch the tune of it once,” said Tuck. “Let me see.” He touched a forefinger to his forehead in thought and hummed to himself, stopping now and then to fit what he had got to what he was searching for in his memory. At last he found it all, cleared his throat, and sang merrily:

“_In the blooming hedge the robin sings,
For the sun is merry and bright,
And joyfully hops and flutters his wings,
For his heart is full of delight.
For the May is in flower,
And there’s little to sour,
And plenty to eat in the Maytime hour.
When the blossoms all fade,
He’ll fly off, unafraid,
To keep himself warm
In some jolly old barn
Where the snow and the wind can do him no harm.

“Such is the wandering friar’s life,
With plenty to eat and to drink;
The goodwife saves him a chair by the fire,
And the pretty girls smile when he winks.
He sings out with a will
As he strolls on uphill,
A rollicking song for the saving of souls.
When the cold winds blow
With the coming of snow,
There’s a place by the fire
For the fatherly friar,
And a crab in the bowl for his heart’s desire_.”
So Friar Tuck sang, in a rich, mellow voice, rolling his head from side to side in time with the music. When he was done, everyone clapped and roared with laughter, for the song suited him well.
“Truly,” said Little John, “that is a fine song, and if I weren’t a yeoman of Sherwood Forest, I would rather be a wandering friar than anything else in the world.”

“Yes, it’s a fine song,” said Robin Hood, “but I thought those two burly beggars told merrier tales and led a merrier life. Don’t you remember what that big black-bearded fellow told us about his begging at the fair in York?”
“Ah, but what about the friar’s tale of the harvest home in Kentshire?” said Little John. “I say he led a merrier life than either of the others.”
“In honor of the cloth,” said Friar Tuck, “I must back my good gossip, Little John.”

“Well,” said Robin, “I stick to my own opinion. But what do you say, Little John, to a merry adventure on this fine day? Take a friar’s gown from our chest of strange clothes and put it on, and I will stop the first beggar I meet and swap clothes with him. Then let’s wander the countryside this sweet day and see what happens to each of us.”
“That suits me,” said Little John. “Let’s be off, I say.”

So Little John and Friar Tuck went to the band’s storehouse and picked out the robe of a Gray Friar for the yeoman. When they came out again, a mighty roar of laughter went up, because the band had never seen Little John dressed like that, and the robe was too short for him by a good hand’s breadth. But Little John’s hands were folded in his loose sleeves, his eyes were cast down on the ground, and from his belt hung a great long string of beads.

Now Little John took up his stout staff, which had a chubby little leather flask hanging from the end, the kind that pilgrims carry at the tips of their staves. But what was in it, I can tell you, was more like good Malmsey wine than the cold spring water that godly pilgrims carry. Then Robin got up and took his own stout staff, and slipped ten golden angels into his pouch. There was no beggar’s outfit among the band’s stores, so he was ready to take his chances on meeting a beggar and buying his clothes.

When all was ready, the two yeomen set out, striding briskly along in the misty morning. They walked down the forest path until they came to the highway, and then along the highway until it forked, one road leading to Blyth and the other to Gainsborough. Here the yeomen stopped.
“You take the road to Gainsborough,” said jolly Robin, “and I will take the one to Blyth. So farewell, holy father, and may you have no reason to tell your beads in earnest before we meet again.”
“Good day to you, good beggar-to-be,” said Little John, “and may you have no reason to beg for mercy before I see you next.”
Each of them went sturdily on his way until a green hill rose between them and one was hidden from the other’s sight.

Little John walked along whistling, for there was nobody near on the whole road. In the budding hedges the little birds twittered merrily, and on either side the green hills swept up to the sky, with the great white clouds of spring sailing slowly and lazily over their crowns. Up hill and down valley went Little John, the fresh wind in his face and his robes fluttering behind him, until at last he came to a crossroad that led to Tuxford. There he met three pretty girls, each carrying a basket of eggs to market. “Where are you off to, fair maids?” he said, and he stood in their path, holding his staff out in front of them to stop them.
They huddled together and nudged one another, and then one of them spoke up. “We are going to Tuxford market, holy friar, to sell our eggs.”

“Well, I never!” said Little John, looking at them with his head on one side. “What a pity that such fair girls should have to carry eggs to market. I’ll tell you this: if I had the shaping of the world, you would all three be dressed in the finest silks, riding milk-white horses with pages at your side, and eating nothing but whipped cream and strawberries. That is the life that would suit your looks.”

At this speech all three pretty girls looked down, blushing and giggling. One said, “Oh!” another, “Goodness, he’s making fun of us!” and the third, “Just listen to the holy man!” But all the while they glanced at Little John out of the corners of their eyes.
“Now, look here,” said Little John, “I can’t bear to see such dainty maidens carrying baskets along a highroad. Let me carry them myself, and one of you, if you like, may carry my staff for me.”
“No,” said one of the girls, “you can’t carry three baskets all at once.”

“Oh, but I can,” said Little John, “and I’ll show you right now. I thank good Saint Wilfred for giving me a clever wit. Watch. I take this big basket, so. I tie my rosary around the handle, like this. Then I slip the rosary over my head and sling the basket on my back, in this way.” And Little John did just as he said, with the basket hanging down behind him like a peddler’s pack. Then he gave his staff to one of the girls, took a basket on each arm, turned toward Tuxford Town, and stepped out merrily, with a laughing girl on either side and one walking ahead carrying the staff. In this fashion they traveled along, and everyone they met stopped and stared after them, laughing, for nobody had ever seen such a merry sight as this tall, strapping Gray Friar in robes much too short for him, loaded with eggs and tramping the road with three pretty girls. Little John didn’t care a bit about that, and when people called out jokes to him, he answered them back just as merrily, word for word.

So they went on toward Tuxford, chatting and laughing, until they came near the town. There Little John stopped and set down the baskets, because he didn’t want to go into the town in case he should meet some of the Sheriff’s men. “Alas, sweet chicks,” he said, “here I must leave you. I hadn’t planned to come this way, but I’m glad I did. Now, before we part, we must drink to friendship.” With that, he unslung the leather flask from the end of his staff, pulled out the stopper, wiped the mouth of the flask on his sleeve, and handed it to the girl who had carried his staff. Each girl took a good drink of what was inside, and when it had gone all around, Little John finished what was left, so that not another drop could be squeezed out. Then he kissed each girl sweetly, wished them all good day, and left them. But the girls stood watching him as he walked away whistling. “What a pity,” said one, “that such a stout, lusty lad should be in holy orders.”
“Well,” said Little John to himself as he strode along, “that was no bad bit of luck. Saint Dunstan, send me more like it.”

He trudged along for a while, and as the day grew warm he began to get thirsty again. He shook his leather bottle beside his ear, but not a sound came from it. Then he put it to his lips and tipped it high in the air, but not a drop came out. “Little John! Little John!” he said sadly to himself, shaking his head, “women will be the ruin of you yet, if you don’t take better care of yourself.”

But at last he reached the top of a hill and saw a sweet little thatched inn nestled in the valley below, where the road dipped steeply down to it. At the sight, a voice inside him cried out, “Joy to you, good friend, for there is just what your heart desires: a sweet rest and a cup of brown beer.” So he hurried down the hill and came to the little inn, which had a sign hanging outside with a stag’s head painted on it. In front of the door a hen was clucking and scratching in the dust, with a brood of chicks at her heels, and the sparrows under the eaves were chattering about their household affairs. Everything was so sweet and peaceful that Little John’s heart laughed inside him. Beside the door stood two sturdy horses with broad, soft, padded saddles, made for comfortable traveling, which told of rich guests in the parlor. Out front, on a bench in the sun, three merry fellows, a tinker, a peddler, and a beggar, sat drinking strong ale.
“Good day to you, sweet friends,” said Little John, striding up to where they sat.

“Good day to you, holy father,” said the merry Beggar with a grin. “But look, your gown is too short. You had better cut a piece off the top and stitch it onto the bottom, so that it’s long enough. But come, sit down beside us and have a taste of ale, if your vows don’t forbid it.”
“No,” said Little John, grinning too, “the blessed Saint Dunstan has given me full permission to indulge in that sort of thing.” And he stuck his hand into his pouch for money to pay his bill.

“Truly,” said the Tinker, “unless your looks deceive me, holy friar, the good Saint Dunstan was wise, for without such permission his follower would have many a penance to do. No, take your hand out of your pouch, brother, for you shall not pay this round. Ho, landlord, a pot of ale!”

So the ale was brought and handed to Little John. He blew the froth aside to make room for his lips, then tipped the bottom of the pot higher and higher until it pointed at the sky, and he had to shut his eyes against the dazzle of the sunshine. Then he took the pot away, because there was nothing left in it, and let out a deep, full sigh, looking at the others with moist eyes and shaking his head solemnly.
“Ho, landlord!” cried the Peddler. “Bring this good fellow another pot of ale, for it does us all credit to have among us a man who can empty a mug so heartily.”
So they chatted merrily among themselves, until after a while Little John said, “Who owns those two horses over there?”

“Two holy men like you, brother,” said the Beggar. “They’re having a fine feast inside right now, for I just smelled the steam of a boiled chicken. The landlady says they come from Fountain Abbey in Yorkshire and are going to Lincoln on business.”
“A merry pair they are,” said the Tinker, “for one is as thin as an old woman’s spindle, and the other as fat as a suet pudding.”
“Speaking of fat,” said the Peddler, “you yourself don’t look any too badly fed, holy friar.”
“No, truly,” said Little John, “you see in me what the holy Saint Dunstan can do for those who serve him on a handful of dried peas and a trickle of cold water.”

At this a great roar of laughter went up. “It’s a marvel, truly,” said the Beggar. “Watching the masterly way you tucked away that pot of ale, I would have sworn you hadn’t tasted plain water in a couple of months. Hasn’t this same holy Saint Dunstan taught you a good song or two?”
“Well, as for that,” said Little John with a grin, “maybe he has helped me learn a tune or so.”
“Then please, let’s hear what he has taught you,” said the Tinker.
Little John cleared his throat, said a word or two about a hoarseness that was bothering him, and then began to sing:

“_Ah, pretty, pretty maid, where are you going?
I beg you, beg you, wait for your lover too,
And we’ll gather the rose
As it sweetly blows,
For the merry, merry winds are blo-o-o-wing_.”

It seemed that Little John’s songs were never meant to get sung, for he had got no further than this when the door of the inn opened and out came the two brothers of Fountain Abbey, with the landlord following them and, as the saying goes, washing his hands with humble soap. But when the brothers saw who was singing, and that he was dressed in the robes of a Gray Friar, they stopped short. The fat little Brother drew his heavy eyebrows together in a mighty frown, and the thin Brother screwed up his face as though he had sour beer in his mouth. Then, just as Little John was taking a breath for a new verse, the fat Brother roared out, “Now then!” his voice coming out like loud thunder from a little cloud, “you rascal, is this a proper place for a man in your clothes to guzzle ale and sing worldly songs?”
“Well,” said Little John, “since I can’t guzzle and sing, as Your Reverence does, in such a fine place as Fountain Abbey, I must guzzle and sing where I can.”
“Shame on you!” cried the tall lean Brother in a harsh voice. “Shame on you, for disgracing your cloth with such talk and behavior.”

“Well, well!” said Little John. “Disgrace, do you say? I think it is more of a disgrace for men of our cloth to squeeze hard-earned farthings out of the grip of poor, thin peasants. Isn’t that so, brother?”

At this the Tinker, the Peddler, and the Beggar nudged one another and all grinned, and the friars scowled darkly at Little John. But they could think of nothing more to say, so they turned to their horses. Then Little John suddenly jumped up from the bench where he was sitting and ran over to where the brothers of Fountain Abbey were mounting. “Let me hold your horses’ bridles for you,” he said. “Your words have struck my sinful heart, so that I will stay no longer in this den of evil, but will go on with you. No vile temptation, I’m sure, will fall on me in such holy company.”
“No, fellow,” said the lean Brother harshly, for he saw that Little John was making fun of them, “we want none of your company, so be off with you.”

“Alas,” said Little John, “I am truly sorry that you don’t like me or my company, but as for leaving you, that cannot be, for my heart is so moved that, whether I like it or not, I must go with you for the sake of your holy company.”

At this talk all the good fellows on the bench were grinning until their teeth shone, and even the landlord could not help smiling. As for the friars, they looked at each other, puzzled, and did not know what to do about it. They were so proud that the thought of riding along the highroad with a wandering friar running beside them, in robes far too short for him, made them sick with shame. Yet they could not make Little John stay against his will, for they knew he could crack the bones of both of them in a twinkling if he wanted to. Then the fat Brother spoke up, more mildly than before. “No, good brother,” he said, “we will ride fast, and you will be worn out trying to keep the pace.”
“I thank you for thinking of me,” said Little John, “but don’t worry, brother. My legs are strong, and I could run like a hare from here to Gainsborough.”

At these words a sound of laughing came from the bench, and the lean Brother’s anger boiled over, like water onto a fire, with great fuss and noise. “Shame on you, you rascal!” he cried. “Aren’t you ashamed to bring such disgrace on our cloth? Stay here, you drunkard, with these swine. You are no fit company for us.”

“Well, there you are!” said Little John. “Do you hear, landlord? You are not fit company for these holy men. Go back to your alehouse. And if these most holy brothers of mine will just give me the word, I’ll beat your head with this stout staff until it’s as soft as whipped eggs.”

At this another great shout of laughter went up from those on the bench, and the landlord’s face turned red as a cherry from stifling his laugh in his belly. But he held his merriment down, for he did not want to earn the ill will of the brothers of Fountain Abbey by laughing at the wrong moment. So the two brothers, since they could do nothing else, mounted their horses, turned their noses toward Lincoln, and rode away.

“I can’t stay any longer, sweet friends,” said Little John, as he pushed in between the two horses, “so I wish you good day. Off we go, we three.” With that, he swung his stout staff over his shoulder and trudged off, matching his pace to that of the two horses.

The two brothers glared at Little John when he pushed himself in between them. Then they moved as far away from him as they could, so that the yeoman walked in the middle of the road while they rode along the footpaths on either side. As they went off like this, the Tinker, the Peddler, and the Beggar ran skipping out into the middle of the highway, each with a pot in his hand, and stood laughing as they watched them go.

As long as they were in sight of the people at the inn, the brothers walked their horses calmly. They did not want to make matters worse by seeming to run away from Little John, for they could not help thinking how it would sound to people when they heard that the brothers of Fountain Abbey had scampered away from a wandering friar, like the Ugly One when the blessed Saint Dunstan freed his nose from the red-hot tongs where he had held it fast. But once they had crossed the top of the hill and the inn was out of sight, the fat Brother said to the thin Brother, “Brother Ambrose, hadn’t we better pick up our pace?”
“Why, truly, friend,” Little John spoke up, “I think it would be good to make our pot boil a little faster, for the day is wearing on. And it won’t jolt your fat too much, so onward, I say.”

The two friars said nothing, but gave Little John another poisonous glare. Then, without a word, they urged their horses on with a click of the tongue, and both broke into a canter. They galloped for a mile and more, with Little John running lightly between them like a stag, not even out of breath. At last the fat Brother hauled back on his reins with a groan, for he could bear the jolting no longer. “Dear me,” said Little John, not so much as panting, “I was afraid this rough pace would shake up your poor old fat belly.”

To this the fat Friar said not a word, but stared straight ahead and chewed his lower lip. Now they went forward more quietly, Little John in the middle of the road, whistling merrily to himself, and the two friars on the footpaths on either side, saying nothing at all.

Soon they met three merry minstrels dressed all in red. The minstrels gaped at the sight of a Gray Friar in such short robes striding down the middle of the road, and of two brothers riding on richly decked horses along the footpaths with their heads hung in shame. As they drew near, Little John swung his staff about like an usher clearing a path. “Make way!” he cried loudly. “Make way! Make way! For here we go, we three!” How the minstrels gaped, and how they laughed! But the fat Friar trembled as if he had a fever, and the lean Friar sank his head down over his horse’s neck.

Next they met two noble knights in rich clothes, with hawks on their wrists, and two fair ladies dressed in silks and velvets, all riding fine horses. They all made room, staring, as Little John and the two friars came along the road. Little John bowed humbly to them. “Greetings, lords and ladies,” he said. “But here we go, we three.”
Everyone laughed, and one of the fair ladies called out, “Which three do you mean, merry friend?”
Little John glanced back over his shoulder, for by now they had gone past one another, and shouted, “Big Jack, lean Jack, and fat Jack-pudding!”
At this the fat Friar gave a groan and looked as if he might fall out of his saddle for shame. The other brother said nothing, but looked straight ahead with a grim, stony face.

Just ahead, the road took a sharp turn around a tall hedge, and about forty paces past the bend another road crossed the one they were on. When they reached the crossroad and were well away from the people they had left behind, the lean Friar suddenly pulled up his horse. “Listen, fellow,” he said in a voice shaking with rage, “we have had enough of your vile company, and we are tired of being made fun of. Go your way, and let us go ours in peace.”

“Well, there now!” said Little John. “I thought we were such a merry company, and here you flare up like fat in a pan. But truly, I’ve had enough of you today, though I can ill spare your company. I know you will miss me, but if you want me again, whisper to Goodman Wind, and he will carry the news to me. But you see, I am a poor man and you are rich. I beg you, give me a penny or two to buy bread and cheese at the next inn.”
“Fellow, we carry no money,” said the lean Friar in his harsh voice. “Come along, Brother Thomas, let’s move on.”

But Little John caught the horses by their bridle reins, one in each hand. “Do you really have no money on you at all?” he said. “Now, I beg you, brothers, for charity’s sake, give me something to buy a crust of bread, even if it’s only a penny.”
“I’m telling you, fellow, we have no money!” boomed the fat little Friar in his big voice.
“Have you, in holy truth, no money?” asked Little John.
“Not a farthing,” said the lean Friar sourly.
“Not a groat,” said the fat Friar loudly.

“No,” said Little John, “that will never do. I couldn’t bear to see two holy men like you go off without a penny. Get down off your horses at once, and we’ll kneel right here in the middle of the crossroads and ask the blessed Saint Dunstan to send us some money for our journey.”

“What do you mean, you limb of the devil!” cried the lean Friar, grinding his teeth with rage. “Are you ordering me, the high cellarer of Fountain Abbey, to climb down from my horse and kneel in the muddy road to pray to some beggarly Saxon saint?”

“Now,” said Little John, “I have a good mind to crack your head for speaking that way about the good Saint Dunstan! But get down this minute, because my patience won’t last much longer, and I might forget that you are both men of the church.” With that, he twirled his stout staff until it whistled.
When they heard this, both friars turned as pale as dough. The fat Brother slid down from his horse on one side, and the lean Brother slid down on the other.

“Now, brothers, down on your knees and pray,” said Little John. He put his heavy hands on each friar’s shoulder and forced them to their knees, kneeling down beside them. Then Little John began begging Saint Dunstan for money in a great loud voice. When he had pleaded with the Saint for a while, he told the friars to feel in their pouches and see whether the Saint had sent them anything. Each man slowly put his hand into the pouch hanging at his side, but nothing came out.

“Ha!” said Little John, “are your prayers worth so little? Then let’s try again.” And he promptly began calling on Saint Dunstan once more, something like this: “O gracious Saint Dunstan! Send some money right away to these poor folk, so that the fat one doesn’t waste away and grow as lean as the lean one, and the lean one doesn’t waste away to nothing at all before they reach Lincoln Town. But send them only ten shillings apiece, so they don’t get puffed up with pride. Anything more than that you send, send to me.”
“Now,” he said, getting up, “let’s see what each man has.” Then he thrust his hand into his pouch and pulled out four golden angels. “What have you got, brothers?” he asked.
Once more each friar slowly pushed his hand into his pouch, and once more it came out empty.
“Nothing at all?” said Little John. “I’ll bet something has slipped into the seams of your pouches, and that’s why you missed it. Let me look.”

He went first to the lean Friar, put his hand into the pouch, and pulled out a leather bag. From it he counted one hundred and ten pounds in gold. “I thought,” said Little John, “that you had missed the money the blessed Saint sent you, in some odd corner of your pouch. Now let me see whether you have some too, brother.” Then he reached into the fat Friar’s pouch and pulled out a bag just like the other, and counted out seventy pounds from it. “You see?” he said. “I knew the good Saint had sent you a little something that you had missed too.”

Then he gave them one pound to share between them and slipped the rest of the money into his own pouch. “You gave me your holy word that you had no money,” he said. “Since you are holy men, I trust you would never go back on a word you pledged, so I know the good Saint Dunstan sent this in answer to my prayers. But I only prayed for ten shillings to be sent to each of you, and everything over that belongs to me by rights, so I am taking it. Good day to you, brothers, and may the rest of your journey be a pleasant one.” With that, he turned and strode away. The friars looked at each other with miserable faces, and slowly and sadly they climbed back on their horses and rode off without a word.
But Little John turned back toward Sherwood Forest, and he whistled merrily all the way as he strode along.
And now we will see what happened to Robin Hood on his adventure as a beggar.

chapters.title: Robin Hood Turns Beggar
paragraphs: After jolly Robin had left Little John at the fork in the road, he walked cheerfully on through the warm, mellow sunshine. Every now and then he would skip and leap or sing a snatch of song, out of pure joy in the day. In the sweetness of springtime his heart was as frisky as a colt turned out to graze. Sometimes he walked a long way gazing up at the great white clouds drifting slowly across the deep blue sky. Then he would stop and drink in the fullness of life all around him, for the hedgerows were just beginning to bud and the meadow grass was growing long and green. Again he would stand still and listen to the pretty songs of the little birds in the thickets, or to the clear crow of the rooster, daring the sky to rain, and that made him laugh, because it took very little to tickle Robin’s heart into merriment. So he tramped sturdily along, always willing to stop for one reason or another, and always ready to chat with any merry lasses he met on the way. And so the morning slipped by, but he still hadn’t met a beggar to swap clothes with. “If my luck doesn’t change soon,” he said, “I’m likely to have an empty day of it, for it’s nearly half gone already. I’ve had a merry walk through the countryside, but I still know nothing of a beggar’s life.”

After a while he began to grow hungry, and his mind turned away from thoughts of springtime and flowers and birds and settled tenderly on boiled capons, Malmsey wine, white bread, and the like. “I wish I had Willie Wynkin’s wishing coat,” he said to himself. “I know exactly what I would wish for, and this is it.” Here he ticked off the things he wanted on the fingers of his left hand, using the forefinger of his right. “First, I would have a sweet brown pie of tender larks, and mind you, not dry, but with a good bit of gravy to soak it. Next, a pretty pullet, nicely boiled, with tender pigeons’ eggs, cleverly sliced, laid all around the platter. With these I would have a long, slim loaf of wheat bread baked on the hearth, warm from the fire, with a glossy brown crust the color of my own Maid Marian’s hair, and that crust should be as crisp and brittle as the thin white ice that lies across the furrows on an early winter morning. That will do for the solid things, but with them I must have three pots, fat and round, one full of Malmsey, one of Canary, and one brimming with my own dear hearty sack.” So Robin talked to himself, and his mouth watered at the corners as he thought of the good things he had conjured up in his mind.

Talking to himself like this, he came to a place where the dusty road turned sharply around the hedge, which was soft with the green of coming leaves. There in front of him he saw a stout fellow sitting on a stile, idly swinging his legs. All around this hearty rogue hung a dozen or more pouches and bags of different sizes and kinds, with wide, gaping mouths like a brood of hungry jackdaws. His coat was belted at the waist and patched with as many colors as there are stripes on a Maypole in springtime. On his head he wore a great tall leather cap, and across his knees lay a stout blackthorn quarterstaff, every bit as long and heavy as Robin’s. He was as jolly a beggar as ever walked the lanes and byways of Nottinghamshire, for his eyes were slate gray and snapped and twinkled and danced with merriment, and his black hair curled tight all over his head in little rings.
“Hello there, good fellow,” said Robin, when he had come close to him, “what are you doing here on this merry day, when the flowers are peeping out and the buds are swelling?”
The other winked one eye and at once sang out in a merry voice:

“_Here on the stile I sit,
And I sing a bit
As I wait for my own true love, O,
The sun is shining bright,
The leaves are dancing light,
And the little bird sings she’s near, O_.
“And that’s how it is with me, bully boy, except that my sweetheart hasn’t come.”
“That is a very sweet song,” said Robin, “and if I were in the mood to listen to you, I could happily hear more. But I have two serious things to ask you, so please listen.”

At this the jolly Beggar cocked his head to one side like a roguish magpie. “I’m a poor jug to pour heavy things into, my friend,” he said, “and unless I’m mistaken, you don’t have many serious words to spare at any time.”
“Oh, but I do,” said jolly Robin. “What I want to say first is the most serious thought in the world to me, namely, ‘Where shall I find something to eat and drink?’”

“Is that so?” said the Beggar. “Well, I don’t make such serious thoughts of it. I eat when I can get food, and I munch my crust when I can’t get a crumb, and when there’s no ale to be had, I wash the dust out of my throat with a trickle of cold water. I was sitting here when you came along, wondering whether to break my fast or not. I like to let my hunger grow good and sharp before I eat, because then a dry crust tastes as fine to me as a venison pasty with suet and raisins tastes to mighty King Harry. I have a sharp hunger on me now, but I think in a little while it will ripen into a nice mellow appetite.”

“Well, truly,” said merry Robin, laughing, “you have a strange tongue in your head. But have you really nothing but a dry crust on you? Your bags and pouches look too plump and hearty for such thin fare.”
“Well, maybe there’s some other cold food in there,” said the Beggar slyly.
“And have you nothing to drink but cold water?” asked Robin.

“Not so much as a drop,” said the Beggar. “Over beyond that clump of trees is as sweet a little inn as you ever laid eyes on, but I don’t go there, because they treat me shabbily. Once, when the good Prior of Emmet was dining there, the landlady set a dear little tart of stewed crabs and barley sugar on the windowsill to cool. Seeing it there, and afraid it might get lost, I took it along with me until I could find its owner. Ever since then they have behaved very badly toward me. Still, truth compels me to say that they have the best ale there that ever rolled over my tongue.”
At this Robin laughed out loud. “Well,” he said, “they treated you badly for your kindness. But tell me honestly, what have you got in your pouches?”

“Well,” said the Beggar, peeping into the mouths of his bags, “here I find a fine piece of pigeon pie, wrapped in a cabbage leaf to hold the gravy. Here I see a dainty streaked slice of brawn, and here a nice lump of white bread. Here are four oatcakes and a cold knuckle of ham. Ha! Strange, but true: here are six eggs that must have come by accident from some poultry yard around here. They’re raw, but roasted on the coals and spread with a bit of butter that I see—”

“Enough, good friend!” cried Robin, holding up his hand. “You make my poor stomach quake with joy at what you tell me so sweetly. If you will give me something to eat, I will go straight to that little inn you mentioned just now, and bring back a skin of ale for you and me to drink.”

“Friend, you have said enough,” said the Beggar, climbing down from the stile. “I will feast you with the best I have and bless Saint Cedric for your company. But, sweet chuck, please bring at least three quarts of ale, one for you to drink and two for me, for my thirst is such that I think I could drink ale the way the sands of the River Dee drink salt water.”

So Robin left the Beggar right away. The Beggar went to a budding lime bush behind the hedge, spread his feast out on the grass, and roasted his eggs over a little fire of sticks, with a skill earned through long practice. After a while Robin came back carrying a good skin of ale on his shoulder, which he set down on the grass. Then he looked at the feast spread on the ground—and a fine sight it was—and slowly rubbed his hand over his stomach, for to his hungry eyes it seemed the fairest sight he had seen in all his life.
“Friend,” said the Beggar, “just let me test the weight of that skin.”
“Yes, certainly,” said Robin. “Help yourself, sweet chuck, and meanwhile let me see whether your pigeon pie is fresh.”
So one of them seized the ale and the other the pigeon pie, and for a while nothing could be heard but the munching of food and the gurgle of ale leaving the skin.
At last, when a good long while had passed in this way, Robin pushed the food aside and sighed deeply with contentment, feeling as if he had been made over brand new.
“And now, good friend,” he said, leaning on one elbow, “I will tackle you about that other serious matter I mentioned a while ago.”
“What!” said the Beggar reproachfully. “Surely you wouldn’t talk about serious business over ale as good as this!”

“No,” said Robin, laughing. “I wouldn’t hold back your thirst, sweet friend. Drink while I talk to you. Here it is: I have taken a liking to your trade, and I would like to have a taste of a beggar’s life myself.”

“I’m not surprised that you like my way of life, good fellow,” said the Beggar, “but ‘to like’ and ‘to do’ are two very different things. I tell you, friend, a man must serve a long apprenticeship before he can learn to be even a clapper-dudgeon, much less a crank or an Abraham-man.(3) I tell you, lad, you are too old to start on something that may take you years to get the hang of.”

(3) Kinds of wandering beggars that overran England until
the middle of the seventeenth century. SEE Dakkar’s
ENGLISH VILLAINIES, etc.

“That may be so,” said Robin, “for I remember that Gaffer Swanthold says Jack Shoemaker makes bad bread, and Tom Baker makes bad shoes. All the same, I have a mind to taste a beggar’s life, and I only need the clothes to be as good as any of you.”

“I tell you, fellow,” said the Beggar, “even if you were dressed as handsomely as good Saint Wynten, the patron of our trade, you would never make a beggar. Why, the first jolly traveler you met would beat you to a pudding for poking your nose into a trade that doesn’t belong to you.”

“All the same,” said Robin, “I would like to try it, and I think I will swap clothes with you, for your outfit looks pretty, not to say gay. So not only will I swap clothes, but I will give you two golden angels on top of it. I brought my stout staff along, thinking I might have to rap one of your brotherhood over the head to make my point, but I like you so much for the feast you have given me that I wouldn’t raise even my little finger against you, so you needn’t have the slightest fear.”
The Beggar listened to this with his knuckles resting on his hips, and when Robin had finished he cocked his head to one side and stuck his tongue in his cheek.

“Well, I never,” he said at last. “Raise a finger against me, would you? Are you out of your mind, man? My name is Riccon Hazel, and I come from Holywell in Flintshire, over by the River Dee. Let me tell you, you rascal, I have cracked the heads of many better men than you, and I’d break yours open right now if it weren’t for the ale you gave me. And you won’t get so much as a scrap of my coat, even if it would save you from the gallows.”

“Now, my friend,” said Robin, “it would hardly be right for me to spoil that handsome head of yours. But I’ll tell you plainly, if it weren’t for this feast, I would do something to you that would keep you from tramping the country for many a day. Keep your mouth shut, lad, or your luck will tumble out along with your words!”

“Well, alas for you, man, because you’ve picked a bad day to be foolish!” cried the Beggar, getting up and grabbing his staff. “Pick up your club and defend yourself, fellow, because I’m going to beat you and take your money too. I’ll leave you without even a clipped groat to buy a lump of goose grease to rub on your cracked head. So defend yourself, I say.”

At that, merry Robin sprang up and snatched his own staff. “Take my money if you can,” he said. “I promise to hand over every last farthing if you so much as touch me.” And he spun his staff between his fingers until it whistled.

Then the Beggar swung his staff and struck a mighty blow at Robin, but the yeoman turned it aside. Three times the Beggar struck, and not once did he touch so much as a hair on Robin’s head. Then sturdy Robin saw his chance, and before you could count to three, Riccon’s staff was flying over the hedge, and Riccon himself lay on the green grass, as still as an empty pudding bag.

“Well now!” said merry Robin, laughing. “Do you want my hide or my money, sweet chuck?” But the other man answered not a word. Robin saw that he was stunned by the blow, so he ran, still laughing, and fetched the skin of ale. He poured some on the Beggar’s head and some down his throat, until the man opened his eyes and looked around, as if he wondered why he was lying on his back.

When Robin saw that the man had gathered up at least some of the wits that had just been knocked out of him, he said, “Now, good fellow, will you trade clothes with me, or must I tap you again? Here are two golden angels if you’ll hand over all your rags and bags, your cap and the rest, and do it willingly. If you won’t, I’m afraid I’ll have to—” And he looked his staff up and down.

Riccon sat up and rubbed the bump on his head. “Well, confound it!” he said. “I thought I’d give you a sweet thrashing, fellow. I don’t know how it happened, but it seems I’ve bought more beer than I can drink. If I have to give up my clothes, I have to. But first promise me, on your word as a true yeoman, that you’ll take nothing from me but my clothes.”
“I promise on the word of a true yeoman,” said Robin, thinking the man had a few pennies he wanted to save.

At that, the Beggar pulled out a little knife that hung at his side and slit open the lining of his coat. Out of it he took ten bright golden pounds and laid them on the ground beside him, with a sly wink at Robin. “Now you’re welcome to my clothes,” he said, “and you could have had them in exchange for yours without paying a single farthing, let alone two golden angels.”

“Well, well,” said Robin, laughing, “you’re a sly one, and I’ll tell you honestly, if I’d known you had so much money on you, you might not have carried it off. I’d wager you didn’t come by it honestly.”

Then each of them stripped off his clothes and put on the other’s, and Robin Hood made as hearty a beggar as you could find on a summer’s day. But sturdy Riccon of Holywell skipped and leaped and danced for joy over the fine suit of Lincoln green he had gotten. “I’m a gay-feathered bird now,” he said. “My dear Moll Peascod would never know me in these clothes. You can keep the cold leftovers of the feast, friend, because I mean to live well and lustily while my money lasts and my clothes are bright.”
With that he turned away from Robin, climbed over the stile and was gone. But Robin could hear him singing from beyond the hedge as he strode off:

“_Polly is smiling and Molly is glad
Whenever a beggar walks in,
And Jack and Dick say he’s a fine hearty lad,
And the hostess runs up his bill.

“Then hey, Willy Waddykin,
Stay, Billy Waddykin,
And let the brown ale pour, let it pour,
The beggar’s the man I adore_.”

Robin listened until the song faded into the distance. Then he too climbed the stile into the road, but he turned his feet the opposite way from the Beggar. The road led up a gentle hill, and Robin walked up it with ten bags or more dangling about his legs. He strolled on for a long while, but he found no other adventure. Nothing was on the road but himself, kicking up little clouds of dust at every step, for it was noontime, the most peaceful hour of the day, next to twilight. The whole earth was quiet and still at eating time. The plow horses stood in the furrow munching from big bags over their noses that held sweet feed. The plowman sat under the hedge, and so did the plowboy, and they were munching too, each with a big hunk of bread in one fist and a big hunk of cheese in the other.

So Robin, with the whole empty road to himself, strode along whistling merrily, his bags and pouches bobbing at his thighs. At last he came to a little grassy path that left the road, went through a stile and down a hill, and led into a small dell. It crossed a stream in the valley and climbed the hill on the other side, until it reached a windmill standing on top of the rise, where the wind bent the trees and set them swaying. Robin looked at the spot and liked it, and for no reason except that his fancy led him, he took the little path and walked down the sunny, grassy slope of the open meadow. So he came to the little dingle and, before he knew it, found four hearty fellows sitting with their legs stretched out around a fine feast spread on the ground.

They were four merry beggars, and each had a little board hung around his neck that rested on his chest. One board read, “I am blind,” another, “I am deaf,” another, “I am dumb,” and the fourth, “Pity the lame one.” But although all these troubles written on the boards seemed so grievous, the four sturdy fellows sat feasting as merrily as if Cain’s wife had never opened the pot that held misfortunes and let them out like a cloud of flies to pester us.

The deaf man was the first to hear Robin, because he said, “Listen, brothers, I hear someone coming.” And the blind man was the first to see him, because he said, “He’s an honest man, brothers, and one of our own trade.” Then the dumb man called to him in a loud voice, “Welcome, brother! Come and sit down while there’s still some feast left and a little Malmsey in the pot.” The lame man had taken off his wooden leg and unstrapped his real one, and was sitting with it stretched out on the grass to rest it. At this he made room for Robin among them. “We’re glad to see you, brother,” he said, holding out the flask of Malmsey.

“Well,” said Robin, laughing, and weighing the flask in his hands before he drank, “I think it’s only fitting that you should all be glad to see me, since I bring sight to the blind, speech to the dumb, hearing to the deaf and a sturdy leg to a lame man. I drink to your happiness, brothers, since I can’t drink to your health, seeing that you’re already sound in wind and limb.”

At this they all grinned, and the Blind beggar, who was the chief man among them and the broadest-shouldered, sturdiest rascal of the lot, slapped Robin on the shoulder and swore he was a truly merry joker.
“Where do you come from, lad?” asked the Dumb man.
“Why,” said Robin, “I came this morning from spending the night in Sherwood.”

“Is that so?” said the Deaf man. “I wouldn’t spend one night in Sherwood for all the money the four of us are carrying to Lincoln Town. If Robin Hood caught one of our trade in his woods, I think he’d cut off his ears.”
“I think he would too,” said Robin, laughing. “But what money are you talking about?”
Then the Lame man spoke up. “Our king, Peter of York,” he said, “has sent us to Lincoln with the money that—”

“Hold on, brother Hodge,” said the Blind man, cutting into the talk. “I don’t doubt our brother here, but remember, we don’t know him. What are you, brother? Upright-man, Jurkman, Clapper-dudgeon, Dommerer, or Abraham-man?”

At these words Robin looked from one man to the next with his mouth hanging open. “Truly,” he said, “I hope I’m an upright man, at least I try to be. But I don’t know what you mean by such jargon, brother. It would be much more pleasant, I think, if that Dumb man over there, who has such a sweet voice, would sing us a song.”

At this a silence fell over them all, and after a while the Blind man spoke again. “You must be joking when you say you don’t understand such words,” he said. “Answer me this: have you ever fibbed a chouse quarrons in the Rome pad for the loure in his bung?”(4)

(4) I.E., in old beggar’s cant, “beaten a man or gallant
upon the highway for the money in his purse.” Dakkar’s
ENGLISH VILLAINIES.

“Well, confound it,” said Robin Hood crossly, “if you’re making fun of me with this gibberish, it will go badly for all of you, I tell you. I’ve got half a mind to crack the heads of all four of you, and I would, too, if it weren’t for the good Malmsey you’ve given me. Brother, pass the pot before it gets cold.”

But when Robin finished speaking, all four beggars jumped to their feet. The Blind man snatched up a heavy knotted club that lay beside him on the grass, and the others did the same. Robin saw that things were likely to go badly for him, though he had no idea what the uproar was about. He leaped up too, caught up his trusty staff, put his back against the tree and stood on guard. “Hey, now!” he cried, spinning his staff between his fingers. “Would you four sturdy fellows jump one man? Stand back, you rascals, or I’ll mark your heads until they have as many scratches as a tavern door! Are you mad? I’ve done you no harm.”

“You lie!” said the one who pretended to be blind. He was the biggest villain of them and the leader of the rest. “You lie! You came among us as a filthy spy. But you’ve heard too much for your own good, and you won’t leave this place unless you leave feet first, because today you die! Come on, brothers, all together! Down with him!” Then he whirled up his club and rushed at Robin like an angry bull charging a red rag. But Robin was ready for anything. “Crick! Crack!” He struck two blows, quick as a wink, and down went the Blind man, rolling over and over on the grass.
At this the others drew back and stood a little way off, scowling at Robin. “Come on, you scum!” he cried cheerfully. “There are cakes and ale for everyone. Now, who’s next to be served?”

The beggars answered not a word. They looked at Robin the way great Blunderbore looked at stout Jack the giant-killer, as if they would gladly eat him, body and bones. Still, they did not dare to come any closer to him and his terrible staff. Then, seeing them hesitate, Robin suddenly leaped at them, striking as he leaped. Down went the Dumb man, and his club flew out of his hand as he fell. The other two ducked to dodge another blow, then took to their heels and scampered off, one one way and one the other, as if they had the west wind’s boots on their feet. Robin looked after them, laughing, and thought he had never seen such a fast runner as the Lame man. But neither of the beggars stopped or looked back, for each could feel in his mind the wind of Robin’s staff about his ears.

Then Robin turned to the two sturdy rogues lying on the ground. “These fellows said something about money they were taking to Lincoln,” he said. “I think I may find it on this big blind fellow, who sees as keenly as any trained woodsman in Nottingham or Yorkshire. It would be a pity to leave good money in the pockets of such thieving rogues.” With that he stooped over the burly rascal and searched through his rags and tatters, until his fingers felt a leather pouch slung around the man’s body beneath his patched and ragged coat. He pulled it off and weighed it in his hands, and it struck him that it was mighty heavy. “It would be a fine thing,” he said to himself, “if this were full of gold instead of copper pennies.” Then he sat down on the grass, opened the pouch and looked inside. There he found four round rolls wrapped in dressed sheepskin. He unrolled one of them, and then his mouth fell open and his eyes stared, I swear, as if they would never close again, for what did he see but fifty pounds in bright golden coins? He opened the other rolls and found the same in each one, fifty bright new-stamped golden pounds. “I’ve often heard that the Beggars’ Guild was overrich,” said Robin, “but I never thought they sent such sums as this to their treasury. I’ll take it with me, because it will do more good spent on charity and my merry band than in making such rogues as these richer.” So saying, he rolled the money up in the sheepskin again, put it back in the pouch, and tucked the pouch into his own shirt. Then he picked up the flask of Malmsey and held it out toward the two fellows lying on the grass. “Sweet friends,” he said, “I drink your health, and I thank you dearly for what you’ve so kindly given me today, and so I wish you good evening.” Then he took up his staff, left the spot, and went merrily on his way.

When the two beggars who had been knocked on the head came around and sat up, and when the other two had gotten over their fright and come back, they were as sad and miserable as four frogs in dry weather. Two of them had cracked heads, their Malmsey was all gone, and they didn’t have so much as a farthing to cross their palms with.

Once Robin had left the little dell behind him, he swung merrily down the road, singing as he went. He was so cheerful, such a sturdy beggar, and so fresh and clean besides, that every pretty girl he passed had a kind word for him and felt no fear. Even the dogs, who usually can’t stand the sight of a beggar, sniffed at his legs in a friendly way and wagged their tails, for dogs can smell an honest man, and an honest man Robin was, in his own fashion.

He went on like this until he reached the wayside cross near Ollerton. Feeling a little tired, he sat down on the grassy bank in front of it to rest. “It’s about time I headed back to Sherwood,” he said to himself, “but I’d love one more merry adventure before I return to my jolly band.”

So he looked up the road and down the road to see who might be coming, until at last he spotted someone riding toward him on a horse. When the traveler came close enough to be seen clearly, Robin laughed, for he cut a strange figure. He was a thin, shriveled man, so dried up, skin and bone, that you couldn’t tell by looking whether he was thirty years old or sixty. His nag was as skinny as its rider, and the pair of them looked as if they had been baked in Mother Huddle’s Oven, where folk are dried out so thoroughly that they live forever.

Robin laughed at the comical sight, but he knew this traveler. He was a rich corn engrosser from Worksop, who more than once had bought up all the grain in the countryside and held on to it until the price rose as high as in a famine. He had made a fortune out of the needs of poor people, and everyone who knew anything about him hated him for it, far and wide.

After a while the Corn Engrosser came riding up to the place where Robin sat. Merry Robin sprang out at once in all his rags and tatters, with his bags and pouches dangling around him, caught hold of the horse’s bridle, and told the rider to stop.
“Who are you, fellow, to dare stop me like this on the King’s highway?” said the lean man in a dry, sour voice.
“Pity a poor beggar,” said Robin. “Just give me a farthing to buy a piece of bread.”
“Get away from me!” snarled the other. “Sturdy rogues like you belong safely in prison, or dancing on air with a hempen rope around the neck, not wandering the roads as free as you please.”

“Tut,” said Robin, “how you talk! You and I are brothers, man. Don’t we both take from poor people what they can hardly spare? Don’t we both make our living without doing anything useful? Don’t we both get by without ever touching an honest day’s work? Has either of us ever rubbed our thumbs over an honestly earned farthing? Come now! We are brothers, I say. The only difference is that you are rich and I am poor, so I ask you once more, please give me a penny.”

“You dare prattle on like that to me, you scoundrel?” cried the Corn Engrosser in a rage. “I’ll have you soundly whipped if I ever catch you in any town where the law can get its hands on you! As for giving you a penny, I swear I don’t have so much as a single groat in my purse. Even if Robin Hood himself caught me, he could search me from head to heel and not find the smallest coin. I’m too sly to travel this close to Sherwood with money in my pouch, with that thief running loose in the woods.”

Then merry Robin glanced up and down the road as if to make sure nobody was near. He stepped close to the Corn Engrosser, stood on tiptoe, and whispered in his ear, “Do you really think I’m a beggar, as I look to be? Look at me. There isn’t a speck of dirt on my hands or my face or my body. Did you ever see a beggar like that? I tell you, I’m as honest a man as you are. Look, friend.” With that, he took a purse of money from his chest and showed the dazzled Corn Engrosser the bright gold pieces inside. “Friend, these rags are only here to hide an honest rich man from the eyes of Robin Hood.”

“Put your money away, lad!” the other cried quickly. “Are you a fool, to trust beggar’s rags to protect you from Robin Hood? If he caught you, he would strip you to the skin, for he hates a hearty beggar just as he hates a fat priest or men of my sort.”

“Is that really so?” said Robin. “If I had known that, maybe I wouldn’t have come this way dressed like this. But I have to go on now, because a great deal depends on my journey. Where are you headed, friend?”
“I’m going to Grantham,” said the Corn Engrosser, “but I’ll spend tonight at Newark, if I can get that far.”

“Why, I’m on my way to Newark myself,” said merry Robin. “Two honest men are better than one on roads troubled by a fellow like this Robin Hood, so I’ll jog along with you, if you don’t mind my company.”
“Well, since you’re an honest fellow, and a rich one,” said the Corn Engrosser, “I don’t mind your company. But I’ll tell you truly, I’m not very fond of beggars.”

“Then let’s go on,” said Robin, “for the day is fading, and it will be dark before we reach Newark.” Off they went, the lean horse hobbling along as before and Robin running beside it. He was shaking so hard with laughter inside that he could barely stay on his feet, yet he didn’t dare laugh out loud for fear the Corn Engrosser would suspect something. They traveled on until they came to a hill on the edge of Sherwood. Here the lean man slowed his lean horse to a walk, because the road was steep and he wanted to save the animal’s strength, since he had a long way to go before Newark. Then he turned in his saddle and spoke to Robin for the first time since they had left the cross. “This is where you are in the greatest danger, friend,” he said, “for here we are closest to that wicked thief Robin Hood and to the place where he lives. Beyond this we come out into open, honest country again, and we’ll be safer on our way.”
“Alas!” said Robin. “I wish I had as little money on me as you have, for today I’m afraid Robin Hood will take every groat I own.”
Then the other looked at Robin and gave him a sly wink. “I’ll tell you, friend,” he said, “I have nearly as much on me as you do, but it’s hidden so well that not a rascal in Sherwood could find it.”
“You must be joking,” said Robin. “How could anyone hide as much as two hundred pounds on his body?”

“Well, since you’re such an honest fellow, and so much younger than I am, I’ll tell you what I have never told anyone in all the world. That way you can learn never again to do something as foolish as trusting a beggar’s costume to protect you from Robin Hood. Do you see these clogs on my feet?”
