“Yes,” said Robin, laughing, “they’re certainly big enough for anyone to see, even if his eyesight were as foggy as Peter Patter’s, who never could see when it was time to go to work.”

“Be quiet, friend,” said the Corn Engrosser, “this is no matter for jokes. The soles of these clogs are not what they seem, for each one is a neat little box. If you twist the second nail from the toe, the upper part of the shoe and a piece of the sole lift up like a lid. Inside, in the hollow spaces, there are ninety bright gold pounds in each shoe, all wrapped in hair so they won’t clink and give themselves away.”

When the Corn Engrosser had finished, Robin burst into a roar of laughter and, grabbing the bridle, stopped the sad-looking nag. “Wait, good friend,” he said between bursts of laughter, “you are the slyest old fox I have ever seen in my life! In the soles of his shoes, he says! If I ever trust a poor-looking man again, shave my head and paint it blue! A corn dealer, a horse trader, a land agent, and as cunning as a jackdaw to boot, I say!” And he laughed again until he shook in his shoes with glee.

All this time the Corn Engrosser had been staring at Robin with his mouth hanging open in wonder. “Are you mad,” he said, “to talk like this, so loudly and in such a place? Let’s get going, and save your laughing until we’re safe and sound in Newark.”

“No,” said Robin, with tears of laughter wet on his cheeks, “on second thought I’m going no farther than this, for I have good friends nearby. You may go on if you like, you sweet pretty fellow, but you’ll have to go barefoot, because I’m afraid your shoes must stay behind. Off with them, friend, for I tell you I’ve taken a great liking to them.”
At these words the corn dealer turned as pale as a linen napkin. “Who are you, to talk like this?” he said.

Then merry Robin laughed again and said, “Men around here call me Robin Hood. So, sweet friend, you had better do as I say and give me your shoes, and hurry, please, or you won’t reach fair Newark Town until after dark.”

At the sound of the name Robin Hood, the corn dealer shook with fear and had to grab his horse’s mane to keep from falling off. Then, without another word, he pulled off his clogs and let them drop onto the road. Robin, still holding the bridle, bent down and picked them up. Then he said, “Sweet friend, I usually invite the people I deal with to come and feast with me in Sherwood. I won’t invite you, because of our pleasant journey together, and because there are men in Sherwood who wouldn’t be as gentle with you as I have been. The name of Corn Engrosser leaves a bad taste in the mouth of every honest man. Take a fool’s advice and don’t come this close to Sherwood again, or some day you may suddenly find an arrow a yard long between your ribs. And with that, I wish you good day.” Then he slapped the horse on the flank, and off went nag and rider. The man’s face was dripping with the sweat of fright, and never again, I’m sure, was he found as close to Sherwood Forest as he had been that day.
Robin stood looking after him. When the man was well out of sight, he turned, laughing, and went into the forest with the shoes in his hand.

Night fell over beautiful Sherwood, and the red firelight flickered over trees and bushes. The sturdy fellows of the band sat or sprawled all around, eager to hear Robin Hood and Little John tell of their adventures. They listened closely, and time after time the woods rang with their laughter.
When the stories were told, Friar Tuck spoke up. “Good master,” he said, “you’ve had a fine time, but I still say that the life of the barefoot friar is the merrier of the two.”
“No,” said Will Stutely, “I agree with our master that his was the more pleasant adventure of the two, for he had two good bouts at quarterstaff today.”
So some of the band sided with Robin Hood and some with Little John. As for me, I think—but I’ll leave it to you to decide which side you take.

chapters.title: Robin Hood Shoots Before Queen Eleanor
paragraphs: The highroad stretched white and dusty under the hot summer afternoon sun, and the trees stood motionless along its edge. Across all the meadows the hot air danced and shimmered. In the clear water of the lowland brook, which was crossed by a little stone bridge, the fish hung motionless above the yellow gravel, and the dragonfly sat perfectly still on the sharp tip of a rush, its wings glittering in the sun.

A youth came riding along the road on a fine milk-white Barbary horse, and the people he passed stopped and turned to look after him, for no one so lovely or so gaily dressed had ever been seen in Nottingham before. He could not have been more than sixteen years old, and he was as fair as any girl. His long yellow hair streamed out behind him as he rode, and he was dressed in silk and velvet, with jewels flashing and a dagger jingling against the pommel of his saddle. This was the Queen’s Page, young Richard Partington, who had come from famous London Town to Nottinghamshire, at Her Majesty’s command, to seek Robin Hood in Sherwood Forest.

The road was hot and dusty and his journey had been long, for that day he had ridden all the way from Leicester Town, a good twenty miles and more. So young Partington was very glad to see a pleasant little inn ahead of him, shady and cool under the trees, with a sign hanging in front of the door that showed a picture of a blue boar. He reined in here and called loudly for a pottle of Rhenish wine, since sturdy country ale was too coarse a drink for this young gentleman. Five hearty fellows sat on the bench in the pleasant shade of the wide-spreading oak in front of the inn door, drinking ale and beer, and they all stared in amazement at the fair and gallant lad. Two of the biggest wore Lincoln green, and beside each of them a great heavy oak staff leaned against the gnarled trunk of the tree.

The landlord came out with a pottle of wine and a long narrow glass on a tray, which he held up to the Page as he sat on his horse. Young Partington poured out the bright yellow wine and, holding the glass high, cried, “Here’s to the health and lasting happiness of my royal mistress, the noble Queen Eleanor! May my journey and her wishes soon be fulfilled, and may I find a certain stout yeoman men call Robin Hood.”

At these words everyone stared, but soon the two big yeomen in Lincoln green began whispering together. Then one of them, whom Partington took to be the tallest and sturdiest fellow he had ever seen, spoke up. “What do you want with Robin Hood, Sir Page? And what does our good Queen Eleanor want of him? I don’t ask this out of foolishness, but for a reason, because I know something about this stout yeoman.”
“If you know anything about him, good fellow,” said young Partington, “you will do him a great service, and our royal Queen a great pleasure, by helping me find him.”

Then the other yeoman spoke up. He was a handsome fellow with a sunburned face and curling nut-brown hair. “You have an honest look, Sir Page, and our Queen is kind and true to all sturdy yeomen. I think my friend and I could safely guide you to Robin Hood, for we know where he can be found. But I tell you plainly, we wouldn’t let any harm come to him for all of merry England.”
“Set your mind at ease; I bring nothing bad with me,” said Richard Partington. “I bring him a kind message from our Queen. So if you know where he can be found, I beg you to guide me there.”

The two yeomen glanced at each other again. “I think it would be safe to do it, Will,” said the tall one, and the other nodded. Then both got to their feet, and the tall yeoman said, “We believe you are honest, Sir Page, and mean no harm. So we will lead you to Robin Hood, as you ask.”
Partington paid his bill, the yeomen stepped forward, and together they set off at once.

Beneath the greenwood tree, in cool shade dappled with flickering light, Robin Hood and many of his band were stretched out on the soft green grass while Allan a Dale sang and played his sweet-sounding harp. They listened in silence, for young Allan’s singing was one of the greatest pleasures in the world to them. As they listened, they suddenly heard the sound of a horse’s hooves, and soon Little John and Will Stutely came out of the forest path into the open glade, with young Richard Partington riding between them on his milk-white horse. The three came toward Robin Hood, and the whole band stared with all their might, for they had never seen a sight as gay as this young Page, dressed so richly in silks and velvets, gold and jewels. Robin got up and stepped forward to meet him, and Partington jumped down from his horse, took off his crimson velvet cap, and met Robin halfway. “Welcome!” cried Robin. “Welcome, fair youth! Tell me, I beg you, what brings someone so handsome, in such noble clothes, to our poor forest of Sherwood?”

Young Partington answered, “If I am not mistaken, you are the famous Robin Hood, and these are your stout band of outlawed yeomen. I bring you greetings from our noble Queen Eleanor. She has often heard of you and your merry doings in these parts, and she would dearly love to see your face. So she asks me to tell you that if you will come to London Town right away, she will do everything in her power to protect you from harm, and will send you safely back to Sherwood Forest. Four days from now, in Finsbury Fields, our good King Henry, a man of great renown, is holding a grand shooting match, and all the most famous archers of merry England will be there. The Queen would like to see you compete against them, since she is sure that if you come, you will very likely win the prize. That is why she has sent me with this greeting, and also, as a sign of her great good will, this golden ring from her own fair thumb, which I now place in your hands.”

Robin Hood bowed his head, took the ring, and kissed it loyally, then slid it onto his little finger. “I would sooner lose my life than this ring,” he said. “Before it leaves me, my hand will be cold in death or cut off at the wrist. Fair Sir Page, I will do what our Queen asks, and I will go with you to London right away. But before we leave, let me give you a feast here in the woods, with the very best we have.”

“That cannot be,” said the Page. “We have no time to waste, so get yourself ready at once. And if there are any of your band you would like to bring along, our Queen asks me to say that she will make them very welcome too.”

“You are right,” said Robin, “and we have little time, so I will get ready at once. I will choose only three of my men to go with me: Little John, my own true right-hand man, Will Scarlet, my cousin, and Allan a Dale, my minstrel. Go, lads, and get ready right away, and we will set off as fast as we can. Will Stutely, you shall lead the band while I am gone.”

Little John, Will Scarlet, and Allan a Dale ran off leaping with joy to get ready, while Robin made his own preparations for the journey. After a while all four came out, and they made a fine sight. Robin was dressed in blue from head to foot, Little John and Will Scarlet in good Lincoln green, and Allan a Dale in scarlet from the top of his head to the toes of his pointed shoes. Each man wore a small head covering of polished steel under his cap, set with golden rivets, and under his jerkin a coat of linked mail, as fine as carded wool and yet so tough that no arrow could pierce it. When all were ready, young Partington mounted his horse again, and after shaking hands all around, the five rode off.

That night they stayed at an inn in Melton Mowbray, in Leicestershire. The next night they lodged at Kettering, in Northamptonshire, the one after that at Bedford Town, and the next at St. Albans, in Hertfordshire. They left St. Albans not long after midnight and traveled fast through the tender dawn of a summer day, when the dew lay shining on the meadows and faint mists hung in the valleys, when the birds were singing their sweetest and the cobwebs under the hedges glimmered like fairy cloth of silver. At last, while the morning was still young and golden in the east, they came to the towers and walls of famous London Town.

Queen Eleanor sat in her royal chamber, where the sweet yellow sunshine poured through the open windows in great floods of golden light. Her ladies-in-waiting stood all around her, chatting in low voices, while she sat dreaming where the mild air drifted softly into the room, heavy with the fresh perfume of the red roses blooming in the great garden below the wall. Someone came and told her that her page, Richard Partington, and four sturdy yeomen were waiting in the courtyard below for her pleasure. Queen Eleanor rose joyfully and ordered them to be shown in at once.

So Robin Hood, Little John, Will Scarlet, and Allan a Dale were brought before the Queen in her own royal chamber. Robin knelt before her with his hands folded on his chest and said simply, “Here I am, Robin Hood. You asked me to come, and see, I do as you ask. I give myself to you as your true servant, and I will do whatever you command, even if it costs me the last drop of my blood.”

Good Queen Eleanor smiled kindly at him and told him to rise. Then she had them all sit down and rest after their long journey. Rich food and noble wines were brought to them, and she had her own pages see to whatever the yeomen needed. When they had eaten as much as they could, she began to ask them about their merry adventures. They told her all the lively tales that have been told in this book, among them the story of the Bishop of Hereford and Sir Richard of the Lea, and how the Bishop had stayed three days in Sherwood Forest. At this the Queen and the ladies around her laughed again and again, picturing the stout Bishop staying in the forest and roaming the woods in hearty sport with Robin and his band. When they had told everything they could remember, the Queen asked Allan to sing for her, because his fame as a minstrel had reached even the court at London Town. Allan picked up his harp at once, and without waiting to be asked again, touched the strings lightly until they all rang sweetly, and then he sang:

“_Gentle river, gentle river,
Bright your crystal waters flow,
Sliding where the aspens shiver,
Gliding where the lilies blow,

“Singing over pebbled shallows,
Kissing blossoms bending low,
Breaking beneath the dipping swallows,
Purpling where the breezes blow.

“Floating on your breast forever,
Down your current I could glide;
Grief and pain would reach me never
On your bright and gentle tide.

“So my aching heart seeks yours, love,
There to find its rest and peace,
For, through loving, bliss is mine, love,
And my many troubles cease_.”

So Allan sang, and as he sang, every eye rested on him and not a sound broke the stillness. Even after he had finished, the silence lasted a little while. And so the time went by until the hour came near for the great archery match in Finsbury Fields.

Famous Finsbury Fields made a gay sight on that bright, sunny morning in the middle of summer. Along the end of the meadow stood the booths for the different bands of archers. The King’s yeomen were divided into companies of eighty men, each with a captain over it, so on the bright green turf stood ten striped canvas booths, one for each band of the royal archers. At the peak of each booth a flag fluttered in the mellow air, in the color belonging to that band’s captain. From the center booth hung the yellow flag of Tepus, the King’s famous bow bearer. Next to it on one side was the blue flag of Gilbert of the White Hand, and on the other the blood-red pennant of sturdy young Clifton of Buckinghamshire. The seven other captains were also men of great renown, among them Egbert of Kent and William of Southampton, but the three first named were the most famous of all. The noise of many voices, talking and laughing, came from inside the booths, and attendants ran in and out like ants around an anthill. Some carried ale and beer, others bundles of bowstrings or sheaves of arrows. On each side of the archery range were rows upon rows of seats reaching high into the air, and in the middle of the north side stood a raised platform for the King and Queen, shaded by gaily colored canvas and hung all around with streaming silk pennants of red, blue, green, and white. The King and Queen had not yet arrived, but all the other benches were full of people, rising tier above tier until it made the eye dizzy to look at them. Eight score yards from the mark where the archers would stand to shoot were ten fine targets, each one with a flag in the color of the band that was to shoot at it. So everything was ready for the King and Queen to arrive.

At last bugles blared a great blast, and six trumpeters rode into the meadow, their silver trumpets hung with velvet banners heavy with rich silver and gold thread. After them rode sturdy King Henry on a dapple-gray stallion, with his Queen at his side on a milk-white palfrey. The yeomen of the guard walked on both sides of them, the bright sunlight flashing off the polished steel blades of their halberds. The Court followed in a great crowd, until the whole lawn came alive with color: silk and velvet, waving plumes and gleaming gold, flashing jewels and sword hilts. It was a gallant sight on that bright summer day.

Then all the people stood up and shouted, and their voices sounded like a storm on the Cornish coast, when dark waves rush at the shore, leaping and breaking and surging among the rocks. Amid the roaring and surging of the crowd and the waving of scarves and kerchiefs, the King and Queen came to their place. They got down from their horses, climbed the broad stairs to the raised platform, and took their seats on two thrones draped with purple silk and cloth of silver and gold.

When all was quiet, a bugle sounded, and the archers came marching in order from their tents. There were forty score of them in all, as strong a band of yeomen as could be found anywhere in the wide world. They came in good order and stood before the platform where King Henry and his Queen were seated. King Henry looked proudly up and down their ranks, for his heart glowed at the sight of such a gallant company of yeomen. Then he ordered his herald, Sir Hugh de Mowbray, to step forward and announce the rules of the contest. Sir Hugh went to the edge of the platform and spoke in a loud, clear voice. This is what he said:

Each man was to shoot seven arrows at the target belonging to his band, and from the eighty yeomen of each band, the three who shot best would be chosen. These three would shoot three arrows apiece, and the best of them would be chosen again. Then each of these would shoot three more arrows apiece, and the one who shot best would win the first prize, the next best the second, and the one after him the third. Every one of the others would receive eighty silver pennies for his shooting. The first prize was to be fifty golden pounds, a silver bugle horn inlaid with gold, and a quiver holding ten white arrows tipped with gold and feathered with the white wing of a swan. The second prize was to be a hundred of the fattest bucks that run on Dallen Lea, to be shot whenever the winning yeoman chose. The third prize was to be two tuns of good Rhenish wine.
Such were Sir Hugh’s words, and when he was done, all the archers held their bows high and cheered. Then each band wheeled around and marched back to its own place in order.

Now the shooting began. The captains took their stands first and sent off their shafts, and then made room for the men, who shot one after another. Two hundred and eighty score shafts were shot in all, and they were shot so skillfully that when the shooting was over, each target looked like the back of a hedgehog when the farm dog sniffs at it. The shooting took a long time, and when it was done, the judges came forward, looked carefully at the targets, and announced in loud voices which three men from each band had shot best. A great hubbub rose from the crowd, each man calling out for his favorite archer. Then ten fresh targets were brought forward, and every sound died away as the archers took their places once more.

This time the shooting was finished more quickly, since each band shot only nine shafts. Not one arrow missed the targets, but on the target of Gilbert of the White Hand, five arrows were in the small white spot that marked the center, and Gilbert had shot three of those five. The judges came forward again, looked at the targets, and called out the name of the man chosen as the best bowman of each band. Gilbert of the White Hand led them all, for six of the ten arrows he had shot had landed in the center. Sturdy Tepus and young Clifton followed close behind him, though the others still had a fair chance at second or third place.

Now, amid the roaring of the crowd, the ten stout fellows who were left went back to their tents to rest for a while and change their bowstrings. Nothing must go wrong in the next round, and no hand must tremble nor eye grow dim from weariness.

While the deep buzz and hum of talk sounded all around like the wind in a leafy forest, Queen Eleanor turned to the King and said, “Do you think these yeomen who have been chosen are the very best archers in all merry England?”
“Yes, truly,” said the King, smiling, for he was well pleased with the sport he had seen. “And I tell you, they are not only the best archers in all merry England, but in all the wide world besides.”
“But what would you say,” asked Queen Eleanor, “if I could find three archers to match the best three yeomen in your whole guard?”
“I would say you had done what I never could,” said the King, laughing, “because I tell you, there are no three archers anywhere in the world to equal Tepus, Gilbert, and Clifton of Buckinghamshire.”

“Well, then,” said the Queen, “I know of three yeomen, and I saw them only a short while ago, whom I would not be afraid to set against any three you could pick from all your eight hundred archers. What is more, I will match them right here, this very day. But I will do it only if you grant a free pardon to everyone who comes on my behalf.”

At this the King laughed long and loud. “Truly,” he said, “you have taken up strange business for a queen. If you bring these three fellows you speak of, I faithfully promise them a free pardon for forty days, to come and go wherever they please, and I will not harm a hair of their heads in all that time. What is more, if the men you bring shoot better than my yeomen, man for man, they shall keep the prizes according to how they shoot. But since you have so suddenly taken a liking to sports of this kind, are you in the mood for a wager?”
“Why, honestly,” said Queen Eleanor, laughing, “I know nothing about such things, but if you want to do something of the kind, I will try to oblige you. What will you wager on your men?”

The merry King laughed again, for he dearly loved a good joke, and he said through his laughter, “I will wager you ten tuns of Rhenish wine, ten tuns of the strongest ale, and two hundred bows of tempered Spanish yew, with quivers and arrows to go with them.”

Everyone standing around smiled at this, since it seemed a merry wager for a king to offer a queen. But Queen Eleanor bowed her head calmly. “I accept your wager,” she said, “because I know very well where to put those things you have named. Now, who will take my side in this?” She looked around at the people standing nearby, but no one spoke up or cared to bet on the Queen’s side against archers like Tepus, Gilbert, and Clifton. So the Queen spoke again. “Who will back me in this wager? Will you, my Lord Bishop of Hereford?”
“No,” said the Bishop quickly, “it hardly suits a man of my calling to deal in such matters. Besides, there are no archers in the world like His Majesty’s, so I would only lose my money.”

“I suspect that the thought of your gold weighs more with you than any wrong to your calling,” said the Queen with a smile, and a ripple of laughter went around, for everyone knew how fond the Bishop was of his money. Then the Queen turned to a knight standing close by, whose name was Sir Robert Lee. “Will you back me in this?” she asked. “You are surely rich enough to risk so much for a lady’s sake.”
“To please my Queen, I will do it,” said Sir Robert Lee, “but for no one else in all the world would I wager a groat, because no man can stand against Tepus, Gilbert, and Clifton.”

Then, turning to the King, Queen Eleanor said, “I want no help like the help Sir Robert gives me. But against your wine, your ale, and your strong yew bows, I wager this belt, set all over with jewels, from around my waist. Surely it is worth more than yours.”
“Then I accept your wager,” said the King. “Send for your archers at once. But here come the others now. Let them shoot, and then I will match the winners against all the world.”

“So be it,” said the Queen. Then she beckoned to young Richard Partington and whispered something in his ear. At once the Page bowed and left, crossing the meadow to the far side of the range, where he was soon lost in the crowd. All those standing around whispered to one another, wondering what it all meant and which three men the Queen was going to set against the King’s famous archers.

Now the ten archers of the King’s guard took their places again, and the whole great crowd fell as silent as death. Each man shot his arrows slowly and carefully, and the silence was so deep that you could hear every arrow thump into the target as it struck. When the last arrow had flown, a great roar went up, and the shooting, I can tell you, deserved it. Once again Gilbert had put three arrows in the white. Tepus came second, with two in the white and one in the black ring next to it. But stout Clifton had dropped back, and Hubert of Suffolk had taken third place, because although both of those good yeomen had put two in the white, Clifton had wasted one shot on the fourth ring, while Hubert had one in the third.
Around Gilbert’s booth the archers cheered until their throats were raw, flinging their caps high and clapping one another’s hands.

In the middle of all the noise and commotion, five men came walking across the lawn toward the King’s pavilion. The first was Richard Partington, whom most of the people there knew, but the others were strangers to everyone. Beside young Partington walked a yeoman dressed in blue, and behind them came three others, two in Lincoln green and one in scarlet. This last yeoman carried three sturdy bows of yew, two of them richly inlaid with silver and one with gold. As these five men crossed the meadow, a messenger came running from the King’s booth and called Gilbert, Tepus, and Hubert to come with him. The shouting quickly died away, for everyone could see that something unusual was happening, and the people stood up in their places and leaned forward to see what the fuss was about.

When Partington and the others came before the spot where the King and Queen sat, the four yeomen knelt and took off their caps to her. King Henry leaned far forward and stared hard at them, but the Bishop of Hereford, when he saw their faces, jumped as if a wasp had stung him. He opened his mouth to speak, but when he looked up he saw the Queen gazing at him with a smile on her lips. So he said nothing, but bit his lower lip, and his face turned as red as a cherry.

The Queen then leaned forward and called out clearly, “Locksley, I have bet the King that you and two of your men can beat any three archers he sends against you. Will you give it your best for my sake?”
“I will,” said Robin Hood, to whom she spoke. “I will do my best for your sake, and if I fail, I swear never to touch a bowstring again.”

Now, although Little John had felt a bit shy in the Queen’s chamber, he was the sturdy fellow he always was once the soles of his feet touched green grass again. So he said boldly, “Blessings on your sweet face, I say. If there is a man who would not do his best for you—well, I will say nothing, except that I would like to crack his rascal’s skull!”
“Quiet, Little John!” said Robin Hood quickly, in a low voice. But good Queen Eleanor laughed aloud, and a ripple of merriment ran through the whole booth.
The Bishop of Hereford did not laugh, and neither did the King. He turned to the Queen and said, “Who are these men you have brought before us?”

Then the Bishop spoke up quickly, for he could keep quiet no longer. “Your Majesty,” he said, “that fellow in blue is an outlawed thief from the Midlands, named Robin Hood. That tall, strapping villain goes by the name of Little John. The other fellow in green is a fallen gentleman, known as Will Scarlet, and the man in red is a rogue of a northern minstrel, named Allan a Dale.”
The King’s brows came together in a dark scowl as he turned to the Queen. “Is that so?” he demanded sternly.

“It is,” said the Queen with a smile. “The Bishop has told the truth, and he should know them well, since he and two of his friars spent three days in merry sport with Robin Hood in Sherwood Forest. I hardly thought the good Bishop would betray his friends like this. But remember that you have given your promise for the safety of these good yeomen for forty days.”

“I will keep my promise,” said the King, in a deep voice that showed the anger in his heart, “but when the forty days are over, this outlaw had better look out for himself, because things may not go as smoothly for him as he would like.” Then he turned to his archers, who stood near the Sherwood yeomen, listening and wondering at everything that went on. “Gilbert, and you, Tepus, and you, Hubert,” he said, “I have promised that you will shoot against these three fellows. If you outshoot the rascals, I will fill your caps with silver pennies. If you fail, you will lose the prizes you have won so fairly, and they will go to the men who shoot against you, man to man. Do your best, lads, and if you win this contest you will be glad of it to the end of your lives. Now go to the butts.”

So the King’s three archers turned and went back to their booths, while Robin and his men walked to the mark where they were to shoot from. There they strung their bows and made ready, looking over their quivers of arrows and choosing the roundest and best feathered.

Meanwhile the King’s archers reached their tents and told their friends all that had been said, and that these four men were the famous Robin Hood and three of his band: Little John, Will Scarlet, and Allan a Dale. The word buzzed through the booths, for every man there had heard of these great yeomen of the Midlands. From the archers it spread to the crowd watching the contest, until at last everyone was on their feet, stretching to get a glimpse of the famous outlaws.

Six fresh targets were now set up, one for each man who was to shoot, and Gilbert, Tepus, and Hubert came out from the booths at once. Then Robin Hood and Gilbert of the White Hand tossed a farthing in the air to see who should shoot first. The toss went to Gilbert’s side, and he called on Hubert of Suffolk to lead.

Hubert took his place, planted his foot firmly, and fitted a fair, smooth arrow to the string. Then, breathing on his fingertips, he drew the string slowly and carefully. The arrow flew true and landed in the white. He shot again, and again he hit the bull’s-eye. He loosed a third shaft, but this time he missed the center and struck the black, though only a finger’s breadth from the white. At this a shout went up, for it was the best shooting Hubert had done all day.
Merry Robin laughed. “You will have a hard time beating that round, Will,” he said, “because it is your turn next. Steady your muscles, lad, and do not bring shame on Sherwood.”

Then Will Scarlet took his place, but because he was too careful, he spoiled his target with the very first arrow he shot, hitting the ring next to the black, the second from the center. At this Robin bit his lips. “Lad, lad,” he said, “do not hold the string so long! Have I not often told you what Gaffer Swanthold says, that ‘too much caution spills the milk’?” Will Scarlet took this to heart, and his next arrow landed squarely in the center ring. He shot again, and again he struck the center. But for all that, stout Hubert had outshot him and made the better target. Everyone watching clapped their hands for joy that Hubert had beaten the stranger.

“If your archers shoot no better than that,” said the King grimly to the Queen, “you are likely to lose your wager, lady.” But Queen Eleanor smiled, for she expected better things from Robin Hood and Little John.

And now Tepus took his place to shoot. He, too, paid too much attention to what he was doing, and so he made the same mistake as Will Scarlet. His first arrow struck the center ring, but the second missed its mark and hit the black. The last arrow was touched with luck, for it struck the very middle of the bull’s-eye, on the black spot that marked it. “That is the sweetest shot that has been fired this day,” said Robin Hood, “but even so, friend Tepus, I think your cake is burned. Little John, it is your turn next.”

So Little John took his place as he was told and shot his three arrows quickly. He never lowered his bow arm during the whole round, but fitted each arrow with his longbow raised. Yet all three of his arrows struck the center, within easy reach of the black. At this no shout was heard, for although it was the best shooting done that day, the people of London Town did not like to see stout Tepus beaten by a fellow from the countryside, even one as famous as Little John.
And now stout Gilbert of the White Hand took his place and shot with the greatest care, and for the third time that day he put all three arrows in the bull’s-eye.

“Well done, Gilbert!” said Robin Hood, clapping him on the shoulder. “I swear you are one of the best archers I have ever laid eyes on. You should be a free and merry ranger like us, lad, for you are better suited to the greenwood than to the cobblestones and gray walls of London Town.” With that, he took his place and drew a fair, round arrow from his quiver, turning it over and over before he fitted it to his bowstring.

Then the King muttered into his beard, “Now, blessed Saint Hubert, if you will only jog that rogue’s elbow so that he hits even the second ring, I will give your chapel near Matching a hundred and sixty wax candles, each three fingers thick.” But perhaps Saint Hubert’s ears were stuffed with tow, for he did not seem to hear the King’s prayer that day.

Once he had three arrows to his liking, merry Robin looked carefully at his bowstring before he shot. “Yes,” he said to Gilbert, who stood close by to watch his shooting, “you should pay us a visit in merry Sherwood.” Here he drew the bowstring to his ear. “In London”—here he loosed his arrow—“you can find nothing to shoot at but rooks and jackdaws. Out there one can tickle the ribs of the noblest stags in England.” So he shot even as he talked, and still the arrow landed no more than half an inch from the very center.
“Upon my soul!” cried Gilbert. “Are you the devil in blue, to shoot like that?”

“No,” said Robin, laughing, “not quite as bad as that, I hope.” And he took up another arrow and fitted it to the string. Again he shot, and again he struck close beside the center. A third time he loosed his bowstring and dropped his arrow right between the other two, into the very center, so that the feathers of all three were ruffled together and looked, from a distance, like one thick shaft.

A low murmur now ran through the great crowd, for London had never seen shooting like this before, and would never see its like again once Robin Hood’s day was over. Everyone could see that the King’s archers were fairly beaten. Stout Gilbert clapped his palm into Robin’s and admitted that he could never hope to draw a bowstring the way Robin Hood or Little John could. But the King was full of anger and would not accept it, though in his heart he knew his men could not stand against those fellows. “No!” he cried, clenching his hands on the arms of his seat. “Gilbert is not beaten yet! Didn’t he hit the bull’s-eye three times? I may have lost my wager, but he has not yet lost the first prize. They will shoot again, and again after that, until either he or that rascal Robin Hood comes out on top. Go, Sir Hugh, and tell them to shoot another round, and another, until one of them is beaten.” Seeing how furious the King was, Sir Hugh said not a word. He went straight off to carry out the order, came to where Robin Hood and the other archer stood, and told them what the King had said.
“With all my heart,” said merry Robin. “I will shoot from now until tomorrow, if it pleases my most gracious lord and King. Take your place, Gilbert lad, and shoot.”
So Gilbert took his place once more, but this time he failed. A sudden little breeze sprang up, and his arrow missed the center ring, though only by the width of a barley straw.
“Your eggs are cracked, Gilbert,” said Robin with a laugh, and right away he loosed an arrow and once more struck the white circle at the center.

Then the King rose from his seat without saying a word. He glared around with such a dark look that it would have gone badly for anyone he caught looking cheerful or merry. Then he, his Queen and the whole court left the place, though the King’s heart was filled to the brim with rage.

After the King had gone, all the yeomen of the archer guard came crowding around Robin, Little John, Will and Allan, to get a look at these famous fellows from the Midlands. Many who had been watching the contest came too, for the same reason. So it was that the yeomen, with whom Gilbert stood talking, were soon surrounded by a ring of people.

After a while the three judges who were to hand out the prizes came forward, and the chief of them spoke to Robin. “As agreed, the first prize rightly belongs to you. So here I give you the silver bugle, here the quiver of ten golden arrows, and here a purse of fifty golden pounds.” As he spoke he handed these things to Robin, and then he turned to Little John. “To you,” he said, “belongs the second prize, which is a hundred of the finest harts that run on Dallen Lea. You may shoot them whenever you please.” Last of all he turned to stout Hubert. “You,” he said, “have held your own against the yeomen you shot with, and so the prize remains yours, which is two tuns of good Rhenish wine. It will be delivered to you whenever you like.” Then he called forward the other seven of the King’s archers who had shot last, and gave each of them eighty silver pennies.

Then Robin spoke up. “I will keep this silver bugle in honor of this shooting match. But you, Gilbert, are the best archer in all the King’s guard, and to you I gladly give this purse of gold. Take it, man, and I wish it were ten times as much, for you are a true yeoman, good and honest. And I give each of the ten who shot last one of these golden arrows. Keep them always, so that you can tell your grandchildren, if you are ever lucky enough to have any, that you are the very best yeomen in all the wide world.”
At this they all shouted aloud, for they were pleased to hear Robin speak of them so.

Then Little John spoke up. “Good friend Tepus,” he said, “I don’t want those harts of Dallen Lea that the judge mentioned just now, for in truth we have plenty and more than plenty in our own country. I give fifty of them to you for your own shooting, and five to each band for their pleasure.”
At this another great shout went up. Many tossed their caps in the air, and they swore to one another that no better fellows ever walked the earth than Robin Hood and his stout yeomen.

While they were shouting at the top of their voices, a tall, burly yeoman of the King’s guard came forward and plucked Robin by the sleeve. “Good master,” he said, “I have something to tell you privately. It is a silly thing, God knows, for one stout yeoman to tell another. A young peacock of a page, one Richard Partington, was looking for you in the crowd without luck, and when he couldn’t find you, he told me he had a message for you from a certain lady you know of. He asked me to pass it on to you in secret, word for word, and this was it. Let me see—I hope I haven’t forgotten it—yes, this was it: ‘The lion growls. Beware your head.’”

“Is that so?” said Robin with a start, for he knew perfectly well that the message came from the Queen and that she was speaking of the King’s anger. “Now I thank you, good fellow, for you have done me a greater service today than you know.” Then he called his three yeomen together and told them quietly that they had better be on their way, since it was likely to go badly for them so near merry London Town. So without waiting any longer, they made their way through the crowd until they were clear of the press. Then, without stopping, they left London Town and set off toward the north.

chapters.title: The Chase of Robin Hood
paragraphs: So Robin Hood and the others left the archery field at Finsbury Fields and, without delay, set out straight away on their journey home. It was well for them that they did, because they had gone no more than three or four miles when six yeomen of the King’s guard came bustling into the crowd that was still lingering there, looking for Robin and his men to seize them and take them prisoner. It was a shameful thing for the King to break his promise, but it all came about through the doing of the Bishop of Hereford, and this is how it happened.

After the King left the archery ground, he went straight to his private room, and the Bishop of Hereford and Sir Robert Lee went with him. The King said not a word to either of them but sat chewing his lower lip, for his heart was sore at what had happened. At last the Bishop of Hereford spoke in a low, sorrowful voice. “It is a sad thing, Your Majesty, that this rascally outlaw should be allowed to escape in this way. For if he gets back to Sherwood Forest safe and sound, he can snap his fingers at the king and all the king’s men.”

At these words the King raised his eyes and looked sternly at the Bishop. “Is that what you say?” he said. “In good time I will show you how wrong you are. When the forty days are over and done, I will seize this thieving outlaw, even if I have to tear down all of Sherwood to find him. Do you think the laws of the King of England can be dodged like this by one poor rascal without friends or money?”
Then the Bishop spoke again, in his soft, smooth voice.

“Forgive my boldness, Your Majesty, and believe that I have nothing at heart but the good of England and Your Majesty’s wishes. But what good would it do, even if my gracious lord uprooted every tree in Sherwood? Does Robin Hood have no other hiding places? Cannock Chase is not far from Sherwood, and the great Forest of Arden is not far from Cannock Chase. Besides these there are many other woodlands in Nottingham and Derby, Lincoln and York. In any of them Your Majesty might as well try to catch Robin Hood as to lay a finger on a rat among the dust and broken things in an attic. No, my gracious lord, once he sets foot in the woodland, he is lost to the law forever.”

At these words the King tapped his fingertips on the table beside him in annoyance. “What would you have me do, Bishop?” he said. “Didn’t you hear me give my word to the Queen? Your talk is as empty as the wind from a bellows blowing on dead coals.”

“Far be it from me,” said the cunning Bishop, “to show the way to one as clear-sighted as Your Majesty. But if I were the King of England, I would look at the matter like this. Suppose I have promised my Queen that for forty days the cleverest rogue in all England shall be free to come and go. But behold, I find this outlaw in my grasp. Should I foolishly cling to a promise given so hastily? Suppose I had promised to do Her Majesty’s bidding, and she then told me to kill myself. Should I shut my eyes and run blindly onto my sword? That is how I would argue with myself. And I would say to myself, besides, that a woman knows nothing of the great matters of government. I would also say that a woman is always apt to take a fancy to something, the way she might pluck a daisy from the roadside and then throw it away when its sweetness is gone. So though she has taken a fancy to this outlaw, it will soon fade and be forgotten. As for me, I have the greatest villain in all England in my grasp. Should I open my hand and let him slip between my fingers? That, Your Majesty, is what I would say to myself, were I the King of England.” So the Bishop talked, and the King listened to his evil advice. After a while he turned to Sir Robert Lee and ordered him to send six of the yeomen of the guard to take Robin Hood and his three men prisoner.

Now Sir Robert Lee was a gentle and noble knight, and it grieved him to the heart to see the King break his promise. Still, he said nothing, for he saw how bitterly the King was set against Robin Hood. But he did not send the yeomen of the guard right away. First he went to the Queen, told her everything that had passed, and asked her to warn Robin of his danger. He did this not for Robin Hood’s sake, but because he wanted to save his lord’s honor if he could. So it happened that when the yeomen of the guard finally went to the archery field, they did not find Robin and the others, and went home with nothing for their trouble.

The afternoon was almost over when Robin Hood, Little John, Will and Allan set out on their way home, trudging merrily along through the yellow slanting light, which soon turned rosy red as the sun sank low in the sky. The shadows grew long and finally melted into the grayness of the mellow twilight. The dusty highway lay white between the dark hedgerows, and four fellows walked along it like four shadows, the pat of their feet sounding loud and their voices ringing clear in the still air as they talked. The great round moon was floating silently up in the eastern sky when they saw the twinkling lights of Barnet Town ahead of them, some ten or twelve miles from London. They walked down through the stony streets, past cozy houses with overhanging gables. In front of the doors sat townsmen and craftsmen in the mellow moonlight with their families around them. On the far side of the village they came at last to a little inn, shaded all over with roses and honeysuckle. Robin Hood stopped in front of it, for he liked the spot well. “Here we will stay and rest for the night,” he said, “for we are well away from London Town and our King’s anger. What is more, if I’m not mistaken, we will find good fare inside. What do you say, lads?”
“Truly, good master,” said Little John, “your orders and my doing always fit together like cakes and ale. Let’s go in, I say too.”

Then Will Scarlet spoke up. “I am always ready to do what you say, uncle, though I wish we were farther along our way before we rested for the night. Still, if you think it best, let’s go in for the night, I say too.”

So in they went and called for the best the place had to offer. A really good feast was set before them, with two stout bottles of old sack to wash it down. It was served by as plump and rosy-cheeked a lass as you could find anywhere in the land. Little John, who always had an eye for a pretty girl, even with food and drink in front of him, planted his hands on his hips and fixed his eyes on her, winking sweetly whenever she looked his way. You should have seen how the lass giggled, and how she peeped at Little John out of the corners of her eyes, with a dimple showing in each cheek, for the fellow always had a charming way with women.

So the feast went merrily, and that inn had never seen such hearty eaters as these four stout fellows. At last they finished eating, though it seemed as if they never would, and sat lingering over the sack. While they sat there, the landlord suddenly came in and said there was someone at the door, a young squire named Richard Partington, of the Queen’s household, who wished to see the lad in blue and speak with him without delay. So Robin got up quickly and, telling the landlord not to follow him, left the others staring at one another and wondering what was about to happen.
Stepping out of the inn, Robin saw young Richard Partington on horseback in the white moonlight, waiting there for him.
“What news do you bring, Sir Page?” said Robin. “I hope it is nothing ill.”

“Well,” said young Partington, “as for that, it is bad enough. The King has been bitterly stirred up against you by that vile Bishop of Hereford. He sent men to arrest you at the archery butts at Finsbury Fields, but when they didn’t find you there, he gathered his armed men, a thousand and more, and is sending them in haste along this very road to Sherwood, either to catch you on the way or to stop you from getting back to the woodlands. He has put the Bishop of Hereford in command of all these men, and you know what to expect from the Bishop of Hereford: short shrift and a long rope. Two bands of horsemen are already on the road, not far behind me, so you had better get away from this place at once, for if you stay any longer, you will likely sleep tonight in a cold dungeon. The Queen asked me to bring you this word.”

“Now, Richard Partington,” said Robin, “this is the second time you’ve saved my life, and if the right time ever comes, I’ll show you that Robin Hood never forgets a favor like that. As for that Bishop of Hereford, if I ever catch him near Sherwood again, it will go badly for him. You may tell the good Queen that I’ll leave this place right away, and I’ll let the landlord believe we’re headed for Saint Albans. But once we’re back on the highroad, I’ll go one way across the country and send my men another, so that if one of us falls into the King’s hands, the others may still get away. We’ll take roundabout routes, and so, I hope, we’ll reach Sherwood safely. And now, Sir Page, farewell.”

“Farewell, bold yeoman,” said young Partington, “and may you reach your hideout safely.” They shook hands, and the lad turned his horse around and rode back toward London, while Robin went into the inn again.

Inside he found his yeomen sitting silently, waiting for him. The landlord was there too, eager to learn what Master Partington could possibly want with the fellow in blue. “Up, my merry men!” said Robin. “This is no place for us. There are men after us, and if we fall into their hands we’ll stand a poor chance. So we’ll push on, and we won’t stop tonight until we reach Saint Albans.” With that he took out his purse, paid the landlord his bill, and they left the inn.

When they reached the highroad outside the town, Robin stopped and told them everything that had passed between young Partington and himself, and how the King’s men were hot on their heels. Then he told them that here they must part company. The three would go east and he would go west, and each would keep clear of the main highroads and make his way to Sherwood by back paths. “So be cunning,” said Robin Hood, “and stay away from the northern roads until you’re well to the east. And you, Will Scarlet, lead the others, for you have a sly turn of mind.” Then Robin kissed the three on the cheek, and they kissed him, and so they parted.

Soon after, at the inn in Barnet Town, a score or more of the King’s men rode up to the door in a clatter of hooves. They sprang from their saddles and swiftly ringed the building, while the captain and four others burst into the room where the yeomen had sat. The birds had flown the nest again, and for the second time the King had been cheated of his catch.

“I thought they were rascals,” said the host, when he heard whom the men-at-arms were after. “But I heard that fellow in blue say they were going straight on to Saint Albans. So if you hurry, you may catch them on the highroad between here and there.” The leader of the band thanked the host heartily for this news, called his men together, mounted, and rode off again, galloping toward Saint Albans on a wild goose chase.

After Little John, Will Scarlet and Allan a Dale left the highway near Barnet, they traveled east without stopping for as long as their legs would carry them, until they came to Chelmsford, in Essex. From there they turned north and passed through Cambridge and Lincolnshire to the good town of Gainsborough. Then they swung west and south, and at last reached the northern edge of Sherwood Forest, without meeting a single band of the King’s men all that time. The journey took them eight days, and they arrived safely in the woodlands. But when they came to the glade in the greenwood, they found that Robin had not yet returned.
For Robin had not been as lucky on his way back as his men, as you will soon hear.

After leaving the great northern road, he turned west and went past Aylesbury to fair Woodstock, in Oxfordshire. From there he headed north, traveling a long way through Warwick Town until he came to Dudley, in Staffordshire. It took him seven days to get that far, and then he decided he had come far enough north. So he turned east, avoiding the main roads and choosing byways and grassy lanes, and made his way by Litchfield and Ashby de la Zouch toward Sherwood, until he reached a place called Stanton. Now Robin’s heart began to laugh aloud, for he thought his danger was past, and that his nose would soon be breathing the spicy air of the woodlands again. But there’s many a slip between the cup and the lip, as Robin was about to find out. For this is how it happened.

When the King’s men found themselves tricked at Saint Albans, and could not find Robin and his men anywhere, they didn’t know what to do. Soon another band of horsemen arrived, and then another, until all the moonlit streets were full of armed men. Between midnight and dawn yet another band came into the town, and with them came the Bishop of Hereford. When he heard that Robin Hood had slipped out of the trap once more, he didn’t waste a minute. He gathered his bands together and rode north at top speed, leaving orders that all the troops arriving at Saint Albans should follow him without delay. On the evening of the fourth day he reached Nottingham Town, and there he at once split his men into bands of six or seven and sent them all across the countryside, to block every highway and byway east, south and west of Sherwood. The Sheriff of Nottingham called out all his men as well and joined the Bishop, for he saw that this was the best chance he had ever had of paying Robin Hood back in full. Will Scarlet, Little John and Allan a Dale had only just slipped past the King’s men in the east. The very next day after they crossed the border into Sherwood, the roads they had traveled were blocked, so that if they had lingered on their journey, they would surely have fallen into the Bishop’s hands.

But Robin knew nothing of all this. He whistled merrily as he tramped along the road beyond Stanton, his heart as free of care as an egg yolk is of cobwebs. At last he came to a place where a little stream spread across the road in a shallow sheet, tinkling and sparkling as it rippled over its bed of golden gravel. Robin stopped there, since he was thirsty, knelt down, made a cup of his hands, and began to drink. For a long way on both sides of the road stood tangled thickets of bushes and young trees, and it warmed Robin’s heart to hear the little birds singing in them, for it reminded him of Sherwood, and it felt as if a lifetime had passed since he had last breathed woodland air. But suddenly, as he bent over drinking, something hissed past his ear and struck the gravel and water beside him with a splash. Quick as a wink Robin sprang to his feet, cleared the stream and the roadside in a single bound, and dived headlong into the thicket without looking back. He knew very well that the thing that had hissed so wickedly past his ear was a gray goose-feather arrow, and that to wait even a moment meant death. Even as he leaped into the thicket, six more arrows rattled among the branches after him, and one of them pierced his doublet. It would have gone deep into his side if not for the tough steel coat he wore. Then some of the King’s men came riding up the road at breakneck speed. They jumped from their horses and plunged into the thicket after Robin. But Robin knew the ground better than they did. Crawling here, stooping there, and now and then dashing across a small clearing, he soon left them far behind, and came out at last on another road about eight hundred paces from the one he had left. There he stood for a moment, listening to the distant shouts of the seven men as they beat back and forth through the thickets like hounds that had lost the scent of their quarry. Then he buckled his belt tighter around his waist and ran swiftly down the road toward the east and Sherwood.

But Robin had gone no more than three furlongs that way when he came suddenly to the top of a hill and saw, in the valley below, another band of the King’s men sitting in the shade beside the road. He didn’t pause for a moment. Seeing that they hadn’t noticed him, he turned and ran back the way he had come, knowing it was better to risk getting away from the men still in the thickets than to run straight into the arms of those in the valley. So back he ran at full speed, and had gotten safely past the thickets when the seven men came out onto the open road. They gave a great shout when they saw him, like the shout a hunter gives when the deer breaks cover, but Robin was already a quarter of a mile and more ahead of them, racing over the ground like a greyhound. He never slowed down, but ran on, mile after mile, until he came close to Mackworth, beyond the Derwent River, near Derby Town. There, seeing that he was out of immediate danger, he slowed down, and at last sat himself under a hedge where the grass was longest and the shade was coolest, to rest and catch his breath. “By my soul, Robin,” he said to himself, “that was the narrowest miss you ever had in all your life. I swear to you, the feather of that wicked arrow tickled my ear as it whizzed past. All this running has given me a terrible craving for food and drink. Now I pray Saint Dunstan to send me some meat and beer, and quickly.”

It looked as if Saint Dunstan meant to answer his prayer, for along the road came plodding a certain cobbler, one Quince, of Derby. He had taken a pair of shoes to a farmer near Kirk Langly and was now going home again, with a fine boiled capon in his pouch and a sturdy bottle of beer at his side. The farmer had given him both for joy at such a stout pair of shoes. Good Quince was an honest fellow, but his wits were rather heavy, like unbaked dough, so that the only thing in his mind was, “Three shillings sixpence ha’penny for your shoes, good Quince—three shillings sixpence ha’penny for your shoes.” This went round and round inside his head, with no other thought getting in, the way a pea rolls round and round inside an empty quart pot.
“Hello there, good friend,” said Robin from under the hedge, when the other had come near enough, “where are you off to so merrily on this bright day?”

Hearing himself called, the Cobbler stopped, and seeing a well-dressed stranger in blue, he answered politely. “Good day to you, fair sir. I’ll tell you that I’m coming from Kirk Langly, where I sold my shoes and got three shillings sixpence ha’penny for them, in as good money as you ever saw, and honestly earned too, I’ll have you know. But if I may be so bold, my fine fellow, what are you doing there under the hedge?”
“Well,” said merry Robin, “I’m sitting under this hedge to sprinkle salt on the tails of golden birds. But truly, you’re the first chick worth the trouble that I’ve seen this blessed day.”

At these words the Cobbler’s eyes grew big and wide, and his mouth went round with wonder, like a knothole in a board fence. “Well, I never!” he said. “Imagine that! I’ve never seen any of those golden birds. And do you really find them in these hedges, good fellow? Please tell me, are there many of them? I’d dearly like to find some myself.”
“Yes, indeed,” said Robin, “they’re as thick here as fresh herring in Cannock Chase.”
“Imagine that!” said the Cobbler, drowning in wonder. “And do you really catch them by sprinkling salt on their pretty tails?”

“Yes,” said Robin, “but this salt is a peculiar kind, let me tell you, for you can only get it by boiling down a quart of moonbeams in a wooden dish, and even then you end up with just a pinch. But tell me now, you clever man, what have you got there in that pouch at your side and in that bottle?”

At these words the Cobbler looked down at the things Robin was asking about, for thoughts of the golden bird had driven them out of his mind, and it took him some time to scrape the memory of them back. “Why,” he said at last, “in one is good March beer, and in the other is a fat capon. Quince the Cobbler will have a fine feast today, if I’m not mistaken.”

“But tell me, good Quince,” said Robin, “would you care to sell those things to me? Just hearing about them sounds sweet to my ears. I’ll give you these fine blue clothes that I’m wearing, and ten shillings besides, for your clothes and your leather apron and your beer and your capon. What do you say, my fine lad?”
“No, you’re joking with me,” said the Cobbler, “for my clothes are coarse and patched, and yours are made of fine cloth and very handsome.”

“I’m not joking at all,” said Robin. “Come, take off your jacket and I’ll prove it, for I tell you I like your clothes well. What’s more, I’ll be kind to you, for I’ll feast right away on the good things you’re carrying, and you’ll be invited to the meal.” With these words he began slipping off his doublet, and the Cobbler, seeing how much in earnest he was, began pulling off his own clothes too, for Robin Hood’s outfit had caught his eye. So each put on the other fellow’s clothes, and Robin gave the honest Cobbler ten bright new shillings. Merry Robin said, “I’ve been many things in my life, but never before an honest cobbler. Come, friend, let’s fall to and eat, for something inside me is cackling for that good fat capon.” So both sat down and feasted with a will, and by the time they were done, the bones of the capon were picked as bare as charity.

Then Robin stretched out his legs with a warm feeling of comfort. He said, “By the sound of your voice, good Quince, I can tell you have a fine song or two running loose in your head like colts in a meadow. Please, let one of them out for me.”
“I do have a song or two,” said the Cobbler, “poor things, poor things, but such as they are, you’re welcome to one of them.” So he wet his throat with a swallow of beer, and sang:

“_Of all the joys, the best I love,
Sing hey, my frisking Nan, O,
And what most moves my soul of all,
Is the clinking can, O.

“All other bliss I’d cast away,
Sing hey, my frisking Nan, O,
But this_—”

The stout Cobbler never got to the end of his song. Suddenly six horsemen came crashing down on the two men where they sat, grabbed the honest craftsman roughly, hauled him to his feet, and nearly tore the clothes off his back while they were at it. “Ha!” bellowed the leader of the band, in a huge voice full of glee. “So we’ve finally caught you, you blue-clad scoundrel! Bless Saint Hubert, we’re eighty pounds richer this minute than we were a moment ago, because the good Bishop of Hereford has promised that much to whoever brings you to him. Oho, you sly rascal! Look at you, putting on that innocent face! We know you, you old fox. Now come along with us, and we’ll have your tail clipped right away.” At these words the poor Cobbler stared around him with his big blue eyes as round as a dead fish’s, and his mouth hung open as if he had swallowed all his words and lost his voice with them.

Robin gaped and stared in amazement too, exactly as the Cobbler would have done in his place. “Goodness gracious me,” he said. “I can’t tell whether I’m sitting here or in No-man’s-land! What’s all this fuss and commotion, my dear good gentlemen? This is surely a kind, honest fellow.”
“‘Honest fellow,’ you say, you oaf?” said one of the men. “Why, I tell you this is the very rogue they call Robin Hood.”

At this the Cobbler stared and gaped harder than ever, for such a threshing of thoughts was going on inside his poor head that his wits were all clouded with the dust and chaff of it. What was more, as he looked at Robin Hood and saw a yeoman who looked just like what he knew himself to be, he began to doubt, and to think that perhaps he really was the famous outlaw after all. In a slow, wondering voice he said, “Am I truly that fellow?—Now I had thought—but no, Quince, you’re mistaken—and yet—am I?—No, I must indeed be Robin Hood! Still, I never expected to rise from an honest craftsman to such a great yeoman.”
“Alas!” said Robin Hood. “Look at that, now! See how your rough treatment has curdled the wits of this poor lad and turned them all sour! I myself am Quince, the Cobbler of Derby Town.”

“Is that so?” said Quince. “Then I really am somebody else, and I can be no one but Robin Hood. Take me, fellows; but let me tell you that you’ve laid hands on the stoutest yeoman who ever walked the woodlands.”

“So you’ll play the madman, will you?” said the leader of the band. “Here, Giles, fetch a cord and tie this rascal’s hands behind him. I’ll wager we’ll bring his wits back once we have him safe in front of our good Bishop at Tutbury Town.” With that they tied the Cobbler’s hands behind his back and led him away on a rope, the way a farmer leads home a calf he has brought home from the fair. Robin stood watching them go, and when they were out of sight he laughed until tears rolled down his cheeks, for he knew no harm would come to the honest fellow, and he pictured the Bishop’s face when good Quince was brought before him as Robin Hood. Then he turned east again and set off, right foot first, toward Nottinghamshire and Sherwood Forest.

But Robin Hood had been through more than he realized. His journey from London had been long and hard, and in a single week he had covered more than a hundred and forty miles. He meant to keep going without a stop until he reached Sherwood, but before he had gone even ten miles he felt his strength giving way beneath him, like a riverbank undermined by the water. He sat down and rested, yet he knew in his heart that he could go no farther that day, for his feet felt like lumps of lead, so heavy were they with weariness. He got up once more and went on, but after a couple of miles he had to give up. Just then he came to an inn, so he walked in, called the landlord, and asked for a room, though the sun was only beginning to sink in the western sky. The place had just three bedrooms, and the landlord showed Robin Hood to the poorest of them. But Robin hardly cared what the room looked like, for he could have slept that night on a bed of broken stones. So he pulled off his clothes without any fuss, tumbled into bed, and was fast asleep almost before his head touched the pillow.

Not long after Robin had gone to bed, a great cloud showed black above the hills to the west. It climbed higher and higher until it stood against the night sky like a mountain of darkness. All along its underside came a dull red flash every now and then, and soon the short, grim mutter of approaching thunder could be heard. Then four stout burghers of Nottingham Town rode up, since this was the only inn within five miles and they didn’t want to be caught in the thunderstorm that was coming. They left their horses with the stableman, went into the best room of the inn, where fresh green rushes lay spread across the floor, and ordered the finest food the place had to offer. When they had eaten heartily they asked the landlord to show them to their rooms, for they were weary, having ridden all the way from Dronfield that day. Off they went, grumbling about having to sleep two to a bed, but their troubles on that account, and every other, were soon lost in the quiet of sleep.

And now came the first gust of wind, rushing past the inn, banging the doors and shutters, smelling of the coming rain, and wrapped in a cloud of dust and leaves. As if the wind had brought a guest along with it, the door suddenly swung open and in came a friar of Emmet Priory, a man of high rank, as the softness and sleekness of his robes and the richness of his rosary showed. He called to the landlord and told him first to have his mule well fed and bedded down in the stable, and then to bring him the very best the house had. Soon a savory stew of tripe and onions with sweet little fat dumplings was set before him, along with a good stout half-gallon of Malmsey, and the holy friar fell to with great courage and heartiness. In a short time nothing was left but a little pool of gravy in the middle of the platter, not enough to keep a starving mouse alive.

Then the storm broke over the inn. Another blast of wind swept past, bringing a few fat drops of rain, and soon the rain was pelting down in sheets and drumming on the windowpanes like a hundred small hands. Vivid lightning lit up every raindrop, and each flash was followed by a crack of thunder that rolled off rumbling and bumping, as if Saint Swithin were busy trundling huge barrels of water over bumpy ground in the sky above. The women screamed, and the merry jokers in the taproom wrapped their arms around them to hush them.

At last the holy friar asked the landlord to show him to his room. When he heard that he would be sharing a bed with a cobbler, he was as sour a fellow as you could find in all England. Still, there was nothing to be done, and he had to sleep there or nowhere, so he took up his candle and went off, grumbling like the thunder that was now far away. When he reached the room where he was to sleep, he held the light over Robin and looked him up and down. Then he felt better pleased, for instead of a rough, dirty-bearded fellow, he saw a lad as fresh and clean as you could find in a week of Sundays. So he slipped off his clothes and crawled into the bed as well, where Robin, grunting and grumbling in his sleep, made room for him. Robin was sleeping more soundly, I’ll bet, than he had in many a day, or he would never have rested so peacefully with one of the friar’s sort lying so close beside him. As for the friar, had he known who Robin Hood was, you may well believe he would have been almost as willing to sleep beside a viper as beside the man he had for a bedfellow.

So the night passed comfortably enough, but at first light Robin opened his eyes and turned his head on the pillow. Then how he gaped and stared, for there beside him lay a man with a shaven head, so that he knew it must be someone in holy orders. He pinched himself hard, but finding that he was awake, he sat up in bed, while the other slept on as peacefully as if he were safe at home in Emmet Priory. “Now,” said Robin to himself, “I wonder how this thing got into my bed during the night.” With that he got up softly, so as not to wake the other, and looking around the room he spotted the friar’s clothes lying on a bench by the wall. First he looked at the clothes with his head on one side, and then he looked at the friar and slowly winked one eye. “Good Brother What’s-your-name,” he said, “since you’ve borrowed my bed so freely, I’ll just borrow your clothes in return.” And he promptly put on the holy man’s garb, though he kindly left the cobbler’s clothes in its place. Then he went out into the freshness of the morning. The stableman, who was up and about the stables, opened his eyes as if he had seen a green mouse, for friars of Emmet were not in the habit of rising early. But the man kept his thoughts to himself and only asked Robin whether he wanted his mule brought out of the stable.

“Yes, my son,” said Robin—though he knew nothing about any mule—“and bring it out quickly, please, for I’m late and must be on my way.” So the stableman soon led out the mule, and Robin mounted it and went off rejoicing.

As for the holy friar, when he got up he was in as sorry a mess as any man in the world, for his rich, soft robes were gone, and so was his purse with ten golden pounds in it, and all that was left was patched clothes and a leather apron. He raged and swore like any layman, but his swearing mended nothing and the landlord couldn’t help him. Since he also had to be at Emmet Priory that very morning on business, he had to choose between putting on the cobbler’s clothes and traveling the road naked. So he put on the clothes, and still raging and swearing vengeance on every cobbler in Derbyshire, he set out on foot. But his troubles were not over yet, for he hadn’t gone far before he fell into the hands of the King’s men, who marched him off, whether he liked it or not, to Tutbury Town and the Bishop of Hereford. He swore in vain that he was a holy man, and showed his shaven crown. Off he had to go, for nothing would do but that he was Robin Hood.

Meanwhile merry Robin rode along contentedly, slipping safely past two bands of the King’s men, until his heart began to dance inside him because Sherwood was so near. He kept traveling east until suddenly, in a shady lane, he met a noble knight. Robin quickly reined in his mule and jumped down from its back. “Well met, Sir Richard of the Lea,” he cried, “for there’s no man in England I’d rather see today than you!” Then he told Sir Richard everything that had happened to him, and said that now at last he felt safe, being so close to Sherwood again. But when Robin had finished, Sir Richard shook his head sadly. “You are in greater danger now, Robin, than you have ever been,” he said, “for ahead of you are bands of the Sheriff’s men blocking every road and letting no one through their lines without questioning them closely. I know this myself, for I have just come past them. The Sheriff’s men are in front of you and the King’s men behind you, and you can’t hope to get through either way, for by this time they will know of your disguise and will be waiting to seize you. My castle and everything in it are yours, but nothing could be gained there, for I couldn’t hope to hold it against a force like the one now in Nottingham, made up of the King’s men and the Sheriff’s.” When he had said this, Sir Richard bowed his head in thought, and Robin felt his heart sink inside him like that of a fox who hears the hounds at his heels and finds his den blocked with earth, so that there is no hiding place for him. But soon Sir Richard spoke again. “There is one thing you can do, Robin, and only one. Go back to London and throw yourself on the mercy of our good Queen Eleanor. Come with me to my castle right now. Take off these clothes and put on the kind my retainers wear. Then I will hurry to London Town with a troop of men behind me, and you will mingle with them, and in this way I will bring you to a place where you can see and speak with the Queen. Your only hope is to reach Sherwood, since no one can touch you there, and you will never get to Sherwood except in this way.”
Seeing the sense in the knight’s advice, and that it offered his one chance of safety, Robin went off with Sir Richard of the Lea and did just as he was told.

Queen Eleanor was walking in her royal garden among the sweetly blooming roses, and with her walked six of her ladies-in-waiting, chattering happily together. Suddenly a man leaped up onto the top of the wall from the other side, hung there for a moment, and dropped lightly onto the grass inside. All the ladies-in-waiting shrieked at his sudden arrival, but the man ran to the Queen and knelt at her feet, and she saw that it was Robin Hood.

“Why, how now, Robin!” she cried. “Do you dare to come into the very jaws of the raging lion? Alas, poor fellow! You are lost indeed if the King finds you here. Don’t you know he is searching for you all over the land?”

“Yes,” said Robin, “I know very well that the King is searching for me, and that is why I have come. For surely no harm can come to me when he has pledged his royal word to Your Majesty for my safety. Besides, I know Your Majesty’s kindness and gentleness of heart, and so I lay my life freely in your gracious hands.”

“I understand your meaning, Robin Hood,” said the Queen, “and that you are reproaching me, as well you may, for I know I have not done by you as I should have. I know very well that you must have been hard pressed by danger to leap so boldly into one peril to escape another. Once more I promise you my help, and I will do all I can to send you back safely to Sherwood Forest. Wait here until I return.” With that she left Robin in the garden of roses, and was gone a long time.

When she came back, Sir Robert Lee was with her. The Queen’s cheeks were flushed and her eyes were bright, as though she had just been arguing hotly. Sir Robert walked straight up to where Robin Hood stood and spoke to the yeoman in a cold, stern voice. “Our gracious Sovereign the King has eased his anger toward you, fellow, and has promised once more that you may leave in peace and safety. He has promised more than that: in three days he will send one of his pages to travel with you and make sure no one arrests you on the road home. You may thank your patron saint that you have such a good friend in our noble Queen, for without her pleading and arguments you would be a dead man, I can tell you. Let the danger you have just come through teach you two lessons. First, be more honest. Second, be less bold in your comings and goings. A man who walks in the dark as you do may get by for a while, but in the end he will surely fall into the pit. You have put your head in the angry lion’s mouth and escaped by a miracle. Do not try it again.” With that he turned and left Robin, and was gone.

For three days Robin stayed in London in the Queen’s household. At the end of that time the King’s head Page, Edward Cunningham, came for him, and the two of them set out northward toward Sherwood. Now and then they passed bands of the King’s men heading back to London, but none of them stopped the pair, and at last they reached the sweet, leafy woodlands.

chapters.title: Robin Hood and Guy of Gisbourne
paragraphs: A long time went by after the great shooting match. During it Robin followed one part of Sir Robert Lee’s advice, namely to be less bold in his comings and goings. Whether he became any more honest (as most people understand honesty) is doubtful, but he took good care never to travel so far from Sherwood that he couldn’t get back to it quickly and easily.

Great changes had come in that time. King Henry had died, and King Richard had taken the crown, which suited him so well after many hard trials and adventures as stirring as any that ever happened to Robin Hood. But however great the changes outside, they did not reach into Sherwood’s shade. There Robin Hood and his men lived as merrily as ever, with hunting and feasting and singing and cheerful woodland sports, and the struggles of the outside world troubled them very little.

The dawn of a summer day was fresh and bright, and the birds sang sweetly in a great tumult of sound. Their singing was so loud that it woke Robin Hood where he lay asleep, and he stirred, turned over, and got up. Little John got up too, and so did all the merry men. Then, after they had eaten breakfast, they set off in different directions to see to the day’s doings.
