Robin Hood and Little John walked down a forest path where the leaves danced and twinkled all around as the breeze shivered through them and the sunlight came flickering down. “I swear, Little John,” said Robin Hood, “my blood tickles my veins as it runs through them this gay morning. What do you say to going off to look for adventures, each on his own?”

“Gladly,” said Little John. “We’ve had more than one pleasant adventure that way, good master. Here are two paths. You take the one on the right, and I’ll take the one on the left, and let each of us walk straight ahead until he tumbles into some merry doing or other.”
“I like your plan,” said Robin, “so we’ll part here. But listen, Little John, keep yourself out of mischief, for I wouldn’t want any harm to come to you for all the world.”
“Well, listen to you!” said Little John. “The way you talk! I’d say you’re the one who usually gets himself into tighter knots than I do.”

Robin Hood laughed at this. “Why, truly, Little John,” he said, “you have a blundering, hard-headed way about you that seems to land you right side up in all your troubles. But let’s see which of us does best today.” With that he clapped his palm to Little John’s, and each went his own way, the trees quickly hiding the one from the other.

Robin Hood strolled on until he came to a broad woodland road stretching ahead of him. Overhead the branches of the trees interlaced in flickering foliage, golden where it grew thin enough for the sun to shine through; underfoot the ground was soft and damp from the shelter of the shade. In this pleasant spot the sharpest adventure that ever befell Robin Hood came upon him. He was walking down the path thinking of nothing but the songs of the birds when he came suddenly upon a man sitting on the mossy roots beneath a broad-spreading oak. The stranger had not noticed him, so Robin stopped and stood quite still, looking at him for a long time before going forward. And the stranger, I can tell you, was well worth looking at, for Robin had never seen a figure like the one sitting under that tree. From head to foot he was dressed in a horse’s hide, tanned with the hair left on. On his head was a cowl made of the horse’s skin, which hid his face, and the ears stuck up from it like a rabbit’s. His body was covered by a jacket of the same hide, and his legs were wrapped in the hairy skin too. At his side were a heavy broadsword and a sharp, double-edged dagger. A quiver of smooth, round arrows hung across his shoulders, and his stout yew bow leaned against the tree beside him.

“Hello there, friend,” cried Robin, coming forward at last, “who are you, sitting there? And what is that you’re wearing? I swear I’ve never seen such a sight in all my life. If I had done some evil deed, or if my conscience bothered me, I would be afraid of you, thinking you were someone from down below, come to tell me to report at once to King Nicholas.”

The other said nothing in answer to this speech. He pushed the cowl back from his head and showed a knitted brow, a hooked nose, and a pair of fierce, restless black eyes, which together made Robin think of a hawk as he looked at the face. And besides this, there was something in the lines of the stranger’s face, his thin, cruel mouth and the hard glare of his eyes, that made your flesh creep to look at him.
“Who are you, rascal?” he said at last in a loud, harsh voice.
“Tut, tut,” said merry Robin, “don’t talk so sourly, brother. Did you feed on vinegar and nettles this morning, that your speech is so stinging?”
“If you don’t like my words,” said the other fiercely, “you’d better be on your way, because I tell you plainly, my deeds match them.”

“No, but I do like your words, you sweet, pretty thing,” said Robin, squatting down on the grass in front of the other. “What’s more, I tell you your speech is as witty and playful as any I’ve ever heard in my life.”

The other said nothing, but glared at Robin with a wicked, menacing look, like the one a fierce dog gives a man before it leaps at his throat. Robin returned the stare with wide-eyed innocence, not a trace of a smile twinkling in his eyes or twitching at the corners of his mouth. They sat staring at each other for a long time, until the stranger suddenly broke the silence. “What’s your name, fellow?” he said.

“Now,” said Robin, “I’m very glad to hear you speak, for I was starting to fear the sight of me had struck you dumb. As for my name, it may be this or it may be that; but I think it’s more fitting for you to tell me yours, since you’re the greater stranger in these parts. Please tell me, sweet chuck, why do you wear that dainty outfit on your pretty body?” At these words the other burst into a short, harsh roar of laughter. “By the bones of the Daemon Odin,” he said, “you’re the boldest-spoken man I’ve ever seen. I don’t know why I don’t strike you down where you sit, for only two days ago I ran a man through, over behind Nottingham Town, for saying not half as much to me as you have. I wear this outfit, you fool, to keep my body warm, and it’s nearly as good as a steel coat against an ordinary sword thrust. As for my name, I don’t care who knows it. It is Guy of Gisbourne, and you may have heard it before. I come from the woodlands over in Herefordshire, on the lands of the Bishop of that same place. I am an outlaw, and I make my living by hook or by crook, in a way that isn’t worth telling now. Not long ago the Bishop sent for me and said that if I would do a certain thing the Sheriff of Nottingham would ask of me, he would get me a full pardon and give me two hundred pounds besides. So I came straight to Nottingham Town and found my sweet Sheriff. And what do you think he wanted of me? Why, to come here to Sherwood, hunt down one Robin Hood, also an outlaw, and take him alive or dead. It seems they have no one here to face that bold fellow, so they sent all the way to Herefordshire for me, for you know the old saying, ‘Set a thief to catch a thief.’ As for killing him, it doesn’t trouble me in the least, for I would spill the blood of my own brother for half of two hundred pounds.”

Robin listened to all this, and as he listened his gorge rose. He knew very well of this Guy of Gisbourne and all the bloody, murderous deeds he had done in Herefordshire, for they were famous throughout the land. Yet although he loathed the very presence of the man, he held his tongue, for he had an end to serve. “Truly,” he said, “I’ve heard of your gentle doings. I think there’s no one in all the world Robin Hood would rather meet than you.”

At this Guy of Gisbourne gave another harsh laugh. “Why,” he said, “it’s a merry thing to think of one stout outlaw like Robin Hood meeting another like Guy of Gisbourne. Only this time it will end badly for Robin Hood, because the day he meets Guy of Gisbourne he will die.”

“But you gentle, merry spirit,” said Robin, “don’t you think this same Robin Hood might be the better man of the two? I know him very well, and many people think he’s one of the stoutest men around here.”

“He may be the stoutest man around here,” said Guy of Gisbourne, “but I tell you, fellow, this sty of yours is not the wide world. I’d bet my life I’m the better man of the two. He, an outlaw? Ha! Why, I hear he has never drawn blood in his life, except when he first came to the forest. Some call him a great archer; well, I wouldn’t be afraid to stand against him every day of the year with a bow in my hand.”

“True enough, some folk do call him a great archer,” said Robin Hood, “but out here in Nottinghamshire we all handle the longbow well. Even I, who am only a modest hand at it, wouldn’t be afraid to shoot a match against you.”

At these words Guy of Gisbourne looked at Robin in wonder, and then roared with laughter again until the woods rang. “Well,” he said, “you’re a bold fellow to talk to me like this. I like your spirit in speaking up to me, for few men have dared. Set up a garland, lad, and I’ll try a round with you.”

“Tut, tut,” said Robin, “only babes shoot at garlands around here. I’ll set up a proper Nottingham mark for you.” With that he got up and went to a hazel thicket not far off, where he cut a wand about twice as thick as a man’s thumb. He peeled off the bark, sharpened the point, and stuck it in the ground in front of a great oak tree. From there he measured off fourscore paces, which brought him back beside the tree where the other sat. “There,” he said, “is the kind of mark Nottingham yeomen shoot at. Now let me see you split that wand, if you’re an archer.”
Then Guy of Gisbourne stood up. “Out upon it!” he cried. “The Devil himself couldn’t hit a mark like that.”
“Maybe he could and maybe he couldn’t,” said merry Robin, “but we’ll never know until you’ve shot at it.”

At this Guy of Gisbourne scowled at Robin, but since the yeoman still looked innocent of any ill meaning, he swallowed his words and strung his bow in silence. He shot twice and hit the wand neither time, missing by a span the first time and by a good palm’s-breadth the second. Robin laughed and laughed. “I see now,” he said, “that the Devil himself couldn’t hit that mark. Good fellow, if you’re no better with the broadsword than you are with the bow and arrow, you’ll never overcome Robin Hood.”
Guy of Gisbourne glared savagely at Robin. “You have a merry tongue, you villain,” he said, “but take care you don’t make too free with it, or I may cut it out of your throat for you.”

Robin Hood strung his bow and took his place without a word, although his heartstrings quivered with anger and loathing. He shot twice: the first arrow landed within an inch of the wand, and the second split it fairly down the middle. Then, without giving the other a chance to speak, he flung his bow on the ground. “There, you bloody villain!” he cried fiercely. “Let that show you how little you know of manly sports. And now take your last look at the daylight, for the good earth has been befouled by you long enough, you vile beast! This day, Our Lady willing, you die—I am Robin Hood.” With that he flashed out his bright sword in the sunlight.

For a while Guy of Gisbourne stared at Robin as though he had lost his wits, but his amazement quickly turned to wild rage. “Are you really Robin Hood?” he cried. “Now I’m glad to meet you, you poor wretch! Say your prayers, for you’ll have no time for them when I’m done with you.” With that he drew his sword too.

Then began the fiercest fight Sherwood had ever seen, for each man knew that one of them had to die and that neither would be shown any mercy. They fought back and forth until the sweet green grass was trampled and ground under their heels. More than once the point of Robin Hood’s sword met soft flesh, and soon bright red drops were spattering the ground, though not one of them came from Robin’s veins. At last Guy of Gisbourne made a fierce, deadly lunge at Robin, who sprang lightly back, but as he sprang, his heel caught on a root and he fell heavily on his back. “Holy Mary, help me now!” he muttered, as Guy leaped at him with a snarl of rage on his face. Guy of Gisbourne stabbed wildly at him with his great sword, but Robin caught the blade in his bare hand, and though it cut his palm, he turned the point aside so that it drove deep into the earth beside him. Then, before Guy could strike again, Robin was on his feet with his good sword in his hand. Despair settled on Guy of Gisbourne’s heart like a black cloud, and he glanced wildly about him like a wounded hawk. Seeing that his strength was failing, Robin leaped forward and, quick as lightning, struck a backhand blow just under the sword arm. The sword dropped from Guy’s grip, and he staggered back from the blow, and before he could steady himself, Robin’s sword ran right through his body. He spun around on his heel, flung up his hands with a shrill, wild cry, and fell facedown on the green grass.

Then Robin Hood wiped his sword and slid it back into its sheath. He went over to where Guy of Gisbourne lay and stood above him with his arms folded, talking to himself. “This is the first man I have killed since I shot the King’s forester in the hot days of my youth. Even now I often think bitterly of that first life I took, but for this one I am as glad as if I had killed a wild boar that was laying waste a fair countryside. Since the Sheriff of Nottingham has sent a man like this against me, I will put on the fellow’s clothes and go out to see whether I can find His Worship, and perhaps pay him back some of what I owe him on this account.”

With that, Robin Hood stripped the hairy clothes off the dead man and put them on himself, bloody as they were. Then he strapped the other man’s sword and dagger around his waist, took his own sword in his hand along with the two yew bows, and pulled the hood of horsehide down over his face so that no one could tell who he was. He left the forest and headed east toward Nottingham Town. As he strode along the country roads, men, women, and children hid from him, for the terror of Guy of Gisbourne’s name and deeds had spread far and wide.
And now let us see what happened to Little John while all this was going on.

Little John followed the forest paths until he reached the edge of the woods, where fields of barley and corn and green meadows lay smiling in the sun here and there. He came out onto the highroad, where a little thatched cottage stood behind a cluster of twisted crab trees, with flowers growing in front. There he suddenly stopped, for he thought he heard someone crying in sorrow. He listened and found that the sound came from the cottage, so he turned his steps that way, pushed open the gate, and went in. Inside he saw a gray-haired old woman sitting beside a cold hearth, rocking back and forth and weeping bitterly.

Little John had a tender heart for other people’s sorrows, so he went to the old woman, patted her kindly on the shoulder, and spoke comforting words to her. He told her to cheer up and tell him her troubles, for perhaps he could do something to ease them. The good woman only shook her head at this, but his kind words soothed her a little all the same, and after a while she told him everything that weighed on her mind. That very morning, she said, she had had three sons beside her, as fair and tall as any in all Nottinghamshire, and now they had been taken from her and were likely to be hanged on the spot. Want had come upon them, and her eldest boy had gone into the forest the night before and killed a doe in the moonlight. The King’s rangers had followed the blood on the grass until they came to her cottage, where they found the venison in the cupboard. Since neither of the younger sons would betray their brother, the foresters had taken all three away, even though the eldest kept saying that he alone had killed the deer. As they left, she had overheard the rangers saying to one another that the Sheriff had sworn to put a stop to the great slaughter of deer that had been going on lately by hanging the very first rascal caught at it on the nearest tree. They said they would take the three young men to the King’s Head Inn, near Nottingham Town, where the Sheriff was staying that day, and there wait for the return of a certain fellow he had sent into Sherwood to look for Robin Hood.

Little John listened to all this, shaking his head sadly now and then. “Alas,” he said when the good woman had finished, “this is a bad business indeed. But who is this man who has gone into Sherwood after Robin Hood, and why is he looking for him? No matter for now. I only wish Robin Hood were here to advise us. Still, there is no time to send for him at this hour, if we are to save your three sons’ lives. Tell me, do you have any clothes around here that I can wear in place of this Lincoln green? Mark my words, if our sturdy Sheriff catches me without a disguise, I’ll be strung up even faster than your sons, dame, let me tell you.”

Then the old woman told him she had some clothes in the house that belonged to her good husband, who had died only two years before. She brought them to Little John, who took off his Lincoln green and put them on instead. Next he made a wig and a false beard out of uncarded wool, covering his own brown hair and beard. He put on a great tall hat that had belonged to the old peasant, took his staff in one hand and his bow in the other, and set off as fast as he could for the place where the Sheriff had made his quarters.

A mile or more from Nottingham Town, and not far from the southern edge of Sherwood Forest, stood a cozy inn with the sign of the King’s Head. That bright morning the place was bustling, for the Sheriff and twenty of his men had stopped there to wait for Guy of Gisbourne to come back from the forest. In the kitchen the cooking hissed and sizzled, and in the cellar there was a great rapping and tapping of wine kegs and beer barrels. The Sheriff sat inside, feasting merrily on the best the house could offer, while his men sat on the bench in front of the door drinking ale, or lay in the shade of the broad oak trees, talking and joking and laughing. All around stood the band’s horses, stamping their feet and switching their tails with a great noise. To this inn came the King’s rangers, driving the widow’s three sons ahead of them. The young men’s hands were tied tightly behind their backs, and a cord ran from neck to neck to fasten them together. They were marched into the room where the Sheriff sat at his meal, and there they stood trembling before him as he glared at them sternly.

“So,” he said in a loud, angry voice, “you have been poaching the King’s deer, have you? Well, I will make short work of you today, for I will hang all three of you up the way a farmer hangs up three crows to scare the rest of their kind away from his field. Our fair county of Nottingham has been a breeding ground for wicked rascals like you for too long. I have put up with it for many years, but now I will stamp it out once and for all, and I will begin with you.”

One of the poor fellows opened his mouth to speak, but the Sheriff roared at him to be silent. He ordered the rangers to take them away until he had finished eating and could see to their case. So the three poor young men were marched outside, where they stood with bowed heads and hopeless hearts until the Sheriff came out after a while. Then he called his men around him and said, “These three villains shall be hanged at once, but not here, or they might bring bad luck on this fine inn. We will take them over to that belt of woodland, for I would gladly hang them from the very trees of Sherwood itself, to show those vile outlaws what they can expect from me if I ever have the good luck to lay hands on them.” With that he mounted his horse, and his men-at-arms did the same, and all together they rode for the belt of woodland he had named, with the poor young men walking in the middle, guarded by the rangers. At last they reached the spot, and there nooses were fastened around the necks of the three, and the ends of the cords were thrown over the branch of a great oak tree that stood there. Then the three young men fell on their knees and begged the Sheriff loudly for mercy, but the Sheriff of Nottingham only laughed scornfully. “Now,” he said, “I wish I had a priest here to hear your confessions, but since there is none nearby, you will just have to travel your road with all your sins packed on your backs, and trust Saint Peter to let you through the gates of Paradise like three peddlers into town.”

Meanwhile, as all this was going on, an old man had come up and was standing there, leaning on his staff and watching. His hair and beard were curly and white, and across his back was a yew bow that looked much too strong for him to draw. As the Sheriff glanced around, just before he ordered his men to string the three young men up to the oak tree, his eyes fell on this strange old man. His worship beckoned to him and said, “Come here, father, I have a few words to say to you.” So Little John, for it was none other than he, came forward, and the Sheriff looked him over, thinking there was something strangely familiar about the face in front of him. “Well, now,” he said, “I think I have seen you before. What is your name, father?”
“If it please Your Worship,” said Little John in a cracked voice like an old man’s, “my name is Giles Hobble, at Your Worship’s service.”

“Giles Hobble, Giles Hobble,” the Sheriff muttered to himself, running through the names in his memory to find one that fit. “I don’t remember your name,” he said at last, “but it doesn’t matter. Would you like to earn sixpence this fine morning?”
“Aye, indeed,” said Little John, “for money isn’t so plentiful with me that I’d throw sixpence away if I could earn it by an honest job. What would Your Worship have me do?”

“Why, this,” said the Sheriff. “Here are three men who need hanging as badly as any I ever saw. If you will string them up, I will pay you twopence apiece for them. I don’t like my men-at-arms having to play the hangman. Will you try your hand?”

“Truly,” said Little John, still in the old man’s voice, “I’ve never done such a thing before, but if a sixpence can be earned so easily, I might as well have it as anybody. But Your Worship, have these wicked fellows made their confession?”
“No,” said the Sheriff, laughing, “not a bit of it, but you may try your hand at that too, if you’re so inclined. But hurry, I beg you, for I want to be back at my inn in good time.”

So Little John went to where the three young men stood trembling. He put his face close to the first fellow’s cheek as though he were listening to him, and whispered softly in his ear, “Stand still, brother, when you feel your bonds cut. But when you see me throw my woolen wig and beard off my head and face, cast the noose from your neck and run for the woods.” Then he slyly cut the cord that bound the young man’s hands, and the young man stood still as though he were still tied. Next he went to the second fellow, spoke to him the same way, and cut his bonds too. He did the same for the third, all so slyly that the Sheriff, who sat laughing on his horse, had no idea what was being done, and neither did his men.

Then Little John turned to the Sheriff. “If it please Your Worship,” he said, “will you give me leave to string my bow? For I would gladly help these fellows along their way, while they’re swinging, with an arrow under the ribs.”
“With all my heart,” said the Sheriff, “only, as I said before, be quick about your business.”

Little John set the tip of his bow against his instep and strung it so deftly that everyone marveled to see an old man so strong. Next he drew a good smooth arrow from his quiver and fitted it to the string. Then he looked all around to make sure the way was clear behind him, and suddenly tore the wool from his head and face, shouting in a mighty voice, “Run!” Quick as a flash the three young men threw the nooses from their necks and raced across the open ground to the woods as swift as an arrow leaves the bow. Little John also flew toward the thicket like a greyhound, while the Sheriff and his men stared after him, bewildered by the sudden turn of events. But before the yeoman had gone far, the Sheriff came to his senses. “After him!” he roared in a mighty voice, for he now knew who it was he had been talking to, and he wondered that he had not known him sooner.

Little John heard what the Sheriff said. He knew he could never reach the woods before they were on him, so he stopped short and wheeled around, raising his bow as if to shoot. “Back, all of you!” he shouted fiercely. “The first man to step one foot closer, or lay a finger on a bowstring, is a dead man!”

When they heard this, the Sheriff’s men froze like posts, for they knew perfectly well that Little John meant what he said, and that disobeying him would mean death. The Sheriff roared at them in vain. He called them cowards and ordered them to charge together, but they would not move an inch. They simply stood and watched Little John walk slowly away toward the forest, his eyes never leaving them. But when the Sheriff saw his enemy slipping through his fingers, he went wild with rage, until his head spun and he hardly knew what he was doing. All at once he wheeled his horse around, drove his spurs into its sides, gave a great shout, and rose in his stirrups and swept down on Little John like the wind. Little John raised his deadly bow and drew the gray goose feather back to his cheek. But luck was against him! Before he could loose the shaft, the good bow that had served him so long split in his hands, and the arrow dropped harmlessly at his feet. Seeing this, the Sheriff’s men let out a shout and came rushing after their master toward Little John. But the Sheriff was well ahead of the rest, and he caught up with the yeoman before he could reach the shelter of the woods. Leaning forward, he swung a mighty blow. Little John ducked, and the Sheriff’s sword twisted in his hand, but the flat of the blade struck the yeoman on the head and knocked him down, stunned and senseless.

“Now I am truly glad,” said the Sheriff, when his men came up and found that Little John was not dead, “that I did not kill this man in my haste! I would rather lose five hundred pounds than see him die like this instead of hanging, as such a vile thief should. Go, William, fetch some water from that spring over there and pour it over his head.”

The man did as he was told, and soon Little John opened his eyes and looked around, dazed and bewildered from the blow. Then they tied his hands behind him, lifted him up, and set him on the back of one of the horses, facing the tail, with his feet strapped beneath its belly. In this way they took him back to the King’s Head Inn, laughing and celebrating all the way. But in the meantime the widow’s three sons had got safely away and were hiding in the woods.

Once again the Sheriff of Nottingham sat in the King’s Head Inn. His heart was glad, for he had finally done what he had been trying to do for years: he had taken Little John prisoner. “This time tomorrow,” he said to himself, “the rogue will be hanging from the gallows tree in front of the great gate of Nottingham Town, and so I will settle my long account with him.” With that he took a deep drink of Canary wine. But it seemed the Sheriff had swallowed a worry along with his wine, for he shook his head and quickly put the cup down. “Now,” he muttered to himself, “I would not lose this fellow for a thousand pounds. Yet if his master should get away from that rascal Guy of Gisbourne, there is no telling what he might do, for he is the craftiest knave in all the world, this Robin Hood. Perhaps I had better not wait until tomorrow to hang the fellow.” With that he pushed his chair back quickly, went out of the inn, and called his men together. “I will not wait any longer to hang this rogue,” he said. “It shall be done at once, and from the very tree where he saved those three young villains by stepping between them and the law. So get ready right now.”

Then they set Little John on the horse again, facing the tail. One man led the horse he sat on while the others rode around him, and so they went to the tree where they had meant to hang the poachers. They went rattling and jingling along the road until they reached it. Just then one of the men called out suddenly to the Sheriff. “Your Worship,” he cried, “isn’t that fellow coming toward us the same Guy of Gisbourne you sent into the forest to find Robin Hood?” At this the Sheriff shaded his eyes and looked eagerly. “Why, so it is,” he said. “That is the very man. Now, Heaven grant that he has killed the master thief, just as we are about to kill the man!”

When Little John heard this, he looked up, and his heart sank at once, for not only were the man’s clothes covered with blood, but he was wearing Robin Hood’s bugle horn and carrying his bow and broadsword.
“Well now!” cried the Sheriff, when Robin Hood, dressed in Guy of Gisbourne’s clothes, had come close to them. “What luck did you have in the forest? Why, man, your clothes are soaked in blood!”

“If you don’t like my clothes,” said Robin in a harsh voice like Guy of Gisbourne’s, “you can shut your eyes. The blood on me belongs to the vilest outlaw that ever walked the woods, and I killed him today, though not without being wounded myself.”

Then Little John spoke up, for the first time since he had fallen into the Sheriff’s hands. “You vile, bloody wretch! I know you, Guy of Gisbourne, for who has not heard of you and cursed you for your wicked deeds of blood and plunder? Is it a hand like yours that has stilled the gentlest heart that ever beat, stilled it in death? Truly, you are a fit tool for this coward Sheriff of Nottingham. Now I die gladly, and I don’t care how I die, for life means nothing to me!” So spoke Little John, with salt tears running down his brown cheeks.
But the Sheriff of Nottingham clapped his hands for joy. “Now, Guy of Gisbourne,” he cried, “if what you tell me is true, this will be the best day’s work you have ever done in your whole life.”

“What I have told you is the truth, and I do not lie,” said Robin, still in Guy of Gisbourne’s voice. “Look, is this not Robin Hood’s sword, and is this not his good yew bow, and is this not his bugle horn? Do you think he would have handed them over to Guy of Gisbourne of his own free will?”
Then the Sheriff laughed aloud with joy. “This is a good day!” he cried. “The great outlaw dead and his right-hand man in my hands! Ask me for anything you like, Guy of Gisbourne, and it is yours!”
“Then this is what I ask of you,” said Robin. “I have killed the master, and now I would like to kill the man. Put this fellow’s life in my hands, Sir Sheriff.”

“Now you are a fool!” cried the Sheriff. “You could have had enough money for a knight’s ransom if you had asked for it. I hate to let this fellow out of my hands, but since I have promised, you shall have him.”
“I thank you heartily for your gift,” cried Robin. “Take the rogue down from the horse, men, and stand him against that tree over there, while I show you how we stick a pig where I come from!”

Some of the Sheriff’s men shook their heads when they heard this. They did not care one bit whether Little John was hanged or not, but they hated the thought of seeing him slaughtered in cold blood. Even so, the Sheriff shouted at them to lift the yeoman off the horse and stand him against the tree, just as the other man had told them.

While they were doing this, Robin Hood strung both his own bow and Guy of Gisbourne’s, though none of them noticed him doing it. Then, when Little John was standing against the tree, he drew Guy of Gisbourne’s sharp, double-edged dagger. “Stand back! Stand back!” he cried. “Would you crowd in on my pleasure, you rude rascals? Back, I say! Farther still!” So they crowded back as he ordered, and many of them turned their faces away so that they would not see what was about to happen.
“Come on!” cried Little John. “Here is my chest. It is only right that the same hand that killed my dear master should butcher me too! I know you, Guy of Gisbourne!”

“Quiet, Little John!” said Robin in a low voice. “Twice you have said you know me, and yet you do not know me at all. Could you not tell it was me beneath this wild beast’s hide? Right there in front of you lie my bow and arrows, and my broadsword too. Take them when I cut your ropes. Now! Grab them quickly!” With that he cut the ropes, and Little John, quick as a wink, leaped forward and snatched up the bow, the arrows, and the broadsword. At the same moment Robin Hood threw back the cowl of horse’s hide from his face and bent Guy of Gisbourne’s bow, with a keen, barbed arrow fitted to the string. “Stand back!” he cried sternly. “The first man who lays a finger on a bowstring dies! I have killed your man, Sheriff. Take care that you are not next.” Then, seeing that Little John was armed, he put his bugle horn to his lips and blew three blasts, loud and shrill.

Now when the Sheriff of Nottingham saw whose face was under Guy of Gisbourne’s hood, and heard those bugle notes ringing in his ears, he felt that his last hour had come. “Robin Hood!” he roared, and without another word he swung his horse around in the road and galloped off in a cloud of dust. The Sheriff’s men, seeing their master running for his life, decided it was not their job to stay any longer, so they spurred their horses and dashed off after him. But fast as the Sheriff of Nottingham rode, he could not outrun a clothyard arrow. Little John twanged his bowstring with a shout, and when the Sheriff dashed through the gates of Nottingham Town at full speed, a gray goose shaft stuck out behind him like the one feather in the tail of a molting sparrow. For a month afterward the poor Sheriff could sit on nothing but the softest cushions that could be found for him.

And so the Sheriff and a score of his men fled from Robin Hood and Little John. When Will Stutely and a dozen or more sturdy yeomen came bursting out of the thicket, there was no sign of their master’s enemies, for the Sheriff and his men were far down the road, hurrying off inside a cloud of dust like a small thunderstorm.

Then they all went back into the forest, where they found the widow’s three sons, who ran to Little John and kissed his hands. But it would no longer be safe for them to wander the forest freely, so they promised that after they had gone to tell their mother they were safe, they would come that night to the greenwood tree and from then on become members of the band.

chapters.title: King Richard Comes to Sherwood Forest
paragraphs: Barely two months had gone by since Robin Hood and Little John had their stirring adventures, when all of Nottinghamshire fell into a great commotion. King Richard of the Lion’s Heart was making a royal tour of merry England, and everyone expected him to visit Nottingham Town along the way. Messengers galloped back and forth between the Sheriff and the King, until at last they settled on the day when His Majesty would stay in Nottingham as the guest of his worship.

And now there was more bustle than ever. Everywhere in the town there was running to and fro, hammering, and a babble of voices, for the people were building great arches across the streets for the King to pass under, and hanging them with silken banners and streamers of many colors. There was a great commotion in the Guild Hall too, because a grand banquet was to be held there for the King and the nobles of his train, and the best master carpenters were busy building a throne where the King and the Sheriff would sit side by side at the head of the table.

To many of the good people of the town it seemed that the day the King would arrive would never come. But come it did, in its own good time, and the sun shone brightly down on the stony streets, which were alive with a restless sea of people. On both sides of the road, great crowds of townsfolk and country folk stood packed as tightly as dried herring in a box, so that the Sheriff’s men, halberds in hand, could hardly push them back far enough to leave room for the King to ride through.

“Watch whom you push!” cried a big, burly friar to one of these men. “Would you dig your elbows into me, fellow? By Our Lady of the Fountain, if you don’t treat me with more respect, I will crack your skull for you, even if you are one of the mighty Sheriff’s men.”

At this a great shout of laughter went up from a number of tall yeomen in Lincoln green who were scattered through the crowd nearby. But one who seemed to have more authority than the others nudged the holy man with his elbow. “Quiet, Tuck,” he said. “Didn’t you promise me before you came here that you would keep a check on your tongue?”
“Aye, indeed,” grumbled the other, “but I never expected some hard-footed scoundrel to trample all over my poor toes as if they were nothing but acorns in the forest.”

Suddenly all the squabbling died away, for the clear call of many bugle horns came winding down the street. Everyone stretched their necks to look toward the sound, and the shoving and swaying got worse than before. Then a splendid company of men came shining into view, and the cheers of the people raced along the crowd like fire through dry grass.

Eight and twenty heralds rode forward in velvet and cloth of gold. A cloud of snow-white plumes fluttered above their heads, and each herald held a long silver trumpet and blew it sweetly. A heavy banner of velvet and cloth of gold hung from every trumpet, with the royal arms of England embroidered on it. Behind them rode a hundred noble knights, two abreast, each in full armor except for his bare head. They held tall lances, and colorful pennons with many designs fluttered from the tips. Next to each knight walked a page in rich silk and velvet, carrying his master’s helmet, from which long feathered plumes floated and waved. Nottingham had never seen anything finer than those hundred noble knights, with the sun flashing dazzlingly off their armor as they rode their great war horses amid the clash of weapons and the jingle of chains. After the knights came the barons and nobles of the Midlands, wearing robes of silk and cloth of gold, with gold chains at their necks and jewels at their belts. After them came a large company of men-at-arms carrying spears and halberds, and in the midst of them rode two men side by side. One was the Sheriff of Nottingham in his robes of office. The other was a head taller than the Sheriff and dressed in rich but plain clothes, with a broad, heavy chain around his neck. His hair and beard were like threads of gold, and his eyes were as blue as a summer sky. He bowed to right and left as he rode, and a mighty roar of voices followed him down the street, for this was King Richard.

Then, above all the uproar and the cheering, a mighty voice came roaring out: “Heaven and its saints bless you, our gracious King Richard! And may Our Lady of the Fountain bless you too!” King Richard looked toward the place the voice came from. There, in front of the crowd, stood a tall, burly, broad-built priest, his legs planted wide apart as he braced his back against the people behind him.

“By my soul, Sheriff,” said the King with a laugh, “you have the tallest priests in Nottinghamshire that I ever saw in all my life. If Heaven never answered prayers because it was deaf, I think I would get my blessings anyway, for that man over there could make the great stone statue of Saint Peter rub its ears and listen to him. I wish I had an army of men like him.”

The Sheriff did not say a single word in reply. All the color drained from his cheeks, and he grabbed the front of his saddle to keep from falling. He had seen the man who shouted, and he knew him for Friar Tuck; and behind Friar Tuck he saw the faces of Robin Hood, Little John, Will Scarlet, Will Stutely, Allan a Dale, and others of the band.
“What is this?” said the King quickly. “Are you ill, Sheriff, that you have turned so white?”

“No, Your Majesty,” said the Sheriff. “It was nothing but a sudden pain, and it will soon pass.” He said this because he was ashamed to let the King know that Robin Hood feared him so little that he dared to come right up to the gates of Nottingham Town.
So King Richard rode into Nottingham Town on that bright afternoon in early autumn, and no one was happier to see him arrive in such royal style than Robin Hood and his merry men.

Evening had come. The great feast in the Guild Hall at Nottingham Town was over, and the wine was flowing freely. A thousand wax candles shone along the table, where lords and nobles, knights and squires sat in fine array. At the head of the table, on a throne draped all over with cloth of gold, sat King Richard, with the Sheriff of Nottingham beside him.

The King said to the Sheriff, laughing as he spoke, “I have heard a great deal about the doings of some fellows in these parts, a certain Robin Hood and his band, who are outlaws and live in Sherwood Forest. Can you not tell me something about them, Sir Sheriff? I hear that you have had dealings with them more than once.”

At these words the Sheriff of Nottingham stared gloomily at the table, and the Bishop of Hereford, who was there, chewed on his lower lip. “I can tell Your Majesty very little about those wicked fellows,” said the Sheriff, “except that they are the boldest lawbreakers in all the land.”

Then young Sir Henry of the Lea spoke up. He was a great favorite with the King, and had fought under him in Palestine. “If it please Your Majesty,” said he, “when I was away in Palestine, my father often wrote to me, and most of the time his letters spoke of this very fellow, Robin Hood. If Your Majesty would like, I will tell you one adventure of this outlaw.”

The King told him with a laugh to go ahead, and Sir Henry told how Robin Hood had helped Sir Richard of the Lea with the money he had borrowed from the Bishop of Hereford. Again and again the King and everyone there roared with laughter, while the poor Bishop turned cherry red with annoyance, for it was a sore subject with him. When Sir Henry of the Lea had finished, others saw how much the King enjoyed this merry tale and told more stories about Robin and his merry men.

“By the hilt of my sword,” said sturdy King Richard, “I never heard of a bolder or merrier rogue than this one. Indeed, I mean to take the matter into my own hands and finish what you failed to do, Sheriff: I will rid the forest of him and his band.”

That night the King sat in the room set aside for his lodging while he was in Nottingham Town. With him were young Sir Henry of the Lea, two other knights, and three barons of Nottinghamshire; but the King’s mind was still on Robin Hood. “Now,” he said, “I would gladly give a hundred pounds to meet this rascal Robin Hood and see something of his doings in Sherwood Forest.”

Then Sir Hubert of Bingham spoke up, laughing. “If Your Majesty has such a wish, it is not hard to satisfy. If Your Majesty is willing to lose one hundred pounds, I promise to bring you not only to meet this fellow but to feast with him in Sherwood.”
“Well, Sir Hubert,” said the King, “that pleases me. But how will you manage to bring me to Robin Hood?”

“Why, like this,” said Sir Hubert. “Let Your Majesty and the rest of us here put on the robes of seven Black Friars, and let Your Majesty hang a purse of one hundred pounds under your gown. Then we will ride from here to Mansfield Town tomorrow, and unless I am greatly mistaken, we will meet Robin Hood and dine with him before the day is over.”
“I like your plan, Sir Hubert,” said the King cheerfully, “and tomorrow we will try it and see if there is anything to it.”

So early the next morning, when the Sheriff came to the King’s lodging to pay his respects, the King told him what they had talked about the night before and what merry adventure they were about to set out on that morning. But when the Sheriff heard it, he struck his forehead with his fist. “Alas!” said he. “What wicked advice you have been given! O my gracious lord and King, you do not know what you are doing! The villain you are going to look for has no respect for either king or king’s laws.”
“But was I not told correctly that Robin Hood has spilled no blood since the day he was outlawed, apart from that of the vile Guy of Gisbourne, for whose death every honest man should thank him?”
“Yes, Your Majesty,” said the Sheriff, “you heard correctly. Even so—”

“Then,” said the King, cutting off the Sheriff’s speech, “what have I to fear in meeting him, when I have done him no harm? Truly, there is no danger in this. But perhaps you will come with us, Sir Sheriff.”
“No,” said the Sheriff hastily. “Heaven forbid!”

Soon seven habits of the kind Black Friars wear were brought in. The King and his companions put them on, and His Majesty hung a purse with a hundred golden pounds in it under his robes. Then they all went out and mounted the mules that had been brought to the door for them. The King told the Sheriff to keep quiet about what they were doing, and they set off on their way. On they rode, laughing and joking, through the open country, between bare fields where the harvest had already been gathered in, and through scattered glades that grew thicker as they went on, until they came into the deep shade of the forest itself. They rode in the forest for several miles without meeting anyone of the kind they were looking for, until they reached the part of the road that ran closest to Newstead Abbey.

“By the holy Saint Martin,” said the King, “I wish I had a better memory for things that really matter. Here we have come all this way and have not brought so much as a drop of anything to drink. I would give fifty pounds right now for something to quench my thirst.”

The King had hardly finished speaking when a tall fellow with yellow beard and hair and a pair of merry blue eyes stepped out of the thicket at the roadside. “Truly, holy brother,” said he, laying his hand on the King’s bridle, “it would be unchristian not to answer so fair an offer. We keep an inn near here, and for fifty pounds we will not only give you a good drink of wine but a feast as fine as any you ever tickled your throat with.” With that he put his fingers to his lips and blew a shrill whistle. At once the bushes and branches on both sides of the road shook and crackled, and sixty broad-shouldered yeomen in Lincoln green burst out of the thicket.
“What is this, fellow?” said the King. “Who are you, you wicked rogue? Have you no respect for holy men like us?”

“Not a bit,” said merry Robin Hood, for the fellow was he. “All the holiness that belongs to rich friars like you could be dropped into a thimble, and the goodwife would never feel it with the tip of her finger. As for my name, it is Robin Hood, and you may have heard it before.”
“Shame on you!” said King Richard. “You are a bold and wicked fellow, and a lawless one too, as I have often heard. Now, please, let me and these brothers of mine travel on in peace and quiet.”

“That cannot be,” said Robin, “for it would look bad of us to let such holy men go on with empty stomachs. But I have no doubt you have a fat purse to pay your bill at our inn, since you offered so much for a poor drink of wine. Show me your purse, reverend brother, or I may have to strip the robes off you and search for it myself.”
“No, use no force,” said the King sternly. “Here is my purse, but do not lay your lawless hands on our person.”
“Hut, tut,” said merry Robin. “What proud words are these? Are you the King of England, to talk to me like that? Here, Will, take this purse and see what is inside.”

Will Scarlet took the purse and counted out the money. Then Robin told him to keep fifty pounds for themselves and put fifty back into the purse. He handed it to the King. “Here, brother,” said he, “take this half of your money, and thank Saint Martin, whom you called on before, that you have fallen into the hands of such gentle rogues, who will not strip you bare as they easily could. But will you not push back your hood? I would like to see your face.”
“No,” said the King, drawing back. “I may not push back my hood, for we seven have vowed not to show our faces for twenty-four hours.”
“Then stay hooded, and welcome,” said Robin. “I would never want to make you break a vow.”

So he called seven of his yeomen and told each of them to take a mule by the bridle. Then they turned toward the depths of the woodlands and journeyed on until they came to the open glade and the greenwood tree.

That morning Little John had also gone out with sixty yeomen following him, to watch the roads and bring a rich guest back to Sherwood glade if luck allowed, since so many travelers with fat purses were sure to be on the roads while such great events were happening in Nottinghamshire. Still, even with Little John and so many others away, Friar Tuck and forty or more stout yeomen sat or lounged beneath the great tree, and when Robin and his party came in they sprang up to greet him.

“By my soul,” said merry King Richard, when he had climbed down from his mule and stood looking around him, “you really do have a fine lot of young men about you, Robin. I think King Richard himself would be glad of such a bodyguard.”

“These are only some of my fellows,” said Robin proudly, “for sixty more are off on business with Little John, my good right-hand man. But as for King Richard, I tell you, brother, every one of us would pour out his blood like water for him. You churchmen cannot truly understand our King, but we yeomen love him with all our hearts, for his brave deeds are so much like our own.”

But now Friar Tuck came bustling up. “Good day to you, brothers,” said he. “I am very glad to welcome some of my own cloth to this wicked place. Truly, I think these outlaw rogues would stand a poor chance without the prayers of Holy Tuck, who works so hard for their well-being.” Here he winked one eye slyly and stuck his tongue in his cheek.
“Who are you, mad priest?” said the King in a serious voice, though he was smiling beneath his hood.

At this Friar Tuck looked all around him with a slow gaze. “Now look at that,” said he. “Never let me hear you say again that I am not a patient man. Here is a rascal of a friar calling me a mad priest, and I do not strike him. My name is Friar Tuck, fellow, the holy Friar Tuck.”
“There, Tuck,” said Robin, “you have said enough. Please stop talking and bring some wine. These reverend men are thirsty, and since they have paid so richly for their bill, they must have the best.”

Friar Tuck bristled at being cut off in his speech, but he went straight off to do Robin’s bidding. Soon a great jug was brought, and wine was poured out for all the guests and for Robin Hood. Then Robin held his cup high. “Wait!” he cried. “Hold off drinking until I give you a toast. Here is to good King Richard of great renown, and may all his enemies be confounded.”
Then all drank the King’s health, even the King himself. “I think, good fellow,” said he, “that you have drunk to your own ruin.”

“Not a bit,” said merry Robin. “I tell you, we of Sherwood are more loyal to our lord the King than those of your order. We would give up our lives for his good, while you are content to lie snug in your abbeys and priories, no matter who rules.”

At this the King laughed. “Perhaps King Richard’s welfare means more to me than you know, fellow,” said he. “But enough of that. We have paid well for our meal, so can you not show us some merry entertainment? I have often heard that you are wonderful archers. Will you not show us a little of your skill?”

“With all my heart,” said Robin. “We always like to give our guests every bit of sport there is. As Gaffer Swanthold says, ‘Only a hard heart would refuse a caged starling the best you have’; and caged starlings is what you are to us. Ho, lads! Hang a garland at the far end of the glade.”

Then, while the yeomen ran off to do their master’s bidding, Tuck turned to one of the mock friars. “Did you hear our master?” he said with a sly wink. “Whenever he hits on some poor scrap of wit, he lays it right away on the shoulders of this Gaffer Swanthold, whoever that may be, so the poor old fellow wanders about with all the odds and ends and tags and rags of our master’s brain packed on his back.” Friar Tuck kept his voice low so Robin would not hear, because he was still a little stung that Robin had cut his talk so short.

Meanwhile the mark they were to shoot at was set up one hundred twenty paces away. It was a garland of leaves and flowers two spans wide, hung on a stake in front of a broad tree trunk. “There,” said Robin, “that is a fair mark, lads. Each of you shoot three arrows at it, and if any fellow misses with even one arrow, he shall get a punch from Will Scarlet’s fist.”

“Listen to him!” said Friar Tuck. “Why, master, you hand out the blows from your sturdy nephew as if they were love taps from some bouncing girl. I’ll wager you’re sure to hit the garland yourself, or you wouldn’t be so generous with his thumping.”

David of Doncaster shot first, and put all three of his arrows into the garland. “Well done, David!” cried Robin. “You’ve saved your ears from a warming today.” Next Midge the Miller shot, and he too landed his arrows in the garland. Then came Wat the Tinker, but alas for him! One of his shafts missed the mark by two fingers’ breadth.

“Step over here, fellow,” said Will Scarlet in his soft, gentle voice. “I owe you something, and I’d like to pay it right now.” Wat the Tinker came forward and stood in front of Will Scarlet, screwing up his face and squeezing his eyes shut, as if he could already hear his ears ringing from the blow. Will Scarlet rolled up his sleeve and rose on tiptoe to give his arm a bigger swing, then struck with all his strength. “WHOOF!” went his palm against the Tinker’s head, and down went sturdy Wat onto the grass, heels over head, just like the wooden figure at the fair when a skillful player hurls a club at it. Then, as the Tinker sat up on the grass, rubbing his ear and winking and blinking at the bright stars dancing before his eyes, the yeomen roared with laughter until the forest rang. King Richard laughed until the tears ran down his cheeks. So the band shot, one after another, some getting off free and some earning a blow that always sent them to the grass. Last of all, Robin took his place, and everyone fell silent as he shot. His first arrow chipped a piece off the stake that held the garland, and his second landed within an inch of the first. “Upon my word,” King Richard said to himself, “I would give a thousand pounds to have this fellow in my guard!” Then Robin shot for the third time, but alas for him! The arrow was badly feathered, and it wavered to one side and struck an inch outside the garland.

At this a great roar went up. The yeomen sitting on the grass rolled over and over, shouting with laughter, for they had never before seen their master miss his mark. Robin, though, threw his bow to the ground in annoyance. “Now, enough of that!” he cried. “That arrow had a bad feather, for I felt it as it left my fingers. Give me a clean one, and I’ll promise to split the wand with it.”

At these words the yeomen laughed louder than ever. “No, good uncle,” said Will Scarlet in his soft, sweet voice, “you’ve had your fair chance and missed your aim completely. I swear the arrow was as good as any shot today. Come here. I owe you something, and I’d like to pay it.”
“Go on, good master,” roared Friar Tuck, “and may my blessing go with you. You’ve handed out Will Scarlet’s love taps very freely. It would be a shame if you didn’t get your own share.”

“That cannot be,” said merry Robin. “I am king here, and no subject may raise a hand against the king. But even our great King Richard might yield to the holy Pope without shame, and even take a tap from him as a penance. So I will yield to this holy friar, who looks like a man of authority, and take my punishment from him.” With that he turned to the King. “Please, brother, will you take my punishing into your holy hands?”
“Gladly,” said merry King Richard, getting up from his seat. “I have a debt to pay you, since you relieved my purse of a heavy fifty pounds. Clear a space on the green for him, lads.”

“If you make me tumble,” said Robin, “I’ll gladly give you back your fifty pounds. But I tell you, brother, if you don’t make me feel the grass all along my back, I’ll take every farthing you have for your boastful talk.”

“Agreed,” said the King. “I’m willing to take the chance.” He rolled up his sleeve and showed an arm that made the yeomen stare. Robin, however, stood firmly planted with his feet wide apart, smiling as he waited. Then the King swung back his arm, steadied himself for a moment, and struck Robin a blow that came down like a thunderbolt. Robin went headlong onto the grass, for that stroke could have knocked down a stone wall. How the yeomen shouted with laughter, until their sides ached, for in all their lives they had never seen such a blow! Robin soon sat up and looked all around, as if he had dropped from a cloud and landed in a place he had never seen before. After a while, still gazing at his laughing yeomen, he softly put his fingertips to his ear and felt carefully around it. “Will Scarlet,” he said, “count this fellow out his fifty pounds. I want nothing more from him, neither his money nor his company. A plague on him and his hitting! I wish I’d taken my payment from you instead, for I truly believe he has deafened my ear for good.”

Then, while gusts of laughter still broke from the band, Will Scarlet counted out the fifty pounds, and the King dropped it back into his purse. “Thank you, fellow,” he said. “And if you ever want another box on the ear to match the one you have, come to me and I’ll give it to you for nothing.”

So spoke the merry King. But just as he finished, the sound of many voices came suddenly from the thicket, and out burst Little John with sixty men, Sir Richard of the Lea in the middle of them. They came running across the glade, and as they ran, Sir Richard shouted to Robin: “Hurry, dear friend! Gather your band together and come with me! King Richard left Nottingham Town this very morning, and he is coming to look for you in the woods. I don’t know how he is coming, for I only heard a rumor of it, but I know it is true. So hurry, with all your men, and come to Castle Lea. There you can lie hidden until your present danger passes. Who are these strangers you have with you?”

“Why,” said merry Robin, rising from the grass, “these are some gentle guests who came with us from the highroad over by Newstead Abbey. I don’t know their names, but I’ve become well acquainted with this sturdy rascal’s palm this morning. Indeed, the pleasure of his acquaintance has cost me a deaf ear and fifty pounds besides!”

Sir Richard looked keenly at the tall friar, who drew himself up to his full height and looked steadily back at the knight. Suddenly Sir Richard’s cheeks went pale, for he knew who stood before him. He leaped quickly from his horse and threw himself on his knees in front of the friar. Seeing that Sir Richard knew him, the King threw back his cowl, and all the yeomen saw his face and knew him too, for every one of them had been in the crowd in the good town of Nottingham and had seen him riding side by side with the Sheriff. Down they fell on their knees, unable to say a word. The King looked all around him, very grimly, and at last his gaze came back and rested again on Sir Richard of the Lea.

“What is the meaning of this, Sir Richard?” he said sternly. “How dare you step between me and these fellows? And how dare you offer your knightly Castle of the Lea as a refuge for them? Will you make it a hiding place for the most famous outlaws in England?”

Then Sir Richard of the Lea raised his eyes to the King’s face. “Far be it from me,” he said, “to do anything that would bring Your Majesty’s anger upon me. Yet I would sooner face Your Majesty’s wrath than allow any harm that I could prevent to fall on Robin Hood and his band, for I owe them my life, my honor, everything. Should I then abandon him in his hour of need?”

Before the knight had finished speaking, one of the mock friars standing near the King came forward and knelt beside Sir Richard. Throwing back his cowl, he showed the face of young Sir Henry of the Lea. Sir Henry took his father’s hand and said, “Here kneels one who has served you well, King Richard, and who, as you know, stepped between you and death in Palestine. Yet I stand by my dear father, and I say here as well that I would gladly shelter this noble outlaw, Robin Hood, even if it brought your anger down on me, for my father’s honor and my father’s welfare are as dear to me as my own.”

King Richard looked from one kneeling knight to the other, and at last the frown faded from his brow and a smile twitched at the corners of his lips. “Well, Sir Richard,” said the King, “you are a bold-spoken knight, and your frank speech does not weigh heavily against you with me. This young son of yours takes after his father in bold words and bold deeds. As he says, he once stepped between me and death, and for his sake I would pardon you even if you had done more than you have. Rise, all of you, for none of you will suffer any harm from me today. It would be a pity to let a merry time end in a way that spoils its joy.”
Then everyone rose, and the King beckoned Robin Hood to come to him. “Well now,” he said, “is your ear still too deaf to hear me speak?”

“My ears would have to be deafened by death before they stopped hearing Your Majesty’s voice,” said Robin. “As for the blow Your Majesty struck me, I would say that although my sins may be many, I think they have been paid off in full by it.”

“Do you think so?” said the King, with some sternness in his voice. “Now I tell you that if not for three things, namely my mercy, my love for a stout woodsman, and the loyalty you have sworn to me, your ears might have been shut more tightly than any blow from me could ever have shut them. Don’t talk lightly of your sins, good Robin. But come, look up. Your danger is past, for I hereby give you and all your band a free pardon. Truly, though, I cannot let you roam the forest as you have done in the past. So I will take you at your word, when you said you would give your service to me, and you shall go back to London with me. We will take that bold rascal Little John as well, and your cousin Will Scarlet, and your minstrel Allan a Dale. As for the rest of your band, we will take down their names and have them properly recorded as royal rangers. I think it wiser to turn them into law-abiding keepers of our deer in Sherwood than to leave them running loose as outlawed killers of it. But now get a feast ready. I want to see how you live in the woods.”

So Robin told his men to prepare a grand feast. At once great fires were lit and burned brightly, and tasty things roasted over them with a sweet smell. While this was going on, the King told Robin to call Allan a Dale, for he wanted to hear him sing. Word was sent for Allan, and soon he came, carrying his harp.
“Well,” said King Richard, “if your singing matches your looks, it should be good enough. Please strike up a tune and let us have a taste of your skill.”
Then Allan touched his harp lightly, and everyone fell silent as he sang this song:

“’_Oh, where have you been, my daughter?
Oh, where have you been today,
Daughter, my daughter?’
‘Oh, I have been down by the river’s edge,
Where the waters lie gray and wide,
And the gray sky broods over the leaden tide,
And the shrill wind sighs, straining.’

“’What did you see there, my daughter?
What did you see there today,
Daughter, my daughter?’
‘Oh, I saw a boat come drifting near,
Where the trembling rushes hiss and sigh,
And the water murmurs as it gurgles by,
And the shrill wind sighs, straining.’

“’Who was in the boat, my daughter?
Who was in the boat today,
Daughter, my daughter?’
‘Oh, there was one dressed all in white,
And a pale glow hung about his face,
And his eyes shone sharp as stars at night,
And the shrill wind sighed, straining.’

“’And what did he say, my daughter?
What did he say to you today,
Daughter, my daughter?’
‘Oh, he said nothing, but he did this:
Three times he pressed a kiss upon my lips,
And my heartstrings shrank with a dreadful joy,
And the shrill wind sighed, straining.’

“’Why are you growing cold, my daughter?
Why are you growing cold and white,
Daughter, my daughter?’
Oh, the daughter never said a word,
But sat straight up with her head bowed low,
For her heart was stilled and her face was dead:
And the shrill wind sighed, straining_.”

Everyone listened in silence, and when Allan a Dale had finished, King Richard heaved a sigh. “Upon my life, Allan,” he said, “you have such a wonderfully sweet voice that it strangely moves my heart. But what a gloomy song this is for the lips of a stout yeoman! I would rather hear you sing of love and battle than a sad thing like that. Besides, I don’t understand it. What do the words mean?”
“I don’t know, Your Majesty,” said Allan, shaking his head, “for I often sing things that I don’t clearly understand myself.”

“Well, well,” said the King, “let it pass. But I’ll tell you this, Allan: you should turn your songs to the subjects I mentioned, love or war. For truly you have a sweeter voice than Blondell, and I thought he was the best minstrel I ever heard.”

Now someone came forward to say that the feast was ready. So Robin Hood led King Richard and his companions to where it lay spread out on fair white linen cloths upon the soft green grass. King Richard sat down and ate and drank, and when he had finished he swore heartily that he had never sat at such a hearty meal in all his life.

That night he lay in Sherwood Forest on a bed of sweet green leaves, and early the next morning he set out from the woods for Nottingham Town, with Robin Hood and all his band going along. You can imagine what a stir there was in the good town when all these famous outlaws came marching through the streets. As for the Sheriff, he didn’t know what to say or where to look when he saw Robin Hood in such high favor with the King, and his whole heart was filled with bitterness at his own annoyance.

The next day the King left Nottingham Town. Robin Hood, Little John, Will Scarlet, and Allan a Dale shook hands with the rest of the band, kissing each man on the cheek and swearing that they would often come to Sherwood to see them. Then each mounted his horse and rode away in the King’s company.

chapters.title: Epilogue
paragraphs: So end the Merry Adventures of Robin Hood. Despite his promise, it was many a year before he saw Sherwood again.

Little John spent a year or two at court, then returned to Nottinghamshire. There he lived quietly, though within sight of Sherwood, and won great renown as the quarterstaff champion of all England. After a while Will Scarlet went back to the home he had been driven from when he unluckily killed his father’s steward. The rest of the band served well as the King’s rangers. But Robin Hood and Allan a Dale did not return to Sherwood so soon, and this is why:

Robin’s fame as an archer made him a favorite of the King, and he quickly rose to be chief of all the yeomen. In time the King saw how faithful and loyal he was and made him Earl of Huntingdon. So Robin went with the King to the wars, and his days were so crowded that he could not get back to Sherwood even for a single day. Allan a Dale and his wife, the fair Ellen, went wherever Robin went and shared all the ups and downs of his life.

And now, dear friend, you who have traveled with me through all these merry doings, I will not ask you to follow me any farther. If you like, I will let go of your hand here and say a cheerful “good day.” What comes next is about the breaking up of things, and it shows how joys and pleasures that are dead and gone can never be stood on their feet to walk again. I will not linger over it, but will tell as quickly as I can how that sturdy fellow Robin Hood died as he had lived. He died not at court as Earl of Huntingdon, but with a bow in his hand and his heart in the greenwood, a true yeoman to the last.

King Richard died on the battlefield, as a lion-hearted king should, as you yourself no doubt know. So after a time the Earl of Huntingdon (or Robin Hood, as we still call him, just as before) found that there was nothing left for him to do abroad and came back to merry England. Allan a Dale and his wife, the fair Ellen, came with him, for the two of them had run Robin’s household ever since he left Sherwood Forest.

It was springtime when they landed again on English shores. The leaves were green and the little birds were singing happily, just as they used to in fair Sherwood when Robin Hood wandered the woodland shade with a free heart and light feet. The sweetness of the season and the joy of everything around him reminded Robin of his life in the forest, and a deep longing came over him to see the woods once more. So he went at once to King John and begged leave to visit Nottingham for a short while. The King told him he could come and go as he pleased, but ordered him not to stay at Sherwood longer than three days. So Robin Hood and Allan a Dale set off at once for Nottinghamshire and Sherwood Forest.

They spent the first night at an inn in Nottingham Town, and did not go to pay their respects to the Sheriff, since his worship held many bitter grudges against Robin Hood, and Robin’s rise in the world had done nothing to soften them. Early the next morning they mounted their horses and rode off toward the woods. As they went along the road, Robin felt he knew every stick and stone he saw. There was a path he had often walked on a mellow evening with Little John beside him. Here was another, now almost choked with brambles, along which he and a little band of men had walked when they set out to find a certain short-frocked friar.

So they rode slowly on, talking about these old, familiar things, which were old and yet new, for they found more in them now than they had ever noticed before. At last they came to the open glade and the great, wide-spreading greenwood tree that had been their home for so many years. Neither of them said a word as they stood beneath that tree. Robin looked around at the well-known sights, so like what they used to be and yet so different. Where once there had been the bustle of many busy men, there was now only the quiet of an empty place. As he looked, the woods, the grass and the sky all ran together in a blur through his tears. A great yearning came over him at the sight of these things, which he knew as well as the fingers of his right hand, and he could not hold back the tears.

That morning he had slung his good old bugle horn over his shoulder, and now, along with the yearning, he felt a great desire to sound it once more. He raised it to his lips and blew a blast. “Tirila, lirila,” went the sweet, clear notes, winding down the forest paths and coming back in faint echoes from the far-off leafy shadows, “Tirila, lirila, tirila, lirila,” until they faded away and were lost.

It happened that on that very morning Little John was walking through a corner of the forest on some business of his own. He was deep in thought as he went along when the faint, clear notes of a distant bugle reached his ear. As a stag leaps when an arrow strikes its heart, so Little John leaped when he heard that far-off sound. It felt as if all the blood in his body rushed into his cheeks like a flame as he bent his head to listen. The bugle sounded again, thin and clear, and then once more. Then Little John let out a great, wild cry of longing, of joy and of grief together, and, lowering his head, he charged into the thicket. On he crashed, snapping and tearing, like a wild boar through the underbrush. He hardly cared about the thorns and briers that scratched his skin and ripped his clothes, for his one thought was to take the shortest way to the greenwood glade where he knew the bugle was sounding. At last he burst out of the thicket with a shower of broken twigs falling around him, and without stopping for a moment he rushed ahead and threw himself at Robin’s feet. He wrapped his arms around his master’s knees, and his whole body shook with great sobs. Neither Robin nor Allan a Dale could speak. They stood looking down at Little John with tears rolling down their cheeks.

As they stood there, seven of the King’s rangers came rushing into the open glade and gave a great shout of joy at the sight of Robin, with Will Stutely at their head. A little later four more arrived, panting from their running, and two of these four were Will Scathelock and Midge, the Miller. All of them had heard the sound of Robin Hood’s horn. They ran to Robin and kissed his hands and his clothes, weeping loudly.

After a while Robin looked around through tear-filled eyes and said in a husky voice, “I swear now that I will never leave these dear woods again. I have been away from them, and from you, too long. Here and now I put aside the name of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon, and take up once more that nobler title, Robin Hood, the Yeoman.” At this a great shout went up, and all the yeomen shook hands with one another for joy.

The news that Robin Hood had come back to live in Sherwood as before spread like wildfire across the countryside, and within a week nearly all his old yeomen had gathered around him again. But when word of it reached King John, he swore long and loud and took a solemn vow that he would not rest until he had Robin Hood in his power, dead or alive. At court there happened to be a knight named Sir William Dale, as brave a soldier as ever put on armor. Sir William knew Sherwood Forest well, for he was head keeper of the part of it near good Mansfield Town. So the King turned to him and ordered him to take an army and go at once to hunt down Robin Hood. The King also gave Sir William his signet ring to show the Sheriff, so that the Sheriff would call out all his armed men to join the others in the chase. So Sir William and the Sheriff set out to carry out the King’s orders and search for Robin Hood, and for seven days they hunted up and down the forest without finding him.

Now if Robin Hood had been as peaceable as he once was, the whole business might have ended in smoke, as other such attempts had done before. But he had fought for years under King Richard and was no longer the man he used to be. It stung his pride to run away from those sent against him, like a fox chased by hounds. So in the end Robin Hood and his yeomen met Sir William, the Sheriff and their men in the forest, and a bloody fight followed. The first man killed in it was the Sheriff of Nottingham, who fell from his horse with an arrow in his brain before ten shafts had been shot. Many a better man than the Sheriff bit the dust that day. At last Sir William Dale was wounded and most of his men were dead, and he withdrew in defeat and left the forest. But scores of good fellows lay behind him, stiff and still beneath the sweet green boughs.

Robin Hood had beaten off his enemies in a fair fight, but it all weighed heavily on his mind, and he brooded over it until a fever took hold of him. It held him for three days, and though he struggled against it, he had to give in at last. So on the morning of the fourth day he called Little John to him and told him he could not shake off the fever. He said he would go to his cousin, the prioress of the nunnery near Kirklees in Yorkshire, who was a skilled healer, and ask her to open a vein in his arm and let a little blood, to help his health. Then he told Little John to get ready to go with him, since he might need help on the way. So Little John and Robin said good-bye to the others, and Robin told Will Stutely to lead the band until they came back. They traveled in easy stages and at a slow pace until they reached the Nunnery of Kirklees.

Robin had done a great deal for this cousin of his, for it was through King Richard’s affection for him that she had been made prioress of the place. But nothing in the world is so quickly forgotten as gratitude. When the Prioress of Kirklees heard that her cousin, the Earl of Huntingdon, had thrown away his earldom and gone back to Sherwood, she was vexed to the soul and afraid that being his cousin might bring the King’s anger down on her as well. So when Robin came to her and said he wanted her help as a healer, she began plotting evil against him in her mind, thinking that harming him might win her favor with his enemies. She kept this carefully to herself, however, and welcomed Robin with seeming kindness. She led him up the winding stone stair to a room just under the eaves of a high, round tower, but she would not let Little John go with him.

So the poor yeoman turned away from the nunnery door and left his master in the hands of the women. But though he did not go in, he did not go far either. He lay down in a little glade close by, where he could keep watch on the place where Robin was staying, like some great, faithful dog turned away from the door his master has gone through.

Once the women had taken Robin Hood to the room under the eaves, the Prioress sent everyone else away. Then she took a little cord and tied it tightly around Robin’s arm, as if she were going to bleed him. And bleed him she did, but the vein she opened was not one of those that lie close and blue beneath the skin. She cut deeper than that and opened one of the veins through which the bright red blood leaps from the heart. Robin did not know this, for although he saw the blood flow, it did not come fast enough to make him think anything was wrong.

When she had done this wicked deed, the Prioress turned and left her cousin, locking the door behind her. All that long day the blood ran from Robin Hood’s arm, and he could not stop it, though he tried every way he could. Again and again he called for help, but none came, for his cousin had betrayed him, and Little John was too far away to hear his voice. So he bled and bled until he felt his strength draining away. Then he got to his feet, swaying, and, holding himself up with the palms of his hands against the wall, he finally reached his bugle horn. Three times he blew it, but weakly and faintly, for his breath came in flutters from sickness and loss of strength. Even so, Little John heard it where he lay in the glade, and with a heart sick with dread he came running and leaping toward the nunnery. He pounded loudly on the door and shouted at the top of his voice to be let in. But the door was made of heavy oak, strongly barred and studded with spikes, so the nuns felt safe and told Little John to go away.

Then Little John’s heart was wild with grief and fear for his master’s life. He looked frantically around him, and his eyes fell on a heavy stone mortar, one that three men today could not lift. Little John took three steps toward it, bent his back, and heaved the stone mortar out of the place where it stood deeply rooted. Staggering under its weight, he came forward and hurled it crashing against the door. The door burst open, and the frightened nuns fled shrieking at his approach. Then Little John strode in, and he said not a word, but ran up the winding stone steps until he reached the room where his master was. Here he found that door locked too, but he put his shoulder against it and burst the locks as if they were made of brittle ice.

Inside he found his own dear master propped against the gray stone wall, white-faced and haggard, his head lolling with weakness. With a wild cry of love, grief and pity, Little John sprang to him and caught Robin Hood in his arms. He picked him up the way a mother picks up her child, carried him to the bed, and laid him down on it with great tenderness.

Just then the Prioress hurried in, frightened at what she had done and afraid of the revenge of Little John and the rest of the band. With clever bandages she stopped the bleeding, so that it flowed no more. All the while Little John stood by grimly, and when she had finished, he sternly ordered her to go away, and she obeyed, pale and trembling. After she had gone, Little John spoke cheering words, laughing loudly and saying that it was all a childish fright, and that no stout yeoman would die from losing a few drops of blood. “Why,” he said, “give it a week and you’ll be roaming the woodlands as boldly as ever.”
