Lying there, Robin only smiled weakly and shook his head. “Dear Little John,” he whispered, “may Heaven bless your kind, rough heart. But my friend, the two of us will never ramble through the greenwood together again.”

“Oh, but we will!” Little John said loudly. “I say it again, yes—away with this talk! Who dares say any more harm will come to you? Am I not here? Let me see who dares touch—” He broke off suddenly, for the words choked him. At last he said in a deep, husky voice, “Now, if any harm comes to you because of what was done today, I swear by Saint George that the red rooster will crow over the roof of this house, for the hot flames will lick every crack and corner of it. And as for these women”—here he ground his teeth—“it will be a bad day for them!”

But Robin Hood took Little John’s rough, brown fist in his pale hands and scolded him gently, in his low, weak voice. Since when, he asked, had Little John ever thought of harming women, even for revenge? He went on talking this way until at last the other promised, in a choking voice, that no harm would come to the place, whatever happened. Then a silence fell. Little John sat holding Robin Hood’s hand in his, gazing out of the open window and every now and then swallowing a great lump in his throat. Meanwhile the sun sank slowly toward the west, until the whole sky blazed with red glory. Then Robin Hood, in a weak, faltering voice, asked Little John to lift him up so that he could look out once more over the woodlands. The yeoman raised him in his arms as he asked, and Robin Hood’s head rested on his friend’s shoulder. For a long time Robin gazed out with a wide, lingering look, while the other sat with bowed head, the hot tears rolling one after another from his eyes and dripping onto his chest, for he felt that the time of parting was near. Presently Robin Hood asked him to string his stout bow and to pick a smooth, fair arrow from his quiver. Little John did so, without disturbing his master or getting up from where he sat. Robin Hood’s fingers closed lovingly around his good bow, and he smiled faintly to feel it in his grasp. Then he set the arrow on the part of the string that his fingertips knew so well. “Little John,” he said, “Little John, my own dear friend, whom I love better than anyone else in the world, please mark where this arrow lands, and dig my grave there. Lay me with my face toward the east, Little John, and see that my resting place is kept green, and that my weary bones are not disturbed.”

With those words he pushed himself upright all at once. His old strength seemed to flood back, and he pulled the string to his ear and shot the arrow out through the open window. While the shaft was in flight, his hand slowly dropped, bow and all, onto his knees, and he fell back into Little John’s loving arms. Yet something had gone out of him, just as the feathered arrow had gone from the bow.

For some minutes Little John sat without moving. Then he gently laid down what he was holding, folded the hands upon the chest, covered the face, turned on his heel, and left the room without a word or a sound.

On the steep stairway he met the Prioress and some of the leading sisters. In a deep, trembling voice he said to them, “If you come within twenty feet of that room, I will pull your nest of a house down over your heads, so that not one stone is left standing on another. Keep my words well in mind, for I mean them.” With that he turned and left them, and they soon saw him running swiftly across the open ground in the falling dusk, until the forest swallowed him up.

The first gray of the coming morning was just beginning to lighten the black sky in the east when Little John and six more of the band came hurrying across the open ground toward the nunnery. They saw no one, for the sisters, frightened by Little John’s words, were all hiding out of sight. The men ran up the stone stairs, and soon a great sound of weeping was heard. After a while it stopped, and then came the shuffling and scuffling of men’s feet as they carried a heavy weight down the steep, winding stairs. So they went out of the nunnery, and as they passed through its doors, a great, loud sound of wailing rose from the glade that lay dark in the dawn, as though many men, hidden in the shadows, had raised their voices in sorrow.

So died Robin Hood, at Kirklees Nunnery in fair Yorkshire, with mercy in his heart toward those who had brought about his death. In just this way he had shown mercy to the erring and pity to the weak throughout his whole life.

From then on his yeomen were scattered, but no great harm came to them afterward. The sheriff who followed the one who was gone was a more merciful man and did not know them so well, and since they were separated here and there across the countryside, they lived in peace and quiet, so that many of them lived to pass these tales down to their children and their children’s children.
Someone says that there is an old inscription on a stone at Kirklees. I give it here in the ancient English in which it was written, and this is how it goes:

Hear undernead dis laitl stean lais Robert Earl of huntingtun nea arcir ver as hie sae geud an pipl kauld im Robin heud sick utlaws as hi an is men vil England nidir si agen obiit 24 KAL. DEKEMBRIS 1247.
And now, dear friend, we too must part, for our merry journeys are over. Here, at the grave of Robin Hood, we turn and each go our own way.
